Sports.title: Third time lucky for Pocognoli as Scotland mark Robertson's 100th cap with win
Sports.content:
Sebastien Pocognoli secured his first Scotland win at the third time of asking as captain Andy Robertson became just the second player to reach 100 caps.

The head coach insisted there was no extra pressure after drawing a blank in their opening two Nations League games, but he and the players silenced some critics with a strong performance in Skopje despite a second red card inside a week as they beat North Macedonia 2-0.

Robertson missed two brilliant chances before Kieron Bowie - hooked after Jack Hendry's early sending off against Switzerland in midweek - smashed the ball into the bottom corner to earn his first international goal and Scotland's first in over 420 minutes.

Play was stopped by a dog running onto the pitch before Scotland continued to dominate with Bowie, Robertson and Ben Gannon-Doak going close before the break.

Scotland were awarded a penalty when Gannon-Doak went down in the box after half-time, only for the referee to overturn his decision after being called to the monitor.

VAR did then award the visitors a penalty soon after. Rangers striker Bojan Miovski was judged to have stopped Bowie's rebound with his arm after Scott McKenna hit the post.

Questions had been asked about John McGinn's Scotland future but the Aston Villa skipper sent the 'keeper the wrong way to double their lead. It was his 22nd goal for his country.

Image: John McGinn celebrates making it 2-0 from the penalty spot

But with the visitors looking comfortable, it was a repeat of Hendry's red on Tuesday as McKenna was sent packing late on for his last-man challenge on Agon Elezi.

Scotland host Solvenia at Hampden Park on Tuesday night in the final Nations League match of this extended international break.

Image: Scotland's Scott McKenna (R) was sent off late on

The key moments from the Philip II Arena

5: SAVE! A clean strike from Andy Robertson, a brilliant save from Stole Dimitrievski.

7: GOAL SCOTLAND! Kieron Bowie hammers the ball into the bottom corner from outside the box.

10: CLOSE! Robertson again. The Scotland captain fires wide of the far post with Oli McBurnie screaming for the pass.

10: PITCH INVASION! Well, there's a dog on the pitch. They catch the pooch quickly and the game gets back underway.

Image: A dog ran onto the pitch during the first half in Skopje

13: OVER! Robertson is a man on a mission, with this effort going just over the bar.

28: OVER! Bowie waits for the opening and cuts the ball back to Ben Gannon-Doak, but he gives it too much and it's over.

30: HUGE CHANCE! Bowie chases down the ball and just has to take it around the 'keeper, but it's eventually blocked.

34: SAVE! Dimitrievski does well to hold onto Gannon-Doak's effort from the edge of the box.

50: CHANCE! McGinn does well to set up Gannon-Doak, but he hits it straight at the 'keeper.

51: PENALTY FOR SCOTLAND! Gannon-Doak is brought down as he bursts into the box, and the referee points to the spot.

54: NO PENALTY! The referee is called to the monitor, and after a review it is overturned.

Image: Referee Francois Letexier overturns Scotland's penalty decision

56: SAVE! Brilliant again from Gannon-Doak as he takes a touch before firing towards goal.

57: CLOSE! John McGinn is so close to Scotland's second, but the Aston Villa captain's effort is just wide.

64: PENALTY FOR SCOTLAND! Scott McKenna hits the post and Bowie's rebound looks to be stopped by Bojan Miovski.

69: GOAL SCOTLAND! John McGinn sends the 'keeper the wrong way and Scotland are two up.

83: RED CARD! It was all going so well, but Scott McKenna is sent packing for a last-man challenge on Agon Elezi.

Progress under Pocognoli

Image: Scotland's Kieron Bowie celebrates with Oliver McBurnie and John McGinn after scoring the opener against North Macedonia

"Not much to say" was Sebastien Pocognoli's verdict after their midweek defeat to Switzerland but the new boss will be far more encouraged by what he saw in Skopje.

They looked far more like the side that impressed in the second half of their goalless draw in Slovenia a week ago.

Controlled and dominant, although the level of opposition cannot be overlooked given North Macedonia's place at the bottom of the group.

Kieron Bowie looked brilliant and should have added to his first international goal. Pocognoli's new call-ups, Stephen Welsh and Luis Binks, also impressed.

Image: Brondy captain Luis Binks has started Scotland's last two games

Scotland have ended their last two games with 10 men and in Skopje that made the last few minutes more uncomfortable that it should have been.

That will be a concern, but the chances created will bring confidence. Now, they just need to finish a few more of them.

Robertson: 'It means everything'

Image: Andy Robertson applauds the Scotland fans at full time

Scotland captain Andy Robertson speaking to BBC Scotland about his 100th cap:

"It means everything to me, it means everything to my family.

"I've been away now 100 times, I've got to feel sorry for my wife! It's been an unbelievable journey, I remember my first game and it's been a process since then.

"It's emotional for me. I love this country, there's only one person before me in the men's game to do that, it's a pretty special achievement.

"I thought Kenny Dalglish was going to be worried about his goalscoring record in the first five minutes! I had about six shots.

"They did a nice presentation for me, I told them I wanted the win. The lads did so well to get the win, it'll be a special one for me and my family."

On Scott McKenna's sending off, which came from a tackle after Robertson's short pass, the captain adds: "I apologise for the pass to Scott McKenna, I'll have to go in and apologise to him for that.

"We played really well on a really difficult pitch. We made it a wee bit interesting with the sending off but we defended so well for the last 10 minutes. All of the lads were magnificent and it was a big win. You want to get it as early as possible for the new manager and thankfully we did that tonight."

Pocognoli refuses to get carried away

Image: Sebastien Pocognoli celebrated his first win with Scotland

Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli speaking to BBC Scotland.

"I'm very pleased with this first win. But, we stay stable because we have a game in three days, and we want just to have another good game before the end of the first break.

"We played a very good game, we created a lot of chances, we keep two times a zero in three games, which for me means a lot also.

"We played with the right attitude, and for me it was a nice game, not everything was perfect, because we should have scored more goals, but we are in the continuity of the second half from Slovenia, and I hope we can have another good game at home."

On Kieron Bowie's first Scotland goal, he added: "He scored the most difficult one from the game. I was really pleased for him, because I know that the topic about not scoring will be on the table after 25 minutes.

"I was really pleased with his performance, and from many of the lads."

Sports.title: 'Our boys can't believe it' - Powell on Wakefield's 'phenomenal, immense' title run
Sports.content:
Wakefield Trinity head coach Daryl Powell revealed members of his playing squad were in shock following their stunning Super League Grand Final victory, two years on from playing in England's second tier.

Wakefield were crowned Super League champions for the first time in the club's history with a resounding 23-10 victory over Warrington Wolves in the Grand Final at Old Trafford, a week on from travelling to huge favourites Wigan Warriors and dispatching of them 33-6 in the semi-finals.

The success proved Wakefield's first league title for 58 years dating back to 1968, and all the more remarkable considering they were relegated from Super League in 2023, playing the 2024 season in the Championship under Powell.

"I'm just amazed really at the players and how good they've been," Powell said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Super League Grand Final between Warrington Wolves and Wakefield Trinity

"Obviously it's pretty sweet for me as an individual but for the club, the players, the coaching staff, everything that we've built up over the last three years is phenomenal.

"We've been building for a while but the last two weeks in particular have been just incredible performances from an unbelievable group of players.

"The boys have got such confidence in each other, that if we all do our jobs then we can do anything we want. We've done that this year. It's just immense.

"It's been an amazing finish to the season, wow. I couldn't speak more highly of the boys about everything they do, really.

"I know there's quite a few boys in there who just can't believe it. That we've been able to do all that.

"But it's just a testament to how good they are. I'm so proud of everything. The club, the fans - the way that they've been - obviously the players. They are just such a pleasure to coach and be around. It makes it an easy job."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tom Johnstone's sensational finish proved the key try of the second half to snuff out Warrington's fightback

For Powell, 61, it was his first time leading a side out in a Super League Grand Final since 2017, when he was Castleford Tigers head coach and lost heavily to Leeds Rhinos.

Saturday's success was made even sweeter for Powell by the fact it came against Warrington, where he coached for two seasons before being dismissed in 2023.

"This is the best [achievement], really," he added. "It looked like maybe I'd slip through my career and not win the big game after 2017 and it's been a long time.

"I had a tough time at Warrington, and then to come back and do this with Wakefield, it's phenomenal.

"For me, it's right up there. Just being at Wakefield and feeling at home again in a place and being able to get a group of men together who can do special things, it's unbelievable.

"I've had some great times in my coaching career, but this is the best."

"A rollercoaster of a year for me personally after dropping down to the reserves, not finding form, but I got my opportunity at the back end of the year.

"For this to be my last game for Wakefield, I will never forget it."

Sports.title: Whittaker clings on to beat Wallace despite final round fright
Sports.content:
Ben Whittaker was left clinging on as he got through a torrid final round to outpoint Conor Wallace.

An Olympic silver medallist and unbeaten professional hope, Whittaker was looking to advance to world level in this IBF title eliminator against Wallace in Birmingham.

Whittaker showed off his skills over the first half of the fight, dominating proceedings as he commanded the distance between them.

He whipped hard shots into the Irishman, now based in Australia. Wallace however withstood them but Whittaker, who sprinkled in some of his trademark showboating, was so comfortably ahead through nine rounds that he seemed to be in complete control.

Image: Whittaker dominated the first nine rounds of the fight with Wallace.

But that all suddenly changed. Wallace hurt him with a big shot in the 10th round. He punished Whittaker for holding his hands low, keeping that pressure on the Olympic star.

Wallace badly shook up Whittaker in the 12th and last round. He had Whittaker reeling and lunging in to clinch and grab Wallace. That saw Whittaker slipping and stumbling to the canvas, falling three times but the referee deemed none of them to be a knockdown.

Image: Whittaker slumps into Wallace on the ropes

Whittaker ultimately won unanimously, taking it 117-111, 116-112 and 115-113 on the cards.

Bilal Fawaz retained the British and Commonwealth super-welterweight titles with an impressive knockout finish as he took out Eithan James in their eighth round.

Sports.title: Let there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honour there | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
At half-time in the 2014 League Cup final, Sunderland led Manchester City 1-0. Yaya Touré equalised with a casually brilliant 30-yard clip 10 minutes after the break, and City went on to win 3-1. City, we now know from the independent commission, were at the time involved in a prolonged and calculated act of cheating, while Touré, the leaks in Der Spiegel suggested, was being paid via a dual contract to disguise exactly how much City were spending. Although precise details were left to the appendices, the commission’s report refers to payments “not recorded in an employment contract … but instead recorded in a consultancy agreement”.

Had Sunderland won, they would not merely have ended a 41-year wait for a trophy but would have qualified for the following season’s Europa League. It’s possible, of course, that the strain the extra games placed on the squad would have led to relegation in 2015, rather than the familiar trope of sacking a manager, in this case Gus Poyet, midway through the season, and surviving thanks to a bump under his successor, Dick Advocaat.

But it’s also possible that the greater exposure brought by European football, the surge of positivity engendered by unfamiliar and unexpected silverware, may have led to Premier League consolidation, stability and semi-regular European qualification.

Should Sunderland feel cheated? Of course they should, just as those who came second behind Lance Armstrong should feel cheated; just as Liverpool and Arsenal should feel cheated over the League Cup finals of 2016 and 2018; just as Stoke should feel cheated over the 2011 FA Cup final; just as Manchester United should feel cheated over the Premier League titles in 2012 and 2018 and Liverpool should in 2014; just as every club who played in the same competitions as City between 2009 and 2018 should feel cheated. But does that mean the 2014 League Cup should be taken from City and awarded to Sunderland?

These are two different questions, and it’s probably best to deal with the latter first – and this, unfortunately, is where subjectivity is unavoidable. I can’t speak for other Sunderland fans but, personally, I wouldn’t want it.

Perhaps this comes from never having seen my club win a major trophy. If it happens, I want it to be pure. I want images that will be remembered down the generations, like the highlights of 1973 – Ian Porterfield’s goal, Jim Montgomery’s save and Bob Stokoe’s celebratory skip across the pitch in mac and trilby.

I want the surge of adrenaline when a goal is scored, the agonised wait of injury time, the rush of the final whistle. I want tears and hugs and community and togetherness, all the things my dad’s generation banged on about. I want to get drunk and sing on a train. I don’t want to find out via an alert on my phone 12 years after the fact as I unpack the dishwasher.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City’s Yaya Touré equalises against Sunderland in the 2014 League Cup final. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/Reuters

Others may feel differently but the arithmetic of trophies won seems far less important than the experience of winning and the memories and sense of comradeship it provokes. Glory denied cannot be rectified a generation later by an independent commission, no matter how august.

Awarding rivals league titles seems even less satisfactory. In the 2017-18 season, for instance, the league was effectively over by the end of January with City 15 points clear.

As City went on to amass 100 points, there was little point in the four sides behind them – Manchester United, Liverpool, Chelsea and Tottenham, who were separated by five points – exerting themselves to try to rein City in.

Their priorities changed. United, Chelsea and Spurs all reached the FA Cup semi-finals. Liverpool got to the Champions League final. In those circumstances, why would any of them have prioritised the league? To award United, who finished second, the title, would seem not just empty but arbitrary.

That, though, does not mean City should not be stripped of those titles. They won them unfairly; why on earth should they be allowed to keep them? (And yes, something similar could be said of Chelsea, but that’s an argument for why Chelsea should also have been stripped of titles, not for why City should not be).

How can those trophies be left in the record books for future generations unquestioningly to see? How can City stand as the fourth-most successful side in league history when so much of that success was achieved by cheating?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The argument will be made that City’s players strived hard for those trophies. But so did players for those other teams, the ones who weren’t cheating. And how much easier to win in a deep squad full of high-grade players, drawn to City by the money they were offering, money whose source, the independent commission concluded, had been disguised in contravention of Premier League regulations.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City with the League Cup in 2014, one of seven major trophies won between 2009 and 2018. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Euphoric memories cannot be expunged, but it is for City fans (and players and coaching staff and directors) to decide what to do with them. If they still want to exult in Sergio Agüero’s 94th-minute winner to claim the 2012 Premier League title, nobody can stop them. But the rest of the world knows what it was based on, that as the rest of the Premier League played to regulations voted in by the clubs themselves, City did not.

That would mean that there was no Premier League champion in 2012, 2014 or 2018, no FA Cup winner in 2011 and no League Cup winner in 2014, 2016 or 2018 (and it does not seem unreasonable to wonder, when all this is done, whether there might be more to be investigated after 2018). If there are blanks on the roll of honour, let them be; there was no honour there.

Let the spaces stand as testimony to what those seasons were. Let them stand as a memorial to the years when a foreign entity tried to subvert English football, when a foreign entity took this country’s greatest cultural mode, and all the passion and all the feeling, all the sorrow and all the joy, all the love it has entailed, and tried to twist it for its own political ends. Let them stand as a warning of the dangers of laissez-faire capitalism, when everything, no matter how beloved, could be sold off to the highest bidder.

And let them stand as a monument to a Premier League that finally – belatedly? – took action, to a process that maintained its independence, to an institution that, at no little risk to its own wellbeing – a risk that has not gone away – in the end preferred justice and fairness and decency over grubby deals with the rich and powerful.

Let the years without a champion stand for ever vacant, both as a rebuke and as a tribute. Sometimes, emptiness can be the most eloquent statement of all.

Sports.title: Bellingham stands out for high-grade England but Uefa sends out wrong message on racism | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
So … can we play another World Cup, then? Can we just undo and rewind? Forget whatever it was you thought you saw in Atlanta. We’re actually ready now.

Although not, repeat not, if any part of this involves playing football in front of 6,000 excitable children, the combined effect of which was to create an atmosphere in Rijeka the adult human ear is simply not designed to process.

This was a dreamlike occasion on many levels, from its quietly farcical staging, to a relentlessly high-grade England performance and a deserved 7-0 win, all of it glossed in the moment by the striking beauty of the setting.

Rijeka is a gently crumbling Italianate coastal town, the stadium lodged up in the hills facing into the blue of the Adriatic. From the stands here you could switch between watching Jude Bellingham cruise about the pitch like a human superyacht to following the cargo ships crawling across the curve of the bay, the grey-green fade of the hills below, white towers by the shore, like a pocket-sized Balkan Rio de Janeiro.

Against this background, two key things happened. The first was an administrative abomination. At 6pm Croatia and England kicked off this closed-doors, stadium-banned Nations League game in front of a packed and boisterous home crowd with barely a spare seat in the house.

The ban was imposed as punishment for a mass fan march to the Stade de France in Paris last March, accompanied by Nazi salutes and the discovery, later, of a stash of combat-ready weapons, including “iron rods, telescopic batons and sharp wooden sticks”.

In response to this, the Croatian Football Association said no to racism here by saying: yes, come along to the game you’re not allowed to come to because of racism. A very simple suggestion to Uefa. If you’re in any way serious about making this point, just close the loophole that allowed the stands here to be filled with 6,000 children plus their designated “handlers”.

View image in fullscreen Adult Croatia supporters were not allowed in but 6,000 children were, plus ‘handlers’, but it was not a pretty sight for the locals.

Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

It is at the very least a confusing message. It seems to say: racism and children, this is a good combination. And given this seems to happen quite regularly, that racism is now a kind of children’s holiday event around here, football Christmas. And here’s your bonus bag of free tickets, brought to you by today’s matchday sponsor, racism.

Playing the game in Rijeka also punished England’s fans, with just a hundred allowed to make the two-hour drive down a two-lane highway from Zagreb. Although this was still a lovely place to be, with its jaunty open stands, the haze of sea, land and sky merging in the middle distance, and not forgetting the Brutalist away end, a fully enclosed steel prison cage, albeit so scenically placed you could probably Airbnb it in the off-season.

On the pitch things were clearer, as England produced a sustained and genuinely high-grade performance from first to last. They did so in an interesting way too. Often England teams can look good but flawed. Here they were tight and mobile, just a powerful, high-technique modern team. They looked like what people imagine Premier League-era England teams might look like, but never really do, a team with the capacity to take on anyone, playing like this.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

And yes, steady on there. They did all this against a Croatia team that gave a performance, given the audience, that verged on child cruelty. But who else around the world is good in exactly this way? France, perhaps. A balanced, focused England team, with Bellingham and Kane, is a serious proposition.

Thomas Tuchel fielded an interesting team, with much to like in a fluid-looking Alex Scott-Elliot Anderson-Bellingham midfield trident. And with seven minutes gone England were 1-0 up. The goal was made by Scott’s drive, Bellingham’s slick pass and Harry Kane roofing it with a zing you could hear from the stands.

England pressed busily, smothered Croatia everywhere and looked assured in their touches. And Bellingham duly made it 2-0 on 20 minutes after some nimble stuff from Anthony Gordon. The goal was his eighth in eight games for England after six in his previous 37. Bellingham just looks irresistible right now.

It was 3-0 on 38 minutes, Gordon heading in a whipped cross from Jarell Quansah, then 4-0 with another brilliant breakaway goal just before half-time, Bellingham running 80 metres to retake the ball, then crossing for Bukayo Saka to tap in.

View image in fullscreen Jude Bellingham slots the ball past Dominik Livakovic to score England’s second goal. Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/Reuters

Modric came and went after half-time, a slightly sad spectacle in itself. For the majority of his career he has looked like a little boy dressed up as a witch. He doesn’t look like this any more. Now he looks like a gnarled middle-aged footballer dressed up as a witch. He still has the brilliance, and the touch, but not in this team of old men. It was 5-0 shortly after, Kane getting his second after a good cross from Anderson, who was just too much for Croatia here. Saka got another, set up by Kane.

By the end, 7-0 really didn’t seem very flattering. And yes, yes, the opponents were poor. But the real point was the style, the balance, the intensity of England’s performance. It felt repeatable. It certainly felt like progress from the World Cup.

The final takeaway, as the shrieks died away, was that Croatian children are far better behaved at football than their adult counterparts. And Croatia does have a genuine problem here. We’re not talking cultural misunderstanding or disputed micro-aggressions. These are macro-aggressions. It’s far-right, actual Nazi-adjacent stuff, and domestic ultra culture still pegged out around white supremacy symbols and references to the wretched Ustase, the notably vicious puppet regime of the second world war.

As Gianni Infantino would say, football unites the world. Sometimes it even unites it in fascism. Filling the stands with kids is not taking your sanctions seriously. Although here the occasion was saved by another kind of punishment and by a genuinely gripping England performance.

Sports.title: Lamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect start
Sports.content:
Lamine Yamal says he feels like Superman or Spider-Man sometimes, and Spain’s fans are starting to wonder if he just might be. There is something comic book hero about what the teenager is doing right now, some unexplained super power swelling inside him. For the third consecutive game he scored inside six minutes, curling in another outrageous goal as Spain completed their World Cup homecoming in Oviedo with a 3-1 win over Czechia that leaves them a single point from the Nations League quarter finals already. Spain’s manager, Luis de la Fuente, put it simply: “Lamine Yamal is on course to become a legend.”

And yet in a game which seemed to have been done at half-time, when Spain led 2-0 after Rodrigo Hernandez had added the second and Lamine Yamal was withdrawn, his show seemingly over, the danger returned. Czechia, vastly improved after the break, pulled one back through Jiri Slama on 69 and then were denied a 79th-minute equaliser when Vassilis Fotias, the referee, who rescued Spain, harshly ruled out a Ryan Naderi goal – apparently for a foul on Robin Le Normand as the free-kick that led to it was swung in.

Reduced to 10 men soon after, still furious, Czechia finally fell with two minutes left when Mikel Merino made Spain safe. The seleccion’s first visit to the Carlos Tartiere in 11 years had ended the way they had hoped. Welcomed back as world and European champions once more, they were applauded off as winners again. A night that had begun with Rodri being presented with the World Cup by Santi Cazorla and Juan Mata, academy products at Real Oviedo and members of the generation to which all others would forever be compared, ended with a jeopardy no one anticipated when it started in a way that has become implausibly, absurdly familiar.

Lamine Yamal had scored after 104 seconds at Wembley and 70 in Seville, as Spain defeated England and Croatia. And the silly thing was that here, his goal might have come even sooner. Fifteen seconds in, the first frisson of excitement went round this place as he chased down the goalkeeper and after just fifty-seven Oviedo almost exploded. But, running on to a Dani Olmo pass, Lamine Yamal calmly guided a shot past the goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky … and past the post.

He would just have to wait until the sixth minute was up instead. Playing a quick one-two with Dani Olmo, Lamine Yamal took possession on the top right corner of the area and curled another outrageous shot into the far corner, the ridiculous becoming routine. They had been playing five minutes 20 seconds, another stadium letting out a roar that spoke of delight but also a kind of disbelief. 320 seconds he had been out there, taking him to 494 seconds to score three.

View image in fullscreen Rodri reacts after scoring Spain’s second in Oviedo Photograph: Petr David Josek/AP

Spain weren’t hurrying but they were controlling, and the chances were accumulating: by half-time they had taken 13 shots to one, and enjoyed 70% of possession. They had also added a second on 32 minutes. Rodri collected near the centre circle and did something he rarely does. The man who sometimes seems to be walking, effortlessly controlling the game with his mind and without fuss, happy enough to drop the ball off to others to do their thing, went off on a run. Advancing through the midfield, he slotted to Pedri whose return, with the help of a defender’s touch, set him up to shoot high into the net.

Next Lamine Yamal slipped in Alex Baena, denied by Kinsky. A little dinked pass from Baena then found Lamine whose shot, slightly scuffed, went wide. At the break Baena, who had drawn “oohs” with one glorious touch, was withdrawn and so too was Lamine Yamal, his work here done, another show over. The game, on the other hand, was not. That at least was Czechia’s intention and it should probably have been their reward too, the visitors taking a decisive step forward and a degree of control. They also reduced the deficit with 20 minutes to go.

The move began deep: as it progressed up the right and through the middle, Jiri Slama was sprinting to catch up. Adam Hlozek saw him coming and played the ball into his path for him to steer it low and true beyond David Raya.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A first error from Spain’s keeper almost gave Czechia an equaliser when Raya stepped out to play and his misplaced pass only found Ondrej Lingr, and a second error really should have done soon after. But if there was relief for Spain when Lingr’s shot drifted wide of an unguarded goal, it was even greater when the referee ruled out Ryan Nadel’s effort.

For Czechia there was disbelief. Michal Sadilek’s long cross had been headed goalwards by Ladislav Krejci, and Raya, reaching by the bar, could not hold on. The ball dropped on the line, where Nadel nudged it in. The referee, though, had blown. For Santi Denia on the touchline it was hard to take and it was equally difficult not to feel sympathy. All the more when Krejci was soon sent off and then Víctor Muñoz was sent clear, dashed into the area where Kinsky blocked and Merino, forever alive, finished off the festivities.

Sports.title: Bowie gets Pocognoli off mark with Scotland victory in North Macedonia
Sports.content:
This was an occasion on which Scotland dare not stumble. By the time Kieron Bowie smashed home a seventh minute opener against a North Macedonia side not without its troubles to seek, it was already clear they would not. Bowie afforded Sébastien Pocognoli his first goal as the Scotland manager. Later, the Belgian had his maiden victory confirmed. Anything else, against such a dismal level of opposition, would have been worthy of significant Scottish embarrassment.

John McGinn’s 22nd goal for his country, coming from the penalty spot, meant the scoreline at least almost reflected Scotland’s dominance. Only Scott McKenna’s late sending off and a failure to notch three, four or five could have irked Pocognoli. Scotland remain alive and kicking in section B1 of the Nations League while aware they will face far, far stiffer challenges. Scotland needed to be professional in North Macedonia and met that task appropriately.

On the occasion of Andy Robertson’s 100th cap, it appeared in the early stages that the Tottenham full-back had been stung by criticism of recent performances in Scotland colours. Robertson marauded forward at will, including inside five minutes where he forced Stole Dimitrievski into a fine save. McGinn, like Robertson, has been the subject of some scathing words. McGinn’s response was as forceful as his teammate.

It was Bowie, though, who afforded Scotland crucial early leeway. Jack Hendry’s red card in the early stages of Tuesday’s loss to Switzerland led to Bowie being withdrawn from the Scotland attack. Pocognoli retained faith in Bowie in Skopje. Bowie had plenty to do when collecting Billy Gilmour’s pass, 25 yards from goal and with two defenders in close proximity. He set himself before firing a terrific left-foot shot beyond the helpless Dimitrievski.

McGinn’s outrageous pass from the right-back position to Robertson, who was operating as a left winger, should have ensured a Scotland second. Robertson opted to shoot and dragged his shot wide when a square pass to Oli McBurnie was the more sensible option. As Ben Gannon-Doak and Bowie missed opportunities, North Macedonia opted for two substitutions with just half an hour played.

View image in fullscreen Kieron Bowie fires Scotland ahead during the first half. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Scotland’s lack of ruthlessness was their only concern. Gannon-Doak was clean through on Dimitrievski within five minutes of the restart but shot tamely at the goalkeeper. Gannon-Doak and Scotland soon believed they had won a penalty, only for the video assistant referee to rightly highlight the Bournemouth player had stood on the foot of Matej Gashtarov rather than vice versa. North Macedonia were clinging on as Bowie tested Dimitrievski from close range.

Officialdom was soon to smile on Scotland. The match referee had originally given a foul against McKenna as the centre-back nodded the ball down towards Bowie from a Scotland corner. Not only was that decision reversed but Bojan Miovski was penalised for blocking Bowie’s shot with an arm. McGinn finished low and hard to close this game as a contest. Only three players have scored more Scotland goals than the Aston Villa midfielder.

Ryan Christie’s arrival at half-time added composure and creativity to the Scotland midfield. He looks the ideal candidate to link play in Pocognoli’s final third. It will be a surprise if Christie does not start when Slovenia visit Glasgow on Tuesday. Angus Gunn, whose position as the Scotland goalkeeper was questioned before this game, had nothing whatsoever of consequence to do.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

McKenna will miss Slovenia’s visit after upending Agon Elezi, six minutes from time. The episode was regarded as the denial of an obvious scoring opportunity. Robertson’s slack pass had landed his teammate in bother.

Robertson later admitted he owes McKenna an apology before reflecting on his cap milestone. “It means everything to me and my family,” said the 32-year-old. “It has been an unbelievable journey. It is emotional for me because I love this country and this is a special achievement. I believe I still have a lot to give.”

Handily for Pocognoli, Scotland did not need 11 men to win. McGinn was denied his second of the evening in stoppage time. North Macedonia, who have now gone seven games without scoring a goal, are a desperate lot.

Sports.title: Alexander’s absence weighs heavy as Bradford try to keep promotion push on track
Sports.content:
It was a bruising start to the week for Bradford City when news filtered through to the players that Graham Alexander had stepped down as manager. They were top of the League One table and his departure was a sudden and unexpected blow for a side that had started to let imaginations run wild about a return to the second tier for the first time in 23 years.

Coaches Mark Trueman and Colin Doyle took interim charge and called a meeting with the squad on Monday. “Some of the players were a little unsettled, didn’t know what was going on or who was taking the team,” Trueman said. “But the players have just got on with business, and that’s the key. It shows the mentality of the team. This could quite easily derail them, but they’ve continued to do the right things.”

If any caretaker can keep Bradford on track, it is Trueman, who has now stepped in temporarily five times since joining the club as an Under-18 coach six years ago.

This time, though, is different. Previously his job was to raise the team during low periods. Now the task is to maintain the upward trajectory that began the moment Alexander arrived in 2023.

Bradford were stuck in the bottom tier of the EFL and sitting in 16th when Alexander took over. They finished ninth in his first season, then third in his second to earn automatic promotion, followed by a stunning fourth-place finish back in League One, losing in the playoff semi-finals last May.

It has been a thrilling ride rarely enjoyed by Bradford fans. They twice reached the EFL Trophy semi-finals in successive seasons. At one stage, they won 10 consecutive home games, breaking a club record set in 1953. Last year [2025] they had the best home record of any side in Europe’s top five leagues. Alexander won 79 times in 158 games – the best win rate of any Bradford manager in charge for at least 65 games.

Chief executive Ryan Sparks said Alexander and assistant manager Chris Lucketti, who has followed him to Preston, delivered “some of the most incredible moments in our recent history”.

They looked set to deliver more, with Bradford top of League One when the Preston opportunity came out of the blue. Alexander told the club he had ambitions to manage in the Championship, but you wonder if he might have achieved that with Bradford had he stayed. Perhaps he realised two promotions in two years would leave them relegation fodder in the Championship, whereas Preston presents a more stable platform.

Ultimately, the lure of a club in the tier above that he once captained – playing 400 games during an eight-year spell from 1999 to 2007 – in the city where his children were raised proved too strong.

View image in fullscreen Graham Alexander’s sudden departure has left Bradford to rebuild early on in the season. Photograph: Paul Thompson/ProSports/Shutterstock

On forums and social media, fans shared a mixture of sadness, anger and anxiety. Most believe Alexander has left the club stronger, but frustration is shared among a sizeable minority about the timing – less than two months into a season after a summer spent recruiting specifically for his aggressive, direct, high-pressing football.

After Jake Beesley headed Bradford into a fourth-minute lead at Reading on Saturday, the 1,118 travelling supporters who made the 400-mile round trip sang about being top of the league, but did not chant for their departed manager once.

Rapid developments in the space of a few weeks leave a huge hole. Bradford now find themselves in unfamiliar territory: it is the first time in 43 years they have lost a manager mid-season, and fans are nervous about the executives’ aptitude for finding a suitable replacement, given the shaky record before landing Alexander.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In the opposition dugout at Reading’s Select Car Leasing Stadium stood one of the favourites to take over. Before the match, Leam Richardson faced questions about whether he was interested. His response – that he would be in the Reading dugout for the match – neatly sidestepped the prospect that he might not be beyond this weekend, though he insisted he had not been contacted.

Nonetheless, Sparks and sporting director David Sharpe would have been watching closely from the directors’ box to see whether Reading showed signs of a style of football that would fit the framework Alexander built.

Plenty makes Richardson a logical candidate. He previously worked with Sharpe, who was chair at Wigan when Richardson was manager, and he has also coached Callum Connolly, in the Bradford starting XI, and Nick Powell, who came on from the bench.

Others are in the frame, including the Plymouth manager Tom Cleverley, the former Manchester United midfielder – a Premier League winner in 2013 – who at 37 has quietly built his managerial reputation these past two years. Udoka Godwin-Malife’s second-half equaliser meant Plymouth moved above Bradford on goal difference.

The next appointment is crucial. Getting Alexander so right makes getting it wrong so much more costly.

Sports.title: Cavan Sullivan’s long-range chip highlights USMNT’s 3-0 romp over Mexico
Sports.content:
The last time the United States and Mexico played at this building, Jimmy Conrad and Landon Donovan provided the goals in one of several 2-0 wins for the US. On Saturday, the US squad included eight players who hadn’t yet been born when that happened.

The young United States went one better from their forebears, though, silencing a sizable pro-Mexico contingent in a composed 3-0 triumph that fully announced the arrival of an exciting new generation of players. Cavan Sullivan, just a few days after turning 17, became the youngest goal scorer in the history of the program with an eye-catching long-range chip. Julian Hall, 18, scored his third goal in as many games. Malik Tillman capped the scoring in the 85th minute, humbling a ten-man Mexico after they’d opened the match with far more strength.



The US haven’t played an away game since 2024, but today might be as close as they’ve gotten with the heavily pro-Mexico crowd. The tailgates cooked up far more fajitas than frankfurters, and the red seats of State Farm Stadium were filled by a hearty influx of green jerseys as the anthems commenced for Tyler Adams’ first shift as Mauricio Pochettino’s captain.

The disparity of support was a fitting embodiment of the match’s early balance. Mexico came out of the gates with intent, while the nominal hosts struggled to get the ball off of their feet. Despite fielding a backline that could credibly be considered the first-choice options to start the cycle, all four US defenders struggled to pass through Mexico’s aggressive man-marking scheme.

After five minutes of Mexico maintaining a steady attack, the United States adjusted. Leaning into Kochen’s experience playing out from the back, the hosts opted for short restarts with Auston Trusty prodding goal kicks to his young goalkeeper. The conservative approach took the sting out of El Tri’s attack, but hardly helped activate their own. After 15 minutes, Mexico had managed to take 38 touches in the opposing half, to the United States’ five.

By the 28th minute, as the hosts worked to keep Mexico off the ball, the crowd at State Farm Stadium had been lulled into quiet observation.

Then, the United States struck.

Sebastian Berhalter lobbed a ball to the right flank to Alex Freeman, who drew Mexico’s focus as he headed toward the corner. He feigned a retreat before deftly rolling a through-ball between two opponents, with Gio Reyna collecting the ball in-stride inside the box. Reyna tried to center the ball in search of a target, leaving Raúl Rangel to flub his attempt to claim the low cross, shanking the ball directly to a lurking Hall. The New York striker made no mistake with his connection, slotting his first-time attempt across goal and far from Rangel.

The 18-year-old turned to the crowd and cupped his ears in front of the American Outlaws, cheekily acknowledging the silenced sect of Mexican support. The act of poaching gave Hall his third US goal in as many caps to bolster his case for regular involvement throughout the cycle.

Mexico strove to regain control of the match, frequently fouling Malik Tillman whenever he tried advancing upfield. Playing without the dynamic midfield duo of Gilberto Mora and Hirving Lozano, Mexico struggled to turn ample possession into genuine quality, with just four shots taken after 40 minutes and none landing on frame. The sea of green shirts began to ripple, with waves of Mexico fans beating the lines for concessions and restrooms with five minutes left in the half.

Their impatience kept them from witnessing Mexico’s best chance of the half from a moment of reverse deja vú. A speculative effort by Luís Romo to the far post forced Kochen into a clumsy diving save. Much like the sequence leading to Hall’s opener, his spill fell right to Santiago Giménez, giving Mexico a golden chance to equalize from inside six yards. Instead, the Porto loanee shanked his effort well wide of goal, sparing US blushes just before half-time.

Allow content provided by a third party? This article includes content hosted on embed.bsky.app . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'. Allow and continue

The hosts weren’t shy once play resumed, spraying the ball to Sullivan down the right flank and up the channel to Tillman or Reyna. The visitors finally put a shot on goal in the 58th minute, with Roberto Alvarado attempting a half-volley on a redirected corner kick. Kochen parried it over the bar with youthful ease, keeping his side in control with half an hour remaining.



Both teams saw their intensity wane a bit as the half progressed, leading to some carelessness in possession. Just after the hour mark, Rangel collected a back pass from Érik Lira and took his time finding his next target for distribution while positioned far upfield. His undercooked pass to Diego Campillo instead found Sullivan, the leader of the US’ makeshift press and as instinctive a player as anybody in the United States pool.



Players with rare spatial awareness like Sullivan’s tend to manifest moments like these more often than most. Rather than look to retain possession, as his team had so often after turnovers, Sullivan snared the ball with his left foot, stopping its progress in close proximity, then returned to his preferred left foot to chip Rangel and curl his effort underneath the crossbar. Sullivan was beyond jubilant, clattering into the corner flag as his teammates converged before patting the US crest over his heart.

Sullivan’s first international goal was always bound to be a staple of his and the team’s highlight reels, an occasion years in the making as the nation’s latest wunderkind-in-waiting. The quality of his solo effort warrants ample replays on its own merit, making his nation’s great rival know his threat from his very first shift.

Something of a Mexican meltdown ensued as the players struggled to return to their former state of control. Substitutes collided in the 67th minute, with Yunus Musah’s attempt to dribble upfield being thwarted by a Mateo Chavez kick through the legs. The foul brought both teams together in a confrontation as referee Selvin Brown raised a red card to the AZ Alkmaar defender, much to the fans’ dismay.



For years, El Tri fans have infamously soundtracked opponents’ goal kicks by chanting a homophobic slur. After considerable mistakes on both goals, the supporters instead bellowed the bigoted cry on Rangel’s restarts, with the stadium operators declining to follow through on their pre-match threats to stop the game if the chant emerged. The fans also took to booing Rangel’s every touch, taking one item off of a hosting fanbase’s usual list of responsibilities.



Perhaps inevitably, Rangel struggled with the unusual jeering. Another poor backpass, this time from Álvaro Fidalgo, rolled right into the box with Rangel staying near his goalline in hopes a center-back would collect. Instead, Malik Tillman strode on to the loose ball and placed it into the upper corner, closing what once looked like a comfortable day for Mexico into downright humiliation.

In the lead-up to the game, Adams spoke about how the winner of this matchup tends to be seen as the region’s current power. In this case the US took that power because it was given, and taken advantage of.

Sports.title: Celtic fans throw tennis balls at club owner Dermot Desmond during golf tournament
Sports.content:
Celtic’s principal shareholder Dermot Desmond had tennis balls thrown towards him during his visit to the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament at St Andrews in a protest from fans.

The 76-year-old – who has been criticised by supporters for an apparent lack of progress on the pitch – was taking part in the pro-am event on Saturday when the disruption happened on the green of the 15th hole.

Tennis balls with pictures of Desmond’s face crossed out were thrown on to the green, with Desmond then escorted off the course by security.

The Celtic Fans Collective later released a statement on X, which included video and pictures of the protest, calling for change at the top of the club.

View image in fullscreen Dermot Desmond is driven away from the course after the fans’ protest. Photograph: Stuart Wallace/Shutterstock

“Dermot Desmond has essentially been allowed to run Celtic Football Club whilst using his wealth to hide from supporters and accountability,” the statement said. “Fans took the chance today to send a message that this arrangement cannot continue.”

On Saturday evening, Celtic issued a lengthy and strongly-worded statement against the “premeditated action” which “brought shame upon” the name of the club.

The statement read: “Celtic Football Club has never sought to prevent supporters from expressing criticism of the club, its board or its shareholders. Supporters are entitled to disagree with decisions, to make their views known and to protest peacefully. What occurred at St Andrews represents a significant and unacceptable escalation.

“Those responsible have brought shame upon the name of Celtic Football Club and upon a reputation which generations of Celtic supporters have spent more than a century building. The club no longer accepts that the Celtic Fans Collective can credibly claim to represent the wider Celtic support. Those responsible for today’s events certainly do not speak for the many thousands of Celtic supporters who express their views passionately, peacefully and responsibly.”

Celtic said the club would not be “intimidated or coerced by organised acts of disruption”, adding “there is a line between protest and deliberate disruption. Today that line was crossed … The club will protect its employees, directors, shareholders and supporters. The reputation of Celtic Football Club is non negotiable.”

Martin O’Neill’s side – who claimed the Premiership title ahead of Hearts after a final-day decider last season as part of a domestic double – currently sit top of the table, two points clear of rivals Rangers.

Celtic, though, lost the last three games before the international break, including two defeats by Rangers, one at Parkhead, and were also beaten 3-1 at home by Ferencvaros in their opening Europa League fixture.

Sports.title: Ex-Premier League player admits it’s tough to ignore noise around wonderkid son who inherited Cristiano Ronaldo shirt
Sports.content:
The Derry Boys is a coming-of-age story about a UK teenager that Shaun Derry is fighting to keep contained to just one household.

The former Crystal Palace and Queens Park Rangers captain is the proud father of son Jesse, who is starring on loan at Sporting Lisbon.

7 Jesse Derry is making a name for himself at Sporting in Portugal Credit: Getty

The 19-year-old has endured a whirlwind past few months since making his Premier League debut for Chelsea at the start of May.

The teenager, who only arrived at the Blues academy last year, was handed his senior debut in a 4-0 FA Cup victory over Hull in February.

The ex-Palace youth star signed a six-year contract extension with Chelsea in July before joining Sporting Lisbon on a season-long loan.

His dad Shaun knows all about the trials and tribulations of making a name for yourself in the professional game.

But, in the modern age, his youngster is faced with more distractions and noise than the generation before him, and it's an issue Derry Sr. has been trying to navigate.

He explained to Kick Off hosts Hugh Woozencroft and Perry Groves on talkSPORT: "It's obviously difficult, isn't it?

"You've got all these trappings that the game brings so early in your career as well. But you must never forget about the game and what you do it for.

"And I can only speak on behalf of us as a family, and in particular for Jesse - I do want to mention about the topic of as a wonderkid.

"For us, he's just our kid. He's our boy. And we love him dearly.

"It doesn't matter where he gets to in his football career. And it's just that humility that I want him to understand throughout his young career, and throughout his senior career.

7 Derry made three appearances for the Blues last season, but his Premier League debut was cut short by a head injury Credit: Getty

"Let's hope he gets to that stage," The 48-year-old continued. "And he has a brilliant time being a footballer.

"But just for us as a family, it's just keeping it consistent with him, and just treating him as our boy and still teaching him life lessons.

"He's gone on a journey. He's had an incredible two or three years. He's moved from Crystal Palace to Chelsea.

"Now he's on his first loan at a remarkably big football club, and he lives away from us now.

"He's not coming home every night. We're not cooking him tea. We're not doing him dinner.

"And we're not making sure that he's getting in bed at the right time. But we've got to try and do that from afar, which is a different challenge."

7 Derry has inherited Ronaldo's first shirt number in professional football Credit: Getty

7 Ronaldo donned the number at his boyhood club before switching to the No.7 at Manchester United Credit: Getty

Jesse Derry at Sporting Lisbon

The England Under-20 international is wearing the same number Cristiano Ronaldo wore during his time at the Portuguese giants.

He underlined his talent with a goal in the pre-season friendly win over Monaco at the Estadio do Dragao.

Derry has since featured in three of Sporting’s four games in August, all off the bench, and his dad couldn't be prouder of his progress.

"Of course I am," He added. "We all are. I'm really proud of the decision that he made and that the club Chelsea made as well.

"I completely respect the pyramid of English football; it's so difficult. It's difficult playing in League Two, never mind in the Premier League.

7 Derry has played for England's youth teams from U17 level up until the U20s Credit: Getty

"This is a hard game that we play, so you don't take anything for granted, of course. But we spoke long and hard about what this challenge would look like. And he really bought into it.

"And he wanted to take himself out of this, and I won't call it a comfort zone, because a lot of being involved in football is being uncomfortable.

"Whether you're uncomfortable playing in the youth team, whether you're striving to be in the second team, especially when you're on that top table when you're in the first team.

"There's moments where you really feel uncomfortable. So to go and experience this 6-12 months over in Portugal, listen, he needs guidance, and he needs perseverance.

"And he needs to get his head down and work extremely hard to try and break into that team."

7 Derry has been challenged by his dad to break into Sporting's first-team after three sub appearances Credit: AFP

Key lessons as dad of a wonderkid

Derry, who was was named Palace’s Under-18s player of the season in 2023/24, was wanted by a host of European giants before joining Chelsea.

On paper, it would seem as a second-generation star in his family that he would have had the ideal blueprint to follow in his dad's footsteps.

Yet Shaun Derry insisted one of the key things he's learnt through his son's academy journey was to avoid becoming an extra coach.

"I think the one thing that really stuck out for me is watching Jesse from the age of 6-7 in the Crystal Palace Academy all the way through is; just watch him and enjoy it.

"There's enough coaches on the sideline to give him that advice and all the information that these kids require.

"You don't need a dad or a mum or a family member shouting on the sideline and screaming sometimes.

7 Shaun Derry - pictured with Ole Gunnar Solskjær - has highlighted how important it is as a parent to enjoy the journey of their children Credit: Getty

"I've seen everything these last 8-9 years. And don't miss those moments of looking back and watching your son and your daughter; if your daughter's playing as well, just watch them and actually enjoy watching your kids play football.

"Don't coach them - Don't coach them on the sideline; they get enough information.

"These boys and girls, they go into the academies 4-5 times a week. They're missing valuable school time. You're going to miss it.

"It flies by so quickly. I remember Jesse's first game as a 6-7 year old playing for the Under-8s at Crystal Palace. I remember it like yesterday, and I'm so pleased that I did say nothing on the sideline, and I just watched, because when he comes out and he gets in that car, and we talk about different things, you're a dad.

"And hopefully at 45-50 years old when Jesse's there, and I'm hopefully still around, I'm still going to be his dad first and foremost.

"I don't ever want to think that he would look at me as if I'm the coach.

"I'm the guy who's putting him under added pressure because there's enough pressure in this game."

'Don't lose that individuality'

"100 per cent [you have to enjoy it]," he added. "Even now, as a 19-year-old and because I'm not there every day and I don't live in Portugal, unfortunately I can't see him and share this experience with him the way that I would like.

"But even when he's getting ready for his games at the weekend, my last text with him will be: enjoy the moment, enjoy the game, enjoy the occasion.

"And I always leave it like this because he's a different type of player to what I was. He's obviously a winger, and he's got this individual flair and ability that is exciting to watch."

"But I'll say to him, 'What would you like to watch?' If he was watching yourself, what would you like to watch? And I say, you'd like to watch yourself being that individual flair player.

"I'm not saying you shouldn't conform to what your manager wants; of course you should. You should always try and do what the manager wants.

"But for him, don't lose that individuality that he's got and he's had since he was five years old; try and take that onto the pitch when he's playing."

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo in cryptic swipe at Portugal teammates over Lionel Messi view
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo in cryptic swipe at Portugal teammates over Lionel Messi view

Cristiano Ronaldo has liked a social media post accusing his Portugal teammates of not treating him with the same respect as Lionel Messi.

The 41-year-old is facing a potential six-month ban from international duty if he is found guilty of abandoning the national team.

2 Ronaldo's international career could be over - 23 years after making his Portugal debut Credit: AFP

Ronaldo's Portugal legacy has been called into question after he walked out of their training camp midweek.

Why did Ronaldo pull out of the national team camp?

The five-time Ballon d'Or winner made the decision in the aftermath of his side's 2-1 win away at Norway in the Nations League.

For the first time since Euro 2008, Ronaldo was an unused substitute.

He has since vowed 'to tell the truth' over his shock departure, with boss Jorge Jesus standing by his choice to leave the veteran forward on the bench.

In the aftermath of Ronaldo's exit, his iconic No.7 shirt was immediately given to Galatasaray winger Rafael Leao.

Meanwhile, Paris Saint-Germain midfielder Vitinha has declared Portugal 'took a step forward' in their attacking play after beating Denmark 4-2 - their first game without Ronaldo.

Though Manchester United skipper Bruno Fernandes has defended Ronaldo's actions, declaring he remains his country's greatest sporting icon.

What post did Ronaldo like on Instagram?

Speaking after that match, ex-Brazil international Felipe Meslo scolded Portugal's squad.

The former Juventus and Inter Milan star stated Ronaldo's long-time rival Messi was worshipped during his time at Argentina - a far cry to how the Real Madrid icon was treated.

His comments were shared by Sport TV's Instagram account, which earned a like from Ronaldo.

In the clip which has gone viral, Melo said: "I see a grotesque difference in the players’ treatment with Cristiano Ronaldo in relation to Argentina players with Messi.

"I see much more respect from the opponents who play against Cristiano Ronaldo, I think that’s wrong.

"No one reaches the level of Cristiano Ronaldo. It’s unacceptable.

"You can’t let the best player in history leave like that, as if nothing had happened. You can’t."

What did Ronaldo say in his statement?

While Ronaldo has not commented on his Portugal future - unlike his sister who has hinted he has retired from international football - he didn't hold back when taking to Instagram.

He wrote: "After the press conference of the national team, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team camp.

2 Ronaldo may never don the famous Portugal jersey again with the forward in danger of receiving a ban Credit: Getty

“In time, I will tell all the Portuguese the truth about the reasons that motivated me to leave the national team, to which I always devoted myself.

“Now is the time to wish Portugal and all my teammates good luck, without exception.”

Sports.title: Celtic owner ambushed and escorted out by security during golf round alongside Brooks Koepka
Sports.content:
Celtic owner Dermot Desmond had to be escorted off Dunhill Links at St Andrews golf course on Saturday as Celtic fans launched tennis balls at him.

The 76-year-old Irish billionaire was the target of the protest while he was playing a round with five-time major winner Brooks Koepka.

3 Desmond is an unpopular figure at Celtic at the moment Credit: Getty

The incident happened on the 15th hole and the tennis balls had pictures of the owner's face on them.

Desmond completed his round of golf with the LIV Golf star before he was escorted away by security.

The Irishman was competing in the Pro-Am ahead of the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship, where his son Ross will be a contender.

And despite the disruption, the duo did finish their rounds.

Since the incident, the Celtic Fans Collective have claimed responsibility and issued a statement.

They said: “Dermot Desmond has essentially been allowed to run Celtic Football Club whilst using his wealth to hide from supporters and accountability.

“Fans took the chance today to send a message that this arrangement cannot continue.”

Desmond has been involved with Celtic since 1995 and is the largest shareholder at the club, owning between 34.6 and 34.9 per cent of the Scottish giants.

Celtic response

The club subsequently released a lengthy statement, saying they no longer engage with the Celtic Fan Collective.

It read: “Celtic Football Club condemns in the strongest terms the deliberate disruption which took place today at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship at St Andrews.

“This was a premeditated action. The club is aware that it was discussed and planned in advance at a meeting of the Celtic Fans Collective committee. Minutes of that meeting record a proposal specifically to disrupt the event at St Andrews using tennis balls and banners, coordination with supporters intending to attend, and an agreement that Collective funds would be used towards materials for the protest.

“Following today’s incident, the Celtic Fans Collective published footage of the disruption on its own social media account together with a statement supporting the action and the message it was intended to convey.

“Celtic Football Club has never sought to prevent supporters from expressing criticism of the club, its Board or its shareholders. Supporters are entitled to disagree with decisions, to make their views known and to protest peacefully. What occurred at St Andrews represents a significant and unacceptable escalation.

“A group purporting to act in the interests of Celtic supporters deliberately took a dispute concerning Celtic Football Club beyond Celtic Park and beyond football, to the home of golf, and disrupted an internationally recognised sporting event involving participants, organisers and spectators who have no involvement whatsoever in that dispute. In doing so, those responsible have sought to attach the name of Celtic and its supporters to their conduct on a public and international stage.

“Celtic’s reputation has been built over generations, and our supporters have earned a worldwide reputation for the extraordinary passion, loyalty and commitment with which they support their club. That reputation was built over many decades by generations of Celtic supporters.

“Those responsible have brought shame upon the name of Celtic Football Club and upon a reputation which generations of Celtic supporters have spent more than a century building.

3 Celtic Park isn't a happy place at the moment with fan anger growing Credit: Getty

“Over the past year, however, the conduct of the Green Brigade and those operating through the Celtic Fans Collective has increasingly threatened to undermine that hard-earned reputation. Repeated acts of disruption and escalation, culminating in today’s pre-planned disruption of an entirely unrelated sporting event, risk creating an image of Celtic supporters which is wholly unrepresentative of the overwhelming majority of those who follow the club.

“The reputation of Celtic supporters belongs to the entire Celtic family. It does not belong to any self-appointed group, and no such group is entitled to diminish it in pursuit of its own agenda.

“The club no longer accepts that the Celtic Fans Collective can credibly claim to represent the wider Celtic support. Those responsible for today’s events certainly do not speak for the many thousands of Celtic supporters who express their views passionately, peacefully and responsibly.

“The club will not be intimidated or coerced by organised acts of disruption. Nor will decisions concerning the stewardship of Celtic Football Club be dictated by those prepared continually to escalate their behaviour in an attempt to exert pressure upon the club, its employees, directors, shareholders or others associated with Celtic. There is a line between protest and deliberate disruption. Today that line was crossed.

“The club has repeatedly sought engagement with supporter groups and, where restrictions have previously been imposed, has sought to provide a route by which relationships could be rebuilt on the basis of responsible conduct. Most recently, the club met representatives of the Celtic Fans Collective in good faith in an effort to engage constructively with the concerns they wished to raise.

“It is therefore particularly regrettable that, while the club was continuing to engage in good faith, the Collective was planning and authorising further organised disruption. This follows the pattern of events surrounding the Stuttgart fixture earlier this year, when constructive engagement was similarly accompanied by plans for disruptive action.

“Today represents a further and more serious escalation. This time, the disruption was taken entirely outside Celtic and outside football, intruding upon an unrelated sporting event and targeting an individual while participating in that event in a private capacity.

“The conduct of the past year, culminating in today’s events, has demonstrated that the basis for constructive engagement has been fundamentally undermined. Accordingly, the club will no longer recognise the Celtic Fans Collective as a representative body speaking on behalf of Celtic supporters and will cease all engagement with the Collective with immediate effect. The club is examining today’s events. Any individuals or groups who are established to be involved in planning, facilitating or participating in this action will be banned indefinitely from Celtic Park.

“No supporter requires the permission of Celtic Football Club to disagree with its Board. But equally, no supporter group has an entitlement to repeatedly disrupt events, intimidate individuals or seek to coerce the club and then claim to do so on behalf of the Celtic support.

“Celtic will continue to listen to and engage with supporters who wish to make their voices heard constructively and responsibly. There are many established channels through which supporters can do so, and today’s decision does not diminish the club’s commitment to meaningful supporter engagement. But engagement requires responsibility. The club will protect its employees, directors, shareholders and supporters.

“The reputation of Celtic Football Club is non negotiable.”

3 Martin O'Neill is also under increasing pressure as well Credit: Getty

Why is Dermot Desmond being targeted?

Opposition towards Desmond is a steady build-up of frustration at the Celtic ownership from fans, rather than frustration over a poor start to the season from the SPFL champions.

The supporters want the board to match their ambitions, recruit wisely and communicate with them.

In the latest set of financial accounts, Celtic posted a loss of £4.8million, which was a startling drop from £22m profit the year before.

This led to a statement from the Celtic Fans Collective in September.

They said: "Anger at recent shambolic results on the park in big games was compounded yesterday by Celtic plc latest financial results.

"The statements from the 'interim' chairman (Brian Wilson) and CEO (Michael Nicholson) typically lacked humility and did little to improve the mood. Supporters are not fooled.

"The stark reality is that Celtic FC is underachieving across the club and the trajectory is alarming.

"We have highlighted the signs of this decline since our formation. We will continue to hold the club to account and fight for the standards that the Celtic support deserves.

"Celtic Fans Collective representatives met with Celtic FC yesterday to discuss the club's fan engagement strategy. We also the took opportunity to express the deep frustration at the continued mismanagement of the club. A full update will be shared with members shortly."

The unrest can be traced further back to the summer of 2025 when Brendan Rodgers asked for more signings and didn't get them, while Adam Idah was sold to Swansea City without a replacement.

The end result was an open letter to the board and a vote of no confidence in them once they responded.

Rodgers resigned shortly after with Frenchman Wilfried Nancy arriving for a brief but shambolic spell.

This further eroded fans' confidence in the board, and despite Martin O'Neill's arrival and dramatic title win last season, the concerns remain.

Celtic fans will now hope that there is a response from the board.

Sports.title: Ex-Chelsea star forced to intervene after vicious tackle sparks on-pitch brawl
Sports.content:
Former Chelsea star and assistant manager Jody Morris was forced to jump in and defend his teammate in a huge on-pitch brawl.

Morris was representing St. Johnstone in the Tennent's Sixes on Saturday evening when things got incredibly heated.

4 A brawl broke out on the opening night of the Tennent's Sixes on Saturday following an aggressive tackle Credit: Premier Sports

Frazer Wright, who played over 100 games for St. Johnstone, smashed into Dundee's Morgaro Gomis, sparking total chaos.

Gomis had his legs completely wiped out from underneath him as he was clattered by Wright on the edge of the box.

The aggressive tackle instantly saw Gomis try and get back to his feet to confront Wright, but the latter was already coming towards him, with other players then storming towards the pair.

Wright was pushed over by a Dundee United player, falling to the ground, with Gomis being held back in the brawl.

Former Chelsea midfielder Morris then tried to intervene, pulling multiple people away from the clash, including Wright, who had plenty directing their anger his way after his challenge.

Things eventually calmed down, but the referee instantly brandished the red card for the ex-St Johnstone centre-back once he was finally separated from the chaos.

Wright then slumped off to the sin bin, sitting there for the remainder of the game at the Braehead Arena.

Fortunately for him though, St. Johnstone managed to hang on to a 2-1 win against Dundee United.

'We're a little bit old school'

Morris spoke about the incident post-match after trying his best, and seemingly failing, at breaking things up on the pitch.

He said: “I suppose it’s just two teams that want to win, isn't it?

4 Wright flew into a challenge on Gomis, clattering his opponent and taking his legs from underneath him Credit: Premier Sports

4 Players from both teams then surrounded the pair and a brawl ensued with plenty of pushing and shoving Credit: Premier Sports

“A little bit of rivalry – I recognise quite a few faces from back in the day. We just wanted to protect the lead.

“It was a strong tackle from Frazer, but I don’t think it was a red. I think he got the ball.

“It was maybe a little bit too much for today’s game, but it is what it is, isn't it? We’re still a little bit old school.

“I think when you come across most footballers, whether they’re playing golf, Monopoly, they want to win and we’re no different.”

What is the Tennent's Sixes?

The Tennent's Sixes is a six-a-side tournament that is held over two days, including all 12 Scottish Premiership clubs.

This year's edition is the first since 1993, with legends of all teams coming together to play against each other.

4 Wright was sent off by the referee on the opening night of Tennent's Sixes, after Morris did his best to break things up Credit: Premier Sports

It is being held indoors at the Braehead Arena in Renfrewshire.

The event started on Saturday, with the brawl between St. Johnstone and Dundee United coming on opening day.

The final will take place on Sunday evening, with the winning club collecting a brand-new Tennent's Sixes trophy.

Sports.title: Bruno Fernandes shares Cristiano Ronaldo plea after phone call with superstar
Sports.content:
Bruno Fernandes has declared Cristiano Ronaldo remains Portugal's greatest icon - despite the striker walking out on the team.

The 41-year-old's international career could be at an end after he departed the Euro 2016 champions' training camp midweek.

3 Fernandes remains supportive of Ronaldo, as he urged Portugal fans to not be divided by his exit Credit: Getty

In last week's 2-1 win away at Norway, Ronaldo was an unused substitute.

It was the first time in 18 years that the veteran forward had been left on the bench for Portugal.

Ronaldo subsequently issued a bombshell statement on social media to announce his exit - vowing to 'tell the truth' regarding his decision.

Portuguese journalist Pedro Sepulveda told talkSPORT in the aftermath that the five-time Ballon d'Or winner had been lied to about his game time by boss Jorge Jesus.

While many fans have been left hurt and disappointed by Ronaldo's shock exit, Fernandes has come to his defence - hailing him for what he has achieved for Portugal.

The world's most capped international player with 234 outings and top scorer with 146 goals, Ronaldo helped his side win the European Championship and two Nations League titles.

Insisting that Ronaldo has not tarnished his legacy, Fernandes, who also played with the ex-Sporting Lisbon man at Manchester United, has implored supporters to not be divided by the news.

What has Bruno Fernandes said about Ronaldo?

Revealing he is still in direct communication with Ronaldo ahead of Sunday's return meeting with Norway, Fernandes said: "Regarding Cristiano, I had a conversation with him.

"What I told him, and what I repeat here, is regardless of what happens, Cristiano Ronaldo will never cease to be the greatest symbol of our national team, of our football, and of the country, for what he has done not only in Portugal but throughout the world.

"He has a reserved place not only among the best of all time, but also in the hearts of all Portuguese people, and the most important thing is that we stop dividing things.

3 Ronaldo, who is four goals shy of 150 international goals, could be banned over decision to walk out Credit: Getty

"There are no divisions in the national team. It is one and will remain so, despite any noise that may come from outside.

"We are outside of this controversy, but what I ask is that the country does not divide itself, does not make choices, that it respects all sides.

"Cris is and will be the biggest icon of our national team, he deserves everyone's respect, regardless of who likes him more or [who likes him] less."

Fernanded also remarked: "Matters must be resolved internally and conclude well for both parties."

Could Ronaldo ever play for Portugal again?

It now remains to be seen whether the Real Madrid and Manchester United will ever play for Portugal again.

He faces a possible six-month banishment by the Portuguese Football Federation if he is found guilty of abandoning the national team.

3 The last time Ronaldo was an unused sub for Portugal came at Euro 2008 Credit: AFP

And with his contract to expire at Al Nassr at the end of the 2026/27 season, Ronaldo could decide to call time on his glittering career upon the expiration of his deal.

How have Portugal fared in the Nations League?

Portugal have won all three of their opening matches, and remain on course to reach the Finals in 2027.

Jesus' side are the defending champions having triumphed over Spain in the final in 2025 under Roberto Martinez's tutelage - which saw Ronaldo get on the score sheet.

They also won the inaugural competition in 2019 - beating the Netherlands 1-0.

Sports.title: Dele Alli trains at non-league club after building fitness at Barnet
Sports.content:
Dele Alli was pictured training with semi-professional side Windsor & Eton as he prepares to return to football.

The ex-Tottenham star remains on the lookout for the next chapter of his career having spent over 12 months without a club.

2 Alli was last on the books at Como - featuring just once for the Italian outfit Credit: Getty

Alli has been without formal employment since September 2025 after having his contract terminated at Como.

Lasting just eight months of his 18-month contract, the 30-year-old featured in just one match for the Italian side.

And that proved to be a nightmare outing having been sent off against AC Milan just minutes after coming off the bench.

Alli, who won the PFA Young Player of the Year award twice at White Hart Lane, struggled for consistency at Everton after leaving Tottenham in 2022. He then flattered to deceive during his loan spell at Besiktas.
