World.title: Malawi, Zambia And Zimbabwe Bishops Stand With Archbishop Banda
World.content:
Regional Catholic Bishops Back Archbishop Banda, Call For Fair And Transparent Process

Two regional Catholic bodies, the Association of Catholic Bishops’ Conferences of Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe (ACBC-MAZAZI) and the Zimbabwe Catholic Bishops’ Conference (ZCBC), have declared solidarity with Lusaka Archbishop Alick Banda and appealed to Zambian authorities to guarantee him a fair and transparent process as his case moves through the courts. In separate communiqués, the bishops said they were troubled by his arrest and the legal proceedings against him, and called for due process and respect for human dignity.

ACBC-MAZAZI, in a communiqué signed by its president, Rt Rev Raymond Mpandasekwa, said it was expressing profound sadness and deep concern over the proceedings, the arrest and the detention of the Archbishop. It said it stood in unwavering fraternal solidarity with him and extended spiritual support to the clergy, religious and lay faithful of the Archdiocese of Lusaka, as well as the Zambia Conference of Catholic Bishops (ZCCB). The association represents the Catholic bishops of Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

Its appeal to the authorities was direct. “We earnestly appeal to the relevant authorities and the legal framework of Zambia to guarantee Archbishop Banda a fully just, transparent and due process in accordance with both national laws and international legal norms,” the association said. The bishops added that the Catholic Church consistently upholds the rule of law, respects national sovereignty and recognises the role of civil institutions. They stressed, however, that justice must be administered with fairness, transparency and respect for human rights and human dignity.

The regional bishops also appealed for calm. They urged the faithful and the wider public to reject any form of escalation and to pursue dialogue. “We urge all parties, the faithful and the wider public to remain calm, united and prayerful, rejecting any forms of escalation while pursuing the path of constructive dialogue and mutual respect,” ACBC-MAZAZI said.

The ZCBC issued its own message, expressing fraternal solidarity and prayerful closeness to the ZCCB, Archbishop Banda and the Catholic Church in Zambia. The Zimbabwean bishops said they had followed developments with concern, from the Archbishop’s appearance before the Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC) on 28 September to his arrest and appearance before the Lusaka Magistrates’ Court. They noted that he pleaded not guilty and was subsequently released on bail.

The Zimbabwean bishops said the Church recognises the legitimate responsibility of state institutions to administer justice and uphold the rule of law. They said judicial procedures must nonetheless respect the rights of those involved. “The dignity of every human person requires that judicial procedures be conducted fairly and impartially, with full respect for due process and the rights of those involved. We therefore join you in praying that truth and justice may prevail,” the bishops said.

They said the bond between the two national conferences runs deeper than geography, resting on shared communion and mission under ACBC-MAZAZI. “When one local Church passes through a moment of difficulty, we cannot remain indifferent. Its joys and hopes, trials and anxieties become our own,” they said.

The ZCBC urged the clergy, religious and lay faithful in Zambia to remain united in prayer, peaceful in spirit and steadfast in hope as the judicial process continues. The bishops assured the Archbishop and the ZCCB of continued prayers and fraternity, entrusting them to the intercession of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Queen of Peace.

Others have also spoken on the case. Movement for Economic Emancipation president Given Chansa questioned what public interest is served by prosecuting a prominent clergyman over a motor vehicle he received as a gift, and urged the State to discontinue the case. He said prosecutorial discretion requires that even where there is enough evidence to charge, a case should proceed only if it is in the public interest.

Former Cabinet minister Given Lubinda said in an interview that the Archbishop is a man of fixed abode and no flight risk. He found it hard to accept that Dr Banda spent a night in the Chimbokaila cells, and most of the following day, after bail was granted. Mr Lubinda said the Archbishop is not above the law.

The Archbishop pleaded not guilty and has been released on bail, and his case remains before the courts.

World.title: Lubinda Is Back: Questions Kafwaya’s Death, Treason Detentions And Archbishop’s Night In Cells
World.content:
Lubinda Demands Independent Inquest Into Kafwaya Death, Questions Treason Detention Delays

Given Lubinda, the former Cabinet minister who acted as Patriotic Front president, has called for an independent inquest into the death of former Cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya, saying the state owes his family and the nation a full account of how he died during a security operation in Lusaka. In an interview, he also asked how long the state may hold treason suspects before presenting them to a court, and warned that the country is dividing into those who won the election and those who lost it.

Mr Lubinda said he would not comment on how the vote was run because he stood apart from the process. “It would be remiss of me to claim to have sufficient knowledge to judge the conduct of those elections,” he said. Asked why he stayed out of public view during the campaign, he said the answer would take an entire programme and should wait for another day.

His concern, he said, is what has happened since the 13 August vote, which has left the country looking split between winners and losers. “Elections, like I said in my statement, should not be a determinant of who is a citizen and who is not a citizen,” he said. Those given the mandate to govern, he added, must deal fairly with the people who voted against them. “You do not wish them out of the way. What you do is to embrace them and ensure that they feel that they still continue to enjoy the full rights of every citizen.”

Mr Lubinda listed the death of Mr Kafwaya, public talk of militias and insurgents, reports that detainees were denied lawyers, family and medical care, and talk of tribalism as signs the country is not heading that way. On Mr Kafwaya, he said word of the death first emerged on the 14th, when people heard of gunfire and that a life may have been lost. Confirmation took almost four days, and the state later disclosed that its security officers were involved.

The first real information, he said, came from the family, who found the body in a morgue at Maina Soko after the widow, the children and friends pleaded for answers. Nobody has stepped forward to say they placed it there. “It’s still a mystery,” he said. He also faulted remarks made after the death suggesting Mr Kafwaya brought it on himself. “You don’t say things like that after a citizen has died,” he said.

Mr Lubinda said he has no evidence of how Mr Kafwaya died and would not point a finger at anyone, but he said the silence leaves families to guess. He put himself in that position. “I shudder to imagine that this happened to me. That all of a sudden, I’m dead, and the state says we were at that place and there was a skirmish, but then the state does not explain the circumstances under which I died,” he said. “I expect a little bit more. As a citizen, I expect that even in my death, I shall be treated with some humanity.”

He was reminded that Secretary to the Cabinet Patrick Kangwa had spoken on the matter and described a clash involving gunfire. Mr Lubinda said that account leaves out what the public most wants to know: whether a state officer shot Mr Kafwaya, and what led security officers to the premises. “That I missed,” he said of both points. He noted that the law requires a post-mortem even where a person dies in a car crash, so that no mystery surrounds the death.

That, he said, is why he is asking for an independent inquest, which he sees as the best way out given how long government took to explain. “The state has a duty to protect my life. And if I was to lose this life under circumstances that my family and friends do not understand, the state must assist them to get to the bottom of it,” he said. “I’m afraid that at this point, citizens may not listen to government anymore.”

Mr Lubinda rejected suggestions that his statement was written in fear. Some people on Facebook, he said, predicted he could be arrested or airlifted for issuing it. “Shouldn’t I express my opinion as a citizen? Shouldn’t I ask questions to my government as a citizen? No, I don’t have such fear,” he said.

He then turned to those arrested after the election, including Brian Mundubile. Mr Lubinda said the nation was told by Mr Kangwa that the matter had been followed up for three years, which left him expecting strong evidence. “They were investigating this for three years, and now they have effected an arrest. So they must certainly have cogent evidence,” he said. Later, he said, the public heard that investigations were still going on, when suspects should have been presented before a judge within 48 hours as the Penal Code provides.

He was asked whether Zambians were being impatient, given how long some past treason cases took. Those cited included the case of Edward Jack Shamwana and 12 others, and the 2017 treason case against President Hakainde Hichilema, then in opposition. Mr Lubinda said those timelines measure how long trials ran, not how long suspects waited to be presented in court. “Jack Shamwana and friends were nabbed, taken into prison, quickly presented before a judge. And then the matter in court is the one that took three years, not investigations,” he said.

The real issue, he said, is the law and not patience. He asked whether the Constitution permits a citizen to be arrested and kept in detention for as long as the state takes to investigate, and he wants Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri to answer for Zambians. “If it takes 10 years for them to be satisfied with the evidence, should we keep quiet and say this is alright?” he said.

Mr Lubinda said delay also damages the accused in the public eye, because a person who is arrested cannot speak until they appear before a judge. “The more you delay to present a person before a judge, the more it sinks in the public that that person is facing this criminal offence,” he said. An accused person who has not been told the charges cannot defend himself, he added, comparing it to being accused of theft without being told the day or the item.

On Archbishop Alick Banda, Mr Lubinda said he has been through the experience of being granted bail in the morning and then waiting while the arresting officer cannot be found. That made the Archbishop’s night in the Chimbokaila cells, and most of the next day, hard for him to accept. Dr Banda is not above the law, he said, but officers have the ability to judge a person’s standing and flight risk. “Where can Dr Alick Banda hide? Where in this world can Dr Alick Banda hide?” he said.

Asked which institutions need strengthening, Mr Lubinda said all of them, naming the executive, the legislature, the judiciary, the police, the anti-corruption and drug enforcement commissions, and the political parties. He said the opposition cannot yet be called strong, noting that every opposition is shaken after defeat, as the PF was in 2021. “I think the opposition is still finding its feet after the defeat. I’m sure that we will find our feet,” he said.

Asked what advice he would give Mr Hichilema for a second term, Mr Lubinda offered three points. The first is to pray and treat every Zambian as one of God’s creation. The second is to use the term to address what people complained about in the first, because “he is capable of ending his second term, leaving a legacy that he would be proud of.” The third is to govern for all Zambians in a way they can see.

Mr Lubinda said he would turn down a place in the President’s team, as he did when lobbied in the past. “If you think that I can add value to government, then I would rather use that value to strengthen the opposition,” he said. He said pressure on those in power is needed, citing the price of fuel and delays in paying farmers by the Food Reserve Agency. Asked whether he still wants to be president, he said he has never run from that ambition.

Mr Lubinda said he would return to explain his silence whenever he is invited again.

World.title: Don’t Be Distracted By “Pe Lampi” Chants; Focus On Delivering!
World.content:
When there was a power outage at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium during the Zambia-Togo match in Ndola the other day, a pocket of fans erupted into “Pe Lampi!” chants as they flashed the Tonse Alliance symbol.

It is common knowledge that PF cadres who have since metamorphosed into Tonse are stubborn in their support. This is not likely to change any time soon. Just look at how Tonse supporters led by the likes of Jay Jay Banda, Binwell Mpundu, Lillian Mutambo and Emmanuel Mwamba behave on social media. Not a single day passes without them offloading cheap propaganda. How can they be spreading lies that the President is indisposed or even calling for his assassination, and yet we have Church leaders cheering them on? Hypocrites!

We would like to urge the President and his incoming administration to keep ignoring these dimwits and minions and focus on his Grow Zambia Agenda – the 10-10-5-3-3-1-1-1 blueprint that speaks to real issues: maize, electricity, tourism, copper, soya, wheat, sugar and beef exports.

Let the work speak for itself!

President Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda is ambitious. But for it to work, it must move like lightening from every village, city and province.

1. 10 Million Tonnes of Maize – Who Will Grow It?

Is it only the commercial farmers? How does the villager in Shangombo or on Chilubi Island participate and benefit? This is where Cooperatives come in. The whole concept of cooperatives needs to be overhauled and adapted to changing seasons. We need genuine, production-based cooperatives – not briefcase cooperatives formed just to share FISP. Let us equip them with irrigation, mechanization and guaranteed markets.

2. 10,000 MW of Electricity – Diversify Now.

With El Nino always looming around the corner, the country must speed up diversification into alternative sources of energy. We cannot continue to depend on hydro alone. Councils must prioritize using part of the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) to invest in solar power plants and even waste-to-energy plants. Every district has an abandoned dump site or sewer ponds that can host a solar plant.

3. 5 Million Tourists – Clean Up Zambia First.

No tourist is going to come to a dirty country. They are afraid of contracting cholera or malaria. The Mayor-Elect of Lusaka is already doing a commendable job cleaning up Lusaka. We hope this will be replicated countrywide. We expect clean cities, paved walkways, street lights, working traffic lights and flowers blossoming everywhere! Tourism starts with order and cleanliness.

4. 3 Million Tonnes of Copper – Not Raw.

Is this copper going to be exported in its raw form as we have done for 60 years? We expect to see value addition. We want to see copper cables, electrical wiring, motor windings and EV battery components manufactured right here in Zambia. That is how we create jobs.

5. 3 Million Tonnes of Soya Beans – The Feed and Oil Link.

Soya is the new gold. It links directly to stock feed, cooking oil and exports. Let us support out-grower schemes and oil processing plants in every province.

6 & 7. 1 Million Tonnes Wheat and 1 Million Tonnes Sugar – Winter Cropping.

This calls for serious irrigation investment. We have water everywhere but we only farm in the rainy season. Wheat and sugar are winter crops that can be grown under irrigation.

8. $1 Billion Beef Exports – Bring Back Ranches.

We had great ranches in Mumbwa, Chisamba and Southern Province. They collapsed. Let us revive them with proper breeding, veterinary services and abattoirs that meet export standards.

In short, 10-10-5-3-3-1-1-1 is possible – but only if we decentralize it to cooperatives, councils and ordinary Zambians.

Prince Bill M. Kaping’a

Secretary General

HH Mpaka 2O31 People’s Alliance

World.title: Zambia Post‑2026: Can the Grow Zambia Agenda Coexist with Civic Space Decay?
World.content:
By Venus N Msyani

The aftermath of Zambia’s 2026 general election has ushered in a period of deep uncertainty, marked by what many observers describe as a rapid decay of civic space. President Hakainde Hichilema’s administration appears intent on pushing the nation to “move on,” yet the methods being used to enforce this political closure have raised serious concerns.

Arrests, intimidation, and punitive actions against critics have become increasingly visible, creating an atmosphere of fear rather than unity. This is occurring against the backdrop of an election whose credibility has been questioned by the European Union and several other reputable monitoring bodies, all of whom expressed dissatisfaction with the conduct and outcome of the polls.

One of the most striking developments has been the targeting of religious leadership. The Archbishop of Lusaka, Alick Banda, widely respected for his defense of human rights, democracy, and the marginalized, spent a night in jail on charges related to a previously settled stolen‑vehicle case.

For many Zambians, this incident symbolized a troubling shift: even the Church, historically a moral anchor and mediator during political crises, is no longer safe from state pressure. Archbishop Banda’s consistent advocacy for truth and justice appears to be the very reason he is now facing persecution.

Beyond the clergy, ordinary citizens and political actors have also felt the weight of state power. Passports have been confiscated from individuals who refuse to accept what they view as a compromised election victory. Others have been detained for prolonged periods without clear timelines for court appearances. These actions collectively paint a picture of shrinking civic freedoms at a moment when national cohesion is desperately needed.

It is within this tense environment that President Hichilema unveiled the Grow Zambia Agenda during his inauguration on 1 September 2026. The agenda promises job creation, wealth generation, and shared prosperity over the next five years. His first international trip of the new term, a working visit to the United Arab Emirates from 29 to 30 September, was framed as the official launch of this development program. Upon his return to Lusaka, the President confirmed to reporters that the UAE trip was indeed aligned with the Grow Zambia vision.

However, not everyone interpreted the trip as a confident stride into Zambia’s developmental future. Notably, there was no media interaction during his departure, in contrast to the engagement seen upon his arrival. This absence of transparency fueled speculation.

Days earlier, Hichilema had explained that he delegated attendance at the United Nations General Assembly to the Foreign Affairs Minister to reduce costs associated with presidential travel. Critics seized on this explanation, suggesting that the UAE trip may have been an emergency visit, possibly for medical reasons. Some even speculated about serious illness. While such claims remain unverified, their circulation reflects a broader erosion of public trust.

Returning to the central question: Can the Grow Zambia Agenda coexist with democratic decay? History suggests the answer is NO. Zambia’s most successful national initiatives have relied on collective effort, public confidence, and broad civic participation. Development is not merely a technical process; it is a social contract. When citizens feel silenced, intimidated, or excluded, they cannot meaningfully contribute to national progress.

The failure of Hichilema’s anti‑corruption campaign during his first term, widely viewed as ineffective due to lack of inclusive engagement, serves as a recent example of how initiatives falter without collective effort.

The current trajectory indicates that the Grow Zambia Agenda is being launched on a fractured foundation. Prosperity cannot be built where dissent is criminalized. Economic growth cannot flourish in an environment where civic freedoms are shrinking. A development program that requires national unity cannot succeed while key voices, clergy, activists, opposition leaders, and ordinary citizens, are suppressed.

The logical conclusion is clear: fresh elections may be necessary to restore legitimacy, rebuild trust, and create the collective environment required for Zambia’s development. Only a renewed mandate, earned through a transparent and credible process, can reconcile the Grow Zambia Agenda with the democratic principles essential for its success.

World.title: Chellah Tukuta is on point; the President is on his own!
World.content:
Presidential photographer Chellah Tukuta has lamented that some Presidential appointees – Cabinet Ministers, Permanent Secretaries and District Commissioners have neglected to rise to the occasion and defend the President whenever he has come under attack from the opposition.

“There’s no way you can be watching your President being disrespected, being called names and being insulted everyday and you are just there enjoying the fruits and the benefits of the appointments he gave you….” charges Tukuta.

The camera man has hit the bull’s eye! The conduct of most of these government officials leaves much to be desired. Most of them are reluctant to put their necks on the chopping board for the President for fear of being pursued in future for whatever wrongs they may have committed.

Such misgivings and frustrations were equally shared with us by a Chingola-based senior clergyman when we had a meeting with him in his office.

“How come senior government officials choose to remain silent when the President is being abused and attacked daily,” wondered the pastor. “Could it be because they’re eating with both hands or their hands have come dirty?”

We are left with no choice but to keep reminding the President that he’s on HIS OWN. He needs to urgently audit those he’s working with to establish their loyalty and commitment to help him realise his Grow Zambia Agenda otherwise some of them don’t mean well at all.

When we as concerned members of the public came up with a mass movement, HH Mpaka 2O31 People’s Alliance whose mission is to help defend and protect the President from unnecessary attacks, we sought appointments with most government officials to gather the necessary data so as to engage the media or the public better equipped. But lo and behold, most of them weren’t willing to interact with us let alone picking up our calls and yet we’ve going extra miles defending the President!

Clean up the system before it’s too late, Sir.

Thank you,

Prince Bill M. Kaping’a

Secretary General

HH Mpaka 2O31 People’s Alliance

World.title: Mbala Central MP urged to address water challenges
World.content:
Village Headmen in Maround and Overspill townships in Mbala District have called on Mbala Central Member of Parliament, Raphael Chilufya to help address the persistent water challenges affecting residents in the two areas.

One of the Village Headmen in Maround, Penza Siame says residents have been facing challenges to access clean and safe drinking water for a long time, forcing them to walk long distances to fetch the commodity from the Lucheche stream.

Mr Siame told ZANIS in Mbala that there is an urgent need for a lasting solution to the water challenges facing the two communities.

And Mbala Central Member of Parliament, Raphael Chilufya, said he had taken note of the concerns raised by residents from the respective townships.

Mr Chilufya said he will engage the council and other departments to explore ways of addressing the problem.

He urged the Village Headmen to remain united, regardless of their political affiliations, in order to contribute to the development of the constituency.

“Water is a basic need, and I have taken note of the challenges raised by the residents. I will engage the relevant authorities to see how best this problem can be addressed. I also encourage Village Headmen to remain united, regardless of their political affiliations, because unity is important for the development of Mbala Central Constituency,” he advised.

World.title: Nigeria: Boko Haram Fighters Gun Down Farmers in Borno
World.content:
Suspected Boko Haram insurgents have ambushed and killed 15 farmers, while abducting three others in Marte Local Government Area of Borno State.

According to local sources, the tragic incident took place across the Ala, Gumna, and Musune wards near the headquarters of the area council, on Wednesday.

While initial reports of the attack reached the community on Wednesday evening, the task of recovering the bodies could not be completed until Thursday morning.

Recounting the borrowing aftermath of the assault, an anonymous source said, "Five bodies were initially recovered from the field, while others were found later. Three persons are still missing, and sources indicate they were abducted by the insurgents."



The Public Relations Officer, Borno State Police Command, DSP Kenneth Nahum Daso, confirmed that 15 people lost their lives and confirmed that authorities were actively investigating the situation.

"We are making efforts to determine the whereabouts of the three people still missing," Daso said.

A grieving relative, whose cousin was among the victims, shared details of the execution-style killings.

She explained that the victims had gone to their farms to harvest crops when they were ambushed.

"They were forced to lie down and were shot in the head at close range. It was a gory sight," she said.

According to the relative, local community members bravely mobilized to scour the fields, retrieve the bodies, and ensure they were buried according to Islamic rites.

The massacre has drawn widespread outrage, with the human rights organization Amnesty International strongly condemning the violence as a horrific violation of international humanitarian law.

In a statement released on Friday, the organization expressed deep concern over the escalating violence against vulnerable populations in Northeast Nigeria.

"Amnesty International strongly condemns the horrific killing of at least 15 people in Marte Local Government Area of Borno State," the statement read. "The victims, who were local residents venturing into the surrounding areas to earn a living or harvest their crops, were ambushed and targeted by a suspected Boko Haram group."

The rights group emphasized that the deliberate targeting of civilians by non-state armed groups constitutes a war crime.

"Amnesty International calls on the Nigerian authorities to take immediate, transparent, and human-rights-compliant measures to protect vulnerable communities living in the region," the statement concluded.

Despite ongoing military operations in Nigeria's Northeast, farming communities continue to face severe security threats as insurgents frequently target agricultural workers in remote areas

World.title: Somalia: Somaliland Detains Austrian Over Spiny-Tailed Lizard Smuggling
World.content:
Hargeisa — Somaliland police and the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change have detained an Austrian national in the port city of Berbera after he was allegedly caught attempting to purchase and collect spiny-tailed lizards, locally known as caasho-badhi.

The Ministry of Environment said the man was apprehended in a joint operation with police in the Sahil region.

"The Ministry of Environment, in cooperation with the police, arrested an Austrian national in Berbera who was collecting spiny-tailed lizards, locally known as caasho-badhi," the ministry said.

Authorities said the animals were allegedly being collected with the intention of taking them to Europe. Officials displayed containers and other equipment they said were connected to the case.

The ministry did not identify the Austrian national or specify how many lizards had been recovered. It also did not immediately say whether formal charges had been filed.

Spiny-tailed lizards, commonly known as Uromastyx, are reptiles distinguished by their thick, heavily spiked tails and are found in arid regions of Africa and the Middle East.

The case has raised concerns about the collection of Somaliland's wildlife for the international exotic-pet trade, in which reptiles and other wild animals can be captured and sold abroad.

The Somaliland government warned residents against illegally capturing, selling or trafficking wildlife and urged the public to report suspicious activities to the Environment Ministry or security authorities.

(Reporting by HornDiplomat News Desk)

World.title: Ethiopia: AU Urges Restraint As Ethiopia, Eritrea, Egypt Tensions Rise
World.content:
Addis Ababa — The African Union Commission has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise maximum restraint amid heightened tensions between the three countries, warning against actions or statements that could further destabilise the region.

In a statement issued in Addis Ababa on Oct. 1, the commission said it was closely following the situation with concern and called on the three African Union member states to avoid further escalation.

"The Commission calls on all three Member States to exercise maximum restraint and refrain from actions or statements that could further escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability," the statement said.

The AU Commission also stressed the importance of maintaining channels of communication between Addis Ababa, Asmara and Cairo as tensions have increased across the Horn of Africa.

It urged the three governments to address their differences through established diplomatic channels and peaceful dialogue, in accordance with the principles of the Constitutive Act of the African Union.

"The Commission further underscores the importance of preserving channels of communication and urges the three countries to address their differences through established diplomatic channels and peaceful dialogue," it said.

The commission said it was prepared to assist the three countries in efforts to reduce tensions and resolve their differences peacefully.

"The AU Commission stands ready, in consultation with the countries concerned, to support efforts towards de-escalation, dialogue and the peaceful resolution of differences," the statement said.

Reporting by HornDiplomat News Desk)

World.title: Uganda: Mountain Gorilla Population Rises to 1,063 Amid Calls to End Illegal Tracking
World.content:
The population of mountain gorillas in Uganda, Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo has risen to 1,063, up from about 300 in 1990, conservation officials have announced.

Of these, 459 are found in Uganda's Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, while the others live in Rwanda's Volcanoes National Park and the Democratic Republic of Congo's Virunga National Park.

The figures were revealed during Uganda's national World Gorilla Day celebrations held at Ruhija Community Playground in Rubanda District. World Gorilla Day is marked globally every September 24 to promote gorilla conservation.

This year's celebrations, hosted under the theme "Securing the Future: Restoring Indigenous Trees, Healthy Gorillas and Resilient Communities," brought together conservationists, government officials, local leaders and communities.



Uganda rotates the national World Gorilla Day event among Rubanda, Kisoro and Kanungu districts.

Officials attributed the increase in the gorilla population to habitat protection, regular monitoring, law enforcement and greater involvement of communities living near protected areas.

Ruhija Town Council Mayor Geoffrey Tumuhimbise commended communities around Bwindi for embracing conservation and urged the Uganda Wildlife Authority (UWA) to increase support to residents so they can benefit tangibly from protecting wildlife.

"Conservation should not only focus on protecting wildlife, but should also consider the welfare and livelihoods of communities living alongside protected areas," Tumuhimbise said.

Representing the Minister of Tourism, Wildlife and Antiquities, Commissioner John Magambo, Tom Butiime welcomed the increase but warned against illegal gorilla tracking in Kigezi, saying it undermines conservation and tourism.

"Gorillas are a key tourism asset that boosts national revenue and community incomes. Tracking must follow established guidelines. Some conservation partners use their positions to facilitate irregular tracking," Butiime noted.

World.title: Sudan: 'I Have Not Lost My Dreams' - Refugee Education Funding Cuts Threaten Millions
World.content:
Refugees wait to be registered at UNHCR is Cairo (file photo).

A teenage girl who fled war-torn Sudan for neighbouring Egypt and hopes to pursue a technology degree is an example of why countries must ensure that young refugees can continue to learn.

"When we left Sudan, I was worried that my education would stop," said Jamila Mostafa, 19, one of the estimated 13.1 million refugee children of school age worldwide in 2025.

Yet nearly half - 5.8 million - remain out of school as funding cuts threaten to roll back years of progress in educating children and adolescents forced to flee their homelands due to war, conflict, violence or persecution.

A generation at risk

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The warning comes in a new report by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR.

"At a time of severe pressure on humanitarian and development financing, cuts to education risk reversing decades of collective investment and closing opportunities for a generation of young people," said UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih, a former refugee from Iraq.

The transition to secondary education remains one of the biggest challenges for refugee children, according to the report. Only 32 per cent were enrolled in high school in 2025, compared to 65 per cent at the primary level.

However, many young refugees arrive at primary school unprepared. Two in three lack the foundational learning that prepares them for the classroom.

Gender gap, enrollment goals

Even though refugee girls and boys attend primary school at similar rates, the gap widens sharply in secondary education. Increasing numbers of adolescent girls leave school due to poverty, early marriage, safety concerns and other pressures.

Meanwhile, progress in higher education underscores the value of sustained investment. Refugee enrollment at the tertiary level reached a record 11 per cent in 2025, with more than 450,000 students attending university or undertaking technical and vocational training.

This means UNHCR and partners are on track to ensure that 15 per cent of refugee youth can access higher education by the end of the decade, known as the 15x30 pledge.

Faiza Qudrati from Afghanistan grew up in Kazakhstan and studied medicine before switching to psychology.

"For me, higher education gives me a chance to grow, learn and one day help other people in the same way that support was once provided to me," she said.

© UNHCR/Hélène Caux UN High Commissioner for Refugees at the digital learning center in Farchana, Chad. (file) Unequal access

Although higher education can significantly improve the lives of refugee women and girls, providing them with access to skills, qualifications, employment and greater financial independence, access is still deeply unequal.

Close 

Refugee enrollment remains below the national average in more than 80 per cent of reporting countries. In low-income and conflict-affected countries, only two per cent of refugees were enrolled in higher education, compared to 13 per cent of nationals.

UNHCR stressed that improving refugee education also means strengthening national education systems by investing more in teachers, classrooms, learning materials and financing to benefit both refugees and host communities.

Shaping their own future

UNHCR called for the international community and development partners to safeguard education funding and invest in the national systems of countries hosting refugees.

"Education gives young people the tools to shape their own future," said Mr. Salih. "Our responsibility is to make sure they have that chance."

Jamila, the young Sudanese woman in Egypt, is continuing her high school education through UNHCR-backed support. She has developed a particular interest in artificial intelligence (AI) and how it can help address social and economic challenges. She hopes to study technology at university.

"School gives me confidence," she said. "It reminds me that even though I lost my home because of the war, I have not lost my dreams."

World.title: Kenya: Lecturers and University Staff Down Tools Over 2025-2029 Cba Dispute
World.content:
Nairobi — Lecturers and other staff in public universities have begun a nationwide strike after their unions rejected a counter-offer by the Inter-Public Universities Councils Consultative Forum (IPUCCF) over the 2025-2029 Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA).

The industrial action involves members of the Universities Academic Staff Union (UASU), Kenya Universities Staff Union (KUSU) and Kenya Union of Domestic, Hotels, Educational Institutions, Hospitals and Allied Workers (KUDHEIHA).

The unions announced the strike after talks with IPUCCF ended without an agreement in Machakos on Thursday.

They said the latest counter-offer failed to address key issues raised during negotiations, including salaries, allowances, medical benefits and the recruitment of additional academic staff.



The unions also argued that the proposal did not honour provisions contained in the registered 2021-2025 CBA, particularly on the harmonisation of allowances under the new agreement.

A major point of disagreement is the proposed salary increment. The unions have rejected an automatic annual increase of four per cent, arguing that it is below the prevailing inflation rate and would not adequately cushion university workers against the rising cost of living.

UASU National Organising Secretary Jacob Musembi, speaking on behalf of the three unions, said the counter-offer was inadequate and failed to respond to their concerns.

The unions have also raised concerns over medical cover, saying the proposed package does not match benefits available to civil servants in equivalent job grades.

Staff shortages have emerged as another major issue, with the unions demanding increased recruitment of academic staff to cope with rising student enrolment in public universities.

The IPUCCF has recommended an 8.25 per cent cumulative increase in basic salaries over the four-year 2025-2029 CBA period, with the adjustment implemented at two per cent annually.

The employers' forum considered several salary review options before settling on the proposal submitted to the Salaries and Remuneration Commission (SRC).

The unions, however, had submitted substantially higher salary demands. UASU proposed increases ranging from 36 to 68 per cent, while KUSU sought increases of between 36 and 113 per cent. KUDHEIHA had proposed increases ranging from 75 to 193 per cent.

The strike follows months of stalled negotiations over the new CBA.

Close 

UASU had issued a seven-day strike notice in September, accusing university councils, the Ministry of Education and the National Treasury of failing to honour commitments contained in the Return-to-Work Formula signed in November 2025.

KUSU also issued a strike notice, citing delays in concluding, registering and implementing the 2025-2029 CBA.

The industrial action is expected to disrupt teaching, examinations, research and other services in public universities and constituent colleges across the country.

The unions have maintained that they are willing to engage in negotiations but want their outstanding demands addressed as part of the process of concluding the 2025-2029 CBA.

The dispute now places pressure on university councils, the government and the unions to return to negotiations and resolve the outstanding issues affecting thousands of university employees and students.

World.title: Ethiopia: Who Gets to Author Ethiopia's Political Order? Why the Crisis Is About More Than Identity Politics
World.content:
analysis

Addis Abeba — A familiar explanation of Ethiopia's recurring crises starts with identity: politics organized around nationality can harden boundaries, reward exclusionary mobilization, and expose minorities, migrants, mixed communities, and dissenters to exclusion when democratic protections are weak. International Crisis Group and other scholars have long raised these concerns.

But that explanation begins too late and risks reversing causality. For many historically subordinated peoples, collective mobilization grew from conquest-based incorporation, land confiscation, cultural and linguistic exclusion, displacement of Indigenous institutions, and rule from above. Collective national claims are therefore not the original disturbance in an otherwise neutral state; they are responses to an older political order whose terms were never jointly authored.

The thesis here is that Ethiopia's crisis is better understood as an unresolved foundational bargain: the basic settlement that determines membership, territory, land and resources, authority, and protection. Political authorship asks whether peoples and citizens merely live under rules made elsewhere or have meaningful power to shape, contest, and revise the political order. The distinction is between being governed as a population and participating as a co-author of the polity.

This framing also puts the state inside the analysis. State institutions have helped organize political categories, privilege some histories and languages, allocate land, define territory, and determine which claims counted as national. The disagreement is therefore not only over identity but also over how the state was made and whose authority, history, and institutions were built into it.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

This is an interpretive historical argument based on scholarship, Oromo historiography, constitutional texts, human-rights documentation, and institutional reports rather than new field data. It does not claim that history mechanically causes present conflict: leaders, parties, movements, security institutions, regional authorities, local actors, media, and diaspora groups make contingent choices. The standpoint is Oromo-centered but not Oromo-exclusive. Nor does the framework romanticize any actor: all political projects remain accountable for civilian protection and basic rights. Here, "the center" means historically dominant institutions, narratives, and governing coalitions, not northern Ethiopians as a population or everyone who values Ethiopian unity.

Historical bargain that was never fully settled

Ethiopia's state formation is deeply contested. State-centered narratives often describe late nineteenth-century expansion as national unification; Oromo-centered and other critical histories describe much of the same process as conquest and incorporation into an imperial order. These rival accounts matter because they produce different answers about who built the state, who was incorporated into it, and on what terms.

Ethiopia's crisis is an unfinished argument about political membership." Discover moreBusiness news analysisRead Travel GuidesBook Local ToursPoliticsBreaking news alertsInternational relations analysiscourtDaily news updates

For many Oromo and other peoples incorporated from the south and east, the problem was not simply unequal citizenship. They were incorporated as subjects of administration rather than as equal citizens and co-authors. Expansion reordered landholding, labor, tribute, taxation, and political authority; studies of Ethiopia's frontiers connect territorial expansion to extraction and administrative hierarchy. Oromo-centered scholarship likewise treats incorporation as a political-economic rupture that displaced locally grounded authority and made land a continuing site of contestation.

Political incorporation also displaced Indigenous institutions. Asmarom Legesse documents Gadaa as an internally generated political order with deliberative assemblies, rotating leadership, checks on power, and public accountability. Its marginalization was therefore a loss of recognized political authority, not merely cultural loss. This condition--incorporation without equal standing as a constituent author--is what I mean by subjecthood. It echoes Mahmood Mamdani's citizen/subject distinction: formal inclusion in a state can coexist with administrative rule rather than equal political rights.

Oromo political thought adds a normative layer. Safuu names the foundational order, Seera Waaqaa, to which Gadaa, as human law, Seera Namaa, is answerable. Cubbuu marks rupture through domination, dispossession, exclusion, or other violations of legitimate relationship; Nagaa names the order toward which repair is directed. Displacing Gadaa therefore displaced not merely an institution but an internally grounded conception of legitimate authority.

Land and language made this hierarchy material. Land links livelihood, identity, development, and political authority; official language shapes access to schools, courts, public employment, administration, and public memory. When a people's land, language, institutions, and history are subordinated, citizenship may be formally universal while remaining politically hierarchical. That is asymmetric political authorship: some groups helped define the state's institutions, official language, national narrative, and claims to legitimacy, while others were governed largely through institutions they did not author.

The 1974 revolution abolished the monarchy, nationalized land, and proclaimed equality, but the Derg remained centralized and militarized. It acknowledged the nationalities question without creating a democratic process through which constituent peoples could negotiate political association, while wars, forced recruitment, displacement, famine governance, and militarized administration deepened distrust. Equality declared from the center could not substitute for meaningful authority over land, language, and local governance.

Why nation-based federalism emerged

Seen against that history, the post-1991 federal system looks different. For many Oromo, Somali, Sidama, Wolaita, Anuak, and other nations, nationalities, and peoples, centralized statehood had meant land loss, language suppression, displacement of Indigenous institutions, weak local authority, or coercive administration. Collective claims were not invented by federalism; they were produced by the earlier denial of collective political existence. Nation-based federalism promised recognition as constituent peoples, authority over territory, self-government, language and cultural protection, and safeguards against renewed assimilation. The 1995 Constitution made those commitments explicit.

The system produced real gains in local-language administration, education, formal recognition, and regional status. It can also reproduce domination where minorities, migrants, mixed communities, or dissenters lack enforceable protections. David Turton and Jon Abbink have identified both sides of the problem: federal recognition can harden exclusion when democracy is weak, while centralized alternatives are not historically neutral. Those risks argue for deeper rights protections, not abolition of collective recognition. Nation-based federalism recognized a real problem, but it did not settle it.

Recognition without dependable power

The post-1991 order developed a central contradiction: peoples were recognized as constitutional subjects while the dominant-party system often limited their capacity to act as political subjects. This is promissory recognition: rights are named, but institutions needed to make them dependable remain weak. Courts, electoral bodies, local administrations, and security institutions often lacked independence, while land administration, infrastructure, revenue flows, credit, investment, and development corridors could be shaped through central ministries, ruling-party networks, and national strategies. Regional states could thus possess constitutional status without enough fiscal and institutional leverage to convert it into material authority.

The post-2018 period makes the distinction between representation and authorship especially clear. The rise of an Oromo prime minister was historically significant, but representation at the federal apex is not political authorship for Oromia as a constituent polity. Article 49(5) recognizes Oromia's special interest in Finfinnee/Addis Ababa, yet the implementing framework that would make that right operative remains deferred; constitutional commentary has described this as recognition without exercise. A right can be named while the power relationship that made it necessary remains intact.

The distinction is between being governed as a population and participating as a co-author of the polity."

The transition from the EPRDF to the Prosperity Party matters for the same reason. The EPRDF was authoritarian and party-managed but formally retained a coalition organized through regional ruling parties. The Prosperity Party absorbed most member and allied parties into a single national ruling party, narrowing already limited arenas in which regional parties could bargain upward as representatives of constituent units.

Oromo politics is not unified: it includes ruling-party actors, opposition organizations, armed actors, local communities, civic networks, and a large diaspora. That plurality does not negate political authorship; it makes protected institutional channels more important. When disputes are managed mainly through emergency, command-post, or military structures, claims over land, representation, and authority are converted into security problems, and residents encounter the state more as an apparatus of containment than a forum for constitutional authorship.

Why Oromia is central to the bargain

Oromia is not simply one regional example. It is Ethiopia's largest regional state; Finfinnee/Addis Ababa is situated within it; it contains major agricultural and urbanizing zones; and it has been central to state formation and mass protest. Oromia is therefore a central site where the legitimacy of the Ethiopian state is continually produced, contested, and tested. Oromo-centered scholarship shows why: Oromo claims concern not peripheral cultural accommodation after the state was formed, but the terms on which a major constituent people was incorporated and the authority it holds within the state today.

The political vocabulary of Oromo claims reinforces this point. Scholarship on Oromummaa links Oromo collective identity to shared historical experience, Afaan Oromo, and struggles against domination. Oromo nationalism is therefore not reducible to reactive identity mobilization; it carries a claim that political authority should be accountable to a people whose institutions, histories, and political standing were subordinated. Likewise, the vocabulary of conquest, colonialism, and imperial domination identifies a real analytical tension: a state celebrated for anti-colonial sovereignty can still contain hierarchies of internal incorporation.

The Finfinnee/Addis Ababa question condenses the wider problem. The city is a diverse federal capital and diplomatic hub, but it is also situated within Oromia and embedded in Oromo land and historical memory. Getahun Benti framed the dilemma as a "nation without a city." The dispute concerns not a self-contained city versus communities outside it, but a capital located within Oromia, Oromia's constitutionally recognized special interest, broader Oromo territorial claims, and authority over metropolitan expansion, land conversion, compensation, cultural recognition, revenue, and representation.

Expansion also raises distributive questions: who loses land, who is compensated, who captures the value created after conversion to urban use, and whose historical presence is recognized. Debelo and Soboka place the city's foundation and horizontal expansion within a longer frontier-making process that displaced Oromo farmers as part of state-building; Regassa and Emmenegger show how monuments, names, and the built environment materialize competing claims about national history and who authored the state. Land, planning, memory, and political authority are intertwined.

The 2014-2016 Oromo protests showed how land, representation, youth precarity, and security could converge. Mobilization around the Addis Ababa/Oromia expansion controversy reflected fears that development centered on the capital would reproduce older patterns of land alienation and political exclusion. Human Rights Watch documented killings, mass arrests, and other serious abuses. Qeerroo networks helped turn localized grievances into a broader challenge to the political order. History did not mechanically produce the protests: activists mobilized, and officials made choices. But blocked futures through unemployment, uneven development, land scarcity, urban expansion, and dispossession gave those choices their structural setting, while securitization helped turn grievance into a wider crisis of legitimacy.

The analytic value of Oromia therefore extends beyond Oromia. The center-periphery question is also epistemic: whose history counts as national history, whose political vocabulary is legitimate, and whose insecurity is treated as a national problem rather than a local disturbance. What appears as fragmentation from the center may appear as unfinished emancipation from the periphery. Oromia is thus one of the principal sites through which the legitimacy of the Ethiopian state itself can be examined.

Oromia is central, but the bargain reaches beyond it

The same problem appears elsewhere. In the Somali region, Human Rights Watch documented counterinsurgency abuses, which it characterized as war crimes and crimes against humanity, and later documented torture in Jail Ogaden. In Gambella, it documented serious abuses against Anuak communities, including violations it assessed as crimes against humanity, and later forced displacement through villagization. These cases connect citizenship to territorial control, security, land, and development.

Western Oromia and Benishangul-Gumuz show how unclear borders, overlapping jurisdiction, weak accountability, arms flows, militia organization, and elite manipulation can intensify intergroup conflict. The Sidama referendum, by contrast, shows that demands for self-rule can be processed through formal institutions. The broader lesson is not that identity is irrelevant, but that it becomes more likely to fuel conflict when institutions cannot credibly adjudicate land, representation, security, and local authority.

The current moment: Test of the bargain

These questions remain visible in 2026. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2026, covering events of 2025, describes continuing armed hostilities in parts of Oromia and Amhara and shrinking space for independent media and civil society. IOM's Ethiopia Crisis Response Plan 2026 reports 3.3 million internally displaced people as of May 2024, with conflict the primary driver. For displaced communities, constitutional debates concern return, compensation, land restitution, minority protection, and credible remedies; fear of permanent land loss can make political compromise harder.

Political association cannot be treated as permanently settled by conquest, inherited borders, ruling-party dominance, or military power."

The 2026 National Dialogue likewise placed state structure, self-determination, federal relations, boundaries, language, rule of law, peacebuilding, and reconciliation on the agenda. Its relevance to the foundational bargain depends less on declarations than on whether recommendations become enforceable rights, institutions, and credible implementation mechanisms.

What the policy problem looks like in practice

If the problem is diagnosed as identity alone, responses tend toward stronger central authority, a common national identity, or removal of collective recognition. If it is an unresolved bargain over authorship, the policy task is institutional. The relevant framework is a dual rights architecture: meaningful collective self-rule and self-determination joined to enforceable individual and minority rights. Collective rights respond to the historical subordination of peoples and their territories, languages, institutions, and political authority; individual rights belong to every person and protect all citizens equally, including minorities, migrants, mixed communities, dissenters, and political opponents within every self-governing region.

Meaningful collective self-rule. Regional authority must involve more than administration: constituent peoples need meaningful authority over territory, language, culture, land, development priorities, self-government, and self-determination.

Enforceable individual and minority rights. Collective self-rule cannot justify exclusion. Equal citizenship, mobility, due process, services, civic freedoms, and political participation need enforceable protection, with courts or constitutional-review bodies able to provide remedies.

Close 

Fair land and metropolitan governance. Expropriation, compensation, development planning, and metropolitan expansion require transparency, affected-community participation, and independent review. In Finfinnee/Addis Ababa, a durable arrangement must protect residents' rights while addressing Oromo land claims, jurisdiction, displacement, revenue sharing, cultural recognition, and representation.

Accountable security institutions. Civilian oversight, transparent deployment rules, investigation of abuses, protection for witnesses and journalists, and credible remedies are essential when political disputes are otherwise managed through military or emergency structures.

Fiscal and development authority. Formal autonomy is hollow without fiscal leverage to protect land, negotiate development priorities, and shape major investments. Growth should be judged by how decision-making, benefits, burdens, and remedies are distributed.

Open political competition. Parties, journalists, civic organizations, and local leaders need protected channels for peaceful organization. A foundational bargain cannot be negotiated by ruling elites and armed actors alone; credible elections, civic space, and inclusive dialogue are part of meaningful consent.

For international partners, short-term stability and humanitarian relief cannot substitute for institutions that make rights, accountability, and negotiated commitments locally enforceable.

Constitutional label is not the first question

None of this predetermines one constitutional outcome. A re-legitimated multinational federation remains possible; a confederal or looser association may better reduce coercive center-periphery control where mistrust remains deep; and negotiated separation should not be treated as inherently illegitimate. Where association can be maintained only through recurring coercion or war, negotiated separation may be less destructive than forced unity. The governing test is consent together with protection of collective political authorship and individual rights.

From coercive cohesion to political consent

The central problem is not that marginalized peoples assert collective rights. Ethiopian state-building repeatedly incorporated conquered peoples as subjects of administration rather than equal citizens and co-authors. Imperial incorporation created durable disputes over land, language, authority, and belonging; the Derg retained centralized and militarized rule; and the post-1991 federation recognized multinational rights while party-state control and securitized governance often weakened their exercise.

Oromo-centered analysis is therefore a corrective lens on the Ethiopian state itself. Oromia exposes the political economy of incorporation, the capital question, the link between land and political authorship, the limits of recognition without effective authority, and the consequences of securitizing constitutional demands. Because Oromia is central to state formation, the capital-city relationship, agricultural and urban transformation, and mass mobilization, Oromo political authorship is not peripheral to Ethiopia's future.

Political authorship does not promise every community everything it demands. It means political association cannot be treated as permanently settled by conquest, inherited borders, ruling-party dominance, or military power. Ethiopia's crisis is an unfinished argument about political membership. A durable future depends less on constitutional labels than on whether peoples and individuals can participate meaningfully in authoring the institutions under which they live. AS

Editor's Note: Dr. Hambisa Belina is an associate professor of accounting at Morgan State University. His research spans auditing, internal controls, and corporate transparency, as well as interdisciplinary scholarship on Indigenous Oromo institutions and their intersections with political economy, peace, development, urban studies, and territorial studies. Hambisa can be reached at hambisa7@gmail.com

World.title: Nigeria: Nigerians Don't Deserve This Hardship, Atiku Tells Tinubu
World.content:
Former Vice President and Presidential Candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, says the Tinubu administration has failed one of government's most basic duties: protecting ordinary Nigerians from crushing economic hardship.

In a statement by Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Atiku said President Tinubu's Independence Day address revealed how far his government has drifted from the people's daily reality.

The President spoke of prosperity while defending policies that have made fuel and basic necessities increasingly unaffordable, and dismissed subsidies as "addictive."

Atiku also challenged his claim that salaries and pensions have been paid "on time and in full," as federal workers report delays and pensioners continue to protest.



He said Germany had cut gasoline and diesel taxes by €0.17 per litre from October through December, at an estimated cost of €2.5 billion and prices at the pump have begun to fall.

"When petrol becomes more expensive, transport becomes more expensive. When transport costs rise, food and other essentials cost more. The hardship follows Nigerians from the filling station to the market and into their homes.

"Germany understands that when fuel prices put families under pressure, government must act. Nigerians deserve the same compassion and urgency.

"Our plan is to restore targeted, budgeted support for fuel refined in Nigeria, with strict auditing and a guarantee that the benefit lowers pump prices. Support will follow the barrel refined here, creating jobs here and easing costs for Nigerians. It will be funded by cutting waste, protected against diversion and price manipulation, and will not apply to imported fuel.

"To every Nigerian forced to choose between feeding a family, paying for transport or meeting another basic need, I am deeply sorry. You did not deserve this hardship. Tinubu made life unbearably expensive and called your suffering the price of reform. I will make life affordable again."

Atiku said lower fuel costs can mean a cheaper bus ride, more affordable goods at the market and more money left in a family's pocket.

"Nigeria's wealth should ease the burden on its people."

World.title: How an Uzbek truck driver’s fatal crash exposed troubling fraud trend in Middle America: ‘Chameleon carriers’
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

CINCINNATI, OH - A young man killed by an Uzbek truck driver earlier this year in Ohio, along with several instances of illegal immigrant truck drivers involved in fatal crashes, has sparked a larger conversation in southwest Ohio about fraud, crime, immigration and how gaps in trucking industry oversight are putting Americans at risk.

Tobias "Toby" Forsythe, a 21-year-old goalkeeper from Ohio on the University of Massachusetts Lowell men’s soccer team, was killed July 5 when authorities say a semi-truck driven by 42-year-old Uzbek national Bekhzod Asrarov, who entered the country under the Biden administration's diversity visa lottery program, rear-ended Forsythe’s Honda Accord on Interstate 71 in Madison County, Ohio.

It was later determined, according to court documents, that Asrarov could not speak or understand English well enough to communicate with responding state troopers without the use of Google Translate, despite holding an Ohio commercial driver’s license, and that he allegedly removed a dashboard camera from his truck after the fatal crash in an effort to conceal or destroy evidence.

"We cannot let truckers like Asrarov, who can’t read our road signs or speak to law enforcement, drive 80,000-pound rigs on America’s highways," Transportation Secretary Sean posted on X after the crash.

IMMIGRANT TRUCK DRIVER ADMITTED TO US UNDER BIDEN ALLEGEDLY KILLS UMASS SOCCER STAR, SPOKE NO ENGLISH

In southwest Ohio, a researcher known as Nodawolf has been sounding the alarm to his growing follower count about a vast network of trucking companies, many of them owned or operated by Uzbek nationals, that have popped up in communities like Loveland, Middletown, and Maineville, where Asrarov resides, in recent years and could be contributing to the unsafe practices that took the life of Forsythe, and many others across the country.

Nodawolf, who Fox News Digital granted anonymity due to the death threats he’s received from his online reporting, said his research has focused on what he describes as an interconnected network of Uzbek-linked trucking companies in southwest Ohio, including companies that have donated money toward construction of a local Islamic center, according to the center's own website.

"All of them have English violations and have manipulated ELDs," Nodawolf said, referring to electronic logging devices that track a trucker’s driving hours and are intended to enforce federal limits on how long drivers can stay behind the wheel.

The Islamic Center, located in Maineville, told Fox News Digital that a "charitable contribution or participation in a community fundraising activity, by itself, should not be interpreted as evidence of an ownership, employment, contractual, commercial, or other business relationship with the Islamic Center or its leadership."

A Fox News Digital review identified hundreds of trucking companies and other trucking entities registered in Maineville and surrounding southwest Ohio communities, including dozens that were registered in recent years. A separate review of companies identified as connected to the local Uzbek community found serious FMCSA safety violations, including drivers cited for failing English-proficiency requirements and other federal trucking violations.

TRUMP ADMIN TRUCKING CRACKDOWN LANDS 51 IMMIGRATION DETENTIONS, 36 ENGLISH LANGUAGE PROFICIENCY VIOLATIONS

"This really concerns me, you know, as a father," Nodawolf told Fox News Digital. "I mean, it's clearly obvious that they either don't understand our laws, they don't care about our laws, or they know our laws and they're taking advantage of it."

Nodawolf has reported on Uzbek trucking networks communicating on the social media platform Telegram. One of those Telegram channels, named "UzbegimAmerica," has routinely mentioned the Uzbek community in Maineville. Court documents show the owner of that channel, Farkhod Faiziev, is a suspected illegal immigrant from Uzbekistan.

The Trump administration has made significant progress on the issue of removing foreign truck drivers who pose a danger being removed from the road – including a recent multi-agency operation in Arizona’s Yuma Sector, which led to the arrest of 95 illegal alien truck drivers earlier this month – striking at the heart of human and drug smuggling operations at the U.S. southern border.

The Departments of Homeland Security, Transportation and Justice recently announced a coordinated crackdown on trucking and CDL fraud targeting fraudulent licensing, unauthorized employment, identity-document fraud, shell companies and other criminal activity. The effort includes inspections at more than 200 driving schools across 23 states, investigations based on more than 1,000 leads, enforcement operations targeting illegal immigrants with commercial licenses and a new multi-state DOJ task force focused on trucking-related fraud and roadway safety.

A trucking-industry veteran with decades of experience who spoke to Fox News Digital under the condition of anonymity for his safety described a developing fraud scheme popular with immigrant communities known as "chameleon carriers", a network of trucking companies that appear separate on paper but, he said, share the same drivers, trucks and operations. The arrangement starts when operators establish one company that is "quote-unquote legitimate," he said, then create additional carriers and authorities while using the same underlying assets across them.

ILLEGAL TRUCKER CASES FUEL GOP PUSH TO CRACK DOWN ON CDL MILLS AS DEMS LARGELY SILENT

The point, the industry expert said, is to "spread out their safety liability across multiple companies." Rather than allowing inspections and violations to pile up under one carrier, he said, the operation can distribute them among multiple motor-carrier authorities.

"If they have 10 inspections and 10 violations across 10 different companies, that doesn’t hurt the safety rating as much," he said. "But if it was one company that had 10 inspections and 10 violations, that one company is going to get hammered."

The separate companies can also serve as a contingency plan, he said. If one carrier is shut down, loses insurance or becomes too damaged by safety problems, "they’re able to immediately move all of the equipment and drivers and everything under one of the different companies," the industry veteran said. "Their operation never stops. There’s no way to shut them down."

He further alleged the structure can facilitate cargo theft, with a company disappearing after obtaining a high-value shipment while the broader network continues operating through its remaining entities. "They lost one of their shell companies, basically, but they just got $5 million in iPads," he said.

The industry expert said the model can be particularly dangerous, in his view, because it allows companies to keep operating despite safety problems while allegedly using drivers who may not be legally authorized to work in the United States. He said operators can make that harder to detect by classifying drivers as independent contractors rather than employees, potentially avoiding the ordinary employee I-9 verification process.

"If you’re using a bunch of people from a third-world country that just showed up in the United States as drivers, whether they’re here legally or not, how well do you think they’re going to maintain their equipment and be able to follow the laws?" he said.

Seven of the trucking schools targeted by the Department of Transportation last month are located in Ohio, DOT told Fox News last month.

A Notice of Proposed Removal was recently issued by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration for Turan CDL School, a Middletown-based company that has advertised CDL training to Uzbek speakers, including s suggesting students could obtain a CDL without first learning English, as well as Google reviews from customers claiming they earned their licenses in as little as one week.

ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’

"There's 'what do the rules say' and then 'what's happening on the ground," Andrew Poliakoff, vice president of the Commercial Vehicle Training Association, told Fox 28 Columbus shortly after the crash that killed Forsythe. "We're seeing now is that there are a lot of people committing fraud, and engaging in a variety of bad actions issuing commercial driver's licenses."

Victor Louis, whose Cincinnati based company Load Secure verifies the identities of drivers entering its network, told Fox News Digital that he has seen local s promising prospective truckers a CDL in as little as a week immediately raise red flags.

"Trucking is such an inherently dangerous activity. Essentially, you're driving a 40-ton missile down the road," Louis said. "To think that someone is going to be certified to do that within a week, that may or may not speak English, like that doesn't make any sense."

Louis said his company is also seeing a significant number of non-domiciled drivers, foreign drivers who hold commercial licenses issued by a U.S. state despite not having their permanent residence in that state. He said roughly 15% to 20% of drivers entering Load Secure's network fall into that category and estimated the figure could be around 20% among long-haul truckers nationwide.

"Whether they're here legally or not, I don't know, but they are essentially foreign nationals," Louis said. He argued that long-haul trucking can be particularly attractive to migrants because drivers can spend weeks at a time living on the road rather than maintaining a permanent home near their workplace.

Louis said cargo theft and the security of the broader supply chain are among his biggest concerns.

"What we see with that market of non-domiciled drivers is a high propensity of cargo theft, an extremely high propensity," he said. "It’s wreaking havoc on our supply chain. Number one, it's extremely dangerous and number two, it is very unsecure. We don't know if things are being tampered with. This exposes our supply chains."

The Ohio Bureau of Motor Vehicles told Fox News Digital that it is reviewing the state’s nondomiciled commercial driver’s license holders in coordination with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. Of the roughly 5,000 nondomiciled credentials originally issued, about 3,500 remain active, meaning approximately 1,500 are no longer active as the review continues.

On Sept. 16, Fox News reported that ICE arrested two Uzbek illegal alien truck drivers in New Jersey as part of nationwide crackdown on fraudulent CDLs.

"We are starting to go into those thousand leads of fraud, waste and abuse into our trucking industry," Mullin said in a press conference last month. "We're going to prioritize going after employees that are suspected of accepting payments to help illegals bypass driver's license and CDL requirements."

In Brown County, Ohio, on Sept. 2, an Indian national with a CDL out of California crashed his semi-truck head-on into the car of 50-year-old Brenda Watson, who died at the scene. The driver, Manjit Singh , was later determined to be an illegal immigrant and ICE announced in a press release that a detainer was placed along with a charge of aggravated vehicular homicide.

"One state’s regulatory failure becomes every state’s highway threat," Ohio attorney Mehek Cooke told News Digital. "Republican governors cannot assume their states were insulated from Biden’s border crisis simply because they opposed his policies."

Fox News Digital reached out to Ohio Governor Mike DeWine's office for comment.

Last month, ICE launched a tip-line for reporting fraudulent CDL licenses.

"Too many American lives have been lost or permanently changed because illegal aliens who have no business being on our roads have been granted CDLs," Mullin said in a press release. "ICE and our federal partners, including the Department of Transportation, will be cracking down on CDL fraud so that not one more American life is lost to a reckless illegal alien behind the wheel of a semi-truck."

World.title: California K-9 Otis helps police seize 440 pounds of cocaine during Alhambra traffic stop
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A California traffic stop took a massive turn when a police K-9 sniffed out approximately 200 kilos, or roughly 440 pounds, of cocaine allegedly packed inside an SUV filled with cardboard boxes, authorities said.

The Alhambra Police Department said the incident began after officers conducted a traffic stop along Valley Boulevard near the 710 Freeway.

Although authorities did not say what prompted the initial stop, they noticed the driver appeared to have an unusual amount of cargo in his vehicle.

"The driver was transporting more cardboard boxes than Amazon on Prime Day," police said in a social media post.

BORDER AGENTS UNCOVER $20M COCAINE STASH HIDDEN BENEATH TRUCK FLOORBOARDS IN MASSIVE BUST

That's when the driver began offering an explanation for the boxes, according to police.

"At first, he said he was heading home to Huntington Park from his cousin’s house and that the boxes were not his," police said in the post.

But that wasn't the man's only story.

"Later came version 2.0 of his lore," police continued, "and he said he was taking diesel parts to a shop that his friend owned."

Up stepped K-9 Otis and his handler to help investigate.

BORDER AGENTS UNCOVER $3.7M IN COCAINE MASQUERADING AS A CUCUMBER DELIVERY

Police said Otis alerted officers to the vehicle, prompting them to search the SUV.

"Thanks to Otis’ top-tier nose, he alerted to the vehicle, and officers discovered the SUV was packed with approximately 200 kilos of cocaine," police said.

The driver, identified as Julio Rangel of Huntington Park, was arrested and booked into the Alhambra Police Department jail, according to police.

Following the drug bust, Otis was hailed as the hero of the operation.

HEROIC FLORIDA K-9 RETURNS TO SHERIFF'S OFFICE DAYS AFTER BEING SHOT PROTECTING 3 DEPUTIES, LOSING LEG

"A round of a-paws for our good boy, K9 Otis," police said.

Users on social media also praised the K-9's work, with many arguing that Otis had earned a promotion — and was perhaps even on track to become police chief one day.

"Give that dog a bone!" another user exclaimed.

One user joked about Otis' ability to sniff out criminals.

"No One escapes from the Long Paw of …. The DOG"
