World.title: Opinion: A Hawk is not the same as a Hawkeye
World.content:
Opinion: A Hawk is not the same as a Hawkeye

toggle caption i Allison Robbert/AP

Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri may not have been exactly hawk-eyed at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing this week when he asked former special counsel Jack Smith if he had gone to an Atlanta Hawks basketball game in February 2024. Schmitt implied that Smith met up in Atlanta with the district attorney who was investigating election fraud charges against then-former President Trump.

Smith said, "I definitely did not go to a Hawks game, I am sure of that," and Sen. Schmitt replied, "I think you've already perjured yourself." Then he called him a "villain" and more names I'd rather not repeat at breakfast time on a Saturday morning.

Sponsor Message

Further questioning from Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota established that Smith had been to a basketball game that night, but not in Atlanta. He was in College Park, Md., to watch the University of Maryland Terps take on Caitlin Clark and the University of Iowa.

The Iowa Hawkeyes. Not the Atlanta Hawks.

Sen. Klobuchar, a Democrat, suggested to Sen. Schmitt, a Republican, "That might be the confusion over the names of the team, but perhaps you should have looked at it more carefully. … I think people should have their facts straight before they accuse people … ."

The names of sports teams can be confounding. If I invite you to a Panthers game would you expect to meet me for a kickoff in North Carolina or a puck drop in Florida?

But was Sen. Schmitt's misstatement an innocent gaffe to be laughed off, like then-Vice President Dan Quayle inadvertently giving the wrong spelling for "potato" to a New Jersey sixth grader, or was it a public effort to discredit Smith with information that would not be hard to fact check?

"We had information, of course, about him being at a basketball game," Schmitt told KTVI-TV in St. Louis the next day. "My job is to ask the questions, and his job is to answer the questions. …

Sponsor Message

"But I guess the one thing that Jack Smith and I can agree on is that we're a fan of college sports and college basketball." This is as close as the senator came to saying he'd made a mistake.

For the record: the Iowa Hawkeyes won that night, 93 to 85. Caitlin Clark scored 38 points. And I'll bet everyone who watched remembers exactly where they were that night.

World.title: Economist Betsey Stevenson breaks down the gender gap in recent hiring reports
World.content:
Economist Betsey Stevenson breaks down the gender gap in recent hiring reports

The U.S. economy added fewer jobs than expected last month and unemployment ticked up to 4.2%. NPR's Scott Simon talks to Betsey Stevenson, an economist at the University of Michigan.

Transcript

SCOTT SIMON, HOST:

The U.S. Labor Department reports that the economy added fewer new jobs last month than expected, and unemployment rose a bit. It's now at 4.2%. We're joined now by Betsey Stevenson, a professor of economics and public policy at the University of Michigan. She was, of course, a member of President Obama's Council of Economic Advisers. Thanks so much for being with us.

BETSEY STEVENSON: Oh, it's great talking with you this morning.

SIMON: Twenty-nine thousand new jobs. What do you see in these latest numbers?

STEVENSON: Well, what I see is a continuation of a low-fire, low-hire labor market. And that is a labor market where if you have a job, you're doing OK. You can hang on to it, but it's hard to get a new job. And that hurts not only the people who need to enter the labor market or have lost their job, but it actually also hurts the people who are employed because most wage gains - big wage gains - come from changing jobs. So that was the other thing we saw in this report, is that, on average, people's wages are not keeping up with inflation.

SIMON: In recent months, a majority of the new jobs have gone to women, though in this report, it was more equal than previous months. What's going on?

STEVENSON: Well, you and I have talked about this before. So I looked at this longer trend because you're right. This month, it was more even. Fourteen thousand of the 29,000 jobs went to women. But if we actually look since July, a hundred percent of the jobs have gone to women, and we now see that women hold 50.1% of the jobs. And this is almost completely explained by the fact that almost all the hiring in our labor market is being driven by healthcare. That is a area where we still need people, and women are the majority of the workers in that industry, and it is growing. That is the engine of job growth, which is very confusing for some people because AI is the engine of GDP growth, but it has not been an engine for job growth.

SIMON: Unemployment among Black workers rose sharply - full percentage point. That is now more than double the rate for white workers. What do you see in that?

STEVENSON: Well, what I see is a series of patterns that reflect a labor market that we're not in a recession, but I wouldn't call this a strong labor market. And what happens in a weak labor market is all sorts of workers who are used to being able to churn and change jobs frequently find themselves getting left out. And when we break down the unemployment rate to groups like Black workers, we do see a lot more volatility. So when you see a big jump in a month - I always want to have a little bit of caution. That's why you're hearing some caution in my voice. But I think it's symbolic of a labor market that matches the K-shaped economy.

People who are doing well are still doing well. And any kind of worker who's struggling to get their foot in the door, keep their foot in the door, get a promotion to the next thing - those are the people who are really struggling right now. And I think that's why we're seeing this real increasing anger over the labor market, because there's no openings and breaks for people to get. I mean, obviously, there's still job openings, but what we've seen is a decline in the availability of opportunities, which has led fewer people to quit jobs. If you're afraid to quit your job, Scott, because you think you'll never find another one, then you can't create another opening for someone else.

SIMON: And that has the effect of depressing wages, which doesn't keep up with inflation.

STEVENSON: Exactly. And it's just a vicious cycle that leaves everybody sort of worse off. We're all much better off in the labor market if we can all chase our dreams, find those new opportunities. The opportunity we're leaving for something else is someone else's opportunity to get ahead.

SIMON: What other data are you looking for between now and Election Day?

STEVENSON: Well, I'm looking at consumer confidence because there's always this, you know, disconnect. People say that they are really unhappy about the economy, but we did see some job growth in leisure and hospitality and people going out to restaurants. So the question is, are they showing behavior that's indicative of being frightened? Because that will start to slow the economy down. But I do think it's time for every policymaker to have jobs and affordability front of mind, because that's certainly the front of mind of most Americans.

SIMON: Betsey Stevenson, economist and professor at the University of Michigan. Thank you so much for being with us again.

STEVENSON: I loved talking with you.

World.title: Just short of its 200th birthday, a landmark natural history museum shuts down
World.content:
Just short of its 200th birthday, a landmark natural history museum shuts down

toggle caption i Andrew Stelzer for NPR

PHILADELPHIA — Every weekend for the past month, the sidewalk in front of the Natural Academy of Sciences has simultaneously felt like a festival, a funeral, and a science fair.

On the Museum's final Friday, there was a line of attendees waiting to get in; Activists circulating petitions and flyers to "Save the Academy"; and a museum educator showed off a giant salamander skull and a rare coat of pangolin scales.

For Philly area kids, visiting this place has been a rite of passage for generations. So when word dropped on September 1st that the nearly 200-year-old museum was closing at the end of the month, thousands of families began a wistful pilgrimage, to make one final visit.

Sponsor Message

"This is a very special place, for my family and also me growing up," said Alexandria McCormick, who was visiting with her husband and six kids. She said when she was a child, her family used to come multiple times a year, awakening her love of natural history.

"It makes me really sad to think that my children might not also grow up having these experiences and being inspired to love nature this way." she said.

Founded in 1812, and opened to the public in 1828, the Academy of Natural Sciences was the first place in the world to display a dinosaur skeleton, back in 1868. There's also mammal dioramas, live animals, and other rotating exhibits.

Its collection of scientific specimens is widely recognized as one of the most important in the world. And its sudden demise comes amidst a continuing decline in funding for cultural and scientific institutions.

"This is the oldest natural history museum in the Americas," says Isa Betancourt , who worked in the Academy's entomology department for 10 years, from 2011 to 2021.

Betancourt now lives in Arizona, but hopped on a plane and came back to Philly to help organize the " Save the Academy " campaign, which included a flurry of rallies, marches, and an online petition to keep the museum open that has over 114,000 signatures.

Sponsor Message

"If this museum can slip away like that, what's stopping other museums from going the same way? We can't let this be a precedent." she added.

toggle caption i Andrew Stelzer for NPR

A sudden closure

Drexel University, which took over financial responsibility for the Academy in 2011, explained on its website that post-pandemic, costs have risen and attendance declined. In its last few weeks, however, museum attendance skyrocketed and revenue was more than 20 times higher than last September.

"Maybe if they had announced this last year, they could have gotten the crowds they have now," said Zoe Abrams, who was visiting with her husband and two children. "This is busier than Grand Central. Could have saved things."

Some people working to save it criticized Drexel for not participating in any efforts to stem the museums' closure, or providing details about how much it would cost to keep it open.

"When they announced the one month notice it was a surprise for everybody," said Betancourt. "It's like the leadership didn't even try to keep it open, and that's why there's a lot of frustration around what's happening. It's just not right." she added.

In response to a request for comment, Drexel said in a statement that it "remains deeply committed to protecting the Academy of Natural Sciences' extraordinary legacy."

Less than a week before the September 30th closing date, the William Penn Foundation offered a year's worth of bridge funding; to buy time to explore more permanent solutions. Drexel said it is exploring the possibility of working with the foundation, but would need a plan for long-term sustainability before considering re-opening the museum.

Hard times for scientific institutions

The Academy houses a massive, irreplaceable library of over 19 million specimens. It includes Thomas Jefferson's fossil collection, and plant samples gathered by Lewis and Clark. It also has an archive of 73,000 holotype specimens— carefully preserved samples which scientists use as references for defining and naming species.

Sponsor Message

Drexel has said it will preserve access to that collection for students and researchers. But it's unclear what that means for the general public. And all this uncertainty comes at a moment when government support for cultural institutions has been in steep decline. "It's certainly a challenging time for the museum field." said Natanya Kashan, a spokesperson for the American Alliance of Museums. A 2025 survey of AAM's members found a third had government grants and contracts cancelled, and more than two-thirds were affected by executive orders in some way."The financial pressures are not only in federal funding, they're also in philanthropy, in corporate donations, in individual giving," she said.

The Academy tied its financial fate to Drexel's, when, in 2011, the two institutions announced an "affiliation." The Academy became a subsidiary of Drexel, but retained its own board and 501c3 organizational status. In a statement announcing the partnership the Academy's president bragged about "a rock-solid balance sheet with a $51 million endowment".

But, like many Universities, Drexel has been struggling financially, in part due to declining enrollment. In 2024, the school reported it was facing a budget shortfall.

And as attendance shrank, in 2025 the museum laid off some staff, and reduced its hours . It soon cancelled its 2026 summer camp program . Earlier this year, The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that the university and the Academy were renegotiating heir relationship ; Drexel wanted a full merger, which would grant it the building, endowment and collections.

Amid speculation that Drexel plans to sell the 150-year-old building housing the Academy, Philadelphia's city council proposed altering local zoning overlays in order to make selling the building or converting it to other uses more difficult. The council also plans to hold special public hearings , to find out how the Academy got to the point of closing, and what possible solutions might look like. The legislation calling for the hearing also gives the council subpoena power over Drexel.

Sponsor Message

"We need to know how this came to be. What were the levers that created this decision, and how do we undo that decision?" said City councilmember Dr. Nina Ahmad.

"There was no campaign in the recent past that we can find to encourage or to tell the city of Philadelphia, 'We're in danger of closing if you don't come and use our museum.' None of that."

World.title: All's fair in love and 'War' — a well-cast, classy-trashy divorce drama
World.content:
All's fair in love and 'War' — a well-cast, classy-trashy divorce drama

toggle caption i Justin Downing/Sky/HBO

Dominic West specializes in playing men who feel victimized by the consequences of their own actions. One of his signature lines as Jimmy McNulty on The Wire was, "What the f*** did I do?" The line was often delivered not in the sense of, "Oh no, what did I do?" But instead, as an indignant, "Why am I getting yelled at? What did I do?" And while West's take on then-Prince Charles in The Crown put him in a completely different setting, he retained that sense of arrogant bafflement, affronted whenever he sensed that he was being perceived as the bad guy.

Sponsor Message

In HBO's new series War, West plays Morgan Henderson — a tech mogul, not a cop or a royal. But he, too, has trouble seeing his own fingerprints on his problems, including his marriage. Morgan is married to Carla Duval (Sienna Miller), an A-list actress whose fame is starting to teeter, inevitably, as she ages. As the first episode begins, they both seem aware that the marriage is on its last legs, but no one has acted — at least not openly — quite yet. Then, at a dinner without Carla where he's receiving an award, he spies a beautiful woman in the crowd. Things progress. Someone acts.

Television The biggest divorce trial in British history is the center of HBO's new series, 'War' The biggest divorce trial in British history is the center of HBO's new series, 'War' Listen · 7:00 7:00

This is the setup for the first battle, as it were, of War, which is intended to be an anthology series about two dueling London law firms. Each season will be about a different case. The first is Morgan and Carla's parting, which one of the lawyers predicts will be the "biggest divorce trial in British legal history." Morgan is working with an old, established firm called Cathcarts — all dark-wood interiors — where he's represented by the terrifying St. John Smallwood (a delightfully wicked Pip Torrens). Carla has hired a young firm called Taylor & Byrne — all glass walls and contemporary furnishings — run by married couple Serena and Nick (Phoebe Fox and James McArdle).

Sponsor Message

In this first hour, we also meet Johnny (Archie Renaux), a young attorney who, for initially unclear reasons, has fled a firm in Manhattan to return to London, and is scrambling to find work while waiting tables and trying to hang on to a frustrated girlfriend. Johnny is a bit desperate, and around the kinds of people he meets in the course of this story, it is never good to be desperate. He naturally includes both firms in his hunt for employment, and he ends up interviewing with both. By the end of the first episode, we know that he will affect the way things progress on both sides of the case.

War was created by George Kay, who also created the Idris Elba action drama Hijack and the fleet-footed and clever Lupin, and he brings a lot of story velocity to this setting, too. Much of War is made up of elements that have always driven heightened, scandal-adjacent legal dramas: intrigue, dramatic reversals of fortune, witnesses who do or do not appear, documents lost, found and suddenly revealed. That these attorneys are also people matters only intermittently: Over on the Taylor & Byrne side, there is a bit of attention given to Serena and Nick's domestic life, but on the Cathcarts side, there's little evidence that St. John or any of the other stone-faced partners think about anything except crushing each opponent into dust and moving on to the next.

But there is, too, the story of Morgan and Carla, who once genuinely loved each other and who learn very quickly that the very last thing any of their lawyers are interested in is protecting whatever amicable relationship they have left — even for the sake of Carla's son, to whom Morgan has been an involved and loving stepfather. On the contrary, the lawyers see it as their obligation (and, they will sometimes admit, their pleasure) to engage in all-out destruction of the other side.

Sponsor Message

There's a tricky tonal balance in treating the lawyers' gasp-inducing ruthlessness as entertaining and even amusing while also allowing its consequences to be clear. At times, the effort to be sincere about the sadness of Morgan and Carla's situation doesn't sit entirely comfortably alongside the more arch, more malicious (and delicious) goings-on at the two firms, where internal competition and backstabbing can be just as dangerous as anything opposite sides can do to each other. The series has a little too much heart to be the ice-cold examination of humanity's underbelly that it sometimes feels like it's going to be.

Still, War offers an impressive cast solidly executing a well-constructed story. You might call it classy-trashy, embracing both its "what will these people do next?" high drama and moments of genuine humanity from West and Miller, both of whom are solid in it. They both, in fact, may fail at first to see what exactly they've done to land in such a miserable state, but if their lawyers teach them anything, perhaps it's to think twice about both marriage and divorce.

This piece also appeared in NPR's Pop Culture Happy Hour newsletter. 

Listen to Pop Culture Happy Hour on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

World.title: The Supreme Court faces another term jam-packed with controversy
World.content:
The Supreme Court faces another term jam-packed with controversy

toggle caption i Roberto Schmidt/AFP via Getty Images

The U.S. Supreme Court formally opens a new term on Monday, with big test cases on religion, bans on semi-automatic weapons, climate change, immigration and — waiting in the wings — election law cases.

It used to be that the first Monday in October marked the beginning of a new Supreme Court term. And that's still true, technically. But for all practical purposes, the formerly quiet summer months after the court finishes its opinions in all argued cases no longer exists.

Sponsor Message

Indeed, as Georgetown University law professor Stephen Vladeck observes, the number of emergency appeals has ballooned during the Trump administration, while at the same time, fully briefed and argued cases have dropped precipitously over the years.

"So now we have twice as many full court rulings on emergency applications as we have on the merits docket," Vladeck observes, adding, "That is a very new phenomenon."

The difference is that decisions on the emergency docket are rendered quickly, with little briefing, no oral arguments, and ultimately little or no explanation of the ruling. In contrast, a decision on the merits is typically worked on for months after full briefing and lengthy oral arguments.

Of late, the court seems to be making an effort to offer some limited explanations of its emergency docket rulings, but lower court judges, both liberal and conservative, complain that isn't enough to provide them with adequate guidance. And the Trump administration often takes what used to be the rare step of getting to the Supreme Court by leapfrogging over lower appellate courts that the administration views as hostile.

With that backdrop, here are the cases the court will be hearing in the coming weeks:

Climate change

The opening case, to be argued Monday, tests whether state and local governments can sue energy companies for allegedly deceiving the public about the damaging effects of fossil fuels.

Sponsor Message

"The theory is that the energy company defendants deceived the public for many years," says Deepak Gupta, who teaches at Harvard Law School and practices law in Washington, D.C. What the companies were telling the public for years, he says, is "the opposite of what the company's own scientists knew, and the local cost of that deception."

That said, however, most court observers see the case as an uphill battle for environmentalists.

Religion

Perhaps the biggest case of the term so far, in terms of ripple effects, involves religion, a subject on which the court's conservative super majority has dramatically changed its legal doctrine. Indeed for the better part of a century, the Supreme Court emphasized the First Amendment's separation of church and state, with the free exercise of religion playing an important — but secondary — role. Since President Trump's appointment of three new justices, however, things have changed.

"It's literally the opposite of what the law was not that long ago, and it's just a complete shift," observes Michigan State University law professor Frank Ravitch.

The court may, in fact, be on the verge of requiring taxpayers to fund religious schools that refuse to admit LGBTQ students and parents. Last term the justices deadlocked on the issue in a separate case after Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself because of a conflict. The 4-4 tie vote automatically left in place an Oklahoma Supreme Court decision that barred overtly religious charter schools from from being funded by the taxpayers. But this year the issue is back in a case from Colorado. The case centers on a state law that provides universal preschool programs that are open to all students, regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation or gender identity.

St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colo., wants the state funding guaranteed in the state's universal pre-k law. But it doesn't want to admit LGBTQ students or students with gay or trans parents. The parish maintains such admissions would violate church's right to the free exercise of religion. The state counters that funding the church school would violate the state's anti-discrimination law.

The court's conservative majority has, in multiple cases, ruled in favor of religious exemptions from generally applicable laws. Until now, however, the court has never said that religious schools are entitled to full taxpayer funding. But given the current court's views, and with Justice Barrett participating in the Colorado case, taxpayers could well end up having to fund religious schools in Colorado and elsewhere.

Bans on semi-automatic weapons

In December the court will hear a case testing whether state and local governments violate the Second Amendment right to bear arms when they ban semi-automatic weapons, like the AR-15.

Sponsor Message

Former Solicitor General Don Verrilli Jr., articulates two different ways to look at the question.

On the one hand the AR-15 "can deliver upwards of 100 bullets per minute" without any enhancements, and 500 bullets per minute with various enhancements. On the other hand, he notes that millions of Americans own AR-15s, "and it would be quite disruptive to suggest all these Americans ... would be dispossessed of their weapons."

Lawyer Erin Murphy, who has litigated lots of cases on behalf of gun owners, says the "single most important question is who gets to decide what guns you have," and he argues it makes no sense to say, "You've got this right against the government, but the government decides which arms you can get."

Immigration

The Trump administration has repeatedly taken positions in immigration cases that no other administration has adopted. Most recently, the court announced it would hear arguments and decide a case testing whether the Department of Homeland Security may deport migrants to so-called "third countries," when their countries of origin refuse to accept them. Since Trump began his second term, his administration has deported thousands of people to third world countries where they have no connections, may not speak the language, have often been jailed and allegedly subject to torture. The court has twice blocked lower court decisions that prevented the third country policy, and now the justices have said they will hear arguments about the policy in December.

In a second immigration case, the issue is the Trump administration's policy of detaining undocumented immigrants without a bond hearing, regardless of how long they have been in the U.S.

Possible cases: The 10 commandments and much more

There are many more cases waiting in the wings that the justices may take up. Among them is a case that seeks to reverse a nearly half-century-old Supreme Court precedent; it bars public schools from posting the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms. Now, however, Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana and Alabama have passed laws that conflict with the Supreme Court's 1980 ruling, and the lower courts are split on the question. That split all but guarantees the the Supreme Court will revisit the question.

Sponsor Message

Another case that could to make it to the court this term tests whether states can regulate Kalshi, the $40 billion prediction market behemoth that has sports fans betting on everything from the next pitch to the point spread or at the other end of the spectrum, betting on the outcome of Supreme Court cases.

And then there are cases that the Trump administration has slow-walked for close to two years, after quickly losing in the lower courts. Prime examples are the administration's attempt to deny medical research grants to Harvard University, and other attempts to deny security clearances to law firms, as well as seeking money damages from law firms Trump views as hostile. Earlier this year the Justice Department told a federal court in Washington that it was dropping the law firm cases. But the next day it went back to court to reverse course.

"They don't want to take up cases that they're going to lose, but on the other hand, they have a boss who wants everything taken up there [to the Supreme Court]," says Stanford University law professor Pam Karlan.

Georgetown's professor Vladeck adds that in his view, "The real story of the upcoming term hasn't been written yet because what we're going to look back on as the biggest cases of the term … are not on the docket yet."

Elections

More immediately, the probability is that like it or not the justices will be drawn into the election. The Trump administration has sought to influence elections in numerous ways, and it's unclear what efforts the administration might take going forward.

Democrats have a battalion of lawyers lined up to deal with problems on the ground — whether it's moving polling places at the last minute or having federal agents stationed near polling places. But if there are serious voting problems, they will likely end up at the Supreme Court's door — on the emergency docket.

World.title: Florida weighs ditching property taxes and sticking Canadians with the bill
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Florida voters are weighing whether to scrap residential property taxes and the state's governor has a solution to that potentially huge revenue loss: tax Canadians more.

Canadians who own property in Florida describe the threats to shake them down for more money as just the latest insult in a series of them since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to power last year with a decidedly anti-Canada agenda.

Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has railed against property taxes, which fund local governments and the services they provide — law enforcement, fire, EMS, disaster preparation and mosquito control, among many others — equating them to a form of modern-day feudalism where homeowners must "pony up money to the government just for the courtesy of using your own property."

To end this, DeSantis is pushing Amendment 3, a ballot measure crafted by his Republican statehouse allies that will be put to voters in the midterm election next month.

If passed, Florida "homesteaders," as permanent residents are called, will see a dramatic increase in an existing property tax exemption.

Any Floridian with a primary residence valued at $250,000 US or less — about 60 per cent of all homesteaders, according to the governor's office, although that figure has been questioned — would pay nothing and those with a home worth more than that would pay much less than they do now. The measure also calls on the state to eliminate homesteader property taxes entirely over time.

Golf carts line the street of a retirement community outside of Orlando, Fla. Florida permanent residents could see a dramatic decrease in property taxes if a ballot measure passes. (Rhona Wise/Getty Images)

This constitutional amendment requires a 60 per cent supermajority, and at least one recent poll suggests it will easily clear that hurdle.

State economists project such a move will cost about $12 billion US annually, forcing local and county governments that depend on these taxes to make deep cuts, find new revenue elsewhere or both.

That's where things could get more expensive for the Canadians who own an estimated $60 billion US worth of property in the Sunshine State. DeSantis has explicitly described them as a resource to tap to close expected budget gaps.

"We need to focus on our Florida residents. And focus on, in this case, Florida homeowners, particularly our homesteaded homeowners, and we need to focus the relief there," DeSantis said at a news conference last year defending his call for lower property taxes instead of a sales tax cut.

"I want Canadian tourists and Brazilian tourists subsidizing the state and making it so Florida residents pay less taxes. I don't want to give Canadians a tax cut."

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaks in Tampa, Fla. DeSantis is pushing a ballot measure to scrap property taxes for Florida residents and has said Canadian snowbirds can make up for some of the lost revenue. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

In an interview with Fox Business in June, DeSantis said that while homesteader property tax revenue will be a fraction of what it once was if the measure passes, Canadian property owners won't see any of that relief, which could help pad local coffers.

"They tax property that is non-homestead: residential, Airbnb, Canadian snowbirds, commercial. That's a lot of money that they have," DeSantis said of local and county governments.

While reducing taxes for Floridians, the ballot measure also dictates that the assessed value of a non-homesteaded property — owned by a Canadian or another non-resident — can increase by up to 5 per cent a year, steadily raising the revenue local governments can collect.

"They are going to start getting more revenue from existing taxes without having to add new taxes and they're going to end up in a very stable situation very shortly," DeSantis said.

Snowbirds 'fed up'

DeSantis has routinely poked at Canada — including its perennially losing hockey teams. He initially mocked the trade war-induced travel boycott, saying he didn't think it would meaningfully materialize, only to see his state tourism bureau report a double-digit drop in Canadian arrivals last year.

Some Canadians who have put down seasonal roots in the state have had enough of the taunts.

Canadian Glenn McGill has wintered in North Fort Myers, Fla., for the last 15 years. He's put his home up for sale after more than a year of U.S. President Donald Trump's taunts and a threat to squeeze more property tax money out of snowbirds. (Supplied by Glenn McGill)

Glenn McGill of Wiarton, Ont., has been wintering in North Fort Myers, Fla., a community once well-populated with fellow Canadian sunseekers, for the last 15 years.

But after Trump's second win there's been what he describes as a "stampede" of Canadians out of the park he and his wife Deb long thought of as a second home.

He says there are only four Canadians left in the sprawling retirement community, a fraction of what there once was when he first started going south.

McGill said DeSantis's threat to lean on Canadians to make up for lost property tax revenue will only drive more of them away, including himself — he listed his home for sale.

"They're a greedy bunch of SOBs," McGill said in an interview with CBC News. "They want to drive Canadians out."

"Those who are well off really don't care but we're not rich, we're not broke, we can do the Florida thing comfortably, but starting to pay extra taxes — that would hurt," he said.

"And this political thing with Trump, I've had enough of it."

With so many Canadians leaving or staying away, McGill says the housing market in Florida has been tough to navigate as a seller.

"The market's pretty dry," he said. "It's listed, but it hasn't sold yet."

Canadians make up the vast majority of foreign property buyers in areas along Florida's Gulf Coast.

According to Realtor.com data, Canadians represent more than 70 per cent of international demand in the Cape Coral metropolitan area, which includes McGill's community.

Deb McGill and her husband Glenn say the political climate has changed dramatically in Florida since the onset of Trump 2.0. They are trying to sell their property in North Fort Myers, Fla. (Supplied by Glenn McGill)

And with Canadian sales nowhere near pre-trade war levels, the firm says local sellers face "real pricing pressure" with properties listed for weeks longer than the national average.

The areas of Florida that have historically attracted the most Canadian interest are projected to see the largest drop in home prices this year, according to the firm's projections.

Edie Ousley, a spokesperson for Vote No on 3, a group opposing the property tax ballot measure, anticipates more housing market shocks given a possible flood of new Canadian-owned home listings if this tax change takes effect.

"Gosh, it wouldn't surprise me if there's an exodus of Canadians — they are going to be hit significantly," Ousley said in an interview.

"Amendment 3 is a train wreck. It's a train wreck for Floridians. It's a train wreck for those who come in the winter. Those Canadian snowbirds are going to be impacted with additional taxes — this is a tax shift, it's not tax relief," she said.

'Everyone is going to lose'

Ousley said a shrinking Canadian population base alone can't replace what will be lost if homestead taxes disappear.

Many municipalities are already warning that a sudden erosion in their tax base will decimate public services, most notably law enforcement and 911 response times.

"Everyone is going to lose with cuts," she said.

John May of Ottawa offloaded his Key West, Fla., condo after getting sick of hearing people he thought were friends parrot Trump's harsh rhetoric about Canada.

He said he felt like he was swimming in "a sea of stupidity" with falsehoods about his country commonplace.

"Trump would say something stupid, Governor Trudeau, 51st state and all that, and they'd stand there and laugh and I'd say to myself, 'Well, I just lost all respect for you,'" May said in an interview.

"And then you start avoiding people because you know what the conversation is going to be. If you try and have a logical discussion with somebody who's a Trumper, just forget about it," he said.

Canadian Jo-Ann Rowe wintered in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., but when her American friends started making jokes about Canada and its people, she felt she had to leave. Rowe now spends her time in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico. (Submitted by Jo-Ann Rowe)

Jo-Ann Rowe, a Canadian who was wintering in Fort Lauderdale for years with no issue before Trump's return, had the same experience.

"The 51st state thing, my American friends all thought that was quite funny. And I really don't," she said.

She left Florida for a rental property in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico. "I found it totally disrespectful. And I just couldn't do it anymore, this was my little part to do," she said.

Lilly White of Almonte, Ont., spent the last 25 years going to Tarpon Springs, Fla., near Tampa and then Flagler Beach on the other side of the state to escape Canadian winters.

White describes her time there in glowing terms, but said things changed dramatically in the Trump 2.0 era and she had to leave.

"It's not that we don't like it. We're just uncomfortable now. We'll always love the U.S. They'll always be our neighbours. They will always be friends. That's a choice we can make. But we can also choose not to fall down the rabbit hole of what's going on over there right now," she said in an interview.

"I don't like rabbit holes."

Lilly White of Almonte, Ont., spent 25 years in Florida but she had to take a step back from the state in the current political climate. She says a possible ballot measure to lean on Canadians for more property tax revenue is unfair. (Submitted by Lilly White)

White said any move to take more property taxes from Canadians is unfair to those who have pumped a lot of money into the state's economy over the years.

The many small businesses that rely on an influx of Canadian snowbirds are surely hurting as visitor figures plummet amid the bilateral bad blood, she said.

Canadians are by the far largest single source of international tourism to the state, and the number of trips dropped by 20 per cent in the prime winter season this year, data shows.

"I can't imagine how much the businesses are losing. I know how many of my friends are not going down anymore. And we were big spenders," she said.

World.title: 'The Night of the UFOs': Remembering the Oct. 4, 1967, skies over Nova Scotia
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Chris Styles was just 12 years old on a clear night when he looked out his bedroom window and spotted a strange light moving along the shoreline a few blocks from his house.

He grabbed his grandfather's binoculars to get a better look and then ran out of the house, much to his dad's dismay, down to the water's edge.

"There's this huge sphere and it was a very dull orange, and it was glowing just like a poker in a fireplace," said Styles about what he saw on Oct. 4, 1967, around 10 p.m. AT.

While that date is best known for a UFO sighting in Shag Harbour in southwestern Nova Scotia, Styles was in Dartmouth, N.S.

Primarily between the Halifax area and southwestern Nova Scotia, people recorded seeing things in the sky that night, which has led ufologists to call it "The Night of the UFOs."

"If you were outside that ... night and you looked up, and for some hours afterwards, you would have seen something," said Styles. "It was a clear night. People were seeing the faintest stars without binoculars."

Chris Styles has written or co-written three books about UFO sightings. (Submitted by Chris Styles)

Styles has written or co-written three books about UFO sightings, including Impact to Contact: The Shag Harbour Incident. He said coverage of Shag Harbour meant other sightings fell out of the press, such as what the crew of the MV Nickerson saw in the waters off Sambro.

Around 9 p.m., Capt. Leo Mersey said he spotted an object with three flashing red lights. The object, which showed up on radar, was about 25 kilometres away.

"It was very clear that night and we could see the lights of Halifax," Mersey said in a statement he filed with the RCMP.

The radar also showed three objects about 10 kilometres away, but he could not see them.

Around 11 p.m., the object he could see went into the air, but by then had only one red flashing light.

This is the statement the RCMP took from the captain of the MV Nickerson, regarding something he and his crew saw in the sky on Oct. 4, 1967. (Submitted by Chris Styles/RCMP)

"I had never seen anything like that before but it sounds like the thing they are looking for down off Shelburne or Barrington Passage," Mersey said in the statement, which was taken Oct. 7, 1967.

The RCMP statement, taken by a corporal with the Lunenburg detachment, noted: "Capt. Mersey is considered to be a reliable type individual and bears a good reputation in his community."

But Shag Harbour has long remained the focus, said Styles, in part because of the large witness pool, what authorities said at the time, and the subsequent paper trail left behind.

In Shag Harbour, an object with flashing lights crashed into the waters off the tiny fishing village.

Besides the many eyewitnesses, adding credence to the account was that a responding RCMP officer, Const. Ron O'Brien, described seeing a light from the object floating about 800 metres offshore.

"It was being carried out to sea by the tide and disappeared before we could get a boat to it," he told the Chronicle-Herald in an Oct. 7, 1967, article.

An Oct. 6, 1967, memo by a National Defence official describes some of the details surrounding the Shag Harbour UFO incident. (Public Archives Canada)

Styles said RCMP officers commandeered two fishing boats to see what was in the water and if there were any survivors, assuming a plane had crashed. They were joined on the boats by local fishermen and other residents.

He said depending on who you talk to, the object either disappeared or submerged, but there was a yellow foam on the water that some say smelled of sulphur.

On Friday, Oct. 6, a naval diving team was brought in, and seven divers searched through the weekend, but reported finding nothing.

This CBC News footage shows the search in the days following the Oct. 4, 1967, Shag Harbour UFO incident. (CBC)

The investigation reached the highest levels of National Defence.

An Oct. 6, 1967, memo by Col. W.W. Turner, the director of operations at National Defence headquarters, noted: "The Rescue Co-ordination Centre conducted [a] preliminary investigation and discounted the possibilities that the sighting was produced by an aircraft, flares, floats, or any other known objects."

His son, John Turner, told CBC News his father often mentioned to the family that he received reports of alleged UFO sightings.

"Many were easily discounted as photos of a Frisbee or a hubcap, but he often said others simply could not be explained," Turner wrote by email.

The Shag Harbour investigation was the cover story in the Oct. 7, 1967, Chronicle-Herald. (Oct. 7, 1967, Chronicle-Herald)

Styles wasn't the only person to see something in Dartmouth on Oct. 4, according to the Chronicle-Herald on Oct. 7, 1967. The newspaper reported that a woman on her way home from work saw a bright, round object in the sky moving from the Halifax-Dartmouth ferry terminal.

"She described it as brighter, more vivid than a star, with an orange hue like a halo around the circumference," the reporter wrote.

The woman looked at it through binoculars when she got home and saw it was not a star.

The newspaper checked with CFB Shearwater's control tower to see if anything was on the radar during the window the woman described. Control tower personnel said no one was monitoring the radar at the time.

World.title: Cornell president calls alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' pledges greater transparency
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Cornell's president called the alleged gang rape of a student at a fraternity house in 2024 "deeply disturbing" Saturday, said it would weigh on the university for years to come and pledged greater transparency amid mounting outrage over the school's handling of the case.

In an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community, Michael Kotlikoff described the past week as one of the most difficult in the university's history and acknowledged troubling questions about the investigations that followed the allegations.

"My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," Kotlikoff said. "It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use."

Kotlikoff reaffirmed his commitment to supporting an independent review of Cornell's handling of the case called for by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and said the school's Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also expressed support for Hochul's decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the state attorney general.

WATCH | N.Y. governor appoints special prosecutor to Cornell sexual assault case: N.Y. governor appoints special prosecutor to Cornell sexual assault case | Duration closed caption 4:40 New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has appointed the office of Attorney General Letitia James as the special prosecutor to oversee the criminal investigation into a woman's allegations that she was gang raped at a Cornell University fraternity house. Hochul said she had lost faith in the local district attorney's ability to handle the case.

"I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say," Kotlikoff said. "We don't have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves."

Scrutiny has mounted in recent days over Cornell's response to allegations that the woman was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members in 2024. The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, has sued the university and seven former students.

During a student assembly hearing Thursday that gave students an opportunity to voice concerns and discuss proposals to improve Cornell's response to sexual assault, several speakers called for Kotlikoff's resignation.

Hochul, asked at a news conference Friday whether she believed Kotlikoff should resign over the university's handling of the case, declined to take a position, saying she did not yet have enough information.

Kotlikoff acknowledged frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough, saying that has led to distrust. While citing "real legal and privacy limits" on what the university can disclose, he pledged greater transparency and more opportunities for students, parents and others to engage with university leaders.

WATCH | Student journalists demand answers in ‘Cornell 7’ case: Student journalists demand answers in ‘Cornell 7’ case | Duration 1:08 Student journalists at The Cornell Daily Sun have reported extensively on the alleged gang rape at their university two years ago. The case came into the spotlight after the victim filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16. Editor-in-chief Sophia Dasser spoke with CBC Radio's As It Happens.

He also committed Cornell's support to legislative efforts to change New York's sexual assault laws.

The case has renewed scrutiny of a state law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving people who voluntarily consume alcohol or drugs, even if they became too intoxicated to consent.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited the law in defending his initial decision not to pursue charges, saying the woman's original statement to police described voluntary drug use and sexual activity.

Critics have long sought to close what they call the "voluntary intoxication loophole," which distinguishes between people incapacitated by drugs administered without their consent and those who voluntarily became intoxicated. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to the law.

Kotlikoff also called for a "serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life," saying Cornell would engage students, alumni and others in examining how to preserve the benefits of Greek life while strengthening accountability and transparency.

"Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others or for speaking up when someone may be at risk," he said.

World.title: Mark Carney for Nobel Peace Prize? Probably not, but his name's out there
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If relations between Canada the U.S. are cool now, the temperature could plummet if Prime Minister Mark Carney were to win the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize this year.

"[Donald] Trump will be unhappy whoever gets the Nobel," Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, told The Associated Press. "If Carney got it, it would make relations with Canada rockier than they are."

Carney's name has been mentioned as a possible recipient of the prestigous prize, an award Trump has made no secret he wants to win.

On Oct. 9, the Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce the winner of the annual Peace Prize in Oslo.

Last year, the award went to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado presented Trump with her medal at the White House in January. Although Trump accepted it, the Nobel Committee stressed that the prize itself remains hers.

Trump has repeatedly said he has ended eight wars, but experts say his invasion of Iran and attack on Venezuela make him an unlikely recipient this year.

Prizes in other categories will also be awarded that week, with several Canadians being discussed as possible recipients.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million US), whether awarded to an individual, small group of laureates or an organization. The deadline for nominations was Jan. 31. After months of discussions and evaluations, the committee votes in October.

Nobel Peace Prize (Oct. 9)

Earlier this week, traders on the U.S.-based prediction market Kalshi put Carney's chances of winning at 14 per cent. His odds later fell.

"I don't think his chances are great," Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, told CBC News.

His organization releases an annual list of potential candidates for the prize. Gjerløw said the Nobel laureate has to meet three broad criteria to win: international co-operation, disarmament and the promotion of peace.

"So it's whoever did the most for these three criteria over the past year," he said.

He said Carney's name has likely been floated because of his resistance to Trump, along with the prime minister's efforts to strengthen ties with Europe — both seen as signs of international co-operation.

But Gjerløw pointed to other possible candidates, including the International Space Station.

Will Canada's prime minister lose the Nobel Peace Prize to the International Space Station? (NASA)

"It would be a symbol of what we can achieve when we are able to co-operate as humanity," he said.

Gjerløw's other candidates include Mykola Kuleba and Save the Children, Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms, the Committee to Protect Journalists, and the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court.

Nobel Prize for physiology or medicine (Oct. 5.)

When The Scientist magazine asked its readers to suggest potential Nobel Prize winners in science, Canadian researcher Dr. Daniel Drucker was among the names put forward.

Canadian researcher Dr. Daniel Drucker is a lead contender for this year's Nobel prize in physiology or medicine. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

The endocrinologist won a 2025 Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences for discovering the GLP-1 hormone used in diabetes and obesity medications — including Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro — that have changed the lives of millions of people around the world.

Prediction market Kalshi has also listed Drucker as one of the top contenders to win.

Nobel Prize for Literature (Oct. 8)

Traders on the U.S.-based prediction market Kalshi see author Anne Carson as a top candidate for the Nobel Prize in literature. (Craig Barritt/Getty Images for The Shed)

Another Canadian being discussed is poet and essayist Anne Carson, who has frequently been mentioned as a strong Nobel contender. Carson is a two-time winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize, and author of Autobiography of Red, Antigonick and Red Doc>.

However, one of Canada's most famous authors, Margaret Atwood, is also a contender according to Kalshi, but at lower odds. The Handmaid's Tale author has won two Booker prizes, and for years her name has been mentioned as a possible candidate for the Nobel Prize.

The last Canadian to win in this category was Alice Munro in 2013.

World.title: Canada's spy agency shakes up hiring process to 'meet operational needs': documents
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian Security Intelligence Service is shaking up its hiring process to meet operational needs, internal emails show — a signal the service continues to face recruitment issues.

CSIS brought in a suite of changes earlier this year to "meet operational needs and emerging demands," according to documents obtained by CBC News through an access to information request.

"These changes represent a shift in how we recruit, classify, deploy and empower our people," reads one of a series of emails sent to managers at CSIS.

"These developments and initiatives will enable us to be more efficient and effective … and better positioned to meet the demands of our changing, more challenging environment."

Most of the changes are aimed at addressing "structural bottlenecks," increasing external hires and making changes to shorten the time between recruitment and operational deployment, according to the documents.

That includes setting up a new team dedicated to external recruitment to bring in people "efficiently and responsibly," the documents say.

As of March 2026, CSIS's hiring ratio is 85 per cent internal appointments to 15 per cent external hires, the documents show. The emails tell managers to strongly consider external talent for certain skilled positions.

Unlike other government positions, most jobs at CSIS require enhanced top secret clearance — a rigorous process diving deep into a candidate's personal background, character, family history and financial history that can take 12 to 18 months.

CSIS looking to outsource more tasks

While sections of the documents were heavily redacted, they also show a push to accelerate deployment.

Changes would see candidates apply directly to their region of choice which CSIS says would enable targeted hiring for regional vacancies. It's also bringing in adjusted official language requirements "where appropriate," and shortening training classes," according to the documents.

"It will empower us to recruit individuals who can fill critical vacancies in regions that will augment our operational capacity," reads one of the emails.

The documents show the secretive and often insular agency is looking to outsource recruitment steps including some screening, targeted recruiting and psychological assessment services.

WATCH | Canada's security screening questioned after alleged spy arrested: Canadian NATO spying suspect raises questions about country’s security screening | Duration closed caption 10:35 A CBC News investigation has identified Biwei Zhang as the Canadian woman recently arrested on suspicion of spying at NATO’s military headquarters in Belgium. According to her online resume, Zhang previously worked for both the Canadian Space Agency and Statistics Canada prior to her NATO internship. The case has raised questions surrounding Canada's security screening process for sensitive government roles.

The service has already increased its use of outsourced, standardized written testing tools to streamline the testing process. It's also restructuring how it bridges co-op students into full-time positions, it said.

CSIS is looking at acquiring new technology that "enables recruitment," but there are few details about what that could look like.

The service didn't answer questions about how many employees it needs to hire but said it's seeking to fill vacant positions for intelligence officers, engineers, analysts, IT and communications professionals "and more."

"CSIS faces growing demands due to evolving security threats, including espionage, foreign interference and terrorism," said spokesperson Magali Hébert.

"To date, CSIS has continued to have high levels of qualified applicants for its work, and recruitment efforts have garnered positive results."

Staff shortages pose risk: former analyst

Stephanie Carvin, a former CSIS analyst and now an assistant professor at Carleton University, said recruitment and retention "has for a long time been a priority concern" at the service.

"Its unique value is that it has human intelligence officers going out, speaking in the community, getting information, developing relationships, developing sources. It can't do that without people," she said.

"When you have staff shortages, you have people working overtime, they burn out, they get tired and that is a risk for the organization."

CSIS Director Dan Rogers has made culture change one of his top priorities at the spy agency. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

As an intelligence agency and Five Eyes partner, onboarding at CSIS is always going to be a long and "demanding" process, said Carvin, but "attempts to find efficiency are welcome."

"Someone can quit with two weeks' notice, but at the same time, it can take somewhere between a year and two years to replace them given the security requirements," she said.

"The demands on the service have probably never been greater, but at the same time, the ability to bring people in largely the same as they were in the 1980s."

A further sign the agency is worried about its staffing is its initial move to bar employees from taking the government's early retirement incentive. As CBC News reported in April, CSIS and other security agencies like the Communications Security Establishment, signalled to employees that it wouldn't accept applications citing "continued operational pressures and growth requirements."

The National Post reported that Privy Council Clerk Michael Sabia then stepped in, leading to both agencies walking back their approach. According to a source who spoke to the Post, Sabia sees the early retirement offers as "a golden opportunity to breathe fresh air into the mid- to senior-levels of the public service and promote younger bureaucrats."

CSIS Director Dan Rogers, who took the reins in late 2024, has made culture change one of his top priorities.

As part of changes to the service, he brought in a new executive lead in recruitment and staffing in February, the emails shared with CBC News show.

"Welcome to the new role, I hope I didn't scare you off earlier today :)," Rogers wrote in an email.

"Given that context, you've got a very important job for the service — so glad you decided to take it on."

World.title: The King will never live at Buckingham Palace. What does that mean for the monarchy?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hello, royal watchers and all those intrigued by what's going on inside the House of Windsor. This is your biweekly dose of royal news and analysis.

For quite a while now, it's been clear that King Charles is quite happy living at Clarence House and has little interest in moving out of that stately home and going down the road to reside in Buckingham Palace.

So it was perhaps not a huge surprise when word emerged that he would never live in that historic central London landmark — even though in ways it has become the most high-profile and visible symbol of the monarchy itself.

While there have been efforts to emphasize that the palace will continue to be the working and ceremonial headquarters of the monarchy, the confirmation that the King won't be living there could also be sending signals about the institution and its future.

"It's a real shift away from what we expect from the monarchy and … it's an example of perhaps slimming down," Craig Prescott, a constitutional expert and lecturer in law at Royal Holloway, University of London, said in an interview.

With fewer senior members of the Royal Family, there is perhaps a move to start to "rationalize some of the properties," he said.

The shift in emphasis for the palace could also be a harbinger of a more subtle but noteworthy shift in focus for the House of Windsor as the monarchy, an institution steeped in tradition, tries to fortify its relevance in a modern world.

From left, Queen Camilla; King Charles; Prince William; Prince Louis; Prince George; Catherine, Princess of Wales and Princess Charlotte stand on the balcony of Buckingham Palace during Trooping the Colour in London on June 14, 2025. (Alberto Pezzali/The Associated Press)

"The King will, in effect, use Buckingham Palace … as his office and in a sense go to work every day," said Prescott, who sees it as part of a potential distinction emerging between the institution of the monarchy and the person who holds the role of monarch at any given time, effectively becoming a custodian.

"There seems to be a shift, which perhaps is more modern thinking, because with Elizabeth II, she was the monarchy — the two were totally sort of one in the same, whereas perhaps we're teasing out a distinction between the monarchy and the monarch at any particular time."

Buckingham Palace was built in 1703 and converted into a royal palace in the 1820s.

While it had been the home of every monarch from Queen Victoria up to Elizabeth, no monarch had actually lived there since the COVID-19 pandemic. At that time, Elizabeth moved to Windsor Castle, just as a 10-year, 369-million-pound ($692 million Cdn) refurbishment project at the palace was also underway.

When Charles started his cancer treatment in 2024, there were also some advantages to the royal residence and the royal office being in separate places, Toronto-based royal historian Carolyn Harris said in an interview.

"At a time when there was an enormous amount of concern about King Charles III's health and the aftermath of his cancer diagnosis, the fact that he had a short commute from Clarence House to Buckingham Palace had the effect of keeping him in the public eye without a need for formal public occasions," she said.

"Some of the symbolism that came out of that moment might also have informed this decision."

King Charles waves as he and Queen Camilla leave their Clarence House residence by car in London on Feb. 6, 2024. Buckingham Palace announced the previous evening that the King had begun outpatient treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer. (Frank Augstein/The Associated Press)

A shift in royal residences has precedents.

"There have been many periods where an established royal residence that seemed as though it would always be a royal residence — it didn't necessarily suit the needs of the next dynasty or the next generation in the Royal Family," said Harris.

"George III refused to live at Hampton Court, which had been a royal residence all the way from Henry VIII to his grandfather George II, because he didn't have good memories of that palace. He remembered his grandfather … boxing his ears there."

Still, the move away from the monarch calling Buckingham Palace home feels significant.

"In the 21st century, this is being treated as a seminal moment as Buckingham Palace is so closely associated with the Royal Family today that we sometimes forget about palaces that no longer exist or mostly no longer exist, such as Whitehall or Greenwich, [which] were at one time the centre of royal power," said Harris.

With the monarch no longer living at Buckingham Palace, it remains to be seen what effect — if any — that will have on public perceptions of the monarchy.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, left, speaks with King Charles, right, during an audience at Buckingham Palace on March 16. (Aaron Chown/Getty Images)

"So many people — when they visit London, [they] visit Buckingham Palace and peer through the gates, watch the changing of the guard … always hoping they might catch a glimpse of a member of the Royal Family," said Harris.

"So it'll be interesting to see if what Buckingham Palace symbolizes transcends whether there are royalty in residence or not, or whether we see … more interest in some of the other royal residences."

Harris isn't writing off Buckingham Palace just yet.

"I think Buckingham Palace's name recognition, its appeal as a tourist destination, I think there's still going to be a lot of interest."

An 'unusual' royal phone call with Canada

Prince William, left, laughs with his wife Catherine, then Duchess of Cambridge, after they both competed in a dragon boat race in Dalvay-by-the-Sea, P.E.I., on July 4, 2011. It was their first overseas visit after their marriage. (Phil Noble/Reuters)

As far as royal phone calls go, there don't seem to be many precedents — at least not any calls that get public attention drawn to them.

After Prince William and Prime Minister Mark Carney were on the phone together the other day, their spokespeople let it be known they'd had a chat.

The Prime Minister's Office didn't share any details of what they talked about, but a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the heir to the throne "discussed the enduring strength of the U.K.-Canada relationship" with Carney.

William also expressed his "longstanding affection for Canada and its people," the spokesperson said.

The call "certainly seems to be unusual," royal historian Justin Vovk said via email.

"In most situations like this, the prime minister would be speaking directly with the King as sovereign."

King Charles, left, takes a video call with Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau during a virtual audience at Buckingham Palace on March 6, 2024. (Victoria Jones/AFP/Getty Images)

It's also rather unusual that the PMO would release a statement announcing that a phone call had taken place and then provide no details of what was discussed, Vovk said.

"We know that William will not speak about the conversation, so without more information, we have to assume that the PMO disclosed this conversation as an optics exercise and a reminder that Canada maintains close ties with the United Kingdom in no small part because of our shared monarchy."

The call, says Harris, shows that William's diplomatic role is expanding and he's building a "strong rapport" with political figures in the Commonwealth realms along with the United Kingdom.

Harris also noted the public reference to William's feelings toward Canada, a country he first visited as a child with his parents and younger brother, going up the CN Tower in Toronto and visiting Niagara Falls.

Diana, Princess of Wales, right, enjoys a ride on the Maid of Mist in Niagara Falls, Ont., in October 1991 with her sons Prince Harry, left, and Prince William, centre. (Hans Deryk/The Canadian Press)

"Canada was the first country William and Catherine visited as a married couple and during this visit William quoted his great-grandmother Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother in 1939, who stated: 'Canada made us.'"

Traditionally, Harris said via email, the heir to the throne has built relationships with Commonwealth prime ministers through royal tours and official engagements.

But there might have been another factor at play in the call between William and Carney.

"There is a personal connection between Prince William and Prime Minister Carney," Harris said.

"Prime Minister Carney's brother, Sean Carney, is chief operating officer at Kensington Palace."

Back to the U.S. and Canada

Prince Edward, Duke of Edinburgh, talks to a Revolutionary era re-enactor during a tour of Mount Vernon, the estate of George Washington, in Virginia on Thursday. Washington led the Continental Army to win independence from British rule and became the first U.S. president. (Tierney L. Cross/Reuters)

After spending several days in New York and Washington, D.C., this week, Prince Edward was in Toronto Friday, drawing to a close a North American visit that focused on areas of particular interest to the Duke of Edinburgh.

Youth opportunities and the arts were front and centre in the visit that was scheduled to take him to the Lassonde Art Trail in Toronto, along with engagements supporting the Duke of Edinburgh Awards.

Edward planned to meet with educators, award providers and students at Queen's Park Friday. The Ontario government recently announced it is investing $4 million and expanding access to the award program in schools across the province.

"Talent is everywhere; opportunity is not," Fouzia Younis, British consul general to Toronto, said in a release. "This investment into young people delivers just that: opportunity."

Earlier in the week, Edward was at the Metropolitan Opera in New York meeting representatives of the city's cultural sector. In Baltimore, he visited Western High School, the oldest all-girls public high school in the U.S., as they became a new partner school for the Duke of Edinburgh Award.

Dr. Lindsay M. Chervinsky, executive director of the George Washington Presidential Library, gives Prince Edward a tour of the library at Washington's Mount Vernon estate on Thursday. (Tierney L. Cross/Reuters)

While in the Washington area, Edward also visited Mount Vernon in recognition of the 250th anniversary celebrations in the U.S. this year.

Edward's U.S. visit follows the high-profile trip there earlier this year by his elder brother, King Charles.

Edward is a more frequent royal visitor — he was last in both the U.S. and Canada in 2025.

A brother's swan song for his sister

Copies of Charles Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, my sister, are displayed at a bookshop in London on Sept. 22. (Jack Taylor/Reuters)

There is little doubt that Charles Spencer's recent book about his late sister Diana, Princess of Wales — published amid a mad swirl of headlines around its more incendiary claims — adds to the debate and interpretation of her legacy.

Beyond those claims — perhaps the most incendiary being that King Charles said his former wife would soon be forgotten after her death — the book offers new anecdotes and insights into Diana, particularly in the early years she shared with her little brother.

More broadly, Swan Song: Diana, my sister raises more questions over recent history within the upper echelons of the Royal Family, and ultimately reflects the impossibility of ever fully knowing what Diana thought or felt.

To read more of my review and analysis of the book, click here .

click here Listen to Matt Galloway's interview with Charles Spencer for CBC Radio's The Current.

WATCH | Charles Spencer doubles down on King Charles claims: Diana's brother doubles down on scathing King Charles allegations | Duration closed caption 1:55 Princess Diana's brother Earl Spencer doubled down on his allegation King Charles sounded elated on the night she died in a BBC interview promoting the release of his book Swan Song: Diana, my sister.

Royally quotable

"I created my Reading Room simply because, like all of us here, I love books and their life-enhancing power and I want to share that love with others."

— Queen Camilla, in a speech at the Queen's Reading Room Festival at Chatsworth House.

Queen Camilla, second from right, views exhibits in the Chatsworth's House of Stories exhibition during a visit to The Queen's Reading Room Festival at Chatsworth House, near Bakewell in northern England on Sept. 19. (Aaron Chown/AFP/Getty Images)

Royal reads

King Charles plans to tour Caribbean countries beginning this month, and will "not shy away from" what he has called the "darkest days" of colonial rule and slavery, Buckingham Palace announced, but is not expected to apologize. [Guardian and ITV]

Police are investigating after two men, believed to be photographers, were seen surveilling the British school that Harry and Meghan's children attend. A spokesman for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex called the incident "extraordinarily reckless." [ITV]

Charles Spencer has apologized to Piers Morgan for incorrectly claiming in his new book about Diana, Princess of Wales, that the former tabloid editor was behind the publication of intrusive photos of the late royal in the mid-1990s. [The Guardian]

Catherine, Princess of Wales, enjoyed a morning outdoors as she joined people recovering from drug and alcohol addictions for a gardening session for Addiction Awareness Week. [The Daily Mail]

The Prince and Princess of Wales laughed with Tom Cruise as the royal couple were greeted by the movie star at the premiere of his new film Digger in London. [The Standard]

Prince Harry fought back tears as he gave a speech on stage at a children's charity that is very close to his heart. [ITV]

World.title: Juno-award-winning singer Sass Jordan dies at 63
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Sass Jordan, the Montreal-raised rock singer whose career spanned nearly four decades, has died at 63.

A post on Jordan's social media page on Saturday says she died the day before, "surrounded by her loving family" and calls her an "inimitable force of nature" and "irreplaceable being of light and joy."

A cause of death has not been released.

Jordan was born in Birmingham, England, and raised in Montreal.

Her debut album, Tell Somebody, was released in 1988, and she won the Juno award for most promising female vocalist of the year in 1989, as well as being nominated several times for best female vocalist.

Her second album, Racine, released in 1992, included hits like Make You a Believer.
