World.title: I moved to Mexico City in my 20s. Here’s what I learned
World.content:
If you move to Mexico City in your 20s, I hope it becomes a home and not just a destination.

I came to Mexico at 25 thinking I was moving abroad one more time. I had already lived outside Spain, so I knew what it meant to arrive somewhere new, figure out a city, make friends and eventually find my way around. I thought Mexico City would be another chapter in that story.

A year later, I realized something else happened. I didn’t just move to Mexico; I started building a life here.

When you’re in your 20s, it’s easy to romanticize starting over somewhere else. How many of us, after a mental breakdown, have thought about leaving everything behind? Maybe moving to Paris like Blair, or finding the messy, exciting life Carrie Bradshaw had in New York City in her 30s.

I’m not saying New York or Paris won’t give you what you need to find. They might. But I found something in Mexico City that I wasn’t necessarily looking for: a place where I could become a slightly different version of myself.

Asking better questions in a new city

For me, my 20s have become less about figuring everything out and more about asking better questions. Do I want to become a mother? Will I get married? What do I want my career to look like? What kind of woman do I want to become? What do I want my future family to look like? I don’t have the answers yet. But living abroad has made me more conscious of the questions.

When I told my friends in Europe that I was moving to Mexico, some of them were worried. I wasn’t particularly afraid. My biggest concern was more mundane: I love walking, and I simply wondered whether I would be able to walk as much as I did back home. I quickly found out I could. I walk from our apartment in San Miguel de Chapultepec to Condesa to see friends, or go to a class. I walk through Chapultepec Park almost every day, and sometimes all the way to Polanco, which can take close to an hour.

One of the first things Mexico City taught me was how easily we can misunderstand places we’ve never experienced ourselves.

Before coming to Mexico, I only knew two Mexicans. They had been exchange students in Finland when I was studying there in 2020 and 2021. We weren’t friends. I just remember them being very good at beer pong and drinking rum or gin with water.

Then I arrived. And I started meeting people.

Finding kindness in the unlikeliest moments

Before Mexico, the country that completely changed my understanding of human connection was Cuba. I would need to write another article about everything that island gave me, but I truly thought nothing could surprise me in the same way again. Until Mexico did.

On my third day living in Mexico City, I was waiting in line to pay for a haircut. The woman behind me noticed what I was doing and immediately told me there was a cheaper hairdresser in the shop across the street. This act of kindness was the first one that people have shown me here. They aren’t normally dramatic moments, but they happen very often. Sometimes it is smiling in the street, starting a conversation or simply making an effort when they have no reason to.

At home, you move through your busy day surrounded by people and routines that are familiar. Abroad, you become more aware of your interactions, and they end up becoming part of what makes a place feel like yours.

There was another adjustment I was not expecting. As a European — very active and not particularly patient — I was struck by how slowly life seemed to move here. I learned that “ahorita” doesn’t necessarily mean right now. It can mean soon. It can mean later. Most of the time it’s just a polite way of saying something will happen when it happens. And you’ll get your coffee when you’re meant to get it. If you’re in a hurry, I recommend you insist a couple of times.

How different neighborhoods shape who you are

One of the things that continues to amaze me about Mexico City is how different each neighborhood feels. Polanco and Santa Fe have their own rhythm: business, luxury, restaurants, offices, polished cars and people dressed for work.

Then you go to Condesa or Roma, and suddenly you’re surrounded by leafy streets, cafes, parks and lots of dogs. I spend a lot of time in Parque México with a good friend of mine who has lived here since 2024, and we still find ourselves surprised by what we see: people dancing, doing karate, playing pickleball, learning to skate, practicing hula-hoop, someone selling poems, couples sitting on benches, foreigners taking photographs of a scene that locals barely notice because, to them, it’s simply Tuesday. That is Mexico City.

The Historic Center still leaves me speechless: the old buildings, the ruins, the Zócalo, Alameda Central, Palacio de Bellas Artes, Museo Nacional de Arte (MUNAL), the markets and the streets where centuries of history exist on top of each other.

And then there is Coyoacán, Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera, colorful markets, museums, and streets that feel completely different from the rest of the city.

The most interesting part is not just that these neighborhoods look different. They also make you feel different. You become a different version of yourself depending on where you are in the city. And in your 20s, that gives you something I have learned to appreciate: perspective.

Experiencing Mexican art and architecture

I’ve visited many museums since arriving — some of the famous ones and others that are less known. I don’t want to pretend I can explain Mexican art after a year here. But I can say that I have never experienced history through public art in quite the same way. The murals of Diego Rivera are not simply beautiful paintings. They tell stories about Mexico, its people and its history. Artists like Frida Kahlo transformed personal pain into art and became part of a cultural identity recognized around the world. I was also so impressed by Luis Barragán. Have you seen his house in San Miguel de Chapultepec? It was designed in the late 1940s, and I swear if you discover it today, you’ll want to move in there. Mexico City reminds me that contemporary doesn’t always mean new.

The joys of Mexican food

The same happened with food. Unpopular opinion: I’m not a foodie. I enjoy a latte and a cookie as much as avocado toast or a good meal at a cool restaurant every once in a while. Just give me some food when I’m hungry, and I’ll be happy. But even I have been fascinated by Mexican food. Mexican cuisine was recognized as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2010, and one of the things I’ve learned is that there is no single thing called “Mexican food.” Ingredients, dishes and traditions change so much from state to state.

Even as a vegetarian, I have found myself trying things I never expected to eat: nopal, huitlacoche and many other ingredients I did not know of before arriving.

And Mexico City is not only Mexican food. You can eat Thai, Italian, Spanish, Chinese … you name it, you’ll find it. I even discovered one of my favorite Lebanese places here in the Historic Center.

Lessons in community through Día de los Muertos

I moved to Mexico City about a year ago, just as the rainy season was ending and Independence Day celebrations were beginning. I was warned before arriving that people knew how to celebrate. “But isn’t that true everywhere?” I thought. Especially coming from Spain, where we’re always down to party. But I understood quickly that celebration here can mean something bigger than drinking late into the night. There is a sense of community, belonging and gathering together.

To this day, experiencing Día de los Muertos in Mexico has been one of the best experiences of my life. We went to the village of Malinalco, less than two hours from Mexico City, to visit family altars. We entered house after house, each one belonging to families that had lost someone that year. Every house was different. Some had large patios and modern buildings; others were old. In all of them, they replicated the profession of the person who had died through objects, decorations and food: a baker, a secretary, a police officer, a chef. The altars were filled with bright orange cempasúchil flowers and candles.

In some of them, we lit our own candles as a sign of respect. Every family gave us something to eat and drink — from tamales and tacos to mezcal, tequila or warm spiced wine. In some of them, you could really feel the presence of the person being remembered. How generous of those families, after losing their loved ones, to celebrate their lives with us, strangers to them. It was so magical. I left with tears in my eyes from the lesson in humanity I had just experienced.

Building a life together while making it your own

I’m not single, and my boyfriend and I moved here together. Some people might think moving with your partner in your 20s means you miss out on the experience. That hasn’t been our case. If anything, moving here has made us more intentional about building a life, both individually and as a couple.

Marta Delgado is a Spanish writer and marketing professional from Galicia, Spain, currently based in Mexico City. She writes about culture, lifestyle, and what it means to build a life abroad, drawing from her own time living in different countries.

World.title: 2 Mexico City chefs launched an international ‘Pay What You Can’ model. How did it go?
World.content:
Food is, in many ways, the greatest of social equalizers. Everyone, after all, must sit down to eat at various points in the day, and there’s no escaping the fact that we must all break bread together.

But too often, there’s an exclusivity around who gets to actually sit at the proverbial table. In a bustling metropolis like Mexico City, in particular, many residents are gatekept and unable to enjoy the city’s most sought-after offerings, largely due to massive socioeconomic barriers.

Wealth disparities shape capital dining

The gap between those who can, or can’t, access Mexico City’s jeweled offerings is wider than ever. A 2026 report from Oxfam Mexico revealed just how disparate Mexico has become as a nation, with 1% of the population hoarding 40% of the country’s wealth.

The divide is glaringly obvious in high-end neighborhoods like Mexico City’s Santa Fe. Oscar Lopez of The Guardian wrote about how “unbelievably unequal” certain areas of Mexico City actually are: “The stark contrast in this little enclave of the capital is a microcosm of a problem that has plagued Mexico for decades: rampant income inequality, with a small slice of the population living in opulence while millions of families languish in poverty.”

The irony, of course, is that the essential workers who sustain the infrastructure for opulent lifestyles in Mexico rarely — if ever — get invited to partake in it. That trickles down to something like booking a table at a popular restaurant in CDMX, which only a select few get to enjoy.

Taking that reality into account, Norma Listman and Saqib Keval — the married chef-owners of Masala y Maíz, a prominent Michelin-starred eatery in Mexico City’s historic center that serves a blend of Mexican, Indian and East African dishes — have made efforts to raise awareness around such issues in the food industry, including workers’ rights and dining accessibility for all.

A global movement for humane hospitality

This summer, they initiated a “Paga Lo Que Puedas” or “Pay What You Can” (PWYC) day, effectively opening their doors to every diner, regardless of their tax bracket or bank account. A powerful and unprecedented gesture, it triggered a wave of support among participating restaurants who joined the cause throughout Mexico, and beyond, to galvanize a movement centered on humane hospitality.

“As the city becomes more expensive and more oriented toward tourism and higher-income visitors, there are people who have lived here and built these communities who are increasingly unable to participate in the spaces around them. For us, that contradiction is important,” Listman and Keval told Mexico News Daily. “Restaurants are part of neighborhoods and communities, but they can also become spaces that feel increasingly inaccessible to the people who live there.”

The couple went on to say, “Dining out has become a privilege for many people, and as it becomes more expensive, it can become more segregated by class. That goes against how we understand hospitality and why we entered this industry in the first place. ‘Paga Lo Que Puedas’ was one small way of responding to that reality.”

In Mexico City, more than 20 restaurants — including MUX, Sin Nombre, Baldío, Cicatriz and Fideo Gordo — declared their commitment to “Paga Lo Que Puedas,” which took place Aug. 26. More than 100 dining institutions across 14 countries also joined in.

So how did it fare? Masala y Maíz, along with 12 participating restaurants, shared their experiences with us.

The origins, challenges and joys of a novel model

The concept originally emerged years ago, during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, when Listman and Keval — who initially opened their restaurant as a small brick-and-mortar in San Miguel Chapultepec back in 2017 — were experimenting with ways to attract customers during a challenging time for food businesses to keep their staff employed and to provide the luxury of dining out in their community.

That evolved into a regular practice, in which diners would enjoy a meal and leave whatever they could afford inside an envelope. What began as an in-house tradition ballooned into a bigger idea that would, years later, result in a global effort.

“From the beginning, we were thinking about how we could make the restaurant more accessible while also creating a tangible way to support the people around us and keep our staff working,” they noted. “It started as a small gesture, but it was also an experiment in trust: What happens when we remove the fixed price from the menu and ask people to honestly decide what they are able to pay for their meal? In Mexico City, that question felt particularly relevant because we were already seeing how quickly the cost of living was changing around us.”

Social media deepens urban segregation

In the fall of 2026, those factors had only become more urgent. In analyzing the stratification of diners in Mexico City through the increased use of social media, Guillermo Echauri of the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) found that the role and perception of food influencers in Mexico City have only exacerbated the problem of inaccessibility.

He writes that “the attributes, perspectives, and personal experiences of the foodies themselves are integrated into an environment of significant socioeconomic disparities, urban segregation, and ethnic discrimination. This shapes their representation of the culinary landscape in the Mexican capital, as digital dynamics intensify existing inequality.”

In other words, the systemic issues around dining accessibility that Listman and Keval were attuned to nearly a decade ago haven’t disappeared — they’ve arguably worsened with the rise of food influencers and rampant social media usage, among other shifts in the community and global economy at large.

By reviving the PWYC initiative in Mexico City, the founders of Masala y Maíz — and the many restaurateurs who chose to join them — are emphasizing the ongoing need for inclusivity and egalitarianism through local and international gastronomy.

Measuring turnout and financial realities

Despite logistical complications that arose through staffing and clarity around how to accept payments in a PWYC framework (in which some diners paid with non-monetary goods, such as original artwork), a survey of 12 participating restaurants unanimously confirmed a “very positive” experience and that the day “opened doors to new audiences,” with 83% of the restaurants declaring they would “definitely” participate again.

“The response we experienced was largely one of curiosity and solidarity,” Listman and Keval affirmed. “Other chefs and restaurant owners were also thinking about accessibility, rising costs, and what it means to be a restaurant within a community. We did not approach this as a model that every restaurant should adopt. Restaurants have different circumstances and different economic realities, and sustainability for the restaurant and for its workers is important. What we wanted to do was create an invitation to think differently about what hospitality can look like.”

In terms of profitable sales, the results were mixed — although that’s to be expected when the public is invited to pay whatever they wish.

Forty-two percent of the surveyed restaurants reported a “better” day of sales; a combined 33% reported either “much worse” or “about the same.” Conversely, 75% of the food businesses shared that they saw a “much higher” or “higher” turnout than an average day, while 25% believe they saw “about the same” number of diners that they would have during normal hours. In all, it seems that the restaurants saw a boom in diners, but not necessarily in income (in an act of reciprocal care, tips reportedly went up by 42%).

Building connection beyond the dining table

Importantly, 58% of the diners self-identified as first-timers at the surveyed restaurants, indicating demand and engagement from a wider range of customers than usual, and affirming the PWYC blueprint as socially equitable.

“What has stayed with us most is the sense of connection that the initiative created. For us, the success of Paga Lo Que Puedas is not simply measured by how many meals were served or how much money was collected. It is also about what happens when people feel that a restaurant is making room for them,” Listman and Keval said. “We hope that diners experience a sense of belonging and joy, and that they are able to enjoy a meal without the usual anxiety around whether they can afford to be in that space. We also hope the experience encourages people to think about the labor, care and knowledge that goes into a meal, and to recognize the workers who make that experience possible.”

Nourishing a better city

In a city as increasingly divided as Mexico City has become in the past half-decade alone — due to gentrification, mass tourism and other sociopolitical factors — PWYC is a bold, if not necessary, kind of reclamation for the people. However, that responsibility shouldn’t fall solely on small-business owners and their staff to level the playing field (or dining tables, in this case); that work should ultimately be the focus of elected officials and local governments, who should be looking for ways to support not only diners, but those who provide the city’s best dining experiences.

Without them, what would be left to nourish and feed us when we want a transcendent meal or simply a night out? Keeping local culinary arts scenes alive — and attainable for diverse residents — should be every world-class city’s priority. No matter the price.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Does civility in politics still exist? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
I am currently spending a few days visiting family and friends in the U.S. and, being a month away from the midterms, have had the opportunity to experience firsthand the run-up to the elections in multiple states. As is always the case now, the TV ads and political speeches of the candidates are increasingly over the top.

Do I choose the candidate who wants to turn the U.S. into a communist country? Or the one who wants to further enable a dictatorship? Do I prefer the candidate who wants to put a data center in my backyard? Or the one who wants to increase my energy costs and threaten my water supply with a data center that’s not in my backyard? It’s all so silly, so anxiety-producing, so insulting to our intelligence. In Mexico, where paid political ads on radio and TV are prohibited, it’s refreshing to not be subjected to this every two years.

Mexican politics, of course, are far from perfect, but there have been some examples of real civility demonstrated lately that give many of us some hope and inspiration. And that civility comes from the tone being set from the top by President Sheinbaum. Let me explain.

The word I most often hear to describe President Sheinbaum is “classy.” The way she dresses, the way she smiles, the way she carries herself, and the way she interacts with people are all frequently mentioned. Even those who don’t agree with all of her policies are impressed by that aspect of her.

Being an American, I have found the contrast to my native country and the increasing lack of class in politics in the United States to be maddening. I can understand genuine differences of opinion on important issues and on the general direction of the country, but I cannot get past the lack of class being exhibited by politicians that we see on a daily basis. The name-calling, the put-downs and the unwillingness to acknowledge anything positive from the other side is really depressing to watch. And it’s on both sides of the political aisle. I know I am not alone in often thinking, “We pay these people to represent us, find compromise, and make decisions — why can’t they seem to actually do it anymore?”

Which brings me back to Sheinbaum. There have been three incidents in just these past few weeks that were impressive examples of civility.

1. The U.S. administration has been back at it again, attacking Mexico for supposedly not doing enough to combat the cartels. This is despite nearly daily progress on high-profile arrests, drug and weapons seizures, and a significant reduction in homicides throughout the country. Marco Rubio, the U.S. Secretary of State, again hinted that the U.S. could act unilaterally against criminal organizations in Mexico. President Trump, acknowledging progress but not wanting to be outdone, added: “However, Mexico must take additional action against the narco terrorist organizations that dominate vast areas of its territory and continue to threaten the American people,” and arrest “the many corrupt public officials” who have colluded with them.

Sheinbaum responded calmly, saying that Mexico doesn’t need to be judged “from the outside.” She went on to say that she would like to see “a report about what the U.S. government is doing in the United States” to reduce drug use and combat drug trafficking. She asked, “Where is the effort being made to stop drug cartels and distributors in the United States? What’s going on with money laundering in the United States?” Fair questions of a government that has no problem frequently questioning her and her administration.

2. Sheinbaum recently completed her second year in office and as a result, just gave her second annual “state of the union” address. She then did something similar to last year, traveling to each of Mexico’s 32 states over a period of several weeks to personally give a “state of the state” address in which she presented, in detail, what the government has accomplished for the people of the state in the past year and what is planned for the following years.

Regardless of which political party is leading the state she visited, or which candidate they voted for, she showed up and presented a business-like progress report for the state. There was no avoiding the states that didn’t vote for her. There was no minimizing the progress in states that don’t support her. But rather a consistent, fact-based, optimistic outlook on what the government is doing to improve things in the state. It’s inspiring to watch, and impressive to see her making the effort to visit every state and make the individual presentations.

3. Sheinbaum’s visits to two states in particular, Jalisco and Nuevo León, most caught my attention. These states have the second and third largest cities in the country after Mexico City, and neither state has a governor of the Morena political party that Sheinbaum is part of. It didn’t matter; Sheinbaum showed up in both states, was warmly greeted by the governors, and spoke about the progress that the federal and state governments have made working together. This was not a post-natural disaster photo op. This was a real effort to present a progress report to the people of these states and present a united front of government.

The governor of Jalisco greeted Sheinbaum along with famous singer Vicente Fernández’s wife (Doña Cuquita). In Nuevo León, she was greeted by Governor Samuel García, his wife and their two daughters. The images of Sheinbaum kissing their youngest daughter with a beaming Governor García looking on would touch even the biggest cynic of politicians.

What we are seeing lately in Mexico is a welcome reminder that politics doesn’t have to be so classless, so off-putting, so negative, so nasty. It hasn’t always been this way in the U.S. — I’m not sure how it got this bad.

I’m not saying things are perfect in Mexico. They are far from it. But seeing politicians of different political parties together, seemingly genuinely acting like polite, kind, classy people is quite inspiring and uplifting. Perhaps that is why a recent poll just put the level of national pride of Mexicans at 90%, a record high.

Let’s hope it continues for the good of the country!

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Mexico’s fastest-growing states aren’t the ones having the most children
World.content:
The 2025 Intercensal Survey by the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) has revealed a paradox in Mexico’s new demographic map: The states that have seen the greatest population growth are not those with the highest fertility rates.

Mexico reached a population of 130.9 million in 2025 – the country’s highest population in history. However, the population grew at an average annual rate of just 0.7%, its slowest pace in recent decades, with growth concentrated in states in the north and southeast of the country.

Which states lead population growth?

According to INEGI, Baja California Sur led in population growth with an average annual rate of 3.4%, followed by Quintana Roo at 2.2%. Querétaro recorded 1.7%, while Nuevo León and Coahuila grew by 1.5% annually.

Population growth in Quintana Roo is a result of its population dynamics: For years, the state has recorded growth linked to an influx of people from other states and the expansion of its urban and tourist areas, among other factors.

The same pattern is observed in Baja California Sur. Meanwhile Baja California, Querétaro and Nuevo León are attracting new residents thanks to urbanization, employment and internal migration.

In contrast, Guerrero and Veracruz lost population, shrinking by -0.6% and -0.3%, respectively.

Which states have the highest and lowest fertility rate?

The states topping the growth rankings are not the same ones showing the highest fertility rates. The Intercensal Survey revealed that Chiapas had the highest fertility rate at 1.8 children per woman, followed by Guerrero (1.6) and Durango (1.5).

The contrast is particularly striking in Baja California Sur and Quintana Roo. Despite ranking at the top for population growth between 2020 and 2025, their fertility rates were among the lowest in the country — 1.2 and 1.1 children per woman, respectively.

Mexico City has the second largest population of any entity or state, despite having the lowest fertility rate (0.8). According to the survey, its population stands at 9.1 million, just behind México state, which with 17.5 million inhabitants is the most populous state in the country.

With reports from Uno TV

World.title: South Africa’s Gauteng Steps Up Femicide Fight After 12 Women Found Dead
World.content:
A South African Police Service van from the Diepkloof station in Soweto, Johannesburg, showing the 10111 emergency and Crime Stop numbers. (Photo: Dickelbers, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Key Facts — The country South Africa has about 65 million people and a US$427 billion economy, the most industrialised in Africa. Gauteng, home to Johannesburg and Pretoria, is its most populous province and business hub.

— Why it matters South Africa has one of the world’s highest rates of violence against women. Police record tens of thousands of rapes every year, and the government calls gender-based violence and femicide (GBVF) a national crisis.

— Why now The bodies of 12 women have been found since July, most in Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg. On 29 September President Cyril Ramaphosa ordered a four-point national response.

— What happened On Friday 2 October Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi said the province will ring-fence 10 police stations with the most rape cases and audit shelters for survivors.

— The numbers Gauteng lists seven rape care centres, 19 medical-legal clinics, 1,022 volunteer “GBV brigades” in 122 high-risk police precincts and 56 extra social workers.

— What it means for you Residents and visitors can call the 24-hour GBV Command Centre on 0800 428 428 or Crime Stop on 08600 10111. Municipal audits target streetlights, parks and taxi ranks.

— Still open Lesufi gave no new rand figure for the plan. A funded national plan to clear forensic backlogs is due within 60 days, with quarterly public progress reports.

Gauteng, the South African province around Johannesburg, has unveiled a plan to ring-fence its worst police stations for rape cases. The Gauteng GBVF plan follows the discovery of 12 women’s bodies in and around the city.

South Africa’s richest province is under pressure to show it can protect women. On Friday 2 October, Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi presented the Gauteng GBVF plan after a series of killings.

GBVF stands for gender-based violence and femicide, the killing of women because they are women. Gauteng is home to Johannesburg and Pretoria, the capital where the national government sits.

Twelve deaths that triggered a national response

The bodies of 12 women have been found since July, most of them in Ekurhuleni, the metropolitan area east of Johannesburg that includes Kempton Park.

On Friday, Gauteng police commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said police had resolved three of the 12 cases and identified persons of interest in three others, SABC News reported. Three of the women have not yet been identified, and a R400,000 (about US$24,000) reward remains on offer for information.

On Tuesday 29 September, President Cyril Ramaphosa announced a four-point national plan. Lesufi met the province’s mayors, municipal managers and police on Friday to turn it into provincial action.

Khumbudzo Ntshavheni, the minister in the Presidency, also spoke at the briefing. She said reports indicate “a trend of victims being killed by people close to them”.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What Ramaphosa ordered

The first point is a national case-recovery operation. Police and prosecutors must audit unresolved murders, attempted murders, rapes and serious sexual offences involving women and children.

The second point gives the police minister, the national police commissioner and forensic authorities 60 days. They must present a funded plan to cut forensic backlogs, with clear turnaround times for priority cases.

The third point requires every municipality to start a women’s safety audit and map high-risk areas. The fourth asks the trade minister to present a package against alcohol-related violence to Cabinet within 60 days.

An inter-ministerial committee and the National Council on GBVF will issue consolidated public progress reports every quarter, TimesLIVE reported. Forensic backlog progress is also to be published quarterly.

Ten police stations to be ring-fenced

Lesufi said Gauteng will give extra policing, victim support and docket management to the 10 stations with the most rape cases. They include Rietgat, Alexandra, Mamelodi, Diepsloot, Ivory Park, Dobsonville, Redhill, Midrand and Thembisa.

“If we can’t put additional resources… in these police stations, we would have failed the call that the President has given us,” Lesufi said.

The province is strengthening seven Thuthuzela Care Centres, one-stop clinics where rape survivors receive medical care and help to open a case. It is also supporting sexual offence courts, which house 144 victim-friendly rooms.

Nineteen medical-legal clinics will help prevent the loss of forensic evidence. The South African Police Service (SAPS) will expand its GBV desks to handle cases faster.

Gauteng will deploy 1,022 volunteer “GBV brigades” across 122 high-risk police precincts. The provincial Department of Social Development is adding 56 social workers.

A fifth commitment: places of safety

Gauteng added its own fifth point to the national plan. It covers shelters and other places of safety for women and children.

“We are mapping the shelters and identifying what, as a province, we call green doors,” Lesufi said. The province will audit buildings, staffing and funding gaps at these facilities.

All municipalities agreed to report within seven days on local hazards. These include broken streetlights, overgrown spaces, poorly secured parks, hijacked buildings, unsafe routes, taxi ranks and gaps in CCTV coverage.

A new intergovernmental committee on GBVF will meet every Wednesday to track the president’s directives. Lesufi said the draft plan had wide support from municipal, provincial and national officials.

How much money is behind it

Lesufi promised additional resources but did not give a new rand figure on Friday. The existing provincial budget gives a sense of scale.

Finance MEC (provincial finance minister) Lebogang Maile tabled a budget of about R179 billion (about US$10.7 billion) for 2026/27 in March. That was R3.6 billion (about US$216 million) more than the year before.

Community Safety received R2.3 billion (about US$138 million) for 2026/27 and R7 billion (about US$420 million) over three years. That money covers policing oversight, school and road safety, and GBVF victim support and case tracking.

Dollar figures use the rate of about R16.66 to the US dollar at the close of trading on Friday 2 October.

What it means for residents and visitors

Johannesburg is South Africa’s main business and air-travel hub. The new measures focus on townships and high-risk precincts rather than tourist areas, but the helplines serve everyone.

The 24-hour Gender-Based Violence Command Centre answers on 0800 428 428. Crime Stop, the police tip-off line, takes information on 08600 10111.

What to watch next

The first test is the municipal hazard audits due within a week. The second is the funded forensic-backlog plan, which Ramaphosa wants within 60 days.

The shelter audit will show whether places of safety have the staff and money they need. The quarterly reports will show whether the Gauteng GBVF plan reaches the women it is meant to protect.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Gauteng announce on 2 October 2026? Premier Panyaza Lesufi said Gauteng will ring-fence the 10 police stations with the most rape cases and audit shelters for survivors. The measures implement President Cyril Ramaphosa’s four-point plan, with a fifth provincial commitment on places of safety. Why did South Africa act now? The bodies of 12 women have been found since July, most in Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg. Ramaphosa announced a national four-point plan on 29 September, and Gauteng presented its response three days later. Is Gauteng spending new money on the response? Lesufi promised additional resources but gave no new figure. The provincial Department of Community Safety already has R2.3 billion (about US$138 million) for 2026/27, which includes victim support and case tracking. Where can someone in South Africa get help? The 24-hour Gender-Based Violence Command Centre answers on 0800 428 428. Information on crimes can be given to Crime Stop on 08600 10111.

World.title: South Africa’s Top Sugar Producer Runs On as US$150 Million Lifeline Ends
World.content:
Sugarcane fields around Upper Tongaat, north of Durban in KwaZulu-Natal, the area where Tongaat Hulett has its head office. (Photo: Hansueli Krapf, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Key Facts — The country South Africa has about 65 million people and an economy of roughly US$427 billion (World Bank, 2025), similar in size to Denmark’s. It is one of Africa’s biggest sugar producers.

— Why it matters Tongaat Hulett, the country’s largest sugar producer, has been in business rescue, a court-supervised turnaround process, since October 2022. Cane growers and mill workers depend on it.

— Why now The company’s emergency credit line from the Industrial Development Corporation (IDC), a state-owned development lender, ran until 30 September 2026. That date has now passed without a final deal.

— What happened On 2 October the business rescue practitioners said operations continued as normal and talks with the IDC and buyer Vision Sugar remained “constructive”.

— The numbers The IDC facility stands at R2.5 billion (about US$150 million), up from R2.3 billion (about US$138 million) before April 2026, according to the practitioners’ reports.

— What it means for you Investors and traders should watch whether a state lender turns rescue debt into equity. South African sugar import tariffs, which also hit Brazilian exporters, are part of the same fight.

— Still open No new funding deadline has been made public. A rival bidder’s appeal against the rescue plan is also still pending in court.

South Africa’s largest sugar producer is still milling after its state credit line reached its end date on 30 September. Its rescuers say talks on a final deal are “constructive”.

The Tongaat Hulett rescue in South Africa has passed another deadline without a final deal. The sugar group’s emergency credit line from a state lender reached its end date on Wednesday, 30 September 2026.

Tongaat Hulett is the country’s biggest sugar producer, with mills and cane estates in KwaZulu-Natal province on the east coast. Its fate matters to the farmers who sell it their cane and to its mill workers.

On Friday, 2 October, the company’s business rescue practitioners told News24 that operations “continue as normal”. They said discussions with the lender and the buyer, Vision Sugar, remained “constructive”.

Rand figures in this article are converted at R16.66 per US dollar, the market rate at Friday’s close on 2 October 2026.

Where the Tongaat Hulett rescue stands

Tongaat Hulett entered business rescue on 27 October 2022. Business rescue is South Africa’s court-supervised process for keeping a struggling company alive while it is restructured.

The firm had been hit by an accounting scandal uncovered in 2019 and by heavy debts. Former directors still face fraud charges in a criminal case that was in court again in September.

Since then the South African business has run on post-commencement finance, emergency credit that ranks ahead of older debts. That money comes from the Industrial Development Corporation (IDC), a state-owned development lender.

In April 2026 the IDC raised the facility from R2.3 billion (about US$138 million) to R2.5 billion (about US$150 million). In June it extended the end date to 30 September, according to the practitioners’ monthly reports.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on IDC Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How the company escaped liquidation in June

The rescue nearly failed earlier this year. In February 2026 the sale agreements under the rescue plan lapsed, and the practitioners asked the Durban High Court to liquidate the company.

That hearing was postponed in April. On 17 June 2026 the court allowed the practitioners to withdraw the liquidation application after a last-minute deal.

Under that deal the IDC, Vision and Tongaat Hulett signed binding heads of agreement, a framework for the final contracts. It covers refinancing the IDC facility, paying other creditors and concluding new sale agreements.

It also covers money owed to the South African Sugar Association (SASA), the industry body that collects levies from millers. That debt has been the subject of separate litigation.

Vision Consortium and the equity question

The buyer under the adopted rescue plan is Vision Consortium, founded and chaired by businessman Robert Gumede. Creditors approved that plan on 11 January 2024.

In September Gumede told The National that the June agreement provides for the IDC facility to be refinanced or restructured. He said the IDC’s funding would ultimately become an equity stake within Vision’s operating structure.

Gumede also said Vision had committed to funding creditor claims, including the obligations to SASA. These terms are his account and have not been published in a final contract.

The IDC told The National that the outcome of the talks would inform its future funding commitments. It declined to pre-empt its next step.

A cash squeeze, a strike and cheap imports

The practitioners’ August report described a “materially constrained” trading environment. At the end of August they delayed some cane and supplier payments until customer receipts came in.

An industry-wide wage strike that began on 18 August cut cane deliveries and production, the report said. Low-priced imports have also displaced local sugar from South African shelves.

On 28 August the International Trade Administration Commission (ITAC), South Africa’s tariff regulator, raised the reference price behind sugar import duties. It went from US$680 to US$785 a tonne.

SASA had asked for US$905 a tonne. The practitioners said the increase should help slow imports from major exporters such as Brazil, but would not fix the problem alone.

A rival bidder in court

A Mozambican group, RGS, has spent months trying to overturn the Vision plan. On 24 July 2026 the KwaZulu-Natal High Court dismissed its counter-application with costs.

RGS filed for leave to appeal on 20 August, and no hearing date had been set by early September. Until the appeal is decided, the Vision plan remains the adopted rescue plan.

What it means for investors and the region

The case is a test of how South Africa’s state lenders handle distressed companies seen as strategic. Turning rescue debt into equity would leave public money exposed to a private sugar business.

For foreign sugar exporters, including Brazil, the outcome also matters. A weak domestic miller strengthens the industry’s case for tougher import protection.

This fits the pattern covered in Africa: The New Scramble, where control of processing, land and commodity chains is being renegotiated.

What to watch next

No new public deadline for the IDC facility had been announced by Sunday, 4 October. The practitioners did not say whether the facility had been formally extended.

The key test of the Tongaat Hulett rescue is whether the IDC and Vision sign final contracts on the facility. The practitioners usually publish a monthly report early in the month, and the next one should give the clearest update.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Tongaat Hulett in business rescue? Tongaat Hulett, South Africa’s largest sugar producer, entered business rescue in October 2022 after an accounting scandal and heavy debts. Business rescue is a court-supervised process that keeps a company trading while practitioners try to restructure it. What happened to the IDC funding facility? The Industrial Development Corporation’s R2.5 billion (about US$150 million) facility ran until 30 September 2026. On 2 October the practitioners said talks with the IDC and Vision Sugar were continuing and operations were normal. Who wants to buy Tongaat Hulett? Vision Consortium, founded and chaired by businessman Robert Gumede, is the buyer under the rescue plan creditors adopted in January 2024. A Mozambican group, RGS, is appealing a July 2026 ruling that rejected its bid to overturn that plan. Does the Tongaat Hulett rescue affect sugar imports from Brazil? Indirectly, yes. South Africa raised the reference price behind its sugar import tariffs to US$785 a tonne in August 2026, partly to slow cheap imports from exporters such as Brazil.

World.title: Nigeria Court Freezes Prime Lagos Property in Abacha Widow’s Land Dispute
World.content:
Office towers and a construction crane in Victoria Island, the banking and business district of Lagos, Nigeria. (Photo: Timmylegend, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Key Facts — The country Nigeria is Africa’s most populous nation, with about 238 million people. Its economy, roughly US$290 billion in 2025 by IMF estimates, is somewhat smaller than Portugal’s.

— Why it matters Lagos is Nigeria’s commercial capital, and Victoria Island is its prime banking and office district. Title and joint-venture disputes there can lock up valuable land for years.

— Why now A Federal High Court judge in Lagos signed an interim order on Tuesday 29 September 2026, and it was reported by Nigerian newspapers on 2 October.

— What happened Justice Ambrose Lewis-Allagoa named a court officer as receiver and barred the developer from selling, leasing or mortgaging the property, according to the order as reported.

— Who is involved Dr Maryam Sani Abacha, widow of former military ruler Sani Abacha, is the applicant. Levitikal Realties & Construction Ltd, a Lagos developer, is the respondent.

— What it means for you Anyone considering a deal on this site should wait. More broadly, foreign buyers in Lagos should check land titles and joint-venture terms before committing money.

— Still open The order is temporary and decides nothing on ownership. Levitikal’s side of the dispute was not reported, and the case returns to court on 9 November 2026.

A federal court in Lagos, Nigeria’s business capital, has put a disputed plot in upmarket Victoria Island under a receiver. The applicant is Maryam Abacha, widow of the country’s former military ruler.

A Nigerian court has frozen dealings in a Victoria Island property in Lagos and placed it under a receiver during the dispute. Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country, and Lagos is its main commercial hub.

The applicant is Dr Maryam Sani Abacha, widow of General Sani Abacha, who ruled Nigeria from 1993 until his death in 1998. The respondent is Levitikal Realties & Construction Ltd, a local property developer.

What the court ordered

Justice Ambrose Lewis-Allagoa of the Federal High Court in Lagos issued the interim order on 29 September 2026. The case number is FHC/LAG/CS/1245/2026, according to reports in The Guardian and The Nation.

The property stands at No. 68 Molade Okoya Thomas Street, off Ajose Adeogun Street. That address sits in the heart of Victoria Island, a district of banks, corporate offices and luxury flats.

The judge barred Levitikal, its directors, agents and anyone acting through it from selling, transferring, leasing, mortgaging or otherwise encumbering the property. The restriction runs until the court hears Abacha’s application for a longer-lasting injunction.

He also barred the company from presenting itself to third parties as the owner with power to sell or mortgage the land. Any step that could prejudice the subject of the lawsuit is likewise forbidden, according to the order as reported.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Lagos Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who will run the property

The receiver and manager is the Deputy Chief Registrar of the Federal High Court, or another court officer acting as official receiver. That officer is to take possession, custody and control of the site.

As an alternative, the order allows a private firm to do the job. It names estate surveyors Bola Adebule & Company, or another reputable firm registered with the Lagos State Real Estate Regulatory Agency.

The judge also directed the police and the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), Nigeria’s anti-graft agency, to help enforce the order. Abacha was allowed to publish the order in newspapers and online to warn buyers, lenders and investors.

How the dispute began

According to the court papers as reported, the dispute grew out of a joint venture to build a high-rise on the site. The landowner later ended the agreement, alleging fundamental breaches by the developer, Levitikal.

A notice of dispute requesting mediation or arbitration was issued on 7 September 2026. Abacha’s lawyer, Adedayo Adesina, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (the country’s top rank for barristers), filed the urgent application on 10 September.

The application was made ex parte, meaning the judge heard only one side before ruling. The supporting affidavit was sworn by Sadiq Mohammed Abacha, according to The Guardian and The Nation.

The title relied on in the suit is a Certificate of Occupancy dated 4 July 1988. In Nigeria, this document is the state’s grant of the right to occupy land, since the state formally owns all land.

The other side

Levitikal’s response to the order was not reported in the coverage, and the allegations of breach have not been tested in court. An interim order of this kind is not a finding against any party.

The Guardian reported that Levitikal Group names Samuel Mawuyon Ajose as its chairman and chief executive. It said Ajose declared an interest in the 2027 Lagos governorship race in January 2026.

Why foreign investors should care

Victoria Island is where many multinational companies, banks and embassies in Nigeria have offices. Prime plots there are scarce, so developers often build through joint ventures with landowners rather than buying land outright.

When such a partnership breaks down, courts can freeze a project for months or years. Buyers and lenders who deal with the wrong party risk being caught in the litigation.

Foreigners cannot hold freehold land in Nigeria and usually rely on leases and occupancy certificates. The Rio Times has explained how buying property in Nigeria works for foreigners.

Checks at the state lands registry, plus a search for pending suits, are standard precautions. This case shows why lawyers in Lagos insist on both before any deal in the district.

What to watch next

The case returns to the Federal High Court on 9 November 2026. Levitikal may then contest the order or set out its own claim to the site.

Parallel arbitration proceedings are also under way, according to the court papers as reported. Either track could decide who controls the land.

For now, the site stays in court hands. No value for the property was given in the reports.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Nigerian court order? On 29 September 2026, a Federal High Court judge in Lagos put a disputed Victoria Island plot under a court receiver. He barred the developer from selling, leasing or mortgaging it until a further hearing. Who are the parties in the case? The applicant is Dr Maryam Sani Abacha, widow of former military ruler Sani Abacha. The respondent is Levitikal Realties & Construction Ltd, a Lagos property developer. Does the order decide who owns the Victoria Island property? No. It is an interim measure that preserves the site while the case is heard, with the next hearing on 9 November 2026.

World.title: South Africa: Makhanda Mayor Admits Broken Water System, Vows Fix in 2027
World.content:
Church Square in central Makhanda, with the City Hall clock tower, seat of the town’s civic life (Photo: Lysippos, CC BY-SA 2.0 DE, via Wikimedia Commons)

Key Facts — The country South Africa has 64.7 million people and Africa’s most industrialised economy. Its output was about US$427 billion in 2025 (World Bank), a little below Denmark’s. Its 257 municipalities run local water supply.

— Why it matters Makhanda is an Eastern Cape university town and host of the National Arts Festival. It has lived with unreliable taps for more than a decade.

— Why now Mayor Yandiswa Vara spoke a month before the 4 November local elections. In June, the national Human Rights Commission recommended dissolving her council.

— What happened On Friday 2 October, Vara conceded that the town’s water infrastructure is broken and promised uninterrupted supply next year, News24 reported.

— The numbers The main treatment plant upgrade began in 2015 with a R102 million (about US$6.1 million) budget. It has cost R279 million (about US$16.7 million) so far.

— What it means for you Visitors, students and investors should plan for water cuts. Firms and institutions that can afford it already pay for their own supply.

— Still open The final upgrade phase was only 12% complete in September and is due in September 2027. Steady taps next year are far from assured.

A South African mayor has admitted that the Makhanda water network is broken and promised uninterrupted supply next year. The plant upgrade meant to deliver it is only 12% complete and runs to September 2027.

Makhanda, formerly Grahamstown, is a town in South Africa’s Eastern Cape province, home to Rhodes University and the annual National Arts Festival. It is run by Makana Local Municipality, one of 257 municipalities that supply water, power and sanitation across the country.

On Friday 2 October, Executive Mayor Yandiswa Vara told reporters in Makhanda that the town’s water infrastructure is broken, News24 reported. She promised residents uninterrupted water next year.

A mayor concedes the obvious

Vara spoke alongside council speaker Mabhuti Matyumza, a month before South Africa’s local government elections on 4 November. News24 described her as the political head of one of the province’s most dysfunctional municipalities, with her term drawing to a close.

Many residents get water for only a few hours early in the morning, they told the news site GroundUp in September. Some go without for two days.

Businesses, institutions and households that can afford it now fund their own supply, independent of the municipality. Outages have been frequent for at least 14 years, GroundUp reported.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Eastern Cape Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Water exists, but the system fails

The problem is not a lack of water. South Africa’s national water department testified to the Human Rights Commission that local rivers and dams hold enough raw water.

The commission, an independent body set up under the constitution, issued its final report on 10 June. It found “structural and systemic” failures and recommended dissolving the council, News24 and the local paper Grocott’s Mail reported.

The council was not dissolved, and Vara remains in office. Voters will now give their own verdict in November.

The upgrade that never ends

The promise rests on the James Kleynhans Water Treatment Works, the town’s main plant. A national upgrade aims to double its output from 10 million to 20 million litres a day.

Work began in 2015 and was due to finish in 2018 at a cost of R102 million (about US$6.1 million). Amatola Water, the state-owned agency running the project, says it has cost R279 million (about US$16.7 million) so far.

A third and final phase started in March 2026 at an added cost of R223 million (about US$13.4 million). That takes the total above R500 million (about US$30 million), roughly five times the original budget.

Six months into the 18-month phase, the work was 12% complete, Amatola Water spokesperson Nolitha Mbangcolo told GroundUp. The phase is due in September 2027, late in the year the mayor promised steady taps.

Even after the second phase was completed, the plant still does not deliver 20 million litres a day. Grocott’s Mail reported in July that two of the plant’s pumps were away for repair, leaving a single pump running.

The money behind Makhanda water

Makana’s 2026/27 budget shows operating revenue of about R959 million (about US$57.6 million), excluding capital grants. Its capital budget is R116.6 million (about US$7 million).

About 71% of that capital spending, or R83 million (about US$5 million), comes from government grants. The municipality plans to add R33.6 million (about US$2 million) of its own, which the budget says depends on better revenue collection.

The same document says old debts weaken its finances. They include the bulk account with Eskom, the state power utility, and a Development Bank of Southern Africa loan.

National debt relief schemes for electricity and water have brought some write-offs, the budget adds.

Council agendas in August showed water maintenance funding cut from R31.68 million (about US$1.9 million) to R26.29 million (about US$1.6 million). The council approved pay rises for senior managers that month, Grocott’s Mail reported.

Amounts are converted at about R16.66 to the US dollar, the rate at the close of trading on Friday 2 October.

Who gains and who loses

High-lying and informal areas suffer most from the cuts, according to residents and the Human Rights Commission. They would gain most if the upgrade finally delivers.

Rhodes University, the arts festival and local firms also depend on steady water. Some now budget for their own tanks and boreholes, a cost that deters new investment.

The Special Investigating Unit, a state anti-corruption body, has probed water contracts in the municipality since October 2024. It told Parliament in August that the probe had led to two referrals to prosecutors.

The broader South African bind

Makhanda water failures reflect a wider pattern in South Africa. Many towns depend on national grants and state agencies for big projects, while weak collection and maintenance undermine daily supply.

This story fits the wider scramble for functional infrastructure across the continent. Read more in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

The first test is the 4 November election, which will decide who runs Makana and inherits the mayor’s promise. The second is progress on the final upgrade phase at the James Kleynhans plant.

Watch also whether the plant’s pumps are repaired and its second pipeline restored. Without both, doubled capacity on paper may not end Makhanda water cuts.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Makhanda keep running out of water? Ageing pipes, broken pumps and an unfinished treatment plant upgrade keep supply below demand. South Africa’s water department told the Human Rights Commission that raw water is not the problem. What is the James Kleynhans upgrade? It is a national project to double the main plant’s capacity from 10 million to 20 million litres a day. Work began in 2015, and the final phase is due in September 2027. Will Makhanda have uninterrupted water next year? The mayor has promised it, but the final upgrade phase was only 12% complete in September. Municipal elections on 4 November will also bring a new council. What does the crisis mean for visitors to Makhanda? The town remains open to visitors, students and festival crowds. Expect Makhanda water cuts, especially in high-lying areas, and carry bottled water.

World.title: What to Do in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, in October 2026: Festival and Expos
World.content:
TANZANIA · DAR ES SALAAM · Culture

A national cycling tour leaves the coast this week and free trade fairs fill the expo halls. The 44th Bagamoyo arts festival closes the month.

Key Facts — The country Tanzania, on Africa’s east coast, has about 70.5 million people. Its economy, about US$90 billion in 2025, is roughly 2% the size of Britain’s.

— Why it matters Dar es Salaam is the largest city and main port, though Dodoma is the official capital. Most diplomats, aid workers and foreign firms are based here.

— Why now October brings a health summit, four trade fairs, a national cycling tour and the country’s best-known arts festival.

— What happened On Sunday 4 October, 169 riders from 12 countries were set to race 109 kilometres to Bagamoyo. The race opens the Nyerere Cycling Tour.

— The numbers The Bagamoyo festival runs 28 to 31 October. Organisers report 146 applicant groups, 42 from abroad, and expect more than 6,000 visitors.

— What it means for you Banks and government offices close on Wednesday 14 October. The energy, solar and mining fairs are free for trade visitors who register.

— Still open Most ticket prices are unpublished. Deadly unrest followed the October 2025 election, so check your government’s travel advice before you go.

DAR ES SALAAM, Tanzania: this monthly guide is for expats, remote workers and long-stay visitors in the country’s biggest city. It lists what is worth crossing town for in Dar es Salaam in October 2026, with dates, venues and practical notes.

The month opens with a cycling race up the coast and a national health summit. Trade fairs follow, then a public holiday on 14 October, and the Bagamoyo arts festival closes the month.

This week: the Coastal Classic and the Nyerere Cycling Tour

Sunday 4 October Vodacom Coastal Classic Start: Benjamin Mkapa Stadium, Dar es Salaam; finish: Bagamoyo · Free to watch from the roadside A 109-kilometre road race organised by the mobile operator Vodacom Tanzania. A field of 169 cyclists from Tanzania and 11 other countries was set to start. They include riders from Kenya, South Africa, Australia and the Netherlands. Men’s and women’s winners each receive Sh10 million (about US$3,775). Expect support vehicles and spectators on the coast road north to Bagamoyo on race day.

Monday 5 to Wednesday 14 October Nyerere Cycling Tour Bagamoyo to Butiama, Mara Region · Free to watch along the route After the Coastal Classic, the main tour rides more than 1,400 kilometres north through 10 regions, including Tanga, Kilimanjaro, Arusha and Mwanza. Formerly called Twende Butiama, it ends in Butiama, home and burial place of founding president Julius Nyerere.

5 to 11 October: a summit and trade fairs

Monday 5 to Wednesday 7 October 13th Tanzania Health Summit Mlimani City Conference Centre, Ubungo · Registration through the summit website The country’s main annual health-policy forum brings together officials, hospitals, investors and donors. This year’s theme is building health sovereignty and strengthening health systems in a changing global order. It is useful for anyone working in health, development or public policy.

Wednesday 7 to Friday 9 October, 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. 10th POWER & ENERGY Tanzania 2026 Diamond Jubilee Expo Centre, Upanga · Free for trade visitors An international trade exhibition on power generation and energy, run by the exhibition organiser Expogroup. It is a working event, but worth a visit if you follow infrastructure or industry. Bring business cards for registration at the door.

Wednesday 7 to Friday 9 October, 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. 10th SOLAREXPO Tanzania 2026 Diamond Jubilee Expo Centre, Upanga · Free for trade visitors A specialist fair for solar panels, batteries and off-grid power. It runs alongside the energy fair in the same halls, so one trip covers both. Organisers advise visitors to pre-register online.

Saturday 10 and Sunday 11 October Champion Rise Swimming Development Gala Shaaban Robert Swimming Pool, Upanga · Contact Champion Rise Swim Club An annual youth swimming competition run by Champion Rise Swim Club, with about 180 young swimmers expected. Registration closes on 5 October. Families with children in swimming programmes should ask the club about spectator access.

Mid-October: Nyerere Day

Wednesday 14 October Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Day Nationwide public holiday This holiday marks the death in 1999 of Julius Nyerere, Tanzania’s founding president, known as Mwalimu (“teacher”). Government offices, banks and many shops close or run reduced hours. The Nyerere Cycling Tour is scheduled to finish on this day in Butiama, Nyerere’s home village in Mara Region.

Late October: Made in Tanzania, Minexpo and Bagamoyo

Monday 26 to Saturday 31 October, 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Made in Tanzania Expo Conference 2026 Mlimani City Conference Centre, Sam Nujoma Road (as listed by exhibitors) · Free entry, according to exhibitors A trade and consumer exhibition of locally made goods and services, from food and textiles to furniture. Exhibitors such as the Tanzania Institute of Arbitrators list free entry. The organiser has not published dates or a programme online, so confirm before going.

Tuesday 27 October, gala; Wednesday 28 to Saturday 31 October, main festival 44th Bagamoyo International Arts and Culture Festival TaSUBa grounds, Bagamoyo · Price from the organiser Tanzania’s best-known arts festival is run by TaSUBa, the state Bagamoyo Arts and Culture Institute. Expect traditional dance, acrobatics, music, drama, film, crafts stalls and guided tours of the old town. A pre-festival gala opens on 27 October. Bagamoyo lies about 70 kilometres north of central Dar, so it works as a day trip or a weekend away.

Wednesday 28 to Friday 30 October, 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. 10th MINEXPO Tanzania 2026 Diamond Jubilee Expo Centre, Upanga · Free for industry visitors A mining equipment and technology fair with regional and international exhibitors, also run by Expogroup. It is open to industry professionals only. Pre-register online or bring business cards to register at the venue.

Running all month: Alliance Française programme

The Alliance Française de Dar es Salaam, the French cultural centre on Ali Hassan Mwinyi Road, has a full October programme. It has published the titles but not every date, so check its website or social media for times.

Dance opens the month with PEPONI, a Tanzanian dance-theatre piece about paradise by House of Wondar. The Womanmoon Showcase follows later.

Music includes a Marafiki Festival edition of Jumatano Groove with The Birds and Afromob. Veteran musician John Kitime headlines Kalam Salaam #26.

Nasty Nate plays house and amapiano at Tuesday Groove, and the first Usiku wa Hip-Hop brings rap and dance battles. A Singeli Fest Special features Manfongo, Kidewizo and K-Pizo, and Marleen Xplastaz closes the month with Afro-fusion.

Film fans get a screening billed as the ZIFF Opening, set in an imagined Nigeria. Two art programmes, Different and Beyond Awareness, explore autism and disability, and Language Café #14 runs on 31 October.

Planning your month

October is hot and humid, with daytime highs around 30°C and warm nights. It is usually drier than the main rainy season, but the short rains can start late in the month.

Carry water and sun protection for outdoor events such as the cycling tour or a Bagamoyo day trip. Check a current forecast the day before.

Nyerere Day on Wednesday 14 October is the only nationwide public holiday this month. If you need banks or official paperwork, plan around that date.

At night, taxis and ride-hailing apps are the easiest way to get around. For Bagamoyo, allow 90 minutes or more by road and consider staying overnight for several festival days.

Most event prices are not published online. On 2 October 2026, the Tanzanian shilling traded at about 2,649 shillings to the US dollar.

Tanzania’s October 2025 general election was followed by deadly protests and a crackdown. Daily life in Dar es Salaam has continued, but check your government’s travel advice before planning a trip.

For weekly listings, check The Citizen and Daily News entertainment pages, the Alliance Française website and the organisers’ own pages. Event aggregators list many local shows, but confirm details with the organiser before travelling.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the biggest sporting event in Dar es Salaam this October?

The Vodacom Coastal Classic on Sunday 4 October is a 109-kilometre cycling race to Bagamoyo. It has 169 riders from 12 countries and opens the Nyerere Cycling Tour, which runs to 14 October.

Is there a public holiday in Tanzania in October 2026?

Yes. Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Day falls on Wednesday 14 October and is a nationwide public holiday, with government offices and banks closed.

When is the Bagamoyo arts festival in 2026?

The 44th Bagamoyo International Arts and Culture Festival runs from 28 to 31 October at TaSUBa in Bagamoyo. A gala opens it on 27 October, about 70 kilometres north of Dar es Salaam.

Are there free events in Dar es Salaam in October 2026?

The POWER & ENERGY, SOLAREXPO and MINEXPO trade fairs at the Diamond Jubilee Expo Centre are free for registered trade visitors. Roadside viewing of the cycling races is also free.

World.title: Cape Verde Explained 2026: Politics, Money and Entry Rules for Visitors
World.content:
CAPE VERDE · COUNTRY EXPLAINER

Key Facts — The country Ten Atlantic islands, nine inhabited, about 500 km (310 miles) west of Senegal. Some 527,000 people, slightly fewer than Wyoming, share an economy worth about US$3.1 billion in 2025.

— Why it matters One of Africa’s steadiest democracies, with multiparty rule since 1991. It has a euro-pegged currency, record tourism and a large diaspora in the United States, Portugal and France.

— Why now Power changed hands peacefully in June 2026. Voters now choose a president on Sunday 15 November, with the incumbent seeking a second term.

— What happened The African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde (PAICV) won 37 of 72 seats on 17 May 2026. Its leader, Francisco Carvalho, became prime minister on 19 June.

— The numbers 6.3% growth in 2025, 4.8% forecast for 2026 (World Bank), public debt near 100% of GDP. The central bank held its key rate at 2.5% on 17 September.

— What it means for you UK, EU, US and Canadian visitors need no visa for 30 days. They must pre-register online and pay a 3,400-escudo (about US$35) airport security fee.

— Still open Whether President José Maria Neves wins a second term against five rivals. Also whether weaker tourism and dearer fuel push prices up in 2026.

Cape Verde explained: a ten-island Atlantic republic of 527,000 people, with a new government and a presidential vote on 15 November. Visitors and investors find political calm and a euro-linked currency, but also high import costs and big differences between islands.

The country lies off West Africa and was a Portuguese colony until independence on 5 July 1975. Its government asks the world to use the Portuguese name, Cabo Verde.

Geography: ten islands, two groups, one maritime nation

File photo: a beach in Cape Verde.

Cape Verde is an archipelago of ten islands in two groups. The Barlavento, or windward, islands are Santo Antão, São Vicente, Santa Luzia, São Nicolau, Sal and Boa Vista.

The Sotavento, or leeward, islands are Maio, Santiago, Fogo and Brava. Santa Luzia is the only uninhabited island.

Santiago is the most populous island and home to Praia, the capital and political centre. São Vicente holds Mindelo, the main cultural and port city.
