World.title: North Korea fires intermediate-range missile, claiming evasive flight and AI features
World.content:
North Korea announced Saturday that it had test-fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile, claiming the weapon can manoeuvre in flight to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.

 

The launch comes as tensions between the two Koreas run high over landmine explosions along their border.

Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said her brother oversaw the test. She called the missile "strategic", a term that suggests it is meant to carry nuclear warheads. She also claimed it can alter its trajectory at low altitudes and has unspecified artificial intelligence capabilities, which she said would make it extremely hard to intercept.

Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, while the South Korean military, which often accuses North Korea of exaggerating its military capabilities, said the missile travelled more than 700 kilometres.

North Korea claims new missile capabilities

According to South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, the North Korean missile was fired early Saturday from the eastern coastal Wonsan area. Japan's Defense Ministry later put the distance at roughly 680 kilometres.

In her statement, Kim Yo Jong pointed to the gap between the two US allies' figures as proof that they could not follow the missile in flight.

"Whenever we applied the wavelike trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points," she said. "There is no way to avoid this attack."

The launch followed a day after she mocked Seoul's demand that Pyongyang apologise for the 21 September landmine explosions. The blasts went off about 10 metres south of the military demarcation line and wounded three South Korean soldiers.

South Korean army soldiers patrol along the barbed-wire fence near the border with North Korea, in Paju, South Korea, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (AP AP Photo

A joint inspection by South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command concluded that North Korea had planted the mines, and the command later found that Pyongyang had breached the armistice that halted the 1950-53 Korean War.

Seoul has also asked the North to stop fortifying the border with mines and anti-tank barriers. That work has sped up since Kim Jong Un dropped the goal of reconciliation in 2024 and branded Seoul a permanent adversary.

Kim Yo Jong, who may be the second most powerful person in Pyongyang, called Seoul's demands "utterly pathetic" on Friday and rejected any North Korean responsibility for the blasts, warning of retaliation if the South fires on troops working along the border.

Pyongyang's weapons tests are piling up

The Wonsan launch is the newest in a string of recent military displays, which also include missile tests, live-fire drills and the commissioning of a new warship. Kim Jong Un is showing off his expanding nuclear programme even as Washington urges a return to diplomacy.

Wonsan also hosted the Sept. 20 test of what state media described as a hypersonic missile system. It belongs to a family of weapons built to overwhelm missile defences in South Korea and Japan, including solid-fuel intermediate-range missiles first revealed in 2024.

South Korea's military said it had raised its surveillance level for further launches and was sharing information closely with Washington and Tokyo. The US Pacific Command said the launch "does not pose an immediate threat to American personnel or territory or to our allies."

Kim has mostly turned his back on diplomacy with the US and South Korea since his nuclear talks with President Donald Trump broke down in 2019. He has shifted his focus to Moscow, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons to back Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine. After years of heavier testing, his arsenal of nuclear-capable missiles now includes long-range systems that could potentially reach the U.S. mainland and shorter-range ones that threaten South Korea and Japan.

In August, Trump scaled back a large joint exercise with South Korea, apparently hoping to restart talks.

North Korea has brushed off the overture, insisting that Washington first end its "hostile policy", a phrase Pyongyang uses to describe US-led sanctions and joint military drills with South Korea.

World.title: Bosnia votes as pro-Russian politician looms large over race and stalled EU bid dominate election
World.content:
Polls opened Sunday in Bosnia's general election, where some 3.4 million voters are choosing the three members of the multi-ethnic presidency, national lawmakers, and leaders of the country's two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska.

 

The complex system of institutions was created by the US-brokered 1995 peace agreement to manage divisions among Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats.

Early reports show voting was delayed at several polling places due to problems with new digital voting technology, which was introduced to address earlier concerns about vote tampering. Polls close at 7 pm. local time.

The election comes as many citizens in the multiethnic Balkan state face everyday problems, while some leading politicians stoke the war-era tensions that have kept the country divided since the 1992-95 conflict.

New election security measures

For the first time, authorities are using electronic voter identification and ballot scanning to curb the irregularities and organised manipulation that undermined confidence in earlier elections.

Most of the 75 parties running are organised along ethnic lines. The Bosniak nationalist Party of Democratic Action has campaigned on keeping Bosnia united against Serb separatism, while many Bosnian Croats back ethnic parties such as the local branch of Croatia's ruling Croatian Democratic Union.

Izetbegovic, who was beaten by Becirovic in 2022, is seeking a third term as president of the centre-right SDA, the largest Bosniak party in the nation.

A woman places her ballot into an electronic ballot box during the general election in Sarajevo, Bosnia, Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Armin Durgut) AP Photo

Many disillusioned citizens say politicians use nationalism to avoid tackling real problems like low living standards and the exodus of young people. Mostar voter Ivan Silic said nothing has improved since he first voted and that politicians live well while everyone else's situation stays the same.

Dodik looms large despite not being on the ballot

Despite not being on the ballot, the campaign has been dominated by Milorad Dodik, the pro-Russian, separatist former president of Republika Srpska. Dodik is banned from public office after being convicted of defying the international envoy who oversees the peace agreement.

Fresh from meeting Russia's president Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Dodik leads a party, the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, that is likely to win in Republika Srpska.

Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik, right, and Prime Minister of Republika Srpska Savo Minic enter a hall for the talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin. AP Photo

At a final rally Friday in Banja Luka, attended by Russia's ambassador, Igor Khalabukov, Dodik declared Bosnia is "dead" and "an impossible country". "It doesn't make any sense," he stressed.

Off the ballot for the first time in almost 30 years, he is still in command and is present across the country's media, says Dragan Bursac, an analyst. In Bursac's view, the ban is not working, and Dodik is exploiting it.

Ethnic tensions continue to rise

Bosnia has been peaceful in recent years, but its politicians have kept ethnic divisions alive. Bosnian Serb leaders such as Dodik have pushed for their entity to break away, raising Western fears of renewed instability.

The Balkan nation remains one of Europe's poorest countries, still recovering from a war that began after it declared independence from Serb-led Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state. That conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions.

The country is formally seeking European Union membership, but progress has stalled despite EU efforts to push its leaders toward reform.

Major powers continue to influence socio-economic and political life in the small Balkan nation. Russia is holding down the EU's efforts to expand its membership throughout the Balkans, including Bosnia, while continuing to back the Republika Srpska.

While a $1.5 billion pipeline project to import US liquefied natural gas is being pushed by a corporation with ties to the Trump administration as part of the US's efforts to gain influence.

And recently, wartime wounds were reopened by public tributes in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to Ratko Mladic, the wartime army commander who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes.

Bosnian Serbs regard him as a hero, despite his UN court conviction over the killing of more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995.

Senior Bosnian Serb officials attended his funeral in Belgrade, drawing sharp EU criticism and angering Bosniak politicians.

World.title: Increasing influence: Italy marks 800 years since death of Saint Francis of Assisi
World.content:
This Sunday, 4 October, marks the 800th anniversary of the death of Saint Francis of Assisi, Italy's patron saint. From this year, and for the first time since 1977, 4 October once again becomes a national holiday.

 

To mark the occasion, the city of Assisi is celebrating this historic anniversary by exceptionally bringing together all of Italy's Regions and provincial capital municipalities, with 18 Regions and just as many municipalities already represented.

More than 3,000 pilgrims and tourists have arrived in the city to take part in the celebrations, which culminate in an address to the Nation by the President of the Republic, Sergio Mattarella, from the loggia of the Sacred Convent.

Events to celebrate the 800th anniversary of Saint Francis

The day of prayer and festivities follows a tightly scheduled programme that began at midnight on Saturday with the festive ringing of the bells. At 6.00 a.m. mass is celebrated for the community of friars, presided over by the Minister General, Friar Carlos Alberto Trovarelli, followed at 6.50 a.m. by the offering of prayers at the Saint's Tomb.

The arrival of President Mattarella is expected by 9.45 a.m. for the solemn mass in the Upper Basilica, presided over by Cardinal Matteo Maria Zuppi. During the celebration, attended also by ambassadors and representatives of accredited countries, Umbria will offer the oil and the mayor of Assisi, Valter Stoppini, will light the votive lamp on behalf of all Italian municipalities. This will be followed, at 11.20 a.m., by official speeches and, at noon, by the live broadcast of Pope Leo XIV's Angelus prayer on the giant screens in the square.

Cultural initiatives linked to Saint Francis

Alongside the institutional and religious ceremonies, major cultural initiatives have been organised, starting with the exhibition "Saint Francis at the Porziuncola", open to visitors until 25 October 2026.

The exhibition is hosted in the Porziuncola Museum at the Basilica of Santa Maria degli Angeli, which for the occasion has created a new entrance by refurbishing the ancient 15th-century cloister, once a traditional passageway for the friars. This exhibition itinerary, curated by the director Friar Saul Tambini and Donatella Vaccari, offers visitors a profound immersion in Franciscan iconography from its origins in the 13th century.

For the first time, the exhibition brings together the breviary of Saint Francis and that of Saint Clare, highlighting the deep bond between these two key figures of the early Franciscan movement. Visitors can admire paintings and relics, such as the famous portrait-relic attributed to Cimabue, which tradition holds was the lid of the Saint's first coffin, and the table on which Francis greeted death in song.

Among the works on display is also the Crucifix of the suffering Christ painted by Giunta Pisano around 1236. The entire cycle of exhibitions and celebrations forms part of the Franciscan Jubilee Year, proclaimed by Pope Leo XIV, which began on 10 January 2026 and is due to conclude on 10 January 2027.

World.title: Shooting and scoring: Photographer Alex Pantling on capturing the world’s greatest footballers
World.content:
What does it take to photograph the greatest footballers on the planet, in action, on the world's biggest stage?

 

Getty photographer Alex Pantling has spent more than a decade capturing sport’s biggest moments, from FIFA World Cups and Champions League nights to Formula 1 and the Olympic Games. Along the way, he has photographed some of the most recognisable athletes in the world, including F1 racing driver Max Verstappen, footballers, Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, Harry Kane, and 19-year-old superstar Lamine Yamal.

This summer’s World Cup gave him some of his most striking football images yet. As he told Euronews Culture, capturing those moments is less about luck than preparation meeting instinct: "You can plan, you can have ideas in your head, but you've got to react when those ideas change in the moment."

After this summer's unforgettable World Cup, we caught up with Pantling to discuss his path into photography, the challenges of working at the highest level of sport, and the stories behind some of his favourite images from the 2026 tournament.

Could you tell me briefly how you got into photography, and the path that led you to sports photography?

Alex Panning: I always knew I wanted to be involved in sport. Originally it was kind of a fluke, to be honest. At school I actually wanted to do architecture, but the way subjects were bracketed meant I couldn't do architecture and the sport-related subject I wanted at the same time. I also found out architecture was a seven-year course at university, which put me off a little.

Someone suggested photography, so I thought, I'll give that a go - which I know isn't the romantic story you're hoping for. But I gave it a go and absolutely loved it. Then I realised there was a job that combined my two passions: sport and photography.

So I pushed that further and went to university at Nottingham Trent. At the start of the course I wasn't really photographing sport yet - it was predominantly an art photography course, so I was doing still life, street photography, portraiture, that kind of thing.

In my second year, I had a tutor from Italy who'd been at Nottingham Trent in the same year as a colleague of mine, Julian Finney. She put me in touch with Julian, which led to work experience at Getty with another photographer, Michael Regan - one of our best football photographers. And from there, it led into a job with Getty.

How much of your work is careful planning, and how much is reacting in the moment?

You plan everything, but reacting is more important, because what you plan never actually happens - let's be honest. You might get to a game thinking you want to sit in a certain spot because of the light, or because you want to photograph a particular team attacking your side in the first half. Then the captains do the coin toss, they swap ends, or the rain comes - there are so many variables that change in football.

I think that's why I love it. You never work the same day twice as a football photographer, because no game is the same. I might shoot Chelsea versus Tottenham again this year, but it won't be the same as last year or the year before. You can plan, you can have ideas in your head, but you've got to react when those ideas change in the moment.

Kansas City Stadium pictured during the World Cup Credit: Alex Pantling/Getty Images

What changes when you're photographing a World Cup game versus a normal Premier League match?

It does feel very different. The Premier League is amazing - I might be a little biased being English, but I think it's the greatest football league in the world, and it's incredible that we get access to it weekly working in the UK. But when you get to FIFA, it's something really special.

It's not just the Argentinas, the Englands, the Frances - I was lucky enough to being doing Curaçao, smaller countries like this, which were almost as enjoyable because of how much it meant to them to be there, and to their fans. And I love that aspect. So yeah, in terms of how it changes: you're still doing the same job, but the emotion and the felling behind the pictures and games is completely different.

Do you still feel nervous before these big games? You're there to capture huge moments and big players - is there a sense of pressure?

Yeah, 100%. Take Messi, for example - I'm sure we'll come to that. You know he'll arguably be one of the greatest footballers to have ever lived, and in ten, twenty, thirty, forty years, people will look back on pictures of him playing. You've got the opportunity to take the pictures people are going to look at. I find that really exciting.

In terms of nerves - yes, they're always there. Getting the goal picture, the celebration, being in the right place. But it does get easier with time. I was lucky enough to shoot the final of the Qatar World Cup, arguably one of the greatest football matches ever. I was up in the stands, and I remember Messi scoring his first goal - the penalty - on my side of the pitch, and my hands were literally shaking, I was so nervous about missing the shot. I think that was because it was my first World Cup, and there was a lot of pressure on me to do a good job so I could hopefully cover more of these. I don't have that same nervousness now, though there are still elements of it.

David Alaba of Austria pictured in the player's tunnel at the 2026 World Cup Credit: Alex Pantling/Getty Images

So, let's take a closer look at some of your images you took from this year's World Cup. Your portrait of Austria's David Alaba in the tunnel is a very cinematic image - most of the frame is actually in darkness. What was the intention behind it?

We get such great access from FIFA at these events. We're allowed in the tunnel before the game as the players walk out, and that always makes for iconic pictures - the two teams lined up, the referees, the ball kids, the players locked in, wearing their tracksuits. Those pictures are a little busier, there's a lot going on, and that's good in its own way for documenting the moment.

But what I try to do - and I think a lot of my colleagues do too - is use the tunnel at half-time as an opportunity, rather than just before the game. This stadium, Kansas City Stadium, was probably my favourite to work in. The tunnel the players came out of was long and narrow, and at the end, rather than going straight up the stairs, it split: the home team went one way, the away team the other, with a wall in front. At night games, the floodlights cast a shaft of light straight onto the players' faces.

You have to be patient - there were plenty of games where I tried this shot and it didn't quite work out. On this occasion, David Alaba was waiting for some of his teammates to come back from the dressing room, and he took a moment, looking out into the light. It worked out as a really nice picture. I think the colours worked well too - the blue branding against the red kit.

Lionel Messi taking a corner for Argentina at the 2026 World Cup Credit: Alex Pantling/Getty Images

Talk us through your image of Lionel Messi taking a corner.

Absolutely. When I first walked into the stadium, the architecture was fascinating - a lot of the American stadiums are, because they're so different from what we have in the UK, mainly due to their scale. What I loved about the Kansas City stadium specifically was that it had no roof, so a lot more light came in during the day, and the floodlights were more prominent. I knew the wider shots would work really well because of how beautiful the stadium was.

When we work for FIFA, we get exclusive access to shoot from behind the bench, right down at pitch level, without an LED board in front of us - unlike the photographers positioned elsewhere, who can't get as low an angle. Going into this game, I knew this was a shot I wanted. A corner isn't the most athletic thing a footballer does, but as a picture, it lets you get close to the player on a wide lens. As he brings his leg back, that's maybe one of the most athletic positions a footballer can be in. I took around 20 frames of him doing it, but the best one is where his leg is fully extended - a really nice body shape, with the lights right above his head.

The low angle makes him look almost heroic in the frame - like the technique directors use in film, shooting from below to give someone a sense of authority. Where you going for the same effect?

Exactly. The low angle makes a big difference. It was actually quite funny - there's not much space to work in down there. You've got the linesman, the player taking the corner. About 20 minutes before this, Argentina won a corner, and as Messi walked over to take it I thought, this is the moment. But another player joined him and they played it short, so I didn't get the shape I was after. Luckily, the second time, he put it into the box himself. But yes - the low angle makes a real difference. If I'd been standing, it wouldn't have had the same impact.

Cristiano Ronaldo leading his team out at the 2026 World Cup. Credit: Alex Pantling/Getty Images

You also captured this striking image of Ronaldo leading Portugal out. What did you see in that scene that made you want to shoot it differently?

Yes - again, I'm grateful to FIFA for the access. As with the Messi picture, we're allowed tunnel access before the games. I walked into this tunnel about ten or fifteen minutes before the teams came out to warm up, knowing Ronaldo would lead the team out as captain - that was the shot I wanted.

But the light in this tunnel wasn't as good as some others, and there were a lot of stewards around, making it a bit messier for pictures. So I stepped outside and thought about what else I could do. I liked the lettering above the tunnel, and there was a sea of Portugal fans nearby, all clearly about to be on their phones trying to photograph Ronaldo - because that's what everyone was there for. I also noticed the photographers had LED boards pushed back, so they had to stay behind a certain line. I thought if I shot from behind that line, framing the photographers with their cameras and the fans with their phones, it would show that all the focus was on him.

Lamine Yamal pictured during Spain's clash against Belgium at the 2026 World Cup. Credit: Alex Pantling/Getty Images

There's a certain poignancy to your image of Lamine Yamal walking alone on the pitch

Yes - I think this was in the Los Angeles Stadium. There's just something about that stadium - I don't think I'd been anywhere quite like it. The architecture is incredible to work in, and the roof is translucent, so you don't get full sun, but you get these shafts of softer light, which can make for really nice pictures.

What's also interesting about this one: I think it was a round-of-16 or quarter-final match, and FIFA had just started using pyrotechnics before kick-off. After the anthems, flares or fireworks went off from inside the stadium, which created a kind of misty effect in the air - you can see that smokiness in the picture, and I think it adds a lot.

This was just after the anthems - the players had come over for a drink or electrolytes, whatever they take pre-match - and Yamal took a moment to himself. It worked out well that no other player was in frame; it almost looks like everyone's there just to watch him.

Ferran Torres and Lamine Yamal pictured in the changing room after winning the 2026 World Cup. Credit: Alex Pantling/Getty Images

Spain celebrating with the trophy in the dressing room. What was it like being in the middle of that chaos, and how did you go about finding the picture?

I'll never forget this one. I was on the pitch before the players came back to the dressing room, and it was my job to get in there. We were hoping Spain would let us in, and thankfully they did. I tried to time it so I didn't miss too much of the action on the pitch - players with their families and so on - while still getting back in time.

I waited outside for ten or fifteen minutes until we got the nod from FIFA to let us inside. And it was absolutely amazing - David Raya and lots of others were spraying champagne all over the players, and me to be honest, the state of the camera was not ideal when I got back, but it was brilliant. There were pictures everywhere - players celebrating separately, then together. Nico Williams grabbed me at one point because he wanted to replicate Michael Jordan's famous shower photo with the trophy, so we went and did that. There was a lot going on. It was almost hard to know what to shoot, because every time you took one picture, you felt like you were missing another happening somewhere else - which is a rare situation for a photographer, to be honest.

World.title: Where is Europe’s greenest city? Eight finalists announced for 2028 and three are in Spain
World.content:
Next week, eight European cities will find out whether their efforts to cut emissions and make room for nature are enough to win one of the EU’s top green titles.

 

The European Commission’s annual European Green Capital and Green Leaf Awards recognise cities making measurable environmental progress while improving quality of life for their residents.

This June, an independent panel whittled 27 eligible applicants down to eight finalists, judging them on everything from air and water quality to their biodiversity and efforts to cut emissions.

The winners will be announced next week on 8 October in Guimarães, Portugal, the 2026 Green Capital. They are selected more than a year in advance, giving cities time to prepare projects, events and public programmes they want to run during their title year.

Five are in the running for the Green Capital title: Aalborg in Denmark, Bielsko-Biała in Poland, Košice in Slovakia, Porto in Portugal and Zaragoza in Spain.

Another three – Benidorm and Chiclana de la Frontera in Spain, and Estarreja in Portugal – have been shortlisted for the Green Leaf awards for cities with smaller populations.

How are Europe’s greenest cities judged?

The EU launched the Green Capital Award to recognise cities that are making measurable progress on environmental problems and improving quality of life for their residents.

The main prize is open to cities with more than 100,000 inhabitants. Smaller cities with populations between 20,000 and 100,000 compete for the Green Leaf title.

The expert panel judged applicants in seven areas, including how clean their air and water are, how they protect nature and green space, how they manage waste and noise, how quickly they are cutting emissions and how they are preparing for threats such as extreme heat and flooding.

Each finalist has different strengths.

Zaragoza, for example, scored well for biodiversity and green space. The city is connecting parks, riverbanks, wetlands, street trees and surrounding natural areas into one network, designed to give wildlife more room to move and help reduce the risk of flooding.

Porto stood out for its water management, as well as its preparations for a hotter, less predictable climate. Over the past decade, the city has worked to restore the Rio Tinto riverbed and banks, built new parks that hold rainwater during downpours and begun reusing treated wastewater for agricultural irrigation and street cleaning.

The resort town of Benidorm, meanwhile, has earned praise for adding far more greenery to its built-up streets. Since 2012, it has expanded its public gardens from 350,000 square metres to more than 1.5 million and nearly quadrupled its number of trees. Today, 92 per cent of residents live within 300 metres of a public green space.

The finalists will present their plans to an international jury next week, on 7 and 8 October.

The Green Capital winner receives €600,000 to put environmental plans into practice, while Green Leaf winners can take home €200,000 for green projects and public activities.

How are European cities adapting to a hotter climate?

The changes being recognised by the EU are part of a paradigm shift visible in cities around Europe. As summers get hotter and weather patterns become more unpredictable, urban planners are giving more space back to trees, parks and water.

In Barcelona, for example, some streets have been closed to through traffic while others have been turned into parks and pedestrian areas.

Meanwhile, in Milan, the Bosco Verticale has provided a small but important example of ways cities can add greenery even where there’s little room for parks. The two residential towers feature more than 21,000 trees and shrubs on their terraces.

In Breda, the Netherlands, widespread civic involvement has transformed the city since the turn of the century. Concrete tiles have been replaced with grass, flower beds and trees. Homes and schools have added rooftop gardens.

Today, 60 per cent of the city is green space – part of more than a decade of work that helped Breda become the EU’s first National Park City in 2025.

The Green Cities Awards are not only a matter of adding plants to buildings or streets, though. Heilbronn, Germany, won the 2027 Green Capital title after scoring highly for its clean air and water, noise reduction policies and waste reduction, among other things.

When the jury meets next week, it will be judging how far the eight finalists have turned similar ideas into city-wide change.

World.title: The best place to retire abroad is no longer in Europe – but six of the top ten are
World.content:
Uruguay has taken the top spot in a new global retirement ranking, overtaking last year’s leader, Portugal. But Europe remains the most represented region, with six countries in the top ten. The Americas hold three places, while Mauritius ranks second.

 

Global Citizen Solutions’ 2026 retirement index compares 46 retirement and passive-income residence programmes, assessing quality of life, travel freedom and routes to citizenship, taxation, application procedures and costs.

Europe’s strengths lie in its high living standards, strong passports and routes to citizenship, although higher taxes weigh on its scores. Spain, Portugal, Latvia, Andorra, Italy and Greece all make the top ten, with Portugal slipping to fifth this year.

Uruguay leads thanks to solid scores across all five categories, rather than coming first in any one of them. Mauritius follows, combining favourable taxation with good results elsewhere.

The report stresses that the right destination depends on each retiree’s priorities. Fewer than four points separate first and tenth place, making the leaders closely matched.

What are the major priorities for those retiring abroad?

Quality of life carries the most weight in the index, followed by mobility and citizenship, then taxation, application procedures and costs. The weighting reflects the priorities of a typical person retiring abroad, according to the report.

Europe performs strongly on quality of life and mobility but scores less well on taxation, with wide differences between its programmes. The Americas stand out for affordability and favourable taxation, while Mauritius leads Africa’s performance. In the Middle East, low taxes and fast processing are the main attractions. The United Arab Emirates, 19th overall, ranks first for preferential tax regimes. Spain, third overall, also scores strongly on mobility and options for moving with family members.

Strong passports and clear routes to citizenship help European and many Latin American programmes score highly. Gulf destinations offer favourable taxation and fast processing, but their retirement programmes provide no standard route to citizenship.

Europe’s top-performing programmes in the 2026 index

Europe’s ten highest-ranked international retirement programmes are those offered by Spain, Portugal, Latvia, Andorra, Italy, Greece, Austria, Albania, Cyprus and Malta. All ten rank in the top half of the index.

European programmes perform particularly well on quality of life and mobility. The trade-off is taxation. Spain, the best country in Europe to live abroad in retirement, ranks fifth in the world for quality of life and offers a smooth application process taking up to eight months. However, the country also ranks last out of 46 on tax, with worldwide taxation, regional wealth taxes and no special regime for visa holders.

Portugal ranks second in Europe. The country, which topped the global list in 2025, slipped to fifth place this year. This came as Portugal increased the number of years required for citizenship. In May, the requirement increased from five to ten years for most non-EU applicants.

The country has still secured a very high global ranking, helped by its position as one of the most affordable major European routes, with the income requirement set at €920 a month. Portugal also scores highly on mobility, but processing takes up to two years, and its 41st-place tax ranking may make it less attractive to retirees prioritising lower taxes.

The programmes that do perform well on tax, notably Malta, Andorra and Cyprus, often have other demanding requirements, including high income thresholds, large investments or slow processing. Several countries also offer opt-in regimes, such as the 7% flat tax on foreign pensions in Greece and southern Italy.

Processing times and costs vary widely: Latvia, third in Europe, offers processing times of two to four months and one of the lowest-cost programmes. By contrast, the process in Cyprus can take more than two years, but the country offers a 5% tax rate, subject to specific conditions.

Ireland ranks first for quality of life in the index. It combines an English-speaking environment with some of the strongest safety and environmental ratings.

Andorra posts the index’s best safety and environmental scores; it ranks third in the world for quality of life and offers low taxes, with income tax capped at 10% and no wealth or inheritance tax. It is also the most expensive programme in the entire index, requiring a €1 million local investment on top of substantial income.

Italy and Greece rank first and second globally for mobility and citizenship, respectively. They are also Europe’s fifth- and sixth-highest-ranked retirement destinations. Both offer options for lower taxation, but Greece’s monthly income requirement of €3,500 is one of the highest.

How much monthly income do you need to qualify?

Monthly income requirements vary widely, from less than €600 in Nicaragua to more than €9,000 in Bahrain. In Europe, a monthly income of less than €800 could be sufficient in Cyprus if other requirements are met, while in Andorra, monthly income has to be more than €4,500. For comparison, the amounts shown in the chart have been converted to euros, so they may fluctuate with exchange rates.

The qualifying sources of income are also important. In some cases, applicants must show foreign-sourced passive income or a pension; others accept savings or dividends. And while the income threshold may be relatively low, some routes also require savings, deposits, investments or other substantial upfront payments.

Cape Verde, Namibia, Chile, Zambia and Morocco are excluded from the chart because the report does not specify whether their income requirements are monthly. El Salvador is also excluded, as it gives separate thresholds for pensioners and people living on passive income. Income requirements in these countries vary between $825 and $1,800.

How quickly can you get a passport?

A route to citizenship is common, but not guaranteed. The report says 24 programmes offer naturalisation within five years and 17 within six to ten years. Andorra requires 20 years. Four — Malta, the UAE, Ireland and Bahrain — offer no standard route through retirement or passive-income visas.

The shortest timelines are in South America: around two years in Argentina and roughly three in Uruguay, Paraguay and some other countries.

However, 11 countries, including Austria, Andorra, the UAE and Malaysia, do not permit dual nationality, according to the report. Applicants may therefore have to give up their original citizenship. For those unwilling to do so, permanent residence may be the limit.

What other regions offer

The Americas stand out for affordability and favourable taxation. Brazil, Argentina and Chile also offer strong passports and relatively short routes to citizenship, adding to the region’s appeal.

Mauritius is Africa’s strongest performer. In the Middle East, the main attractions are low taxes and fast processing, although retirement routes offer no standard path to citizenship.

World.title: Bosnia-Herzegovina votes amid divisive campaigns, EU bid
World.content:
Polls have opened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where voters are taking part in parliamentary, presidential and local elections.

Polling began in Bosnia and Herzegovina on Sunday, with around 3.4 million voters eligible to take part in the Balkan country's general election.

Citizens are electing officials across multiple tiers of government, including members of the multiethnic, tripartite presidency.

They will also choose lawmakers for the federal parliament and the heads of institutions for the country's two largely autonomous entities — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-run Republika Srpska.

The election comes at a time when the country is struggling with a number of challenges. There's been an economic slowdown, sluggish progress toward EU membership, and a long-drawn-out political gridlock, with the ethnically based dominant parties from the two entities repeatedly stalling decisions by the weak central government that links them.

The election will see adversary ethnic parties, the Bosniak ​SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH, pitted against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party.

Polls close at 7 p.m. local time (1700 GMT), with preliminary results expected to be released late Sunday.

What is the system that governs Bosnia-Herzegovina?

The economic, administrative and political responsibilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina are divided between the multiethnic central government, the self-governing neutral Brcko district and the two semi-autonomous entities.

Both entities are further split into several cantons and communities.

The complicated framework — divided along ethnic lines — was set up during the US-brokered 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, following the 1992-95 Bosnian war which was triggered by the breakup of Yugoslavia.

Simmering ethnic tensions

Currently in Bosnia and Herzegovina's populace, around half are Muslim Bosniaks, while 31% are Orthodox Serb and 15% are Catholic Croat.

The country has been peaceful in recent years but its ethnonationalist parties have kept the divisions alive even as voters say they want to move on from the war-era rhetoric and division.

Milorad Dodik not on the ballot but still dominant in Republika Srpska

In Republika Srpska, secessionist leader ​Milorad Dodik of the SNSD party remains the key figure despite not being on the ballot.

Dodik, the former president of the Serb-majority entity, is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.

Dodik-backed Savo Minic is running for the Republika Srpska's presidency.

Dodik wants close ‌ties with Serbia and Russia. He has just returned from Moscow where he met Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country," Dodik told supporters at the final rally of his in Banja Luka on Friday.

What is happening in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are advocating for a stronger central state.

The main Bosniak SDA party is focused on efforts to keep the country united against Serb separatism.

Bosnian Croats are also largely backing their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union.

Meanwhile, Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak presidency member, has vowed a renewed path to the EU and NATO.

EU ambitions

Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate for EU membership since 2022.

But the actual start of membership talks depends on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, including strengthening judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption ​laws.

World.title: India news: Police order probe amid sexual harassment allegations against officers at Delhi protest
World.content:
10/04/2026 October 4, 2026 Police order probe amid sexual harassment allegations against officers at Delhi protest

Delhi Police personnel are facing allegations of harassment during the Saturday protest at Jantar Mantar Image: ANI/IMAGO

Delhi Police have begun an inquiry into complaints by three women journalists who say they were sexually harassed by police personnel while covering protests against India's chief election commissioner.

In a statement on social media, police said the complaints were referred to the Crime Branch for a "fair and impartial enquiry."

The allegations emerged as police detained protesters near New Delhi's Jantar Mantar for a second day on Saturday, after over 700 people were detained on Friday. Demonstrators have been demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a mass voter-roll revision that has removed millions of names. The commission denies wrongdoing.

Kumar has not publicly commented.

In a video shared by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke, one journalist alleged that an assistant commissioner of police groped her while she filmed the detention of student activist Neha Bora. Police have not publicly responded to the specific allegation.

Journalists and protesters gathered outside the Parliament Street police station demanding a report be filed, local media reported.

The Press Club of India expressed "shock and dismay" at the treatment of journalists and urged swift action. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi asked Home Minister Amit Shah to respond, noting that Delhi Police fall under his ministry.

Several student groups have called for a march from India Gate to Jantar Mantar on Sunday at 3 p.m. local time.

Meanwhile, opposition parties plan to march on the Election Commission on Tuesday, and the CJP has called for a mass mobilization in Delhi on October 10.

World.title: Latvia election: Pro-Ukraine PM Kulbergs set to retain power after historic victory for his United List party
World.content:
Latvia's prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, looks set to retain power after his party appeared to score the country's biggest election victory since independence.

Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs appeared set to remain in power on Sunday after his centrist United List secured 35.3% of the vote in the country's parliamentary election.

The result gives United List 42 of 100 seats and puts Kulbergs in a strong position to form another pro-Ukraine coalition.

What do the results show?

With 97% of ballots counted, United List had secured the country's biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.

The party could secure a parliamentary majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the left-leaning Progressives, political scientist Roberts Kits said.

Kulbergs, a 47-year-old businessman and amateur rally driver, only came to power in May after the previous coalition collapsed over its handling of incidents involving stray Ukrainian military drones.

Latvia vote shaped by Russia fears To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An exit poll put the the populist Latvia First party in second place with 11.3% — nearly double its share at the last election in 2022. It had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority.

Kulbergs said on Saturday night that he would not cooperate with any pro-Russian parties and specifically ruled out forming a coaltition with Latvia First.

Some 1.5 million people were eligible to vote in the country's 11th parliamentary election since independence in 1991.

The election, which saw 100 seats in the Saeima being contested by 14 parties using a proportional system, was dominated by rising living costs and national security concerns in the small Baltic country which borders both Russia and Belarus.

Latvia vote shaped by Russia concerns

Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine is seen as a direct threat to national security in Latvia which, like Ukraine, is a former Soviet state with a sizeable ethnic Russian and Russian-speaking minority.

Unlike Ukraine, however, Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO.

Riga is one of Kyiv's closest partners and supporters, having committed itself by law to spending at least 5% of GDP on defense – leaving less room for spending elsewhere.

Many Latvians complain of high prices and low wages, the economy is sluggish, the health system is under strain, and emigration and an ageing population remain persistent challenges.

Populist movements such as the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and the Latvia First party have attempted to exploit discontent by taking a less stringent line towards Moscow and arguing that a complete economic decoupling from Russia is damaging.

Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Eurofighter jets in Latvian airspace

Nevertheless, no parties proposed any major deviation from Latvia's clear foreign policy alignment with the EU and NATO.

Indeed, four German Eurofighter jets were deployed to protect Latvian airspace during the election in response to a request from Riga.

World.title: Germany news: Many believe Merkel more capable than Merz
World.content:
10/03/2026 October 3, 2026 Steinmeier warns German democracy faces renewed threats

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has warned that Germany's democracy is once again being challenged.

The 70-year-old used his final German Unity Day speech as president to reflect on more than three decades of political change.

"I thought everyone had learned the lesson from history, and now I see supporters of right-wing extremism seeking to erase the memory of the victims of the Holocaust," Steinmeier said at the official ceremony in Bremen.

"I believed our democracy was secure and now have to experience it being challenged anew."

Steinmeier, whose second and final term as president ends in March, said his expectations after the changes that began in 1989 had been greater than what ultimately became reality.

Those expectations had included greater progress for liberal democracy and for "the undeniable reason of international cooperation," he said, acknowledging that there had been "bitter setbacks."

Looking ahead to his successor, Steinmeier warned that the presidency was "not an office to be taken lightly."

He said promoting social cohesion and preserving the country's unity would become more demanding in the coming years.

The official German Unity Day celebrations began earlier Saturday with an ecumenical service at Bremen's St. Peter's Cathedral attended by Steinmeier, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and other senior officials.

More than 550 events are being held in Bremen through Sunday to mark the 36th anniversary of German reunification. The celebrations rotate between Germany's 16 states and are hosted by the state currently holding the presidency of the Bundesrat, the upper house of parliament. Bremen currently holds the presidency.

World.title: Germany's Merz arrives in Kyiv to pledge more support
World.content:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz is expected to announce new measures to support Ukraine, including military aid and plans for the joint production of drones. A Kyiv bridge was struck by a Russian drone during Merz's visit.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Sunday morning, accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a delegation of leading German economic figures.

"If Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us sooner or later," Merz said upon his arrival by train.

The chancellor is expected to announce a new raft of measures to support Ukraine in its fight against the ongoing Russian invasion, including a further billion euros in German military aid, plus €350 million ($395 million) for energy sector repairs, according to German media reports.

Merz is also expected to unveil plans for the co-production of interceptor drones and long-range missiles both in Ukraine and Germany.

Focus on ramping up drone production

According to German government sources cited by the Reuters and dpa news agencies, arms production is expected to focus on the development and delivery of thousands of drones capable of intercepting the rapid, jet-powered drones increasingly being deployed by the Russian military against civilian infrastructure targets in Ukraine.

The production of missiles with a range of over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) is also expected to be ramped up, enhancing Ukraine's ability to strike military and logistical targets far beyond the frontline and inside Russia itself.

Merz is expected to emphasize how Germany also stands to benefit from the expanded cooperation, both in terms of its own defense against Russian hybrid activities and in terms of jobs and technology.

The chancellor is also expected to speak to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the progress of political reforms in Ukraine and the continuing battle against corruption.

Can Ukraine still count on Germany? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia strikes Kyiv bridge during Merz visit

The visit comes just hours after the Russian Foreign Ministry warned foreign diplomats and other visitors to avoid the Ukrainian capital, and military and government buildings in particular.

"The responsibility for any negative consequences lies entirely with those who ignore this warning," read a statement, which claimed that Russian strikes were responses to "terrorist acts by the Ukrainian armed forces against our country's civilian infrastructure."

In recent days, Russia has attacked several bridges across the Dnipro river as well as energy infrastructure, and the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, on Friday said that Kyiv was in a "very dramatic situation."

Another strike followed on Sunday during Merz's visit, with Klitschko confirming that a bridge had been struck.

"Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene," the mayor wrote on the Telegram messaging service.

Air raid sirens had earlier blared, warning of drones approaching the city, but the German delegation has not been deterred, with Merz saying upon arrival that "Ukraine will need all our support in the coming weeks" as winter approaches and Russian attacks intensify.

"A fifth winter of war is about to begin," he said. "Russia is bombarding cities, apartments and power stations. I will tell President Zelenskyy today: 'You can count on our help.'"

Russia targets Kyiv bridge network To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Merz: 'If Germany wavers, Ukraine wavers'

Merz's arrival in Kyiv marks the fourth such visit to Ukraine by a German chancellor since the full-scale Russian invasion began in February 2022.

His predecessor, Olaf Scholz, visited twice during his three-year tenure, while Merz himself first traveled to Kyiv in May 2025 – just four days after taking office. He was accompanied on that occasion by French President Emmanuel Macron, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

Sunday's visit comes just days after Merz had assured Ukraine of Germany's support, despite isolated resistance and criticism at home.

"If we in Germany waver, Europe wavers," he said on Thursday after conferring the international Westphalian Peace Prize upon the NATO military alliance and its secretary general, Mark Rutte. "And if Europe wavers, Ukraine wavers."

Germany remains Ukraine's most important backer, both militarily and financially, but state elections in September saw significant gains for parties at both ends of the political spectrum who are critical of expenditure on Ukraine: the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the socialist Left Party in Berlin.

In his speech on Thursday, Merz called out in particular "the AfD and their Russian backers" and promised Ukraine that Germany would not be divided.

World.title: In Tigray, Ethiopian government forces have advanced against a northern rebel group, reports indicate
World.content:
Reports indicate Ethiopian government forces have made advances against a northern rebel group. Renewed fighting has raised fears the conflict could spill over into the wider region.

Government forces in Ethiopia said they have recaptured an airport in Tigray's capital that was seized by rebel groups last week, in the northern region's worst outbreak of violence since a bloody civil war ended in 2022.

Several news agencies cited anonymous government sources on Saturday as saying Ethiopian federal forces now control Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle.

"The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm," an Ethiopian general told the Associated Press on condition of anonymity.

The AFP news agency, citing a "humanitarian source," reported rebel groups were leaving the city as Ethiopian government forces moved in.

Neither side has issued an official statement on the status of who controls Mekelle, and reporting is complicated by communication blackouts and restricted media access.

Return to civil war?

Pulling out of Tigray's capital would be a setback for the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which recently aligned with several other armed opposition groups in northern Ethiopia.

The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The TPLF has been the dominant force in Tigray since ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year, and then appointing former wartime regional leader Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president.

The Addis Ababa-based government's Ethiopian National Defense Force has been fighting off a renewed rebel offensive since late September.

The TPLF seized the airport in Mekelle on September 23, along with launching attacks on government positions in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, initially having made gains before being pushed back this week.

Gebremichael issued a statement on Thursday, promising to continue guerrilla attacks on government forces, similar to what took place when rebels lost control of Mekelle in 2020.

The TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018, seeks to topple Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. More than 600,000 people were killed in a civil war from 2020 to 2022.

Fears of wider regional unrest

The renewed unrest in northern Ethiopia has led to tensions spilling across the region, with fears of wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa.

For years, Ethiopia has accused its northern neighbor Eritrea of providing support to Tigray rebels, alongside Sudan and Egypt. All three countries deny this.

Last week, Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties, with both countries expelling diplomats and closing embassies.

The African Union said it was concerned by the growing tensions between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt, and has called on all sides to show maximum restraint.

Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to the Red Sea

The TPLF's Debretsion said in his video message that "the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea."

World.title: Peru: Fire burning on road to Machu Picchu kills 1
World.content:
One person has died and two others have suffered burns in a fire near the main access route to the historic sanctuary of Machu Picchu.

A blaze was burning near the main access road to the ancient Inca citadel of Machu Picchu in Peru, leaving one person dead and two injured, officials said on Saturday.

The fire began on Friday in the Sacred Valley of the Cusco region, which also includes the Ollantaytambo train station — the busiest for travelers visiting Machu Picchu.

"We have one elderly person who died in the flames and two others with second-degree burns," Miguel Osco, head of the Cusco Regional Office for Disaster Management and Safety, told RPP radio.

How did the fire start?

Osco said the fire originated from controlled bush burning that farmers carry out to clear land for crops.

The flames spread quickly because of the hot, windy weather and dry vegetation, he added.

The Incas built Machu Picchu in the 15th century.

Located at an altitude of 2,500 meters in the Andes Mountains, the historic sanctuary is regarded as an architectural masterpiece.

UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 1983.

Machu Picchu is Peru's most famous tourist destination, attracting about three million visitors every year.

World.title: Brazil's 2026 presidential election is kicking off with polls showing Lula and Bolsonaro nearly tied.
World.content:
Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former far-right populist President Jair Bolsonaro, is taking on incumbent left-wing President Lula da Silva. Polls show the first round of voting will likely lead to a runoff.

The latest polling points to a tight race in Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, with leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva seeking a fourth non-consecutive term and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro seeking to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro.

The two leading candidates wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo.

Lula vows to 'defeat the far-right'

The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right," and framing the election as choice between "democracy and sovereignty" and "barbarism and corruption." Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city.

Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution.

The 80-year-old Lula is seeking the presidency for a fourth and final time Image: Amanda Perobelli/REUTERS

Bolsonaro's law and order

Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana.

The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent."

Flavio Bolsonaro has said he would pardon his father if elected Image: Douglas Shineidr/AFP

"I am convinced ​that everything is in place for us to win this election in the first round," the ​lawmaker said.

He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him.

Brazil's 2022 election rematch

The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected.

Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump, who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, which the US president called a "witch hunt."

US President Trump had held close ties with fellow right-wing populist Jair Bolsonaro [FILE March 2019] Image: Chris Kleponis/CNP/MediaPunch/picture alliance

The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference."

Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change.

Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely."

What happens next?

Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media.

In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct.

Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Polls show neither candidate is likely to win more than 50% of valid votes on Sunday needed to avoid a runoff that would take place on October 25.

The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency.

In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%.

In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points.

Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators.
