World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.title: When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.content:
SHANGHAI — “Great-grandma, your head seems to be a little loose,” Yu Mingrui jokes as he examines an ancestral portrait depicting nine members of a family across three generations.

The 28-year-old Shanghai restorer was commissioned to repair the Qing dynasty (1644–1911) portrait by a descendant of the family in Ningbo, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, which had been passed down through generations. Yu filmed the process and posted it on Douyin, China’s version of TikTok.

Amid the portrait’s cracks and damage, Yu found clean, deliberate cuts around one woman’s painted head, suggesting the section was once removed and replaced.

Yu commented that the painter might have added the faces after painting the bodies. But viewers offered their own explanations. Some hypothesized the painter had covered up a mistake and repainted the face. Others suggested that descendants of a male ancestor’s concubine had altered the portrait to replace his wife’s image.

The answer may never be known. But the mystery drew widespread attention online, with videos about the painting receiving more than 100 million views and likes across Chinese social media platforms.

On Chinese social media, independent restorers like Yu are demonstrating how damaged paintings, old books, and family records are taken apart, repaired, and preserved.

“A lot of people told me that they simply didn’t know that something damaged could actually be restored before watching my videos,” Yu told Sixth Tone.

The objects brought to independent restorers include ancestral portraits, genealogies, old books, and calligraphy passed down through families and kept in homes rather than institutions.

Often made from paper or silk, these objects are vulnerable to moisture, insects, light, and age. Even when damaged, they can retain names, images, and other details about the families that preserved them.

For restorers like Yu, the videos can also connect that work with owners who might otherwise have left such objects damaged at home. Those commissions provide restorers with work and, in some cases, allow families to recover information from records that had become too fragile or damaged to read.

Face value

When the Qing-era ancestral portrait arrived at Yu’s studio, its ink had faded, its paper had become brittle, and its edges were torn. A patchwork of old advertising flyers held it together, promoting everything from cakes to real estate.

At 3.4 meters long and 1.2 meters wide, the portrait barely fits into the worktable at the center of Yu’s roughly 40-square-meter studio in Shanghai’s rural Songjiang District.

Yu turned the makeshift repairs into another joke for his viewers. Families in China traditionally honor deceased relatives with food and other offerings. The flyers, Yu joked, had given the painted ancestors a modern assortment of their own.

“Whatever the ancestors are missing, they can just take it from behind the painting,” he said.

Repairing the portrait, however, was a more exacting process. Yu said the restoration is divided into four broad stages: washing away dust and stains, removing the backing paper and remnants of earlier repairs, patching tears and holes with paper matching the original, and retouching missing colors and lines.

Each stage depends on the painting’s condition. Even washing it requires the restorer to decide whether to use hot or cold water, whether mold and stains require chemical treatment, and how much the paper can withstand. Chemicals can remove stains quickly, but excessive treatment can damage the paper or alter the painting itself.

“The real difficulty lies in the uncertainty,” Yu said. “A restorer’s experience gives you certainty at the beginning, serving as a safety net to deal with the uncertainty that appears in the process.”

The portrait took around three months to restore. Before treatment, Yu said, face-detection software picked up only three of the nine painted faces. Afterward, when he photographed the restored portrait, the software marked all nine faces on screen. Yu charges around 10,000 yuan ($1,493) for a painting of this size and complexity.

Yu began posting restoration videos while studying Chinese antique restoration in college. After graduating in 2021, he opened his own studio. His videos often begin with an unusual detail, a question about an object’s history, or a joke designed to catch attention.

“History isn’t only made up of famous paintings or nationally protected cultural relics,” he said. “It is also made up of these seemingly insignificant objects. As I restore them, I’m also helping to pass that culture on.”

Genealogies, ancestral portraits, and other family documents offer a view of the past that differs from official histories and local gazetteers, Zhang Yi, a historian at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, told Sixth Tone. Genealogies, for example, can record more than 1,000 people, while larger volumes can include tens of thousands, sometimes with birth and death dates.

“These materials greatly enrich our understanding of the lives and personal histories of ordinary people in Chinese history,” Zhang said.

The videos have also helped Yu turn restoration into a livelihood. His online following attracts commercial sponsorships, which now account for roughly half his income, he said. Many clients bring him just one family object in need of repair, but together, those individual commissions have allowed him to build his own customer base.

Paper trail

Beijing restorer Lian Chengchun also works mainly for private owners, from collectors to families preserving books passed down through generations.

Her videos offer them a first lesson in how to handle and preserve those objects at home, and can prompt people to take a second look at old records before the stories they carry disappear.

“I see little distinction between collections held by organizations and individuals,” Lian said. “Whether a book is restored by a public institution, an independent restorer or a private collector, the goal is the same: to preserve it for future generations.”

Books kept in private hands can arrive in almost any condition. Some have been patched with tape, glue, calendars, or whatever paper was available, repairs that may hold them together temporarily but can cause further and sometimes irreversible damage.

“Others were stored in plastic bags, where trapped moisture can encourage mold and decay,” said Lian, 38, who’s spent 18 years restoring old books by hand.

Before starting such work, Lian studies a book’s age and history, along with its paper, printing style, and other materials, which can vary across periods.

“Only then can I decide how best to repair it,” she said.

Cai Yadong came across Lian’s videos just when members of his clan in Jiaozhu Village, in southern China’s Guangdong province, needed help repairing a badly damaged genealogy.

In 2023, two elderly clan members handed Cai a 111-page genealogy dating to 1920. The wider Huazhou Cai clan today numbers about 20,000 descendants across roughly 110 villages, but Jiaozhu’s own records had almost completely disappeared, leaving residents unsure how their branch fit into the family or even who its founding ancestor was.

“When I first saw it, it was barely recognizable,” Cai, secretary of the Huazhou Cai clan association, said. “The pages were mixed together. Some had been burned, and years of damage had left the book extremely fragile.”

After contacting Lian, Cai flew to Beijing to deliver it himself rather than risk shipping it. “It was simply too valuable to risk any accidents,” he said.

Restoring the genealogy took Lian nearly a year and a half. Because of the genealogy’s age and poor condition, the restoration required careful, piece-by-piece work, Lian said.

“We try to repair it in a way that preserves its original appearance, while retaining as much of the surviving text as possible,” she said.

Lian compared numerous samples before selecting restoration paper that matched the original pages in color and texture. She repaired torn fragments and holes one by one, reinforcing sections where the original characters remained legible.

“Saving each character felt like picking up the brush where the Cai ancestors had left off,” Lian said. “Each page I uncovered felt like a dialogue with people from hundreds of years ago.”

When the work was completed, the volume showed that more than 30 pages were devoted to Jiaozhu, detailing family members and major events.

One entry showed how Jiaozhu’s branch fit into the wider Huazhou Cai clan and identified its founding ancestor as Cai Wende. The restored volume also helped three other villages establish their own connections to the clan.

“If our generation does not do this, the family memory may be gone after another one or two generations,” Cai said. “Once it is lost, it will be very difficult to recover.”

Just weeks before the genealogy surfaced, Jiaozhu had held a ceremony to renovate an ancestral tomb. Villagers knew it as the tomb of their founding ancestor but no longer knew his identity. Once the book was restored, they added Cai Wende’s name to the tomb’s inscription.

Cai described the timing as uncanny. “Whenever we talk about it, we all get goosebumps,” he said.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Yu Mingrui at his studio in Shanghai, August 2026. Lü Xiao/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019092/Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.title: Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019092/Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.content:
Beijing Wildlife Park has turned its fight against a surge of invasive caterpillars into a public contest, offering up to 10 park tickets to visitors who collect the heaviest haul each day. From Sept. 28 to 30, participants caught an estimated 120,000 larvae weighing a combined 18.5 kilograms.

The safari-style zoo on the capital’s southern outskirts announced the event with a call for “warriors” to battle a leaf-eating pest it dubbed the “forest food monster.” Initially scheduled for two days, the contest was extended through Oct. 7 after drawing strong interest and now runs throughout the weeklong National Day holiday.

Participants first register and receive a brief lesson on identifying the pest before staff hand out disposable gloves, food containers, and chopsticks. They search the park for larvae and submit their catches by 2:50 p.m., when staff weigh them and determine the day’s rankings. The captured caterpillars are destroyed rather than fed to the park’s animals.

Prizes are awarded each day based on the total weight collected. The first-place entry receives 10 park tickets, with five for second place and two for third. Everyone who participates receives a commemorative pin, while those finishing fourth through 10th also receive a themed headband.

Competition was stiff from the opening day. A visitor surnamed Liang collected about 4,000 caterpillars weighing 596.3 grams, filling six containers but finishing second. The winning entry came from a five-person team that brought in 1,069.5 grams, while third place went to a catch weighing 391.4 grams.

“The winners were a team of five and caught nearly twice as many as I did,” Liang, a pianist who has visited the park for a decade, told Beijing Daily. “I couldn’t keep up.”

Liang said there was no particular trick to catching the caterpillars, though she found more in less crowded parts of the park and in the shade beneath taller trees. “I brought my own plastic bottles and tweezers, which I found more convenient,” she said.

The winner on the second day, Zhang Hanfang, 18, collected 1.3 kilograms with a six-person team. A taxidermist who runs a studio specializing in insect, reptile, and bird specimens, he made the two-hour drive from neighboring Hebei province with a friend’s family the day after seeing the park’s announcement. The group shares an interest in natural science.

“There’s no secret,” Zhang told Sixth Tone. “Just keep your eyes on the trees and keep at it. It was intense and thrilling. The contest also satisfied our October itch to go bug hunting.”

A video about the contest posted on the lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, known in English as RedNote, received more than 31,000 likes and 1,400 comments. One commenter described the initiative as “crowdsourced debugging,” while a related hashtag on Weibo attracted nearly 3 million views.

In recent weeks, residents across Beijing have reported seeing fall webworm caterpillars — the larvae of an invasive moth native to North America — on sidewalks, balconies, and even people’s shoulders.

The city is experiencing the peak larval period of the pest’s third generation this year, with mature larvae descending from trees in search of sheltered places to pupate and survive the winter.

Yang Zhongqi, chief scientist at the Chinese Academy of Forestry, said the species is a major invasive pest that threatens more than 300 plant species, including forest and fruit trees, flowers, and crops.

“During severe infestations, the caterpillars can strip a tree of every leaf, damaging urban greenery and hindering the tree’s growth,” Yang said. “But they do not kill the tree.”

Beijing had released nearly 700 million parasitic wasps this year before beginning the release of another 400 million on Sept. 28. Harmless to people and pets, the wasps lay their eggs inside fall webworm pupae, preventing adult moths from emerging.

Yang Sihan, head of monitoring and forecasting at the Beijing Gardening and Greening Resources Protection Center, attributed this year’s surge to a cyclical pattern of severe outbreaks, warmer winters, and frequent summer rain that disrupted spraying.

At sites monitored over five consecutive years, the survival rate of overwintering pupae rose from 65.3% in 2023 to 84.2% this year, Yang Sihan said. Heavy rain also left fewer clear days for spraying and washed away pesticides after they were applied. A single female moth can lay 300 to 600 eggs and sometimes as many as 2,000.



Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A participant tries to catch a caterpillar at Beijing Wildlife Park, September 2026. From @北京野生动物园 on Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019091/In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.title: In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019091/In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.content:
China’s weeklong National Day holiday began Thursday, extending a travel period that started with the Mid-Autumn Festival less than a week earlier and fueling demand for long-distance trips at home and abroad.

The Mid-Autumn Festival, traditionally an occasion for family reunions, fell on Sept. 25 this year. National Day, which marks the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, followed on Oct. 1 and began a weeklong public holiday. With only three working days between them, people who took those days off could combine the two breaks into a 13-day holiday ending Oct. 7.

Chinese airlines are expected to carry 31.19 million passengers from Sept. 25 to Oct. 7, up 3.6% from the same period last year, according to the Civil Aviation Administration of China. Bookings for domestic flights covering more than 2,000 kilometers rose about 14%, according to aviation data provider Umetrip.

International flight bookings for the period were up 22.5% year on year as of Sept. 24, the CAAC said. Flights to Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam, and Laos increased by about 20%, while those to Britain, Germany, and Spain rose by about 15%.

Here are snapshots from the extended holiday period across China.

(Header image: Tourists take photos at Yuyuan Garden in Shanghai, Sept. 27, 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019083/Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.title: Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019083/Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.content:
Chinese Olympic diving champion Zhang Jiaqi has sparked debate after starring in a popular reality show and revealing years of criticism, little emotional support, and financial control from her mother.

The debate intensified Sunday after Zhang’s mother, Xiao Yingjie, read aloud a letter telling her daughter that, despite not having “performed very well,” she still chose to “trust” and “forgive” her. Xiao had written the letter ahead of the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, where Zhang, then 17, went on to win gold in synchronized diving. Related hashtags later trended on microblogging platform Weibo, drawing tens of millions of views.

The 22-year-old from Beijing retired last year. She now studies sports training at Beijing Sport University and also works as a livestreamer. In late August, she joined the current season of “My Little One,” a reality show that follows female celebrities and their parents at home, inviting guests to provide commentary on family dynamics.

The show revealed that before Zhang retired, all of her earnings, including a prize of 810,000 yuan ($120,000) she had received as a teenager, and three bank cards were managed by her mother.

On “My Little One,” Xiao is seen repeatedly criticizing her daughter, complaining about everything from Zhang letting her cats onto the table to drinking ice water, eating snacks, and leaving the tag on her pajamas. On one occasion, she says to the show’s other guests, “Look how lazy she is.”

Xiao’s private communications to Zhang via the instant messaging platform WeChat — messages critiquing everything from her tone of voice to table manners, as well as forwarded educational videos — were also shown to viewers. Zhang largely responded with silence as they were presented. “It’s so suffocating (to watch),” one highly upvoted comment on the microblogging platform Weibo read.

The show also revealed that Xiao, despite having no other job commitments, rarely visited Zhang once she left home to attend training at age 6.

On the show, Zhang told Xiao that she often felt that her mother didn’t love her and that her parents were not what she “imagined.” She added that she “always hated” Xiao as a child and that she believed she had been raised not by her but by her diving team.

Popular social media comments labeled Xiao as “NPD,” short for narcissistic personality disorder, a clinical diagnosis that has become an online shorthand in China for controlling, self-centered, or emotionally manipulative people.

One post with nearly 20,000 likes on Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, called Zhang a “survivor of criticism-based parenting,” praising her for expressing her dissatisfaction with her mother on the show and actively distancing herself from her mother’s control. Others questioned Zhang’s father for his apparent absence from the conflict.

Domestic psychologist Li Songwei, appearing as a guest on the show, described the conflict as “delayed adolescence” on Xiao’s part. In a Weibo post, Li later urged people not to vilify Xiao, saying she had since voluntarily signed up for courses on parent-child communication and apologized to her daughter for her mistakes.

“This is a typical mother who is blinded by anxiety,” Li wrote. “In fact, the reason young viewers see so many parental traits in Zhang Jiaqi’s mother that they find ‘annoying’ or even ‘infuriating’ is that they, too, are working through issues from their own adolescence. It is a path every family has to take.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Zhang Jiaqi (right) and her mother on the show “My Little One.” From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019065/The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.title: The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019065/The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.content:
This summer, “All Wishes Come True!” took in more than 1.8 billion yuan ($268 million) at the Chinese box office, becoming the latest in a string of hit animated films inspired by traditional Chinese myths and legends. The movie reimagines the Eight Immortals, a group of legendary figures in Chinese mythology and Taoism, as ordinary mortals who pose as immortals and venture into the celestial realm of Penglai. There, the mismatched group finds itself caught up in a conflict involving powerful gods, including the warrior deity Erlang Shen.

Despite the film’s widespread acclaim, some Taoist friends of mine were far from impressed. They believe it trivializes important figures in Taoist tradition, completely reimagining their stories while simply borrowing the names of Chinese immortals as a gimmick. But how fixed are the stories of the Eight Immortals in the first place?

Firstly, what makes the Eight Immortals — one of the best-known groups of immortals in Chinese culture — so special? And how exactly are they understood within Taoism?

Let’s start with why there are eight. In traditional Chinese culture, the number eight has long been associated with completeness and balance. The “Zhou Yi” (or “Book of Changes”), for example, describes the eight trigrams; traditional cosmology divides space into eight directions; and ancient people worshipped eight agricultural deities collectively associated with the harvest.

Then there are the “immortals” themselves. The Chinese word xian, or “immortal,” has long been associated with hermits who withdraw into the mountains in pursuit of spiritual cultivation. In Taoism, immortals are distinct from shen, or deities, in that ordinary humans can attain immortality through cultivation. Immortals thus occupy a space between the human and sacred worlds, embodying the Tao in the human realm.

Before the Eight Immortals became established as a group, several individual members had already appeared in historical writings and paintings from the Tang (618–907) and Song (960–1279) dynasties, each associated with their own supernatural feats.

Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin practiced neidan, a Taoist tradition of spiritual cultivation sometimes called “internal alchemy,” and frequently interacted with the influential Taoist priest Chen Tuan. Zhang Guolao once demonstrated various miraculous Taoist arts before Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty. Han Xiangzi could make flowers bloom instantly. Lan Caihe was a beggar who wore a shoe on one foot while leaving the other bare, often singing and dancing while intoxicated and carrying a large clapper.

Once they had formed into a group, however, the Eight Immortals did not simply retreat into the mountains or ascend to heaven. Instead, they remained closely connected to the human world. The most representative figure in this respect is Lü Dongbin, who chooses to remain among mortals and save them. He assumes various guises, including those of a fisherman, an ink and paper peddler, a sick beggar, and even a pregnant nun. Stories and images of Lü spread across China, with saving and enlightening ordinary people becoming a central theme in legends surrounding him.

The Yuan dynasty (1279–1368) mural “The Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea” at Yongle Palace in Ruicheng, in northern China’s Shanxi province, shows that the Eight Immortals had by then become an established subject in Taoist art. But closer inspection reveals that the only female member of today’s group, He Xiangu, is missing. In her place is Xu Shenweng, a Taoist figure associated with the Northern Song period (960–1127) who once ranked among the Eight Immortals. In other words, the Eight Immortals were originally an all-male group.

So, when did He Xiangu become one of the Eight Immortals? One early appearance of her as part of the group comes in the Yuan dynasty drama “Chen Jiqing Mistakenly Boards a Bamboo Leaf Boat” by Fan Kang. By the time Wu Yuantai wrote the mythological novel “Journey to the East” during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), she had become a permanent member of the group.

This change came amid the flourishing of women’s literary and religious activity during the mid-to-late Ming. Like male scholars, educated women participated in religious and intellectual life and produced literary works of their own. In “Journey to the East,” He Xiangu’s defining supernatural ability is her power to foresee good and bad fortune. Born into a family that ran an herbal medicine shop, she possesses medical knowledge and uses encounters with people seeking treatment as opportunities to encourage them to do good.

With the addition of He Xiangu, the lineup familiar today became fixed and increasingly popular. The Eight Immortals eventually became influential enough to attract the attention of European missionaries studying Chinese religion and folklore. French Jesuit Henri Doré (1859–1931), for example, compiled stories about them in “Researches into Chinese Superstitions,” his multivolume study of Chinese popular religion, folklore, and customs.

The Chinese Jesuit priest Pierre Hoang (1830–1909), also known as Huang Bolu, meanwhile, described the Eight Immortals as representing a cross-section of society: the old and young, men and women, the rich and poor, the noble and lowly. In another interpretation, Zhang Guolao represents old age; Lan Caihe and Han Xiangzi, youth; Zhongli Quan, the military; Lü Dongbin, the scholar; Cao Guojiu, the nobility; Li Tieguai, the sick; and He Xiangu, women.

The Eight Immortals thus came to encompass a broad range of social identities and experiences. They had, collectively, seen many sides of the human world, allowing people from different backgrounds to recognize something of themselves in the group. Their differences also created a kind of balance, recalling a passage in Chapter 2 of the “Tao Te Ching,” which states: “Thus existence and non-existence produce each other; the difficult and the easy bring about each other; the long and the short impart form to each other; the high and the low comply [or change places] with each other; sounds and voices harmonize with each other; priority and sequence alternate with each other.”

From the mid-to-late Ming dynasty onward, the Eight Immortals also became a popular decorative motif on ceramics produced in both imperial and private kilns. They often appeared more subtly on everyday objects, including furniture, utensils, clothing, and architectural decorations. Rather than depicting the immortals themselves, artisans represented them through eight objects associated with the group: Li Tieguai’s gourd, Zhongli Quan’s fan, Zhang Guolao’s fish drum, Lan Caihe’s flower basket, Cao Guojiu’s jade tablet, Han Xiangzi’s flute, He Xiangu’s lotus, and Lü Dongbin’s sword. Craftsmen combined these symbols with scrollwork, bats, clouds, and waves to create decorative compositions that also conveyed wishes for longevity, good fortune, and wealth.

Stories about the Eight Immortals were similarly adaptable. Among commoners, plays such as “The Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea” and “The Eight Immortals Assembly Celebrate Longevity” were widely performed. By the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns (1736–1820) of the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), such stories were increasingly associated with birthday celebrations, with gatherings of the Eight Immortals symbolizing longevity, joy, and good fortune.

Among intellectuals, meanwhile, the Eight Immortals served as a source of creative inspiration. One example is “The Record of Handan,” the last of the “Four Dreams of Linchuan” by the great Ming playwright Tang Xianzu. Rather than focusing on reunion, the play uses Lü Dongbin to explore the illusory nature of worldly ambition.

In the play, Lü meets a poor scholar obsessed with achieving fame and gives him a porcelain pillow. After putting on a pot of rice to boil, the scholar falls asleep and dreams that he marries, places first in the imperial examinations, and spends decades navigating political machinations before becoming a powerful and honored official, only to eventually die from overindulgence. Waking to find his pot of rice still cooking, the scholar realizes his entire lifetime of ambition was merely a brief dream. Lü then begins the process of enlightening him, introducing him to the other immortals, who appear one by one to admonish him until he finally awakens to the emptiness of his desires.

All this shows just how adaptable the stories of the Eight Immortals have always been. Taoist traditions and popular folklore have continually shaped and reshaped one another, producing new versions of the group for different audiences and eras.

In that sense, what is happening to the Eight Immortals today is nothing new.

Translator: David Ball.

(Header image: An Eight Immortals room screen at a museum in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019071/She Sold 192 Porsches in a Year. Then Came an AI-Fueled Smear Campaign.
World.title: She Sold 192 Porsches in a Year. Then Came an AI-Fueled Smear Campaign.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019071/She Sold 192 Porsches in a Year. Then Came an AI-Fueled Smear Campaign.
World.content:
Editor’s note: After Mu Qianwen hit the headlines in 2024 as one of Porsche’s top sales consultants worldwide, she became the target of toxic online abuse, including sexually explicit AI-generated videos. For this 35-year-old mother in Qingdao, in the eastern Shandong province, the harassment got so bad that she even contemplated suicide. Rather than give in, she decided to fight back through the courts. Here, Mu shares her ordeal in her own words.

I first started attracting attention online in early 2024. I’d already been “sales champion of the month” at my dealership more than 20 times, but on the last day of 2023, our sales manager presented me with a crystal trophy. I had sold 170 cars that year.

When I posted about the achievement on Xiaohongshu (the lifestyle platform known globally as RedNote), it soon became a trending topic, and more than a dozen media outlets asked me for interviews.

But there was also a huge backlash, with some questioning how I could have sold so many cars and suggesting that the dealership must have inflated my sales figures. Our general manager issued a statement to refute any talk of deception, but the allegations kept coming.

A woman selling luxury cars seems like an easy formula for a viral story. Some people claimed I was making 3 million yuan ($447,000) a year. Porsche pays its salespeople about 2,000 to 3,000 yuan in commission for every car sold. We can earn several hundred thousand yuan a year, but exceeding 1 million is extremely difficult. I make enough to give my family a comfortable life, and I do own an entry-level Porsche, but I’ve never made anything close to that amount.

Rumors also began circulating that I treat my customers to lavish dinners, which is pure innuendo. In reality, I work such long hours that I barely have time to eat, let alone entertain. I’ve never dated a customer or had any kind of inappropriate relationship. More than 60% of my buyers are women.

After people claimed that the dealership had exaggerated my sales figures, I set myself a goal: In 2024, I would sell another 170 cars, no matter what. On Dec. 31, I was still one car short of the target. But then a female customer walked in. I told her about my goal and offered her an attractive price on a model. It was win-win. A little after 3 p.m., she placed an order.

In 2025, I sold even more cars — 192. At this point, I felt I’d answered all my critics. But the online abuse had only gotten worse. Early that year, I discovered that someone had spread a sexually explicit rumor about me using an overseas social media platform. They claimed that I slept with customers, and posted as “proof” a fabricated video and audio recording using a different woman, whose face was concealed throughout.

I tried to brush it off and told myself not to take it too seriously, that this was just the price of publicity. But my friends urged me to report it to the police, so I ultimately filed a report.

At first, the explicit material mainly circulated on overseas websites and social media, so the impact was limited. But last October, things escalated. Someone shared a misleading video via (the instant-messaging platform) WeChat that combined one of my sales-promotion posters with footage of a woman with a completely different body shape to me undressing in a hotel room. There were also some demeaning AI-generated videos.

This time, the content spread incredibly fast among my circle. Friends, colleagues, and customers all started asking me what was going on. I felt like my world was collapsing. I again reported the videos to the police.

My phone number was also leaked, and I began receiving harassing calls, sometimes at one or two in the morning. A man in Qingdao called out of the blue to ask me to “come over and spend the night with him.” I recorded the conversation and sent it to the police, who issued the man a warning.

My WeChat was blowing up, too. I didn’t know whether a new friend request was from someone looking to buy a car or for something else. Some people would start by talking about cars and then steer the conversation toward asking me out. Others were more covert, asking me to record a video showing the “backseat legroom.” I knew what they really wanted. One person messaged, “I know it’s not you in those videos, but I fantasize that it is. Can you provide me with services?”

Social media is an important source of customers for me, so I couldn’t just ignore it. I still had to livestream. But when I was on camera introducing cars, I’d always see inappropriate comments pop up, like “I saw that video” or “You’re so hot.”

I even overheard some customers in the showroom talking about me. That hit me hard. I could no longer pretend that this online smear campaign wasn’t affecting me.

By now, the enthusiasm and confidence I used to have with customers was gone. I feared talking with people, paranoid that they must be gossiping about me.

At my lowest point, I briefly considered jumping from a building. I felt there was no point in being alive, that the world had become dark. It seemed everyone looked at me differently.

I told my supervisor that I had reached breaking point and needed time off. I was given three days, so I took my son back to my hometown, Yantai (about a three-hour drive from Qingdao), where we stayed at a beautiful guesthouse. I told myself that I had to keep living for my child and be responsible for my family. I had to clear my name.

When I returned to work, I was so anxious I couldn’t walk straight; my muscles were so tense I unconsciously leaned to one side. I wore a neck brace because even the slightest jolt during a test drive would send sharp pains up my back. I developed insomnia and tinnitus. At one point, I even struggled to speak.

Zero to hero

I started in auto sales in 2013, initially selling Audi and Lincoln cars in Beijing. I joined the Porsche dealership in downtown Qingdao in 2018. At first, my performance was so poor that I nearly lost my job.

Most of the salespeople had years of experience, and I was the youngest. Social media wasn’t the powerful tool it is today; business depended largely on walk-ins and referrals. For the first six months, I barely sold anything. At our 2019 New Year’s meeting, the sales manager asked everyone to share their goals for the year ahead. I said, “I want to survive at Porsche.”

I didn’t know the different models or specifications well enough. If a knowledgeable customer asked me a question, I felt intimidated and out of my depth. I started getting up at 6 a.m. to memorize technical information. I’d stand near colleagues and listen as they explained different cars. I studied the way they talked.

One colleague said I needed to dress better, so I started wearing tailored shirts and paying more attention to the cut and quality of everything I wore. In sales, it’s appearance, not skill, that makes the first impression. When I applied makeup, I felt more confident. Even though I had only four days off a month, I scheduled manicures and eyelash extensions, and sometimes skin booster injections.

I was a core consultant by my second year, became one of the dealership’s top performers in 2020, and was closing 17 deals a month in 2021.

Demand for foreign luxury cars has declined in the past two years, but my sales have continued to increase, largely because of social media. Of my 170 customers in 2023, 15% found me through social media. In 2025, it was 41%.

I also run a Porsche owners’ WeChat group with several hundred members. I organize monthly group events, such as camping trips, yacht outings, and nature walks. If I stop talking to someone as soon as a deal is done, they’ll always be just a customer. But if we spend time together, we can become friends. Referrals are an important part of my sales.

My typical workday runs from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. I’ve hardly taken any annual leave in all these years. If I go on vacation, customers disappear. I’m competitive by nature. I crave deals, performance figures, the feeling of being number one. I’m currently leading Porsche’s global sales rankings for September 2026, but someone could still overtake me.

The hardest word

When selling cars, effort usually pays off. But clearing a damaged reputation? That’s different.

Someone can casually share something about me online, and suddenly I have to spend money, time, and energy to respond. I have to pay lawyers and gather evidence. I filed 31 complaints to Douyin (China’s version of TikTok) alone between October 2025 and April this year about abusive messages, videos that used my image without permission, and people cloning my voice to promote get-rich-quick books.

I hand the most egregious messages directly to the police. One man I reported was initially very cocky. He seemed to think I was bluffing and wouldn’t be able to track him down. The authorities eventually found him, and he sent me an apology.

A 20-something Porsche owner in Qingdao forwarded some offensive material about me in a group chat and was given five days of administrative detention. I later accepted his apology, too, but then his family called my dealership’s customer service line to complain — they couldn’t understand why he still needed to be detained. I had no say in his punishment, but they obviously never stopped to think about how his actions might have affected me.

Even the outcomes of such cases haven’t halted the spread of false allegations; I still encounter vitriol during livestreams and on social media.

In July this year, the police gave me details of a 30-something man in the eastern Fujian province who’d been behind one of the AI-generated videos. I’d never met him. He was given 10 days of administrative detention in last October, but he never contacted me to apologize.

I think receiving punishment is not the same as saying sorry. This man was punished for spreading rumors, but what about the harm he caused? So I decided to file a civil lawsuit against him. All I want is for him to apologize and say explicitly that the woman in that video is not me.

Some friends urged me to press criminal charges, but I don’t want him to bear the consequences for the rest of his life. As a mother, I think about what would happen to his child if he were prosecuted. My lawyer says that if the civil case goes to trial, it could take up to two years. No matter how long it takes, I need to see it through.

Now I’m facing claims that the lawsuit is a publicity stunt, that I’m dredging things up again. In reality, just because the story is no longer in the headlines, it doesn’t mean those negative voices have disappeared from my life.

My son is in kindergarten. He doesn’t have a phone, and he knows nothing about what’s going on. All he knows is that his mom is the top salesperson at Porsche Qingdao. When I asked him what he wanted to do when he grew up, he said he wanted to sell cars. He’s proud of his mom.

What happens when he grows up, gets a phone, and sees what people have said about his mother? What if his classmates use the rumors against him? Who takes responsibility for that? The same goes for my parents. I want to clear my name for my family’s sake.

I still like being number one, but after everything that’s happened, my ambition has waned. I want to focus more on family and my health.

My life used to be a straight line between work and home, but over the past two years, I’ve started leaving more time for myself — meals with colleagues and friends, live music bars, taking my son to the mountains or the beach.

I wonder whether the rumors will disappear once the lawsuit is over. If people keep talking, there might be nothing more I can do. I’ve done everything within my power. If I win the case, that will be the end of it for me.

Women have sent me long messages of support, telling me how brave I am. Many professional women have shared that they have been the targets of similar smear campaigns and felt completely helpless. They ask me what they should do. I don’t know what to tell them.

As told to reporter Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Mu Qianwen at her workplace in Qingdao, Shandong province, August 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.title: Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019076/Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.content:
A northern Chinese village has announced it will spend 30 million yuan ($4.5 million) to recruit 100 character performers — known in China as NPCs, or non-playable characters — to interact with tourists. Successful hires will receive a range of salaries, with the highest reportedly reaching 10 million yuan a year.

Situ Town, a scenic spot located in Situ Village in the northern Shanxi province, will finance the recruitment partly through its publicity budget and partly from startup funds, Zhou Xiaoming, the village Party secretary, told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper on Sunday.

Once a coal town, Situ Village’s coal was gradually depleted by the end of the 20th century. To address its lack of resources, in 2009, the village built an agricultural ecological park — an area that combines farming with ecological protection and tourism — on a slag heap, which later grew into a highly rated national attraction. The village is known for its “iron flower” performances — a folk art in which local blacksmiths hurl molten iron into the air.

Zhou announced the NPC recruitment on Sept. 19 in a video posted on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. “No matter what your talent is, as long as you can make the tourists on stage have fun, and the audience below enjoy themselves, we’ll give you a platform — and 1 million, even 10 million (yuan),” he said in the video.

The plan quickly drew suspicion online, with some arguing that the money would be better spent investing in the scenic area itself, such as by adding amusement parks, building affordable guesthouses, improving green spaces, upgrading the “iron flower” show, or supporting local artists.

Previously, the scenic spot had announced a short video contest — also led by Zhou — in August in which 5 million yuan was offered to participants based on likes and views. Winning the top prize of 1 million yuan required 10 million likes and 300 million views.

Official data showed that in 2025, Situ Town received 2.2 million tourist visits, double the year prior, generating a total revenue of 350 million yuan. Meanwhile, tourism-related jobs grew from 500 to more than 1,000, the latter accounting for roughly a third of the village’s labor force.

Zhou noted, however, that the scenic spot has faced steep losses in recent years. “In 2023 we lost 500,000 yuan, in 2024 we lost 500,000 yuan, and in 2025 we lost money, but not much,” he said.

More than 7,000 people have applied for the NPC positions so far, with video interviews planned for over 50, Zhou said, adding that they have not yet set an application deadline. Zhou added that NPC salaries will range from 500,000 to 10 million yuan depending on the traffic they generate, the emotional value they bring to tourists, and tourists’ degree of satisfaction.

Recruiting NPCs is reportedly the scenic spot’s first step, with the goal of eventually cultivating its own homegrown talent. Its employees, Zhou said, are actually the biggest NPCs, but they need a good environment and role models to imitate — and those recruited with the 30 million yuan are meant to set an example.

Zeng Bowei, a professor at the Tourism College of Beijing Union University, told The Paper that the most important value of NPCs is transforming culture into something tourists can see and participate in.

“Although NPCs have been called ‘non-playable characters,’ their true value to scenic areas is precisely making each tourist into a player,” Zeng said, adding that with the right roles, stories, and cultural backing, NPCs can increase traffic in the long term.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.title: Danggit, mangroves tell story of coastal recovery in Prieto Diaz, Sorsogon
World.content:
Once facing severe decline, the 1,000-hectare Prieto Diaz mangrove forest in Sorsogon has been transformed by local residents into a thriving, community-managed sanctuary that protects both their livelihoods and the coastline

In Prieto Diaz, Sorsogon, danggit is more than a local delicacy. The rabbitfish that become the town’s dried fish thrive in nearly 1,000 hectares of seagrass meadows, part of a larger coastal ecosystem of seagrass, coral reefs, and mangroves that supports both the town’s livelihood and its marine life.

At the center of Prieto Diaz’s coastal conservation story is an ecosystem that has not always been this healthy. After decades of community-led protection, the town’s coastal habitats have recovered. Today, its mangrove forest spans more than 1,000 hectares, making it one of the largest community-managed mangrove forests in the Bicol region.

A Prieto Diaz local paddles his way through the mangrove forest. All photos by Marky Ramone Go

The transformation began in 1993, when the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) selected Prieto Diaz as a pilot site for a coastal rehabilitation project. The program eventually led to the formation of Seagrass, Mangrove, Corals (SEAMANCOR), a community organization whose members became bantay dagat (sea patrol), mangrove wardens, and guides for visitors.

The recovery also involved people who patrol the waters, guide visitors through the bakawan, the Tagalog word for mangroves, and monitor the coastal ecosystem.

The people behind Prieto Diaz’s mangrove recovery

For Victor Emata, a paddler and guide, that work started when he began seeing the mangroves return. He remembers the early rehabilitation efforts in the 1990s, led by the DENR in partnership with the Agta-Tabangnon community and other organizations across the barangays.

“Through the protection of the mangroves, we are able to preserve the different mangrove species that can thrive here, as well as the other species like different birds, that depend on the mangrove ecosystem,” he said in Filipino.

As the forest recovered, visitors began arriving, and Victor became one of the paddlers and guides introducing them to the bakawan.

For Montano Eva Jr., protecting the restored mangroves meant enforcing the rules. When fishing restrictions were introduced, community members organized sea patrols.

Some violators were caught and fined, and Montano says the number of fishermen operating inside the protected area eventually declined. Today, residents continue taking turns guarding the mangroves.

An aerial view of over 1,000 hectares of mangrove forests in Prieto Diaz, Sorsogon.

Manuel Domdom, a fisherman, guide and president of the local guides’ organization, says the bakawan has become a big part of the community’s daily life.

“The bakawan is an important source of income for the fishermen in our community,” he said. “For those of us who live here in Prieto Diaz, we believe the bakawan is also a blessing from God. That is why we feel a responsibility to preserve it for our town and for our people.”

That responsibility is not always easy. Manuel says some people still attempt to cut or collect trees despite regulations, while the area remains an important fishing ground.

For Manuel, protecting the bakawan also means protecting the community’s fishing livelihood and the coast itself from storm surges.

From restoration to community management

Restoration eventually gave way to a system of community management and, later, tourism.

According to Oriculo Despuig Jr., the municipality’s tourism officer-designate, the process began when DENR assessed the condition of the mangrove forest and worked with an indigenous peoples group. Members were encouraged to plant mangrove propagules in designated areas in exchange for payment.

This was followed by the formation of SEAMANCOR in 1994, a community-based organization composed largely of fishermen and their wives. DENR eventually awarded the group a 25-year Mangrove Stewardship Agreement, formalizing its role in managing and protecting the restored forest.

Fisherman Manuel Domdom (top) and the local tour guides (right) in Prieto Diaz.

Mangroves had been cut for charcoal and firewood, with some sold to nearby bakeries and others used by fishermen for fishpen construction. Illegal fishing, including the use of dynamite and poisonous substances, also threatened the coastal ecosystem.

The bantay dagat helped enforce the rules. Some fishermen were later trained as boat paddlers and guides for the community’s Mangrove Tours.

“Now the community, especially the coastal barangays, is aware that DENR regulations pertaining to mangroves are being implemented, especially for their protection and preservation,” says Despuig.

The community’s work eventually earned national recognition. The municipality was named the 2020 national grand winner of the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources’ (BFAR) Malinis at Masaganang Karagatan (MMK) program, receiving P30-million worth of fisheries livelihood projects. The incentive-based program recognizes communities for stronger coastal governance and sustainable marine resource management.

The lush fauna in the Prieto Diaz mangroves in Sorsogon.

Despuig hopes the mangrove forest will continue expanding over the next five to 10 years, eventually stretching from the poblacion toward Barangay Talisayan and the boundary with Sorsogon City.

For Fatit Guttierez Bayle, Prieto Diaz’s tourism officer, the future of the mangrove forest is personal.

Bayle said she chose to build her career in her hometown rather than pursue an opportunity with the United Nations: “As (Prieto Diaz’s) tourism officer, I did not give up a bigger life because I found a better one.” – Rappler.com

World.title: PH nets biggest Asian Games medal haul in 6 decades
World.content:
DELIVER. Carlos Yulo, EJ Obiena, and Jeus Yape banner the Philippines' medalists in the 2026 Asian Games.

Gymnastics star Carlos Yulo, pole vault stalwart EJ Obiena, and taekwondo standout Jeus Yape show the way for the Philippines' 29-medal finish in the 2026 Asian Games

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines recorded its biggest Asian Games haul in six decades as it wrapped up its campaign in the 20th edition in Nagoya, Japan, on Sunday, October 4, with four golds, nine silvers, and 16 bronzes for a total of 29 medals.

Although the country matched its 17th-place finish in 2023 in Hangzhou, China, it came away with its most medals since winning 42 in the 1966 staging in Bangkok, Thailand.

Gymnastics star Carlos Yulo showed the way for the delegation with two golds, while pole vault stalwart EJ Obiena and taekwondo standout Jeus Gabriel Derick Yape scored one each as they all claimed a piece of history.

Yulo ruled in men’s floor exercise and vault — the same events in which he captured his two Olympics golds — to become the first Filipino gymnast to win an Asian Games medal. In doing so, he completed his collection which includes titles from the World Championships, Asian Championships, World Cup, and Southeast Asian Games.

Obiena defended his men’s pole vault crown in record-breaking fashion, setting a new Asian Games mark of 5.91 meters as he emerged as only the fourth back-to-back champion in the event.

Then in a breakthrough in taekwondo, Yape became the Philippines’ first-ever Asian Games gold medalist in the sport following his triumph in the mixed individual virtual taekwondo, an event that debuted in the continental showpiece.

Yape secured the landmark gold for Philippine taekwondo after bagging bronze in the men’s individual poomsae.

With four golds, the country equaled its tally in 2023 and 2018 in Jakarta-Palembang, Indonesia.

The Philippine Olympic Committee and Philippine Sports Commission initially set an eight-gold target — a haul that, if achieved, would have marked the Philippines’ first time winning at least five golds in a single edition since its seven-gold showing in 1962.

But a fifth gold remained elusive, with the country enduring final losses in mixed martial arts, 3×3 basketball, sepak takraw, archery, boxing, taekwondo, and jiu-jitsu.

MMA fighter Jean Claude Saclag (men’s traditional -65kg) delivered the first silver followed by the Gilas Women team of Kacey dela Rosa, Kennan Ka, Amyah Espanol, and Maria Pasilang (women’s 3×3 basketball), the sepak takraw squad of Jean Marie Sucalit, Abegail Sinogbuhan, and Nelly Jay Salon (women’s double), archer Amaya Amparo Cojuangco (women’s individual compound), and taekwondo jin Juliana Mykhail Candelaria (women’s individual poomsae).

The Philippines stayed on track to break through that four-gold ceiling on Friday, October 2, as boxer Carlo Paalam (men’s 55kg) and taekwondo bets Tachiana Mangin (women’s -49kg) and Kurt Barbosa (men’s -58kg) all reached the finals, only to fall short in their respective title bouts.

Jiu-jitsu champion Alexandria Enriquez (women’s -63kg) stood as the Philippines’ last hope for a fifth gold on Saturday, October 3, but she suffered the same fate as Paalam, Mangin, and Barbosa following a narrow loss by advantage to Thailand’s Orapa Senatham.

The Philippines secured 16 bronzes, its most since also bagging 16 in 2002, with the likes of tennis star Alex Eala (women’s singles), gymnast Eldrew Yulo (men’s horizontal bar), weightlifter Albert Ian delos Santos (men’s 70kg), and athletics bets Victoria Bossong (women’s 800m) and John Cabang Tolentino (men’s 110m hurdles) also contributing to the tally.

As expected, China claimed the overall championship, doing so for the 12th consecutive edition as it dominated with 169 golds, 89 silvers, and 83 bronzes.

Host Japan finished second in the medal standings for the third straight time with 83 golds, 95 silvers, and 91 bronzes, while South Korea placed third with 39 golds, 43 silvers, and 68 bronzes.

Meanwhile, Thailand ended up as the best Southeast Asian nation, landing at seventh with 18 golds, 13 silvers, and 21 bronzes followed by Malaysia (9-7-16) at 11th, Indonesia (5-11-23) at 16th, then the Philippines.

World.title: Lula ahead in polls for Brazil’s first-round vote; runoff likely
World.content:
BRAZlL. A flag in support of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for presidential re-election, waves during a rally one day before the general election, in Brasilia, Brazil, October 3, 2026.

If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes on Sunday, October 4, the two frontrunners advance to a second-round runoff on October 25

SAO PAULO, Brazil – A series of polls on Saturday, October 3, showed Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva slightly ahead of Senator Flavio Bolsonaro before Sunday’s first-round vote, and a close race in a likely runoff between the leftist incumbent and his right-wing challenger.

If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes – which exclude blank and null ballots – on Sunday, October 4, the two frontrunners advance to a second-round runoff on October 25.

CNT/MDA POLL

First round (valid votes): Lula 47.8%, Bolsonaro 42.1%, Augusto Cury 3.6%, Ronaldo Caiado 3.4%, Renan Santos 1.7%, Romeu Zema 0.9%

Runoff: Lula 47.3%, Bolsonaro 43.1%

MDA surveyed 2,007 people from September 30 to October 2; margin of error of 2.2 percentage points

DATAFOLHA

First round (valid votes): Lula 45%, Bolsonaro 42%, Caiado 4%, Santos 3%, Cury 3%, Zema 1%

Runoff: Lula 47%, Bolsonaro 46%

Datafolha surveyed 4,006 people from October 2-3; margin of error 2 percentage points

QUAEST POLL

First round (valid votes): Lula 46%, Bolsonaro 45%, Cury 3%, Santos 3%, Caiado 3%

Runoff: Bolsonaro 44%, Lula 42%

Quaest surveyed 3,702 people from October 2-3; margin of error 2 percentage points

ATLASINTEL/BLOOMBERG POLL

First round (valid votes): Lula 47%, Bolsonaro 44.1%, Santos 4.6%, Cury 2.1%, Caiado 1.4%

Runoff: Lula 47.6%, Bolsonaro 47.4%

AtlasIntel surveyed 4,945 people from September 27 to October 2; margin of error 1 percentage point

– Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Largest’ POGO crackdown of 2026: Hundreds of foreigners caught in Zamboanga Sibugay
World.content:
The Bureau of Immigration says those apprehended during simultaneous operations in Zamboanga Sibugay were 'mostly Chinese'

MANILA, Philippines – Authorities on Friday, October 2, apprehended at least 244 foreigners in two municipalities in Zamboanga Sibugay in what the Bureau of Immigration (BI) said was the “largest” crackdown on Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) so far in 2026.

The simultaneous operations targeted suspected POGO-related activities in Barangays Kimos of Siay town, and Barangay Tandiong Muslim of Alicia town, the BI said in a statement on Sunday, October 4.

In Siay, authorities nabbed 113 foreigners, including 110 Chinese, 2 Cambodians, and 1 Hong Konger. Another 131 were apprehended in Alicia, mostly Chinese, along with Malaysians, Indonesians, and Burmese.

The BI said the identities and nationalities remain subject to verification. The raids were conducted by the BI Intelligence Division and its Mindanao units, with the National Bureau of Investigation and Armed Forces of the Philippines.

The foreigners are being investigated for alleged immigration violations, including working without the required work visa, and, in some cases, illegal entry. The BI also cited their alleged involvement in illegal POGO-related online activities.

POGO. Authorities apprehend foreigners during simultaneous operations against illegal POGO activities in Zamboanga Sibugay on October 2, 2026. Photo from the Bureau of Immigration

In Siay, authorities also seized 78 computer monitors, laptops, cellular SIM cards, and around 3,000 mobile phones. The equipment are believed to have been used in an organized online scam operations.

The foreigners will undergo deportation proceedings for their alleged violations of Philippine immigration laws. Those issued deportation orders will be placed on the BI’s blacklist and barred from reentering the Philippines.

The operation is part of the government’s continuing crackdown on POGOs activities, which President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ordered banned during his third State of the Nation Address in 2024. In October 2025, Marcos signed Republic Act No. 12312, or the Anti-POGO Act of 2025, which prohibits offshore gaming operations and the establishment or operation of POGO sites in the country.

But POGO operations have continued despite the ban. Authorities have carried out raids and arrests in different parts of the country in recent years, targeting suspected illegal offshore gaming operations.

BI Commissioner Joel Viado, however, said that his agency is “firmly implementing the government’s policy.”

“We will continue to enforce our immigration laws against foreign nationals who violate the conditions of their stay and ensure that the Philippines is not used as a base for illegal activities,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Dr. Sabrina Berger-Marcelo brings Filipino flavor to space science
World.content:
‘There's actually a huge history of indigenous Filipinos doing astronomy, and we just don't talk about it,’ says Fil-Am astrophysicist Dr. Sabrina Berger-Marcelo

Ever heard someone explain the formation of black holes by comparing it to the classic Filipino sinigang recipe?

This is something only Dr. Sabrina Berger-Marcelo could pull off. Almost instantly, the Filipino-American astrophysicist caught the attention of her listeners during a talk on astronomy in Manila.

For someone who grew up in the US, Berger-Marcelo still makes sure that her teachings reflect her Filipino roots.

“My mom was born in Palawan and immigrated when she was in her teens. Growing up, I was confused about my background,” Berger-Marcelo shared. “My mom had a lot of trauma here as a child — that was one of the reasons why she left, so she’s never wanted to come back. Not because of the Philippines, but because of her family life here. It was really hard to connect to my culture.”

“My family on my dad’s side is just my grandma, so I basically just grew up with my Filipino family. I think, actually, it’s helped me in astrophysics because I just learned this word: kapwa. My grandma and my mom know how to build community.”

Dr. Sabrina Berger-Marcelo hopes to inspire young Filipino students to pursue science.

At 30 years old, Berger-Marcelo visited the Philippines for the first time, accompanied by her 84-year-old grandmother, whom she’s very close with.

“Growing up in the US, there were a lot of opportunities to get involved and do research. That’s one of the reasons why I wanted to come to Manila: to meet Filipino astrophysicists, help diversify astronomy, and find out what people are doing here,” she said.

Berger-Marcelo is a PhD candidate in physics at the University of Melbourne, Australia. Her interests in astronomy, astrophysics, instrumentation, cosmology, and other branches of science have led her to various paths, including indigenous Filipino astronomy.

“There’s actually a huge history of indigenous Filipinos doing astronomy, and we just don’t talk about it. It’s in your blood,” she said. “In Australia, there are big programs dedicated to indigenous Australian astronomy, so it’s slowly evolving.”

Berger-Marcelo graduated with a bachelor’s degree in astrophysics at UC Berkeley in 2018, then took her masters in physics at McGill University in 2022, before becoming a PhD candidate at the University of Melbourne.

In 2019, she worked as a data science intern at NASA Ames, a major research center of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration in California, then later took some time off to travel.

Music dreams

Like many Filipinos, Berger-Marcelo also loves singing.

“I actually grew up wanting to be a musician. I loved singing. I wanted to be like Olivia Rodrigo. In college, they made me choose between music and astronomy, and so I said, ‘Okay, I’ll do astronomy instead,’ because I always knew I was interested in it,” she shared.

“I love it because the problems that I get to work on, I feel like, are some of the most interesting ever. They’re so cool. I just gave a talk on black holes; it doesn’t affect anything we do on Earth, but it’s still really interesting.”

During her talk in Manila, Berger-Marcelo shared why she enjoys teaching.

“In astrophysics, it tends to be very individual — everyone for themselves, a very self-absorbed, narcissistic field,” she said. “I think that’s been one of the greatest things I’ve learned from being Filipino: connecting with people and trying to do it as a group rather than just being on my own. I want to bring other people up with me.”

Berger-Marcelo was a lecturer at the Hackbright Academy and also conducted workshops and private tutoring. So it’s no surprise that she wanted to do the same in her mother’s home province.

“That’s one of the things I want to do in Palawan, at Palawan State University. There’s no astrophysics program in Palawan,” she said.

But then, Berger-Marcelo understands the many gut issues Filipinos have to face.

“Coming here, I think, ‘wow, how can I be studying astrophysics when there are all these people that can barely get to work because of flooding?’ There are so many major political issues and poverty,” she said. “It’s really hard to reconcile, and I don’t think I have an answer for it yet.”

Access to astronomy

Still, Berger-Marcelo noted the importance of pursuing science.

“Everyone should have the opportunity, but simultaneously, we need to work on ways to do astrophysics while also addressing problems like climate change or poverty in the Philippines,” she said.

“First, you need to make sure that kids can get to school and have enough food to study. Kids need to be emotionally and physically healthy to then be able to study.”

“There’s so much potential, there are so many amazing astrophysics students [here],” she added. “They deserve to have access to astronomy just like the rest of the world.”

For now, Berger-Marcelo hopes to continue using her voice and knowledge to inspire future scientists.

“I’m really proud of my mentorship and how I’ve given back to science through science communication and mentoring,” she said. “I care a lot about that — that’s the whole reason I’m here.” – Rappler.com

Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

World.title: [Tech Thoughts] Building safe online spaces requires whole-of-society approach
World.content:
The Safe Online Spaces forum tackles different aspects of online safety, from legal and technological issues to community and family-related efforts, to foster safe spaces for children

At a PLDT and Smart event dedicated toward starting the conversation on building safer online spaces for children, I saw members of the community at large discuss ways on how they could foster safety in the digital age, especially given reports of school shootings and the spread of child sexual abuse material.

The Safe Online Spaces forum, held Tuesday, September 29, convened telecommunications companies, law enforcement agencies, mental health professionals, parents and other stakeholders. They held three panel discussions on different aspects of online safety, from legal and technological issues to community and family-related efforts, to help bring about these safe spaces for kids and teens.

As a member of the media who did not have a child, I felt out of place during the proceedings, but as the day went on, I felt like everyone had a part to play in fostering a safe environment for the young.

PLDT chief operating officer and chief technology officer Menardo Jimenez said during the forum’s opening speech that the problem of keeping and maintaining safe online spaces for the young was one “that can’t be solved by telcos or government playing God.”

MENARDO JIMENEZ. PLDT chief operating officer and chief technology officer Menardo Jimenez speaks at the Safe Online Spaces forum on September 29, 2026.

JImenez added that such a task “will be solved by the sectors in this room talking with each other, understanding what the problem is, and coming up with a solution to solve this problem together.”

There were three panel discussions around specific themes.

The first panel tried to define the safeguards by explaining existing regulations and policies or basically, what can and can’t be done in the process of protecting children online.

During this panel, lawyer Jaye dela Cruz-Bekema, chief legislative staff officer for the Office of Senator Risa Hontiveros brought up the Batang Ligtas Act — formerly Senate Bill No. 1819 or the Sagip Bata Act — which the Senate ratified recently.

Word of the impending ratification at that time was met with applause, and it was nice seeing political will being celebrated and enacted in this way.

The second panel featured Bea Bautista, TikTok’s communications lead for the Philippines, Malaysia, and Thailand; national esports athlete and Philippine Tekken champion Alexandre “AK” Laverez; AK’s father, lawyer Ronie Laverez; and tech journalist Jayvee Fernandez,

During this panel, they shared their views on how to identify and address harmful content, prevent the amplification of such content, and deal with possible online threats. This included reminding people that tech companies, both for the devices being used and the apps on said devices, had built-in features to address parental concerns.

These, however, required an investment of attention and time from parents, who may not be as tech-savvy as their kids. One of the potential problem points in creating safe spaces online is that sometimes, parents or other adults don’t know how to navigate the online world as deftly as their children.

To that end, the final panel discussion dealt with how specific societal units — families, schools, and the communities at large — can strengthen children’s digital resilience and provide support when online threats or harms occur.

In this discussion, it was commonly brought up that parents needed to step up, so to speak, to be there for their kids, even if they don’t have the tech skills required to police kids’ gadgets 24/7.

This panel brought out strategies for parents, teachers, and other community members to allow them to become the safe spaces kids need in times of crisis. It was touching, even though it also felt like it was meant for those privileged enough to be available for children to seek out.

This is something I felt was left not entirely addressed, as not all parents can be there for their kids, especially if they’re OFWs separated by distance. But there may be other times for people to tackle that topic on. Only so much can be done in four hours.

The Safe Online Spaces forum last Tuesday aims to be the first of many such events, allowing different stakeholders to share ideas and ask questions of the community on promoting online safety for children and teens.

Jimenez, during his opening speech, acknowledged that there were limitations to what a telecommunications company could do, and simply reacting to online threats will not solve the issue of online harm; the issue will also not be solved by any one company alone.

He added, “Our role as PLDT is to use our network and our reach to help reduce these digital risks, and to gather different perspectives to come up with clear priorities and practical recommendations as we move forward.”

As a member of the media, I suppose I also have a part to play: that of sharing what threats are out there, and what a whole-of-society approach can do to build better online spaces for everyone. – Rappler.com

World.title: OpenAI safety employee quits, says ‘time for trial and error is over’
World.content:
OPENAI. A keyboard is placed in front of a displayed OpenAI logo in this illustration taken February 21, 2023.

A former OpenAI safety employee who recently resigned criticized the company’s approach to AI safety, arguing that a fast-paced culture focused on rapid development increases the risk of failures.

Writing in “I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken,” published by the Atlantic on Saturday, October 3, David Robinson said AI companies, including OpenAI, were not being “nearly careful enough” and should place greater emphasis on safety expertise and research before developing more capable systems.

“The time for trial and error is over,” Robinson wrote, arguing that advanced AI systems require safeguards more akin to those used in industries such as nuclear power and aviation.

Robinson said OpenAI relies heavily on what it calls “iterative deployment,” releasing systems and strengthening safeguards when problems emerge.

The comments add to a debate within the AI industry over whether companies are moving too quickly to develop increasingly powerful systems. OpenAI and rival Anthropic have faced scrutiny after incidents in which safety controls failed, or experimental systems behaved unexpectedly.

Robinson, who said he spent 3-1/2 years at OpenAI, helped draft the company’s preparedness framework and oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches, wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.”

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement.

Robinson also warned that AI capabilities were advancing faster than researchers’ understanding of alignment, a field focused on ensuring AI systems act in accordance with human goals and values. – Rappler.com

World.title: 3 Japanese scholars examine Filipino migration story in UAE
World.content:
Japanese professors specializing in Philippine studies launch a pioneering book that documents the history and daily lives of OFWs in the United Arab Emirates

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates – Why would three college professors from Japan write a book on overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) in UAE?

Drs. Naomi Hosoda, Masako Ishii, and Akiko Watanabe said they’ve always been interested to study the Philippines — to learn more about its people, and perhaps, provide the world a better understanding of the Filipinos.

Hosoda, who has been in the Philippines for seven years — four in Manila where she worked as a journalist for the Manila Shimbun from 1994 to 1998, and some more years in Samar where she, then a doctorate student, conducted ethnographic research on the Samarnon migration — has long been curious to learn about the Filipino movement elsewhere around the world.

“My interest in the Philippines began when I was a graduate student in Canada and chose the country as the focus of my research topic. Why do so many Filipinos go abroad to work in such a wide range of professions?“ she asked.

Dr. Akiko Watanabe (third from left) at an elementary school in Bicol. Contributed photo

Ishii, who, from March 1995 to March 1996 was based in General Santos City and Sarangani Province, has, since 2022, spent more than a year in total in Cotabato City monitoring the transition process of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).

Watanabe, meanwhile, has stayed mostly in Manila from 2001 to 2006, and traveled to different places in Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao.

All holding doctorates and specializing in Philippine studies, the three Japanese scholars are set to launch a book about Filipino migration to the UAE. Alongside seven contributing authors, the book explores why the country has become one of the top destinations for OFWs.

They decided to write the book to document how the lives of Filipinos in the Gulf have transformed over the years. They noted that it has been over 50 years since the Philippines first began exporting labor to alleviate economic stagnation at home and meet the growing demand for workers in the Middle East during the 1970s oil boom.

“Gulf cities like Dubai have experienced drastic changes since the 1970s. But what about the people living there?” Hosoda asked.

The professors highlighted that while existing literature covers the daily lives of Indian, Arab, and European expatriates in the Gulf, no books have focused specifically on the Filipino community.

“We chose the UAE as our case study site because it is where we conducted most of our research, and it is widely seen as a model country for urban development driven by a global workforce,” Hosoda said.

“The nexus of the Philippines as the sending country and the UAE as the receiving county, we imagined, could be a very interesting case study for us to learn how a massive human flow could transform both urban spaces and migrant people.”

Filipinos comprise the fifth biggest number of foreigners in the UAE at one million, according to official estimates.

“We also need to emphasize the fact that we were able to conduct research in the UAE because of the kindness of people we encountered there, especially Filipinos living in the country,” Hosoda said.

The book, entitled Filipino Migration to the United Arab Emirates: Trajectories of Navigating Long-term Temporariness, also features seven contributors — five Filipinos and two French.

It has 12 chapters discussing subjects from origins of the migration to the UAE, to Filipino entrepreneurship and what lies ahead, among others. Work on the book started in 2024.

Dr. Naomi Hosoda (top), one of the editors of the book ‘Filipino Migration to the United Arab Emirates: Trajectories of Navigating Long-term Temporarines.’

No strangers

The three scholars are no strangers to the contemporary Philippine setup.

“I had been studying about Muslims in Manila and then explored my focus on Filipinos in the Gulf. It’s partly to return the favor for all the kindness they’ve extended to me, and partly because I want to further raise/change their standing in Japan and around the world,” said Watanabe.

Ishii also finds it interesting to note the economic relations between Japan and southern Philippines, and the armed conflict there.

“Mindanao is an island from which Japan has long imported timber, bananas, pineapples, and tuna. Japan and the southern Philippines have therefore long maintained significant historical and economic ties,” she said.

“Nevertheless, the armed conflicts that have taken place in this neighboring country remain relatively little known among the Japanese public. This is one of the reasons why I have continued to study and teach about the southern Philippines.”

Ishii first learned more about the country in 1989, during which she found out about the war in the southern Philippines.

“Since then, I have become interested in studying the armed conflicts in a country neighboring Japan,” she said.

“I have also learned that the armed conflict and the resulting displacement had expanded the physical range of movement of Muslim women. Some eventually began traveling abroad to work as overseas Filipino workers. However, many of them experienced mistreatment while working in the Middle East,” Ishii added.

“This, in turn, compelled me to document the experiences of Muslim Filipina domestic workers and to draw attention to the challenges they faced.”

Hosoda, meanwhile, has been keen to pass on what she has learned to her students.

“After finishing my master degree, I became a journalist and then a doctoral student in Japan. Finally, I became a researcher, and write books and papers. Basically, I have been researching the same topic ever since,” she said.

“I teach my students in Japan and elsewhere what I have learned from my research because the lives of the Filipino migrants I have encountered teach us many important life lessons, such as values, faith, community, nation, and history.”

Filipinology

What’s even more interesting is why their students are taking up Filipinology.
