Once again, as we discussed above, far from everything has been rectified yet.

Alkhas Gagulia: And what specifically needs to be rectified?

Adgur Ardzinba: The persecution of citizens. That is what causes harm. On the whole, however, the agenda has shifted. All those harmful initiatives have receded into the background. Incidentally, they themselves acknowledge that those were not beneficial. Right now, as I see it, very broad opportunities are open before us, before our small country. By the way, similar opportunities were open to us right after recognition, during that flourishing period. Later, to some extent, everything experienced a slight decline, but now there is such a surge. We cited the economic forum as an example. Several federal ministers, governors, heads of republics, and the First Deputy Chief of Staff came to Abkhazia, to the city of Sukhum, to discuss the development of our economy. Those are enormous opportunities. In other words, a tremendous amount of attention is being paid to our relatively small country in this regard. And that ought to be capitalized on in the best sense. I do not see that same level of initiative from our side—from the authorized bodies and structures—to make full use of all this. Because such chances may not present themselves again in the future. Russia is a vast country. It is navigating a very complex period right now. Further escalation could follow, and people will focus on solving their own problems. Why should they travel with entire government delegations to Abkhazia, sit with us here in Sukhum, and try to help us figure out how to make our lives better? That is primarily our own responsibility. There is transportation infrastructure—the train has started running, work is underway at the border, the airport has begun operations. Most importantly, what genuinely pleases me is that very positive information about Abkhazia is circulating across the Russian Federation’s media space. There is outright promotion of Abkhazia as a resort destination. That provides a huge impetus for the growth of our tourism sector and the overall economy.

Yet, returning to those matters: when such promotion is taking place and top officials are calling Abkhazia an ally, prioritizing it, we must work proactively right here on the ground. Do you understand? Rather than simply trailing behind, picking up scattered initiatives, and failing to carry even those through to completion. That is what I am concerned about. And I will tell you why I am so concerned, Georgi. Alkhas, 2008 brought recognition. Following that, starting in 2010, Abkhazia was provided with financial assistance. Substantial financial assistance—exceeding one billion dollars. However, those funds dissolved across various projects. Back then, too, there were no clear priorities or plans. As a result, where we had the opportunity to completely resolve the situation—at least within the energy sector, given the possibilities that opened up at the time—we would not be facing these problems today. We would not be talking about a deficit today had we utilized that opportunity wisely back then. Therefore, I simply do not want history to repeat itself this time, which is why I am so concerned. The fact that there is a warming of relations, a mutual understanding, and that people are frankly paying far more attention to Abkhazia than before—that is a reality. That is a fact. The other question is what we ourselves are capable of proposing and what we ourselves are capable of achieving; that is where the problem lies.

Georgi Berzenia: And what role do you see for Sergei Vladimirovich Kiriyenko?

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, I already noted above that he is a person… First of all, let us be frank. Every official possesses a certain degree of capability. There are a number of leaders in the Russian Federation, and they all have differing levels of capability. As far as I can see, this individual possesses quite substantial capabilities. Within the scope of those capabilities, he is doing everything possible to assist Abkhazia and to involve as many federal leaders in this work as possible. Let us recall—we live here after all—past periods. Let us recall the period from 2020 to 2025. How many federal leaders visited Abkhazia over those five years? The Minister of Sports came. The Minister of Economic Development came a couple of times. To my memory, that was all. Yet now, in a span of a year and a half… Again, when these people visit, our officials and top leaders have the opportunity to sit down over a cup of coffee and discuss specific issues. I assure you, I know the situation in Russia: not every governor or regional leader has the opportunity to sit down with ministers and drink coffee whenever they wish. Yet we have that opportunity. And all of this is thanks to this new team.

At the same time, I cannot fail to mention our people here. Had our people not stood up in 2024—and throughout the period leading up to November 2024—to defend their core interests, none of this would exist. Absolutely no changes would have occurred. Had that entire proposed agenda passed quietly and silently, no one would have given us a second thought. The Abkhazian people courageously defended their interests, their core interests. And the Abkhazian people—who, by the way, are exceptionally friendly toward the Russian people—stood up, protected their interests, and drew attention to themselves. That commands respect, and I observe that respect coming from these leaders.

Georgi Berzenia: Speaking of the development of relations between Abkhazia and Russia, I have also recalled with several guests in this studio the 2014 treaty. It was signed more than 12 years ago now, back in 2014, so ten years have passed. Political events were taking place back then as well, yet no review was conducted, no outcomes were summarized, and it was extended automatically. How would you evaluate these 10 to 12 years of that treaty, and where do we go from here? Does it require refinement, or is a new treaty or a new phase in relations with Russia needed?

Adgur Ardzinba: The treaty is quite thoroughly developed. Moreover, when it was adopted, as you remember, there was a certain degree of opposition here as well. The very people who in the recent past accused us of being pro-Western and anti-Russian were themselves blocking the border to prevent that treaty from being signed, to speak specifically. But the treaty itself became a foundational document following the 2008–2009 post-recognition agreements. Coming after them in 2014, it served as a foundational document that touched upon economic forms of interaction, social matters, and other areas.

Of course, time moves forward. It keeps moving forward. And I am certain that we have not fully realized the potential of that agreement. There is still much to discuss within it. However, Georgi, we can also recall other agreements. We have a whole host of agreements that remain unfulfilled. If we return to defense and security, within the framework of signed agreements regarding joint efforts to strengthen the state border along the Ingur River, nothing has been done—neither from our side nor from the side of the Russian Federation. Furthermore, matters regarding the joint group of forces in that direction remain poorly developed.

If we speak about the economy, we have an agreement on the mutual protection of investments. In that direction, too, we need to look at what genuinely concerns investors from the Russian Federation—not those who sought to create a tailored, exclusive climate for themselves, but regular businesspeople. And they do not necessarily have to be billionaires; they can simply be people capable of investing 10 million rubles, or 20 million rubles, conditionally speaking. We need to communicate with them and examine the rules and standards that exist in the Russian Federation. They could be implemented here. For instance, the public service system in the Russian Federation—the MFC system, “My Documents”—which several years ago was announced to start operating here, has seen nothing done. That system is objectively considered one of the best and most efficient in the world. So, please, let us integrate it here.

Georgi Berzenia: In Russia, which…

Adgur Ardzinba: Yes, in Russia. We all use it, as we are Russian citizens. It is an incredibly convenient system. As for tax administration, one of the most effective systems has been established in Russia. That is a reality; you can see it in all surveys. Russia has specific criteria for evaluating the investment attractiveness of various regions. At the St. Petersburg forum every year, if memory serves, a specific rating and classification is assigned to one region or another. That, too, is a positive thing. Well, as I mentioned above, the entire local economy resides in the districts.

Georgi Berzenia: In September, elections to the State Duma will take place in the Russian Federation. These elections will also be held on the territory of Abkhazia, allowing citizens of Abkhazia who are simultaneously citizens of Russia to participate. What is your view on the significance of these elections for citizens of Abkhazia, and should citizens take part in them?

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, look, posters reading “Abkhazia’s Voice Matters to Russia” are currently hanging all across Abkhazia, right? If Russia, which has provided us with such immense support all these years, sends a message that our voice matters to Russia, is it really that difficult to go and vote if it truly is so important? And it is important, first of all because we are almost all Russian citizens, for the most part, when provided with such an opportunity… I remember in past periods there were issues with the number of polling stations and so forth; as far as I can see, it is being approached more systematically now. Of course, people should go and vote. Why not? It isn’t that difficult to do. If people say it is important, and one can demonstrate civic engagement in that sense, I believe one should go and vote.

As for whom to vote for, that is a separate question. I do not have the right to engage in campaigning here right now, but one should also look at the retrospective. Various political forces have existed throughout Abkhazia’s history; you are younger, but Alkhas and I remember the blockade times and the post-blockade period when the new team came in. We must also understand for ourselves which political force is minded to help Abkhazia, and which political force recognized Abkhazia’s independence. These are different teams with different viewpoints, so here too, I believe our choice is straightforward; we simply need to understand it all.

Alkhas Gagulia: We have spoken at length about relations with Russia—it is our strategic partner—but an event took place in the Turkish parliament recently. People view it in different ways, and opinions vary. In my view, it is a very landmark event when 30% of the Turkish parliament raised the issue of ending the isolation of Abkhazia. Recognition was not on the table, and there were differing opinions regarding the motives behind that speech. It turned out to be primarily the opposition party. But anticipating your answer, I would say—as one Chinese sage or general secretary put it—it doesn’t matter what color the cat is, as long as it catches mice. What is your view on this initiative, and what, in your opinion, actually happened there?

Adgur Ardzinba: Alkhas, your late relative Gennady Leonidovich Gagulia once told me a story about cats and mice too. He said that when you try to play political cat-and-mouse, make sure that you are not the mouse. Yes, of course, it is a positive signal. Incidentally, our organization issued a statement on this matter. The signal itself is positive, even if, as some note, it represents an element of internal political struggle to attract our large diaspora and secure votes. Even if that is the case, it remains positive. It shows the role and significance of our diaspora, which we utilize very weakly—and not only in Turkey. But that is a vast, separate topic. Therefore, it is a positive signal, and that is how we assess it. However, actions and deeds matter most. Words are fine—we approve and welcome them—but deeds are what count. Russia went ahead in 2008 and established diplomatic relations with Abkhazia, recognizing our independence. Those are real actions.

Alkhas Gagulia: There was a caveat there, if I am not mistaken, that there was no question of any recognition.

Adgur Ardzinba: When politicians speak about it to attract votes, again, it is still a good thing that the topic of Abkhazia and ending its isolation is being discussed, forming a positive agenda to attract votes. But I very much hope it will not remain mere words.

Alkhas Gagulia: Adgur Ardzinba of 2024 and Adgur Ardzinba of 2026. What advice would you give today to the person you were back then?

Adgur Ardzinba: That is a good question; I hadn’t thought about it. That is actually too short a time frame. I wouldn’t have changed much.

Georgi Berzenia: Significant events have occurred. First of all, the elections. They surely brought about some…

Alkhas Gagulia: Takeaways from the elections. What mistakes were made?

Adgur Ardzinba: Look, yes, of course, we made a whole host of mistakes. But it is not a given that if I had told my former self to avoid those mistakes, other mistakes wouldn’t have been made instead. Mistakes are part of any process.

Alkhas Gagulia: Nor is it a given that he would have listened?

Adgur Ardzinba: I will tell you this: it has been a rather interesting period of time. I consider myself fortunate. I feel fortunate in that—and I say this sincerely—the Abkhazian people, a portion of the Abkhazian people, and a substantial portion at that, entrusted me with this responsible mission. That is a great, immense honor. There is nothing above that, Alkhas. Any obstacles or hurdles are minor by comparison. When serving your people is not mere rhetoric but a reality—if done sincerely and from the heart—there are no obstacles. That is the highest honor.

Therefore, what would I advise my former self? I would advise him not to doubt, because a person always experiences doubt when faced with immense difficulties. Alkhas, we speak about this so casually now. For instance, when people entered the building in November 2024, some said they shouldn’t have entered, while others asked what would have happened had they not entered. Someone had to take responsibility. Other politicians were there; we were all together. While we achieved a certain goal on the one hand, on the other hand, during all those days—and I slept inside that building for three nights to ensure people wouldn’t clash with one another—it was a difficult period, followed by the election process.

Naturally, any person experiences doubt. Our recent presidential elections were unique—they were engaging and event-filled. But those elections were particularly interesting because our team faced such a formidable, serious opponent equipped with vast resources. When you have a very serious opponent, it mobilizes you immensely. I assure you, had that not been the case, the elections might have turned out very dull. Instead, they unfolded the way they did.

Alkhas Gagulia: To be honest, I dream of dull elections for all branches of power.

Adgur Ardzinba: We are speaking about personality and perception right now. Yes, I too dream that our country, like Switzerland, could have dull elections. But if we talk about what existed then versus now, it has been a very fascinating period during which I came to respect my people even more. I feel immense pride in being part of this nation—small in numbers perhaps, but possessing a grand spirit and a vast heart—a people that cannot be intimidated, no matter how hard anyone tries. And with such a spirit in our hearts, we are bound for success.

I am absolutely certain that we will succeed in everything. All those misunderstandings and unpleasantries, including those in relations between Abkhazia and Russia, are entirely surmountable. I am confident that… Look, we are talking about certain incidents right now, and they are indeed unpleasant. Yet we had a period when the entire country was under a blockade for six to seven years. We were under a blockade—the whole country. Now we are talking about a few individuals being unable to travel, whereas back then it was the entire country.

Even then… Vladislav Grigorievich Ardzinba—for which I will always be grateful to him—was a great, exceptionally wise man. He always maintained that we must orient ourselves toward a union with the Russian Federation; that time would pass, people would change, and understanding would arrive. And he was right. Although you remember, Alkhas, how many different proposals there were, delegation after delegation, yet we did not deviate from our path. All these misunderstandings taking place are simply part of the process. Just as there are mistakes on our side, there are mistakes on theirs as well.

I am confident that everything will be fine. The main thing is to remain vigilant. Times are very dangerous. I will repeat it endlessly: defense and security.

Alkhas Gagulia: Well, I want to say thank you for today’s broadcast, for coming to join us so that a thorough conversation could take place on all the questions that interested us. The only thing I would like to add, of course, is that while we spoke about priority tasks—about defense and education—all of this stems from a single overarching priority: our sovereignty and our independence. If that serves as the main guidepost, everything else is meant to serve that exact priority. There are no other options. You mentioned my age twenty times today; in any case, my generation accepts nothing less. We lost far too many people for this land, and it is thanks to them that we stand on this land today. That is what I want to say to every single politician, without exception, on both sides. Thank you for the broadcast and for coming. I look forward to our next meetings.

Adgur Ardzinba: Thank you, friends. I believe that while our conversation was lengthy, it was candid, and we answered a number of questions. If we missed anything, I think we will have another opportunity to meet. As for sovereignty, Alkhas, that concerns not only your generation. The younger generation and the youth—the rising generation with whom I interact—see no other path across all generations than the building of an independent, sovereign Abkhazian state in Abkhazia. If anyone thinks otherwise, that would be their mistake. All of us have stood, are standing, and will continue to stand for this. Fundamentally, our entire conversation has been dedicated to strengthening that sovereignty, to making our state less vulnerable.

Today, our state is vulnerable. Let us be frank. To eliminate these weak points, we need systemic work, the establishment of priorities, societal consolidation, and defense to preserve our territory, as well as our language—which you raised, Georgi—and our culture. All of this is vital, because knowing a language alone does not make you Abkhaz. The upcoming parliamentary elections are also crucial; the quality and substantive content of that body are of great importance. All of this, as was rightly stated, Alkhas, exists in order to preserve, strengthen, and pass down. Thank you.

Georgi Berzenia: Thank you for an engaging conversation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: ‘We will decide in the coming months’: Pashinyan on choosing model for Armenia’s new nuclear power plant
World.content:
Pashinyan on building a new nuclear power plant in Armenia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has announced a change in the government’s position on the technology and design of a new nuclear power plant.

“I have said dozens of times before that we do not need anything more [powerful] than a modular nuclear power plant. That was our position. But now we have to understand that a modular plant will most likely not be enough to meet our needs,” Pashinyan said.

He explained that the government changed its position because of the construction of AI factories. Armenia now needs to import electricity to meet their power requirements.

Discussions continue over which technology would best suit the new nuclear power plant. The Armenian government expects to make a decision on the issue by the end of 2027.

A day earlier, the prime minister met a delegation led by Alexey Likhachev, director general of the state-owned Rosatom corporation. They discussed proposals from the Russian side.

Armenia is currently working to extend the operating life of the Metsamor nuclear power plant until 2036. Russia has taken part in efforts to extend the plant’s operating life and modernise it throughout this period. The plant originally entered service in 1977.

At the same time, Yerevan is discussing the construction of a new nuclear power plant with several countries, including the US. The prime minister has repeatedly said in recent months that the nuclear power issue is not a geopolitical choice for Armenia: “We will choose the proposal that serves us best.”

Pashinyan does not rule out accepting the Russian proposal

Speaking about the upcoming decision on the technology for the new nuclear power plant, the prime minister stressed that before Armenia signed memorandums of understanding with the US on 8 August 2025, Armenia had a surplus of electricity.

“We had to think about where to direct this surplus energy. A year later, Armenia had become a country with an electricity deficit,” he said.

According to Nikol Pashinyan, this resulted from the construction of two AI factories in Armenia during that period:

“The point is that, given the scale of the investment projects already approved, Armenia has faced an electricity deficit. In other words, these projects are fully absorbing the surplus we have. So we need to decide what to do next.”

The prime minister said the government would make a decision in the coming months. Pashinyan also said that Armenia could accept the proposal put forward by Russia:

“It is quite possible that building a 1,000 MW plant will prove to be the most logical solution. However, I cannot say for certain at this stage because experts are still assessing the issue.”

“The unit should be at least one, with a capacity of at least 1 GW” — Likhachev

Rosatom director general Alexey Likhachev told journalists some details of Russia’s proposal after talks in Yerevan. Likhachev said Armenia would continue to rely on nuclear energy for decades to come. Russia therefore plans to “formulate the most competitive proposal” for building a new reactor unit in the coming months.

“And in our view, this unit should be at least one, with a capacity of at least 1 GW,” Likhachev said.

According to him, the proposal involves a VVER-1000 reactor, a pressurised water reactor with a capacity of 1,000 MW.

The head of Rosatom stressed that this proposal is “the best currently available on the global market”. He added that Rosatom has built and continues to build VVER reactors of this type in India and Iran:

“They combine very high economic efficiency, namely a low cost of electricity, with all the necessary Generation III+ safety systems.”

Details of talks with Rosatom director general in Yerevan

The Armenian prime minister’s office said Pashinyan and Likhachev discussed:

work to extend the operating life of the existing second reactor unit at the Armenian Nuclear Power Plant;

Russia’s proposals for building a new reactor unit.

At the same time, the prime minister told Likhachev that the Armenian government was continuing to consider proposals from other international partners.

Pashinyan stressed that the final decision would depend solely on economic considerations. These would include price, quality, safety, construction timelines and guarantees.

The statement also said Alexey Likhachev described cooperation with Armenian partners as constructive. The Rosatom chief also provided detailed information about the construction of not only large VVER reactors, but also small and medium-sized reactors.

World.title: Iran must be able to benefit from provisions of NPT if it is member – FM spokesperson
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 4. Iran must be able to benefit from the provisions of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) if it is a member of the treaty, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said today at a press conference in Tehran.

“Although Iran has fully adhered to its obligations as a member of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons since 1970, its scientists have been killed and its nuclear facilities have come under attack. This raises a serious question,” he said.

Baghaei said that if a country is a member of the NPT, it should be able to exercise its rights and benefit from the treaty’s provisions rather than face pressure, military attacks and threats.

Baghaei said that, as a rule, the Iranian Foreign Ministry follows the decisions of the country’s relevant authorities. Iran is currently a member of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. As a member of the treaty, it is aware of its obligations.

Iranian Parliament Deputy Speaker Ali Nikzad said that the issue of Iran’s withdrawal from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons is being examined by the relevant committee of the Iranian parliament. Meanwhile, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei also said that a number of actions by the International Atomic Energy Agency could prompt countries to withdraw from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.

World.title: Iran denies offering IAEA inspections in exchange for sanctions relief
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 4. Iran has not made any proposal to allow International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors to inspect the country’s nuclear facilities in exchange for easing sanctions against Iran, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said today at a press conference in Tehran.

“Overall, Iran has not made any proposal in this form. Iran has not put forward any issue in exchange for sanctions relief or concessions on the nuclear issue. In general, the Iranian side has not entered into the nuclear issue,” he said.

Baghaei said that Iran had conveyed its conditions to the other side. These conditions were presented to mediators as part of a plan called the “seven-day plan.” The Qatari side also conveyed them to the United States.

In June last year, the United States and Israel carried out airstrikes on a number of Iranian nuclear facilities. Since then, Iran has restricted access to the country for IAEA inspectors. Inspectors have only been allowed access during certain operations at the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant. Iran has refused to allow inspectors into the country, citing the lack of security at its nuclear facilities and the fact that the IAEA has not condemned attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities.

World.title: Iranian President to visit Turkmenistan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 4. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will visit Turkmenistan in the coming days, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said today at a press conference in Tehran.

“The Iranian president will participate in two important conferences during the visit.

The first conference that the Iranian president will attend is the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity.

The second is the summit of the heads of state of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), which will be held on October 8. The Iranian president will attend the CIS heads of state summit as a special guest,” he said.

Baghaei said that the Iranian president is expected to hold a number of meetings during the visit.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian visited Turkmenistan in December last year. During the visit, the Iranian president participated in the International Conference on Peace and Trust and held bilateral talks with Turkmen officials as well as the heads of state of several countries participating in the conference.

World.title: Iran is currently focusing on issue of Strait of Hormuz – FM spokesperson
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 4. Iran has stated that it is currently focusing its attention on the issue concerning the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said today at a press conference in Tehran.

“The security of the Strait of Hormuz and restoring security to the strait depend on the United States taking certain steps, including not obstructing Iran’s maritime trade, halting the imposition of sanctions, and resolving other issues,” he said.

Baghaei said that Iran has stated its position regarding the implementation of the issues outlined in the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, as well as provisions added over the past several months, and the lifting of sanctions imposed by the United States.

The Foreign Ministry official said that, overall, the proposal presented to Iran by the United States reflects its previous position and mainly concerns the nuclear issue. The U.S. position was conveyed to the Iranian side through Qatari mediation. At that meeting, Iran’s position was conveyed in response. The Iranian side is conducting the necessary review of some details, and once finalized, they will be conveyed to the other side.

The latest escalation in U.S.-Iran relations began on July 8. On that day, the U.S. Armed Forces launched several waves of strikes against Iranian territory, claiming they were in response to an attack on a commercial vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, for the first time since the memorandum was signed between Washington and Tehran. On the same day, U.S. President Donald Trump announced the termination of the ceasefire with Iran. In response, Tehran began launching strikes against U.S. facilities located in Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE and Oman. As a result of the conflict, maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz was brought to a standstill.

World.title: Eight-bed outback hospital costs $67m, three times original budget
World.content:
WA's Health Minister Meredith Hammat has defended the cost of a new eight-bed outback hospital, which has reached practical completion at a cost of $67.6 million, or more than three times the original budget from 2015.

Construction of the new Laverton Hospital began last year to replace the aging facility, which was built in 1973 for the northern Goldfields community, about 950 kilometres north-east of Perth.

WA Premier Roger Cook and Ms Hammat flew into Laverton on Sunday to announce practical completion of the new hospital, which includes a 24-hour, telehealth-equipped emergency department.

The hospital also has flexible care beds, specialist facilities for visiting clinicians as well as outpatient services for community health, mental health, and space for an onsite private GP clinic.

Pat Hill (left) with Ali Kent, Roger Cook and Meredith Hammat at the new Laverton Hospital. (ABC Goldfields: Nick Ward)

When pressed on the cost of the build, Ms Hammat said it reflected the reality of delivering major infrastructure in remote locations.

"What we see with all our health infrastructure projects, particularly in regional Western Australia, is that it's always challenging to deliver them," she said.

"But we are absolutely committed to deliver the health services and the health infrastructure that people need.

"A look at the old Laverton Hospital confirms the reality that this facility is incredibly needed for the community, and we've taken the opportunity to co-locate services like community health, child health, as well as a GP service."

The entrance to the new Laverton Hospital. (ABC Goldfields: Nick Ward)

Long road to new hospital

The Shire of Laverton has been lobbying for a hospital redevelopment for more than a decade.

The former Liberal-National government promised a $19.5 million redevelopment of Laverton Hospital in 2015, before funding was cut by WA Labor when it came to power in 2017.

Mr Cook, who was minister for health in 2017, said the new Laverton Hospital would open its doors to patients from Wednesday.

"I'm a previous health minister and this project has been on the books for a long time," he said.

"It's with a sense of deep relief but great pride that we're now in a position to welcome patients here."

Roger Cook on a visit to the new Laverton Hospital. (ABC Goldfields: Nick Ward)

After years of delays, the state government announced in February 2025, on the eve of the March election that year, that ADCO Constructions had won the tender to build the new hospital at a cost of $37.5 million.

Minister for Health Infrastructure John Carey confirmed in October last year those costs had blown out to $63.6 million.

The final cost of $67.6 million includes a federal government contribution of $16.8 million towards the project.

Hospital vital for Outback Way

Shire of Laverton president Pat Hill said the new hospital would be vital in emergencies due to the projected increase in traffic once the Outback Way was sealed.

The Outback Way stretches 2,719km through central Australia, from Laverton in Western Australia's northern Goldfields to Winton in Queensland, and it is hoped the final stretch can be sealed by 2032.

"It's been on the cards for over 15 years … I know they've had challenges but it's completed and it's a beautiful, first class facility," he said.

"With the development of the Outback Way and more people coming through these isolated, remote communities, and also the mining interests around Laverton, we've got over 7,500 people working fly-in, fly-out, so it's great to see governments working to put infrastructure into these remote areas."

The Outback Way in WA begins at Laverton with the Great Central Road. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Mr Hill has been chairman of the Outback Highway Development Commission since 1997 and is set to attend its annual general meeting in Alice Springs on Tuesday.

Kalgoorlie MLA Ali Kent echoed Mr Hill's sentiments on the hospital's importance due to the Outback Way.

"Laverton is in the middle of the desert, it's a long way from the Perth CBD and to have a hospital of this standard delivered here … it's been a difficult journey because we were putting tenders out and couldn't get builders that could do it," she said.

"When the Outback Way goes through, this hospital is going to become even more important."

World.title: Thousands make arrow sign for Jai as Amy Shark leads grand final tribute
World.content:
Tens of thousands of fans have united by making the arrow gesture during a moving pre-grand final lap by the NRL's Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles, who were both diagnosed with motor neuron disease this year.

Arrow, who had the month of July dedicated to him when NRL players would make the arrow gesture after scoring, was forced into retirement following his diagnosis, rocking the Australian sporting community.

Charles, who played four rugby union Tests for Australia, revealed his diagnosis this week.

The pair were driven around Stadium Australia before the NRL grand final, with Australian music artists Amy Shark, Dave Gleeson and Phil Jamison performing.

Shark began with a rendition of You'll Never Walk Alone as Arrow and Charles began their lap.

Amy Shark performs as the NRL pay tribute to Jai Arrow and Nathan Charles. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Thousands in the crowd did the arrow gesture as they drove past, as prompted in a pre-packaged video by NRL Hall of Fame member Ray Warren.

"Jai's fight against MMD has reached far beyond the football field," Warren said.

"He has and continues to inspire others facing difficult times.

"The way Jai has faced this challenge with his head held high is showing us what true bravery really looks like.

"This is what our game is about. Strength, courage, community and making sure when life gets tough someone is there beside you."

After Shark sang You'll Never Walk Alone, Newcastle legend Dave Gleeson walked onto Stadium Australia to sing What's Up? by 4 Non Blondes.

Grinspoon's Phil Jamieson then joined Shark and Gleeson to end the tribute with the famous Tina Turner rugby league anthem, The Best.

The tribute came after the NRL's negotiations to secure Tones And I fell through.

The NRL has pledged $1 million, which was to be spent on pre-match entertainment, to help underprivileged kids who can not afford to play rugby league play rugby league," Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC this week.

World.title: Thousands of motorcyclists join pothole rally outside Victorian parliament
World.content:
Thousands of motorcyclists descended on Victoria's parliament on Sunday to voice their concerns about safety issues stemming from the state of the road network, with a focus on potholes.

Chants of "fix the roads" could be heard alongside the roar of motorbikes outside state parliament as more than 3,000 attendees joined the rally, which began at 11am.

The so-called broken roads rally was organised by Michael White and Paul Povh, who host a motorcycling YouTube channel.

"We're not here because we're bloody happy," Mr White said as he addressed the crowd.

"We're not here because we care about Labor, Liberal, Greens, One Nation, anyone.

" We're here because of the bloody state of the roads and we're sick of burying our mates. "

The rally was organised in the wake of the death of 71-year-old Peter "Tiki" Mason, who died while riding his motorbike on the Western Highway near Trawalla last month, after he was believed to have struck a pothole.

Police have said they were still investigating the cause of the incident, while Mr Mason's family have shared their heartbreak and said they did not want his death to be used to promote "political agendas".

Police say the rally attracted more than 3,000 attendees. (ABC News)

In recent days, heavy rain in some parts of the state has resulted in fresh potholes on the road network.

Concerns about potholes and poor road maintenance have become a key topic in the lead-up to the November state election.

A recent report from the Victorian Auditor-General's Office on the maintenance of the state's roads found that the proportion of state-managed roads in poor or very poor condition had increased from 39 to 48 per cent between 2021 and 2024.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson attended the rally, while Premier Ben Carroll spoke with the rally's organisers on Saturday.

Ahead of the state election, Labor has promised $1 billion for road maintenance, and has also doubled the amount allocated to fixing potholes this year with an additional $352 million. The Coalition has promised to spend $5 billion over four years to improve the state's roads.

World.title: Brigginshaw's NRLW legend remains eternal
World.content:
As the merciless Roosters ran away with the NRLW grand final it was hard to think of a less fitting end for a career as legendary as Ali Brigginshaw's.

The 36-year old and the rest of the Broncos were helpless to stop a Tricolour massacre that ended 30-6 as the Roosters earned a manner of vengeance for last year's grand final defeat to complete a perfect season.

It was over by half-time because Brisbane did not pick up their guns, let alone fire a shot.

NRLW grand final quick hits The 2026 Sydney Roosters NRLW side has cemented its legacy with a crushing grand final win over the Brisbane Broncos. Here are the quick hits from the NRLW grand final.

They completed just three sets in the entire first half as they drowned under a sea of Roosters points.

From the 15th minute to the 34th minute they only touched the ball to kick it off, drop it or be driven back into the in-goal.

For almost 20 minutes they did not play the ball once, with the Roosters running in six straight tries and between the 15th and 39th minutes they did not complete a set.

All of the weapons that have made Brigginshaw great — her skill, her guile, her cunning and class as a playmaker, which she has carried through her 17 years at the top of women's rugby league — were blunted before she even got a chance to use them.

She did manage to sneak through for a line-break in the second half, a 35 minutes of football that felt like it only happened because it had to happen so we could get to the end, as she held up a pass before hitting a gap with exquisite timing, but had no support.

In the end, her last day was destroyed by a monster of a team who are without question the best NRLW side ever assembled.

They are the culmination of a transformation in women's rugby league that Brigginshaw herself helped bring about through a career that stretches all the way back to the primordial days of women's rugby league.

Brigginshaw's Broncos were helpless before the Roosters onslaught. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

When she started playing for Queensland and Australia in 2009 her Broncos teammate Reegan Hicks was three years old.

Club football was ad hoc, pathways barely existed and the NRL may as well have been a different universe. For the committed few who kept the women's game going it was day-to-day as much as it was hand-to-mouth.

Interstate matches were not played under the State of Origin banner and were held at suburban grounds in front of tiny crowds.

A World Cup final was the only game that could get on television and even then, only if the network was feeling generous.

Footage of those days leading up to the first NRLW season in 2018 is grainy and hard to find. Even basic details of matches — things like team lists, scorers and attendances — aren't always easy to track down.

Brigginshaw has been a top-level footballer for almost as long as some of her teammates have been alive. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

In a very literal sense of the word, it's almost prehistoric.

Today it's a new world, a world Brigginshaw helped create as the premiere footballer and one of the biggest stars of the transitional era and into the early NRLW years.

For proof, look no further than the words of Julia Robinson, who has played with Brigginshaw ever since that first Broncos season.

“She’s a true leader, on and off the field, she’s the heart of the Broncos, she’s going to be this legacy that carries on for generations," Robinson told ABC Sport.

“She’s going to be missed, missed by the team, missed by everyone but she’ll still be around and make a big impact on the rugby league community.”

“I’m so grateful I had the opportunity to play with Ali, she’s one of the greats.”

Brigginshaw was a pioneer and a trail blazer, who set a new mark and standard for others to aspire to and acted as a legend for an entire game to believe in.

To see the Tricolours complete their perfect season is to see the end product of that belief. Today's players are bigger, faster, stronger and more skilful.

They play together for longer and the improvements to the sport are plain to see. They are better athletes and better footballers and so many of the best of them play at the Roosters.

John Strange's side are the culmination of almost a decade of progress, the ultimate example of what's possible when a club with some serious muscle decides to really invest in a women's program.

As Brigginshaw proved what was possible for the women's game in terms of star power and sheer class, the Roosters prove what is possible when those attributes are taken to their very limit.

Now they are what Brigginshaw was — a star for the entire league to sail by, and they are filled with players who can trace their lineage to the retiring Bronco.

In a cruel irony, without Brigginshaw there might be no Tarryn Aiken, who was named the Karyn Murphy medallist with a brilliant display at halfback for the Roosters or Jocelyn Kelleher, Brigginshaw's opposite number, who tortured Brisbane with her kicking game.

Closer to home might be no Tamika Upton, who succeeded Brigginshaw as the world's best player but just could not get into the game for the Broncos until she set up a late try, or Jesse Southwell, who scored that try and is so clearly an evolution of an archetype that Brigginshaw pioneered — not an athlete, but a pure footballer.

She is one of the players who entered the NRLW having played league all their lives, unlike Brigginshaw who had to stop when she was 12 because there were no more teams to play on and that's just one change Brigginshaw has born witness too.

Origin matches are ratings gold and attracts crowds that dwarf what they were even five years ago, the NRLW has been born and expanded twice over and the product and support is edging towards the point where a standalone grand final doesn't just feel possible, it feels like a logical step for a game that continues to grow.

Brigginshaw helped raise that profile as a mainstay in Brisbane's early premierships and a Queensland regular. She was not just a star, she was the star.

She didn't just adapt to the new world, she brought it to heel as she became a legend and now retires as an icon — if they were to rename the women's Dally M after a modern player, the Ali B certainly has a fine ring to it.

NRL live The Sydney Roosters won their third NRLW premiership, thrashing the Brisbane Broncos by seven tries to one in a blowout of a grand final. Follow live.

When you are a player of that stature, to whom greatness has been a constant companion for years and who remained a threat right to the end — even at 36, Brisbane did not win a game this year without Brigginshaw — a grand final massacre is no way for a career to end.

She has given the game so much but the game could not give her the perfect ending.

But as she prepares for the rest of her life, Brigginshaw leaves the game as a figure that sits astride two eras, who helped bring her game to life and make it bigger than anyone in the old days could have dreamed.

There is still progress to be made and in retirement Brigginshaw will not stop pushing for it.

She believes in a brighter future and she knows one is possible, because she has already built one. We are living in it right now.

World.title: NRLW quick hits: Roosters complete 101-year first as Aiken stars
World.content:
The 2026 Sydney Roosters NRLW side has cemented its legacy with a crushing grand final win over the Brisbane Broncos.

Twelve months on from a heartbreaking loss to the women from Brisbane, the Roosters not only won the premiership, but did something no other top-flight rugby league team has achieved in Australia for more than a century.

Here are the quick hits from Sydney's NRLW grand final win over Brisbane.

1. Origin wingers make uncharacteristic errors

It doesn't matter how much experience you have, every player feels some sort of pressure on grand final day.

And the pressure of a grand final was on display in the opening minutes, with a pair of State of Origin representatives making uncharacteristic errors.

Brigginshaw's NRLW legend remains eternal Ali Brigginshaw's decorated rugby league career ended with a heavy defeat but there can be no doubt about the impact the Broncos playmaker has had on the game.

Sydney Roosters winger Jayme Fressard had a proper shocker to begin the grand final, failing to gather the opening kick-off and nudging it into touch.

As the ball came to the NSW State of Origin rep, she tried to trap it with her foot but kicked the footy over the sideline.

The Roosters were able to defend their goal-line and then it was a Broncos Origin rep to have a shocker.

It was Fressard's opposing winger, Julia Robinson, who dropped the ball stone cold in her own half, which gifted the Roosters a golden chance to open the scoring.

Unlike the Broncos, the Roosters were able to score when winger Brydie Parker fielded a great cross-field kick from five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher and touched down in the corner.

2. Tarryn Aiken takes over in 7-minute blitz

The Roosters were dominating the grand final in the first half, as multiple errors from Brisbane kept them under immense pressure.

But Brisbane's goal-line defence was one aspect of their game that was withstanding the impressive Roosters.

That was until Sydney halfback Tarryn Aiken, who missed last year's decider due to an ACL injury, produced three moments of brilliance in a 7-minute stretch that led to a trio of tries for the Roosters.

First Aiken grubbered for herself and when the ball bounced off the arm of Brisbane winger Kerri Johnson, the Sydney halfback caught the ricochet and scored the game's second try.

Four minutes later, Aiken was setting up the third try of the match. The halfback lined up at lock in an attacking scrum 10 metres from Brisbane's goal-line. Aiken passed from the base of the scrum to the left, wrapped around and retook the footy, then gave a perfect short pass to captain Isabelle Kelly who charged over.

The Roosters then charged down the field again and when a sixth tackle play looked to be coming unstuck, it was Aiken again who produced a great kick which Brisbane's Deleni Paitai fumbled, and the Tricolours regathered and Fressard scored in the corner.

3. Brigginshaw on report in her farewell game

The trailblazing career of Ali Brigginshaw, someone who has been instrumental in the growth of women's rugby league, came to an end with an NRLW grand final.

But the legendary Broncos, Maroos and Jillaroo might have considered herself lucky not to have been sin-binned in her farewell game.

With the Roosters on top, Brigginshaw was desperate not to let Aiken put in an attacking cross-field kick.

Aiken did, which led to a try, but Brigginshaw's low dive resulted in her clattering into the planted leg of Aiken.

A hit under the knee led to Aiken landing hard on her back and could have easily resulted in Brigginshaw being sent for a 10-minute break on the sideline.

But referee Belinda Sharpe decided that putting Brigginshaw on report was the only action necessary, which really is academic considering this was her farewell outing.

4. Dally M medallist pulls off one of season's best tackles

Down 26-0 early in the second half, Brisbane's misery looked destined to continue when the Roosters were about to cross over for what would have been their seventh try of the grand final.

Jessica Sergis of the Roosters is tackled by Tamika Upton of the Broncos. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

A high bomb from the Roosters was allowed to bounce, the ball took a wicked turn and landed in the arms of Brydie Parker, and a brilliant flick pass on the inside looked set to end with Jessica Sergis scoring in the corner.

But Brisbane's captain and fullback Tamika Upton, the Dally M medalist this season, produced a try-saving tackle as good as any seen this season.

The Brisbane number one screamed across in cover and was able to twist her body in the tackle and make sure she was under the ball as Sergis fell to the line.

With Upton around her like a snake, Sergis was unable to get her arm free and ground the ball. It didn't change the outcome, but it was another example of why Upton is the best player in the competition.

5. Roosters complete first perfect season in 101 years

The Roosters came into Sunday's decider with plenty of confidence.

They had won 30 of their previous 31 NRLW matches. There only loss was last year's grand final, to the Broncos, denying them an undefeated season.

But the Tricolours regrouped in 2026, won every match on their way to the decider, then exacted revenge with a commanding win to complete the perfect season.

The Sydney Roosters became the first men's or women's side in top grade rugby league to go the entire season without suffering a loss since the 1959 ST George Dragons.

That Dragons team recorded 17 wins, and one draw, on their way to a fourth consecutive premiership, in a dominant era of 11 straight titles.

But the 2026 Roosters NRLW side had no draws, just 13 wins from 13 matches. The last team to win every match in a season was South Sydney, way back in 1925.

World.title: Kangaroos thrash Swans as Demons, Eagles claim crucial wins
World.content:
The Sydney Swans have lost star ruck Ally Morphett to a knee injury in their humiliating 55-point defeat to North Melbourne.

But while the 10.11 (71) to 2.4 (16) victory returned the Kangaroos to the top of the ladder, the reigning premiers have injury concerns of their own, as Emma Kearney sustained a hamstring injury.

In the first quarter at Arden Street Oval on Sunday, Morphett looked to make a tackle but collapsed in the lead-up.

She was left holding her right knee in agony, later emerging from the rooms wearing a brace and on crutches.

St Kilda kick solitary point St Kilda were 90 seconds from failing to score in their AFLW clash against the Western Bulldogs, as Essendon's first win of the year leaves the Saints as the only winless team in the league.

The 22-year-old has played a starring role for the Swans this season, spearheading them into top-four contention.

Kearney, an eight-time All Australian, left the field in the fourth quarter, just two months after missing the Australia-Ireland clash with a hamstring injury.

The loss of the 37-year-old defender would be massive, considering she adds a plethora of experience to the Kangaroos, who are in a tight race for the minor premiership.

"Disappointing way to finish the game. I've been pretty lucky throughout my career not to have too many injuries," Kearney told the Seven Network.

"Probably my age has something to do with it. Hopefully it's not too bad, but we'll get it scanned."

The Kangaroos' Tess Craven (17 disposals, two goals), Tahlia Randall (three goals) and Jasmine Garner (31 disposals, 10 clearances) dazzled, as the Swans were held goalless until midway through the third term.

By that point, the home team had already booted four goals and kicked another six afterwards to demote the Swans to seventh position.

Mia Austin (right) kicked three goals in the Demons' triumph. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

At Victoria Park, Melbourne secured a 6.6 (42) to 2.9 (21) win over a wasteful Collingwood, despite the absence of injured captain Kate Hore.

Fresh off a 31-point defeat to the Kangaroos last round, the Demons rebounded with forward Mia Austin slotted three first-half majors to help the visitors lead 29-10 at the main break.

From this point of the match, midfielders Tyla Hanks (24 disposals, 12 tackle and one goal) and Olivia Purcell (32 disposals) sparkled.

The win moves the Demons into second position, while the Magpies will hope defender Sarah Rowe quickly recovers from a leg injury sustained in the second half.

Meanwhile, the West Coast Eagles thrust themselves firmly into finals contention by beating Fremantle 5.9 (39) to 4.3 (27) in Perth.

Midfielder Ella Roberts (22 disposals, one goal) produced a masterclass to help the Eagles claim their first regular-season win over their cross-town rivals and move level on points with the eighth-placed Dockers.

The Eagles' fourth straight win comes after they lost their first four matches.

AAP

World.title: Shock wake-up for residents as WWII shell detonated on beach
World.content:
Residents on Queensland's Sunshine Coast were woken in shock by an early morning blast when the Defence Force detonated an unexploded World War II-era shell found on a beach.

Police were called to Wurtulla Beach just before midnight after Sean Mackney's friend discovered an object at the base of a sand dune while they were walking his dog.

"She yelled out to me and she thought that she'd found a bomb and I was like, 'What?'" he said.

Curious, Mr Mackney picked up the object before realising what it was.

"I'm a bit of an idiot … I was shitting myself," he said.

"The sheer weight of it was massive.

"I didn't really know what to do … we called the police and they were down there pretty quick.

"I'm surprised nobody else had seen it and [wonder] how long it was exposed."

Police officers attended and guarded the site until Department of Defence personnel arrived.

A Defence spokesman confirmed the unexploded ordnance was "identified as a 25-pound High Explosive projectile (25 Pounder) from World War II".

Explosion wakes residents

Defence bomb squad personnel detonated the 11-kilogram device at about 4am.

The 25-pounder artillery shells were used during World War II. The yellow one, second from right, is similar to the one found on the Sunshine Coast. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

Battery Hill resident Rhiannon McPherson said she was woken by "a massive bang".

"I thought maybe a bad car accident or something … it sounded like something really big had dropped onto cement," she said.

"I was waiting to hear sirens but didn’t hear anything.

"I woke my husband but he hadn't heard it. My dog didn't bark, which threw me off as well.

"I was trying to work out if I'd made it up or I'd dreamt it."

History of unexploded devices

The region was home to a live firing site during World War II and the Wurtulla are is listed on the Defence website as having substantial potential for unexploded ordnance.

Unexploded ordnance is a risk on the Sunshine Coast. The red areas indicate "substantial potential" of the presence of a device.. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

The 25-pounder was "the primary artillery piece of the Commonwealth Forces until the 1960s", according to the Defence department.

The guns were built in Australia from 1942 and were used by the Australian Army until 1965.

The "high explosive" variant was about 30 centimetres long and contained a nose fuse and up to 900 grams of amatol — a mix of TNT and ammonium nitrate.

"Unexploded items of this type are most often found in/near areas used by the Army for artillery practices, typically on the ground surface up to 1.5 metres deep," the Defence website says.

The ADF's bomb disposal squad responds to about 500 unexploded ordnance incidents around Australia each year.

Last year officials detonated three World War II-era bombs on a remote Northern Territory beach, and in 2024 a device was blown up on the NSW South Coast.

World.title: Cornell president vows 'serious look' at fraternities in wake of gang rape allegations
World.content:
Cornell University will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus following an outcry over the school's handling of a student's gang rape allegations, the president says.

In an 8-minute video message to the Cornell community, Michael Kotlikoff said the past week had raised questions around the investigations conducted at the time the allegations were reported, and that the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the future.

That would include "a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life", he said.

"At their best, these organisations can provide students with friendship, belonging, mentorship and a powerful sense of community.

" But being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility. "

The alleged victim is suing the men, the Chi Phi fraternity, the university, an Ithaca bar and others, seeking undisclosed damages.

Cornell University will take a "serious look" at the role of fraternities and sororities on campus. (AP: Heather Ainsworth)

Identified in court documents as Jane Doe, she says she was pressured into taking illicit drugs and drinking alcohol, which completely incapacitated her.

According to investigation records obtained by The New York Times, the woman told a police officer: "I can say with 100 per cent confidence I was raped."

New investigation into Cornell claims Kathy Hochul says the woman who accused a group of Cornell University students of rape has been "failed" at "every turn" by authorities.

But that statement was left out of an official police report that was sent to prosecutors, who ultimately dropped the case.

The school conducted its own investigation and issued sanctions, including expelling some students and suspending others.

Mr Kotlikoff reaffirmed his commitment to supporting an independent review of Cornell's handling of the case, which was called for by New York Governor Kathy Hochul.

He said the school's board of trustees would announce details of the review later this week, and expressed support for Ms Hochul's decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the state attorney-general.

"I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say: We don't have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves," he said.

Loading...

During a student assembly hearing on October 1, several speakers called for Mr Kotlikoff's resignation.

Ms Hochul declined to take a position on whether Mr Kotlikoff should resign over the university's handling of the case when asked at a press conference on October 2, saying she did not yet have enough information.

Mr Kotlikoff acknowledged frustration that Cornell had not communicated enough, saying that had led to distrust.

While citing "real legal and privacy limits" on what the university could disclose, he pledged greater transparency and more opportunities for students, parents and others to engage with university leaders.

The alleged victim is suing members of the Chi Phi fraternity. (AP: Heather Ainsworth)

He also committed Cornell's support to legislative efforts to change New York's sexual assault laws.

State laws make it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults that involved victims who voluntarily consumed drugs and alcohol, even if they became too incapacitated to consent.

Critics say the laws create a "voluntary intoxication loophole", which separates people who were incapacitated by drugs without their consent, and those who voluntarily became intoxicated.

The district attorney who initially chose not to pursue criminal charges cited these laws as reason, saying the woman's original statement to police described voluntary drug use and sexual activity.

Ms Hochul has pledged to push for changes to the law.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Albo, Minns, Greg Norman: The who’s who of grand final VIPs
World.content:
Breaking NationalCBD Albo, Minns, Greg Norman: The who’s who of grand final VIPs John Buckley Updated October 4, 2026 — 8:37pm ,first published 6:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The first big question facing Peter V’landys during his reign as rugby league’s newly minted executive chairman was whether or not the NRL could snatch a victory over the AFL in the TV ratings when the dust settles on the 2026 grand final. Only a few months ago, the NRL chief was holding court with media bosses at the State of Origin opener, with broadcasters Nine Entertainment, owner of this masthead, and Foxtel, owned by the global streaming giant DAZN, jockeying for pride and place in the thick of high-stakes negotiations over a new media rights deal. New US ambassador David Brat with Anthony Albanese inside the Presidents Suite at Accor Stadium on Sunday night for the NRL grand final. Greg Norman is in the background. Those talks would eventually deliver V’landys a $5.3 billion broadcast rights deal, and set a new national record in the process. On Sunday evening, the challenge was to deliver value for money – all without the draw of a major entertainment act to bring in extra eyeballs. But if V’landys was nervous, he didn’t show it, as he pressed the flesh with a cast of powerbrokers from across business and politics.



Among the biggest names to drop into V’landys’ Presidents Suite at Accor Stadium was David Brat, US President Donald Trump’s new ambassador to Australia. Brat, regular readers will no doubt recall, only arrived on Australian shores last month, filling the post after it sat vacant for close to two years. No doubt the grand final will offer the ambassador a speed-run on Australian diplomacy. Labor stars: Premier Chris Minns and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the grand final on Sunday night. Also in the room was former Australian golfing great Greg Norman, who has been a conduit between Australian officials and golf-loving US president Trump. The biggest names usually turn out closer to kick-off, but after a protracted period on the sidelines over summer following last year’s expenses scandal, Communications and Sport Minister Anika Wells eagerly turned up to the stadium early. The minister was among those who showed up to V’landys’ suite in the afternoon, working the room with an eye on the NRLW grand final clash between the Roosters and the Broncos. Also at the stadium early was a man known for his love of a different code: Former Collingwood president Eddie McGuire, who was seen with his wife, Carla Galloway, climbing the escalator to the private suites during the women’s final.



NRL officials were out early. The media types, meanwhile, were also out in force. Among them was Nine Entertainment director Andrew Lancaster and the company’s publishing boss Tory Maguire, who were expected to be joined by the company’s chairman Peter Tonagh. Tonagh, according to The Australian Financial Review, intervened in Nine’s negotiations with V’landys to tie up the company’s free-to-air rights to the NRL. The other side of the rights deal, meanwhile, was represented by Patrick Delany, who just last month was promoted to chief operating officer of Foxtel’s (relatively) new owner, DAZN. Foxtel heavyweight Brian Walsh was also there, we’re told, as was Tom Malone, chief executive of 2GB owner Tapt Media. Prime Minister Antony Albanese and Queensland Premier David Crisafulli at the grand final. But the raw power, as always, lay with who got pride and place with V’landys himself, revelling in his first grand final as executive chairman. There was never any doubt that taking pride of place in the Presidents Suite was Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who had a seat saved next to V’landys, with Albanese’s wife, Jodie Haydon, to the PM’s side on the seating plan. The couple dropped in to work the room well before kick off, by which time Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn was also doing the rounds.



NSW Premier Chris Minns also dropped in to the suite, no doubt a little smug to see the grand final clash locked up by two of his state’s clubs. But that didn’t stop Queensland Premier David Crisafulli from taking up the invitation to make the trip south. NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane was also saved a place for good measure. Rounding out the political contingent was Barnaby Joyce, who showed up well before the men’s kick-off at 7.30pm. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Moving or exploitative? The verdict on the NRL’s grand final pre-match show
World.content:
CultureTV & radioNRL grand final Moving or exploitative? The verdict on the NRL’s grand final pre-match show Garry Maddox October 4, 2026 — 8:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NRL struggled to line up its traditional NRL grand final pre-match entertainment until days before the big game. No Olivia Dean, too expensive. No Tones and I, too complicated, especially if hit song Dance Monkey was off the playlist. No Silverchair reunion given the late notice and the well-known disagreements between the Newcastle band’s members. Retired South Sydney player Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles acknowledge the crowd before they take part in a lap of the field ahead of the NRL grand final. Getty Images The NRL eventually decided there would be no show at all this year. The game’s supremo, Peter V’landys, said he would rather spend $1 million on junior development than a big-name act. So far, so chaotic.



Then came a late turnaround during the week: V’landys said there would be a show, after all. And that would be “the highest-rating 11 minutes you will ever see”. It emerged the NRL planned a tribute to former Souths star Jai Arrow, whose forced retirement after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease has resulted in some of the season’s most emotional moments. Amy Shark and Dave Gleeson perform before the NRL grand final. Getty Images As much love as there is around the rugby league community for Arrow and his family, there was a real risk a tribute dreamt up in the last week would feel exploitative. That it was milking the genuine warmth the game felt for the larrikin Rabbitoh. So after The Kid Laroi and Teddy Swims shone in the last two years, how was it?



As excitement built towards kick-off, the show began with veteran commentator Ray Warren talking about the importance of rugby league heroes and announcing that the $1 million would allow underprivileged kids to play the game. He said Arrow had shown us “what true bravery really looks like” and called on the crowd at the stadium to shoot an arrow for Jai. Loading Then Amy Shark started singing You’ll Never Walk Alone, the Liverpool FC anthem was the moving soundtrack to Arrow taking the field for his 100th and last Souths match and other emotional moments since his MND diagnosis. She greeted him and a surprise guest, former Wallaby Nathan Charles, who has also been diagnosed with MND, as they started a drive on a lap of honour.



David Gleeson from the Screaming Jets, another favourite Newcastle band, took over with Four Non Blondes’ What’s Up, with Shark and the crowd joining in. Then Phil Jamieson from Grinspoon launched into the most famous rugby league anthem of all, The Best. The verdict: it was a simple but effective show. Considering how late it came together, the emphasis on Arrow, Charles and a trio of Australian singers had none of the wow factor of Kylie Minogue’s 20-minute set at the AFL grand final, but it worked well enough on TV. The visual element that should have capped the show – the crowd united in firing an arrow for Jai – came too early and didn’t pay off. Not one of the all-time great NRL grand final shows but it did not feel awkward or contrived. It will work a lot better next year if the planning starts a lot earlier.
