World.title: The private schools with the richest parents in Victoria revealed as extra funding flows
World.content:
Victorian private schools, many of them educating the state’s richest families, benefited from an extra $95 million in Commonwealth funding in 2025, as underfunded public schools’ battle for their share continued to go down to the wire. Melbourne Grammar School, where the median family income was $375,000, the highest in the state, received $1.18 million more than the nationally agreed funding benchmark from the Commonwealth last year. Melbourne Grammar School It was one of 26 Melbourne schools with a median family income of $300,000 or more. At least 12 of those schools received between $134,000 and $1.5 million above their entitled funding, known as the School Resource Standard (SRS), in 2025. The SRS is an estimate of how much public funding a school needs to meet its students’ educational needs, as detailed in the long-awaited Gonski reforms.



Federal Education Department data released in response to inquiries from Greens senator Penny Allman-Payne during budget estimates showed there were 58 overfunded non-government Victorian schools and education authorities in 2025, which received a combined $95,154,592 in funding above SRS. The Commonwealth has now agreed to fund 80 per cent of the SRS of non-government schools, while the states’ target is 20 per cent, but the transition back to their actual entitlement is being done in stages until 2029. Melbourne Grammar School will receive about $986,000 more than the SRS this year, $40,000 more than previous Senate estimates figures revealed. Principal Philip Grutzner said Melbourne Grammar was “keenly aware” of the funding changes and was planning ahead to reduce the impact on families.



Asked whether this would mean fee increases, Grutzner said salaries, inflation, ongoing operating costs, payroll tax and fees all influenced tuition. “Our focus continues to be on offering an exceptional, holistic education focused on the whole child,” Grutzner said. State Education Minister Gabrielle Williams and Premier Ben Carroll. Eddie Jim Christ Church Grammar School, an independent Anglican primary school in South Yarra, educated the second-highest-income-earning families in the state last year. There is no indication that it was overfunded. Parents of Christ Church Grammar students had a median income of $370,000, and the top 25 per cent of earners had an income of $580,000 of more.



It was one of 21 schools where the top 25 per cent of families had an annual income of $500,000 or more in 2025. Principal Kim Wheeler said the school was proud of its community and the many families who had chosen it because they valued a high-quality education for their children. “Our hard-working families make an informed choice in choosing an independent school education, which reflects the importance our community places on education and their desire to provide their children with the best possible opportunities,” Wheeler said. St Joseph’s School in Hawthorn had the third-highest earners last year, with parents having a combined median income of $365,000. The Catholic school’s top 25 per cent of earners brought in $525,000 or more.



The state’s Catholic schools, most of which receive Commonwealth funding via the Victorian Catholic Education Authority (VCEA), received an extra $39.2 million from the Commonwealth last year, dropping to $31 million above their funding entitlement in 2026. Senate estimate data released in November had indicated the peak body would receive $30.6 million this year. VCEA chief executive Elizabeth Labone said the federal government’s data failed to account for enrolment growth and was unlikely to represent the actual funding schools received. “With the new EBA [enterprise bargaining agreement] in Victorian government schools set to increase school costs by a much higher rate than assumed in the SRS model, it is clear that the model no longer sets an accurate funding benchmark for schools,” Labone said. “Catholic education looks forward to working closely with the government to review and improve the SRS model.”



The federal government estimates it will provide $33.3 billion in total recurrent funding for Australian schools this year. This includes $12.7 billion to government schools, $11.1 billion to Catholic schools and $9.5 billion to independent schools. The Commonwealth will provide about $5.3 billion to non-government schools in Victoria. Overfunding has occurred over the past 15 years as Labor and Liberal-led federal governments stuck to a promise that private schools would never be worse off. Public school advocate and Waiting for Gonski co-author Tom Greenwell said successive federal governments “carving out exemptions to placate the private school lobby” had led to overfunding of non-government schools booming.



“[Julia] Gillard guaranteed 3 per cent annual increases for overfunded schools, [Tony] Abbott enthusiastically maintained them, and [Scott] Morrison added fuel to the fire with a multibillion-dollar slush fund and an extension of overfunding for another decade,” Greenwell said. Related Article Private schools Private schools expand scholarships to target ‘late bloomers’, boost diversity Greenwell is among those critical of the pace at which overfunded non-government schools will transition back down to 80 per cent of the SRS. He said the Albanese Labor government would pour more cash into overfunding wealthy private schools this decade than it would into lifting struggling public schools up to the bare minimum standard. “It’s pure political cowardice,” he said. “While the Albanese government is big on rhetoric about fixing public school funding, in reality it’s deferred delivery of real additional funding to the 2030s.” Victoria government schools have been funded at about 90 per cent of the SRS since 2018, despite signing an agreement with the Commonwealth that year to reach full funding by 2028.



The current agreement, which would see the state contribute 75 per cent of the SRS for public schools and the federal government contribute 25 per cent by 2034, is set to expire at the end of the year. The Carroll government has indicated it intends to sign a long-term funding deal ahead of the November election, though it has locked horns with the Commonwealth on the transition and key reforms tied to the federal dollars. The Victorian Education Department has argued that the state is contributing more to school infrastructure than other states and territories, which should be considered when evaluating the state’s investment. Education Minister Gabrielle Williams referred to Victoria’s “$20.1 billion school building program – the largest in the country” in response to questions about SRS funding. “We’re continuing to work with the Commonwealth to secure a long-term funding agreement that delivers full and fair funding for Victoria’s public schools,” she said.

World.title: ‘Makes you happy’: Classic Greek treat finds a new home on Sydney Road
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life ‘Makes you happy’: Classic Greek treat finds a new home on Sydney Road Carolyn Webb October 4, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A serious back injury ended his career as a plumber at age 20, and aside from being painful, it left Kosta Kostidis at a loss as to what to do for a living. But the love and advice of relatives, including his 89-year-old grandfather, helped Kostidis find a sweet but very different career — in the field of Greek pastries. Kosta Kostidis (right), with Yianni Palazi, serves bougatsa pastries at his new shop, Bougatsaki, in Brunswick. Chris Hopkins A few weeks ago, two years after the injury, Kostidis opened a small shop in Sydney Road, Brunswick, whose prime product is a custard-filled pastry called bougatsa. The street-side outlet is named Bougatsaki, meaning, in Greek, “little bougatsa”.



There’s a symmetry to the move, given Kostidis’s pappou (grandfather), Efthimios Oplopiadis, is a former baker. In 2024, Kostidis was a fourth-year apprentice plumber when he “did his back” on a job in Melbourne’s south-east. Former baker Efthimios Oplopiadis with grandson Kosta Kostidis at the new shop. Chris Hopkins “I was out of work for a year, seeing physios and specialists,” he said. He was bedridden for months, and he still receives treatment.



“It was not fun,” he said. “For a couple of months, it was really bad.” When Kostidis felt better, he was keen to work, but there was a problem: “I had no idea what I wanted to do.” A sample of a bougatsa pastry from the shop, Bougatsaki. Andrew Clark While at home in Coburg, he would make bougatsas with his pappou, and had the idea of selling pastries. Oplopiadis had worked as a baker in Melbourne factories for 30 years after migrating from Greece in 1968 and liked to make pastries at home.



His daughter, Kosta’s mother Martha Oplopiadis, says bougatsas have been a staple of family gatherings, as a dessert, for generations. One year ago, Kostidis started a food van selling bougatsas, which took off. He has worked at parties, festivals and soccer games. Kosta Kostidis (right) with his cousin’s husband, LaManna Supermarket CEO Patrick LaManna. Chris Hopkins In February at the Antipodes Festival in Lonsdale Street, in Melbourne’s CBD, Kostidis, his mother, his sister, Danean, and cousin Lynda LaManna helped Kosta sell more than 3000 bougatsas in three days. Opening the shop in Brunswick last month had been a huge but exciting step, Kostidis said.



He was inspired by specialist bougatsa outlets in Greece. And his mentor – his cousin’s husband, LaManna Supermarket chief executive Patrick LaManna – encouraged him to focus on bougatsas. “To be honest, I’m not too sure what I would have done without Patrick and my mum. Coming off a year when I wasn’t working and was just lost, they helped me find myself, pretty much,” Kostidis said. His grandfather, to whom he has always been close, has also been a great support, being a sounding board, and suggesting ingredients, including savoury fillings. It feels right, says Kostidis, to follow his pappou in the baking business.



Oplopiadis said he liked that Kostidis had opened a shop. “He started slowly and has been steadily progressing and coming up with new ideas,” Oplopiadis said. “I’m happy to see the family helping him. It’s a lot of hard work.” Editor's pick Exclusive

Victorian election A cinema chain’s Liberal donation broke the rules. This is why there won’t be consequences Oplopiadis, originally from the city of Serres, in northern Greece, reckons that bougatsas will draw customers. “You see, when you eat bougatsa, it makes you happy, it’s not a heavy dessert. It has light, velvety custard, it’s just delicious,” he said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘We’re going to defend the kingdom’: NRL fans prepare for grand final after tragedy
World.content:
For Newcastle Knights fan Bailey Goodacre, grand final day began 156km from Sydney’s Accor Stadium in the Del Hotel and Pub on Newcastle’s trendy Darby Street. Not long after the pub’s doors opened at 10am, Goodacre and his mates were inside, beer in hand and ready to watch their team in a grand final for the first time in 25 years. Bailey Goodacre (second from the right) and his friends at The Del Hotel and Pub. Tom Decent “We’ll steady ourselves and have some food and drinks,” he said. “Eventually, we’ll have more people come. It’s going to be unreal. I can’t wait. “We defended the table, and now we’re going to defend the kingdom.”



The city woke to promising news after the tragedy of Saturday. Several supporters, including children, were hospitalised after a car crashed into a crowd in Newcastle. But a five-year-old girl struck by the car, who underwent emergency surgery the night before, was now in a critical but stable condition. “We feel really bad for what has happened. It is sad,” Goodacre said, adding that he thought the town, already bonded by their team’s success, had become even closer after the incident. Newcastle fans at Broadmeadow Station start the journey to Sydney. Sitthixay Ditthavong At Broadmeadow Station, three kilometres closer to Accor Stadium, groups of Knights fans left every 30 minutes on trains to Sydney. Most were in Newcastle jerseys, few had any luggage and they seemed prepared to make the return journey after the match. Two of them, Cathy and Michelle Price, wouldn’t have been on the Newcastle express if not for the tickets they won in a competition on the morning of the game.



“I’ve had to change my plans,” Cathy said on the platform. By midday, hundreds had crossed the Hawkesbury River, descending on the state capital by train, bus or car. David Thompson dressed as a knight for the occassion. Oscar Colman Ashlee Storey and her mum, Anissa, were two who made the journey on the Pacific Motorway, arriving at the stadium in jerseys from the collection of their late brother and son Matthew, who died nine years ago from Hodgkin’s lymphoma. “All his friends have been sending messages saying he’ll be here with us. They’re so happy we got tickets,” Anissa said. “He was the number one Knights fan, and even his coffin, he had a Knights coffin.”



Ashlee, who attends every home game, has worn her Knights jerseys to work every day this week, much to the chagrin of her boss, a Roosters supporter. But the events at the fan parade on Saturday were in every fan’s mind. Ashlee and Anissa Storey outside Accor Stadium. Oscar Colman “Just upsetting and devastating,” she said. “I feel so sorry for all the families that were all involved in it. It’s just terrible. “It’s been such a great atmosphere in Newcastle and for one guy to ruin it all for everyone is just really upsetting.”



Although Knights fans dominated the station and pubs around Accor – including one actually dressed as a knight (“It’s not knitted by Nan; I got it on eBay,” David Thompson said) – others were there for the State Championship and NRLW grand final. Adrian Harch with his children, Ella and Lachlan, outside Accor Stadium. Oscar Colman Luckily for 10-year-old Lachlan Harch, his beloved Brisbane Broncos were still in contention in the NRLW. Otherwise, the Broncos jersey, shorts, socks and necklace he received for his birthday on Thursday wouldn’t have seen the inside of a stadium until next year. Sadly for him, the Broncos were well beaten, 30-6, by the Roosters in the women’s decider. Though fewer than the Knights fans, Roosters supporters made a pilgrimage of their own from Sydney’s east to its west and weren’t phased by being in the minority.



“It doesn’t matter,” Harry Zouroudis, who dressed up as a Rooster, said. “It’s the result that matters in the end.” Some Roosters fans made a much longer commute, and only intend to do so once. Harry Zouroudis wasn’t phased about the fewer number of Roosters fans. Oscar Colman Moruya’s Brad Fairbairn has been a fan for more than half a century but has never attended a grand final. He’s in the stands because of a drunken impulse after the Roosters’ 36-20 victory over the Dolphins in the preliminary final at Suncorp Stadium. “Well I got drunk last Friday night and said I don’t care what it costs, we’re going,” he said.



Although Fairburn spent more than $1600 on two tickets – one for himself and one for partner Karen Cooper – he didn’t wake up hungover and regretful the morning after. “It’s a bucket list thing,” he said. “We’re not getting any younger, we won’t be back again.”

World.title: Albo, Minns, Greg Norman: The who’s who of grand final VIPs
World.content:
Breaking NationalCBD Albo, Minns, Greg Norman: The who’s who of grand final VIPs John Buckley Updated October 4, 2026 — 8:37pm ,first published 6:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The first big question facing Peter V’landys during his reign as rugby league’s newly minted executive chairman was whether or not the NRL could snatch a victory over the AFL in the TV ratings when the dust settles on the 2026 grand final. Only a few months ago, the NRL chief was holding court with media bosses at the State of Origin opener, with broadcasters Nine Entertainment, owner of this masthead, and Foxtel, owned by the global streaming giant DAZN, jockeying for pride and place in the thick of high-stakes negotiations over a new media rights deal. New US ambassador David Brat with Anthony Albanese inside the Presidents Suite at Accor Stadium on Sunday night for the NRL grand final. Greg Norman is in the background. Those talks would eventually deliver V’landys a $5.3 billion broadcast rights deal, and set a new national record in the process. On Sunday evening, the challenge was to deliver value for money – all without the draw of a major entertainment act to bring in extra eyeballs. But if V’landys was nervous, he didn’t show it, as he pressed the flesh with a cast of powerbrokers from across business and politics.



Among the biggest names to drop into V’landys’ Presidents Suite at Accor Stadium was David Brat, US President Donald Trump’s new ambassador to Australia. Brat, regular readers will no doubt recall, only arrived on Australian shores last month, filling the post after it sat vacant for close to two years. No doubt the grand final will offer the ambassador a speed-run on Australian diplomacy. Labor stars: Premier Chris Minns and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the grand final on Sunday night. Also in the room was former Australian golfing great Greg Norman, who has been a conduit between Australian officials and golf-loving US president Trump. The biggest names usually turn out closer to kick-off, but after a protracted period on the sidelines over summer following last year’s expenses scandal, Communications and Sport Minister Anika Wells eagerly turned up to the stadium early. The minister was among those who showed up to V’landys’ suite in the afternoon, working the room with an eye on the NRLW grand final clash between the Roosters and the Broncos. Also at the stadium early was a man known for his love of a different code: Former Collingwood president Eddie McGuire, who was seen with his wife, Carla Galloway, climbing the escalator to the private suites during the women’s final.



NRL officials were out early. The media types, meanwhile, were also out in force. Among them was Nine Entertainment director Andrew Lancaster and the company’s publishing boss Tory Maguire, who were expected to be joined by the company’s chairman Peter Tonagh. Tonagh, according to The Australian Financial Review, intervened in Nine’s negotiations with V’landys to tie up the company’s free-to-air rights to the NRL. The other side of the rights deal, meanwhile, was represented by Patrick Delany, who just last month was promoted to chief operating officer of Foxtel’s (relatively) new owner, DAZN. Foxtel heavyweight Brian Walsh was also there, we’re told, as was Tom Malone, chief executive of 2GB owner Tapt Media. Prime Minister Antony Albanese and Queensland Premier David Crisafulli at the grand final. But the raw power, as always, lay with who got pride and place with V’landys himself, revelling in his first grand final as executive chairman. There was never any doubt that taking pride of place in the Presidents Suite was Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who had a seat saved next to V’landys, with Albanese’s wife, Jodie Haydon, to the PM’s side on the seating plan. The couple dropped in to work the room well before kick off, by which time Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn was also doing the rounds.



NSW Premier Chris Minns also dropped in to the suite, no doubt a little smug to see the grand final clash locked up by two of his state’s clubs. But that didn’t stop Queensland Premier David Crisafulli from taking up the invitation to make the trip south. NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane was also saved a place for good measure. Rounding out the political contingent was Barnaby Joyce, who showed up well before the men’s kick-off at 7.30pm. World.title: Moving or exploitative? The verdict on the NRL’s grand final pre-match show
World.content:
CultureTV & radioNRL grand final Moving or exploitative? The verdict on the NRL’s grand final pre-match show Garry Maddox October 4, 2026 — 8:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NRL struggled to line up its traditional NRL grand final pre-match entertainment until days before the big game. No Olivia Dean, too expensive. No Tones and I, too complicated, especially if hit song Dance Monkey was off the playlist. No Silverchair reunion given the late notice and the well-known disagreements between the Newcastle band’s members. Retired South Sydney player Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles acknowledge the crowd before they take part in a lap of the field ahead of the NRL grand final. Getty Images The NRL eventually decided there would be no show at all this year. The game’s supremo, Peter V’landys, said he would rather spend $1 million on junior development than a big-name act. So far, so chaotic.



Then came a late turnaround during the week: V’landys said there would be a show, after all. And that would be “the highest-rating 11 minutes you will ever see”. It emerged the NRL planned a tribute to former Souths star Jai Arrow, whose forced retirement after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease has resulted in some of the season’s most emotional moments. Amy Shark and Dave Gleeson perform before the NRL grand final. Getty Images As much love as there is around the rugby league community for Arrow and his family, there was a real risk a tribute dreamt up in the last week would feel exploitative. That it was milking the genuine warmth the game felt for the larrikin Rabbitoh. So after The Kid Laroi and Teddy Swims shone in the last two years, how was it?



As excitement built towards kick-off, the show began with veteran commentator Ray Warren talking about the importance of rugby league heroes and announcing that the $1 million would allow underprivileged kids to play the game. He said Arrow had shown us “what true bravery really looks like” and called on the crowd at the stadium to shoot an arrow for Jai. Loading Then Amy Shark started singing You’ll Never Walk Alone, the Liverpool FC anthem was the moving soundtrack to Arrow taking the field for his 100th and last Souths match and other emotional moments since his MND diagnosis. She greeted him and a surprise guest, former Wallaby Nathan Charles, who has also been diagnosed with MND, as they started a drive on a lap of honour.



David Gleeson from the Screaming Jets, another favourite Newcastle band, took over with Four Non Blondes’ What’s Up, with Shark and the crowd joining in. Then Phil Jamieson from Grinspoon launched into the most famous rugby league anthem of all, The Best. The verdict: it was a simple but effective show. Considering how late it came together, the emphasis on Arrow, Charles and a trio of Australian singers had none of the wow factor of Kylie Minogue’s 20-minute set at the AFL grand final, but it worked well enough on TV. The visual element that should have capped the show – the crowd united in firing an arrow for Jai – came too early and didn’t pay off. Not one of the all-time great NRL grand final shows but it did not feel awkward or contrived. It will work a lot better next year if the planning starts a lot earlier.
