World.title: Step back in time like it was 1953
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Step back in time like it was 1953 October 4, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. ONE NATION Pauline Hanson stands in front of a banner proclaiming, “Take Victoria Back” (‴⁣⁣In prison by Christmas’: One Nation attacks Andrews, Allan in campaign launch″⁣ 4/10). One wonders if she realises just how accurately this epitomises her approach.

One Nation would take Australia back to a mythical golden age, somewhere around 1953, when the population was a little over 8million; very few people went to university, no one had heard of a bahn mi, inefficient internal combustion engine cars ruled the roads, and the white Australia policy manned the borders.

It was a narrow, inward looking society and, if we are wise, it’s never coming back.

Alan Whittaker, East Kew Labor government has lost all credibility

The sentiment behind ‴⁣⁣In prison by Christmas’: One Nation attacks Andrews, Allan in campaign launch″⁣ (4/10) is nonsense given how our justice system works.

More importantly, Victoria is in the invidious situation of the possibility of One Nation holding the balance of power in the upper house. This is extremely alarming.

The tragedy in all this is that the state Labor government has rightly lost all credibility, having been neglectful of the needs of many communities. One Nation’s rhetoric has no understanding of the climate crisis, how immigration has benefitted Australia and the success of our multiculturalism.

The world of yesteryear is not what is required today. The political landscape is fallow.

Judith Morrison, Nunawading



Conspiracy politics must be rebuffed

Labor and Coalition voters thinking of switching allegiance to One Nation at the Victorian election need to read the senseless and destructive rhetoric of its Victorian leader Warren Pickering and others to see the threat the party represents to our country and our social cohesion. ″⁣

″⁣This is an opportunity to shake the established order to its core″⁣, Pickering said, giving the impression One Nation is the ″⁣real″⁣ Australia.

But it’s a con. Pauline Hanson might claim she understands the anger of her supporters, but this is a fallacy. How else to explain her anti-worker rhetoric?

One Nation offers solutions without truth.

Its racial grievances (a return to the ″⁣good old days″⁣ of white Australia) and conspiracy politics need to be rebuffed by Victorian voters.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne A show of Trumpian kitsch

One Nation’s Victorian campaign launch at the weekend alarmingly reflected Trumpian politics – right down to the kitsch ″⁣bobble-head″⁣ Hanson dolls, the corny copycat MAGA caps (″⁣Make Albo Go Away″⁣), and the threats to jail political opponents.

Hopefully, there are still enough rational, discriminating voters around to ensure that this divisive populist movement doesn’t end up holding the balance of power. And Jess Wilson also needs to ensure that no concessions are made to One Nation for her to become premier, which would send the state down a very dangerous and turbulent pathway.

Bruce Watson, Belgrave MAGA with a local twist

The US has its orange MAGA man, and now our own orange lady is touting MAGA with her “Make Albo Go Away” slogan. Neither orange holds much a-peel for me.

I suggest the compost bin.

Mark Cherny, Caulfield North THE FORUM Greens’ flawed strategy

I am sorry to hear that new Greens leader David Shoebridge is intending that the Greens replace, rather than work with, Labor. The idea of the two main left of centre parties fighting each other for supremacy in the face of a growing threat from the far right is reminiscent of Germany in the 1930s.

Cooperating with a moribund and reactionary Coalition to make life more difficult for Labor only opens the way for One Nation to further exploit people’s frustration and anger. Similarly, I wish that Anthony Albanese would put all his energy into fighting Tories rather than indulging in his well-known loathing of the Greens. A whole lot of energy and resources aimed at flipping a couple of Labor seats to the Greens or vice versa is only lessening what is available to tackle the real threat, which comes from the right.

Ron Exiner, Northcote



Heed history Shoebridge

Greens leader Senator David Shoebridge has said no to providing arms to the democratically elected government of Ukraine. Meanwhile, North Korea and Iran send arms and support to Russia as it invades and tries to overthrow the Ukrainian government.

In the 1930s, England and other allied countries said no to providing arms to the democratically elected government of Spain while Germany and Italy supplied arms and support to Franco as his troops invaded from North Africa to overthrow the Spanish government.

The end result of that was 40 years of repressive fascist dictatorship in Spain, the deaths of innumerable Spanish people and arguably the emboldenment of the Nazis leading into World War 2.

Sometimes if you want peace, you need to learn the lessons of history and fully support the fight to stop the aggressor.

Graham Phelps, Ocean Grove Follow SA lead

Here we go again. ″⁣Big money dodges election laws″⁣ on The Age front page (4/10). When will the penny drop that we can’t have a true democracy and allow political donations, the two are diametrically opposed? Simple logic suggests donors overwhelmingly give money to politicians and political parties to curry favour – there is no such thing as a free lunch.

South Australia’s Premier Peter Malinauskas, understood this and successfully campaigned in 2022 by pledging to ban political donations in his state. Once elected, his law received unanimous support in the SA parliament.

There, the state pays for political campaign costs on an equitable basis depending on party size etc. Malinauskas also severely curtailed the influence of political lobbyists in his state and enacted laws to make them accountable.

When will the rest of Australia follow that lead?

Jack Coffey, Camberwell, Downsizer downdraught

It is simplistic to say that the only people who are negatively affected by falling house prices are investors. Many are regular owner/occupiers and, while it is true that if you are selling and buying into the same market there is little real impact, many retirees are downsizing, and have bought an apartment or unit off-the-plan, up to two years out from occupation. Their purchase was probably conducted at prices near their peak, say early 2025, while their settlement might be in early 2027, with returns down maybe 15 to 20 per cent off the peak.

The developer of their off-the-plan purchase is not about to offer a discount because the market has dropped, so if the home owner’s sale return is necessary to finance their purchase, they are compromised.

Pete Dunne, Highett Doctors’ complaints

Your doctor correspondent (Letters, 4/10) probably knows better than most about the brutal hours and shifts that our young doctors work in the public system. They never stop training. They probably earn less in their 12-hour shifts than someone working at a Big Build site. And our lives and wellbeing are in their hands. If their union (which has to be one of the most conservative) calls a strike, the rest of us should stop and think about what we want from these brave young people.

Hamish McTavish, Brunswick East Medical charge shock

I feel sorry for the women anaesthetists; it seems like the old boys’ club culture, which women have been subjected to in many fields.

But I was more shocked by the $10k a day fee headline; is that what they can earn? Specialist doctors, dental and eye surgeons etc are charging exorbitant fees, and the out-of-pocket expenses are rising at an alarming rate, even if you have private health cover.

Every other industry seems to get mentioned if they price gouge, but not in this field.

Darren Oliver, Daylesford



Who succeeds Boomers?

The article on boomer life expectancy (″⁣Death numbers are climbing as Australia’s Baby Boomers reach their 80s″⁣, 3/10) was a surprisingly good use of statistics, although decimals of a year were unnecessarily precise.

I’m a 1949 Boomer. One feature was the steady introduction of new vaccines in my time, and compulsory injections. The polio and diphtheria epidemics were recent history: we avoided them. We were protected from measles, smallpox and tuberculosis.

I have never understood the thinking of the anti-vax brigade. One feature of the Boomer generation: we started multiple community cultural and preservation organisations, involving regular work sessions or club meetings. Most of the committees of management are still run by the same founders: now into their 70s and 80s.

The younger generation are generally not joiners, or attendees, or volunteers. As we die, many of those clubs and projects will die. Succession is a constant topic at annual general meetings.

There are however some younger people involved. Mixing with enthusiastic and energetic younger generations keeps my brain alive far more than shifting into a retirement home where there might be one death per week.

Roderick Smith, Surrey Hills Book retreat

The article ″⁣In the age of Kindle, books are making it back to our shelves″⁣, (4/10) warmed this old librarian’s heart. Walking into my study I’m surrounded by books about beautiful places, inspiring art, fascinating people and history, and novels that temporarily cocoon me from the problems of the real world. I feel that I’m among old friends, even if they do need dusting. Give me the physicality of a real book and, yes, a print newspaper before another screen any day.

Vikki O’Neill, Ashburton Writers’ write back

As an avid reader, as well as a buyer of books, mostly non-fiction, it’s great to read that books are making a comeback, (4/10). If I read a book that really impresses me, I will write a letter to the author to tell them.

I have written many such letters. Most authors do reply. Two authors that stick in my mind, are famed crime novelist Donald Westlake, and the Pulitzer Prize winning author Robert Caro.

Mr Westlake wrote to say: “You’re letter made my day.” Mr Caro, not only thanked me for my letter on his book “The Power Broker”, but also asked for me to let him know what I thought of the first volume on his biography of Lyndon B. Johnson.

It’s obvious that authors appreciate hearing from the people who read their books for pleasure, not as a critique.

Chris Burgess, Port Melbourne Noisy children

Recent letters about noisy children disturbing the peace reminds me of a story I heard once. A couple were overheard talking about having children. They decided they didn’t want children, and were going home to tell them.

Sue Fisher, Coburg Your voting choice

Your correspondent (Letters, 3/10) does not appear to understand how each political party’s “How to Vote” cards actually function. They state that “the preferential system advantages the parties that preference each other”.

However, the numbered lists on these handouts are not mandatory, it is OK for each of us to make up our own minds about which party we prefer first, second and so on.

Sandra Weller, Mount Helen



Pot and parma option

Rising prices and cost of living pressures are two topics that, understandably, appear daily in our newspapers and television. Why, then, do many newspapers continue to run with columns of luncheon interviews with famous people, the total cost of such lunch for the interviewer and interviewee often amounting to a staggering $180 to $300?

It would be more realistic in these times of falling real purchasing power for these interviews to be conducted over a ″⁣pot and parma″⁣ pub meal – total cost $85. As another option, the interviews could be held in warm spring weather or autumnal bliss, with fish and chips on a park bench at $40. Shareholders would be happy.

James Henshall, Richmond You’re not in an ad

During the recent rain storms (I refuse to call them ″⁣events″⁣), there were repeated warnings for motorists to not drive through flood waters.

However, ads for massive SUVs currently on sale in Australia inevitably depicts them conquering rugged terrain and negotiating their way through creeks and waterways of varying depth. Is it any wonder the drivers of these vehicles think they are invincible in flood waters?

Narelle Murray, Glen Waverley AND ANOTHER THING Leadership

I wish we had an Australian politician like Bernie Sanders in the United States. Old but articulate, wise, smart, savvy and super intelligent, with the ability to read the room and offer cautions that are very real. I think everyone could learn from this long-serving independent congressman.

Frank Flynn, Cape Paterson The attempted execution of Christa Pike, even 30 years after her imprisonment in the US, shows just how uncivilised and abhorrent that country is.

David Eames-Mayer, Balwyn



One Nation

It is apparent that some of One Nation’s political operatives don’t understand the separation of powers given their threat to imprison former Labor premiers. Another concern to add to the many should they form government next month.

Tony Delaney, Warrnambool Gosh, I bet former premiers Dan Andrews and Jacinta Allan are quaking in their boots.

Fiona White, Alfredton One Nation’s Warren Pickering rails against foreign ″⁣globalists″⁣, yet his party’s threat to imprison Dan Andrews and Jacinta Allan is straight out of US President Donald Trump’s playbook. And look what he’s done to his and the world’s economies.

George Djoneff, Mitcham Perhaps Pauline Hanson was unaware when evoking Ned Kelly at her launch that Kelly and his gang were bank robbers who murdered three policemen. Not ideal role models for an aspiring leader.

Sandra Torpey, Hawthorn When One nation voters (as with Brexit) have emotionally blown up traditional government, will they accept responsibility for any negative results?

Malcolm McDonald, Burwood



Finally

Rich people are using multiple businesses to circumvent the $4970 cap to donate to state political parties. The solution is simple: only registered voters can donate. No businesses. That means no loopholes. No non-citizens.

Rob Skelton, Ballarat The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: The private schools with the richest parents in Victoria revealed as extra funding flows
World.content:
Victorian private schools, many of them educating the state’s richest families, benefited from an extra $95 million in Commonwealth funding in 2025, as underfunded public schools’ battle for their share continued to go down to the wire. Melbourne Grammar School, where the median family income was $375,000, the highest in the state, received $1.18 million more than the nationally agreed funding benchmark from the Commonwealth last year. Melbourne Grammar School It was one of 26 Melbourne schools with a median family income of $300,000 or more. At least 12 of those schools received between $134,000 and $1.5 million above their entitled funding, known as the School Resource Standard (SRS), in 2025. The SRS is an estimate of how much public funding a school needs to meet its students’ educational needs, as detailed in the long-awaited Gonski reforms.



Federal Education Department data released in response to inquiries from Greens senator Penny Allman-Payne during budget estimates showed there were 58 overfunded non-government Victorian schools and education authorities in 2025, which received a combined $95,154,592 in funding above SRS. The Commonwealth has now agreed to fund 80 per cent of the SRS of non-government schools, while the states’ target is 20 per cent, but the transition back to their actual entitlement is being done in stages until 2029. Melbourne Grammar School will receive about $986,000 more than the SRS this year, $40,000 more than previous Senate estimates figures revealed. Principal Philip Grutzner said Melbourne Grammar was “keenly aware” of the funding changes and was planning ahead to reduce the impact on families.



Asked whether this would mean fee increases, Grutzner said salaries, inflation, ongoing operating costs, payroll tax and fees all influenced tuition. “Our focus continues to be on offering an exceptional, holistic education focused on the whole child,” Grutzner said. State Education Minister Gabrielle Williams and Premier Ben Carroll. Eddie Jim Christ Church Grammar School, an independent Anglican primary school in South Yarra, educated the second-highest-income-earning families in the state last year. There is no indication that it was overfunded. Parents of Christ Church Grammar students had a median income of $370,000, and the top 25 per cent of earners had an income of $580,000 of more.



It was one of 21 schools where the top 25 per cent of families had an annual income of $500,000 or more in 2025. Principal Kim Wheeler said the school was proud of its community and the many families who had chosen it because they valued a high-quality education for their children. “Our hard-working families make an informed choice in choosing an independent school education, which reflects the importance our community places on education and their desire to provide their children with the best possible opportunities,” Wheeler said. St Joseph’s School in Hawthorn had the third-highest earners last year, with parents having a combined median income of $365,000. The Catholic school’s top 25 per cent of earners brought in $525,000 or more.



The state’s Catholic schools, most of which receive Commonwealth funding via the Victorian Catholic Education Authority (VCEA), received an extra $39.2 million from the Commonwealth last year, dropping to $31 million above their funding entitlement in 2026. Senate estimate data released in November had indicated the peak body would receive $30.6 million this year. VCEA chief executive Elizabeth Labone said the federal government’s data failed to account for enrolment growth and was unlikely to represent the actual funding schools received. “With the new EBA [enterprise bargaining agreement] in Victorian government schools set to increase school costs by a much higher rate than assumed in the SRS model, it is clear that the model no longer sets an accurate funding benchmark for schools,” Labone said. “Catholic education looks forward to working closely with the government to review and improve the SRS model.”



The federal government estimates it will provide $33.3 billion in total recurrent funding for Australian schools this year. This includes $12.7 billion to government schools, $11.1 billion to Catholic schools and $9.5 billion to independent schools. The Commonwealth will provide about $5.3 billion to non-government schools in Victoria. Overfunding has occurred over the past 15 years as Labor and Liberal-led federal governments stuck to a promise that private schools would never be worse off. Public school advocate and Waiting for Gonski co-author Tom Greenwell said successive federal governments “carving out exemptions to placate the private school lobby” had led to overfunding of non-government schools booming.



“[Julia] Gillard guaranteed 3 per cent annual increases for overfunded schools, [Tony] Abbott enthusiastically maintained them, and [Scott] Morrison added fuel to the fire with a multibillion-dollar slush fund and an extension of overfunding for another decade,” Greenwell said. Related Article Private schools Private schools expand scholarships to target ‘late bloomers’, boost diversity Greenwell is among those critical of the pace at which overfunded non-government schools will transition back down to 80 per cent of the SRS. He said the Albanese Labor government would pour more cash into overfunding wealthy private schools this decade than it would into lifting struggling public schools up to the bare minimum standard. “It’s pure political cowardice,” he said. “While the Albanese government is big on rhetoric about fixing public school funding, in reality it’s deferred delivery of real additional funding to the 2030s.” Victoria government schools have been funded at about 90 per cent of the SRS since 2018, despite signing an agreement with the Commonwealth that year to reach full funding by 2028.



The current agreement, which would see the state contribute 75 per cent of the SRS for public schools and the federal government contribute 25 per cent by 2034, is set to expire at the end of the year. The Carroll government has indicated it intends to sign a long-term funding deal ahead of the November election, though it has locked horns with the Commonwealth on the transition and key reforms tied to the federal dollars. The Victorian Education Department has argued that the state is contributing more to school infrastructure than other states and territories, which should be considered when evaluating the state’s investment. Education Minister Gabrielle Williams referred to Victoria’s “$20.1 billion school building program – the largest in the country” in response to questions about SRS funding. “We’re continuing to work with the Commonwealth to secure a long-term funding agreement that delivers full and fair funding for Victoria’s public schools,” she said.

World.title: Doughnuts and Donald Trump: Behind the scenes of the One Nation campaign launch
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD Doughnuts and Donald Trump: Behind the scenes of the One Nation campaign launch Fiona Byrne October 4, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Premier Ben Carroll has been at pains to separate himself from his predecessors, but a One Nation threat to put Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan in jail by Christmas had him lamenting the alarming “Americanisation” of the orange mob’s rallying cry – and that was before he heard about the doughnuts. Pauline Hanson with One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, (right) at Crown in Melbourne on Saturday. Chris Hopkins At One Nation’s Victorian campaign launch on Saturday, MC and candidate Mark Nicholson provocatively threatened to jail the two former Victorian premiers if the right-wing party won November’s state election. His aggressive comment in front of the revved-up 1000 party supporters at Crown mirrored US President Donald Trump’s threat a decade ago to “lock up” political rival Hillary Clinton. Related Article Victorian election ‘In prison by Christmas’: One Nation attacks Andrews, Allan in campaign launch



Trump and America were an obvious but unspoken influence at the sold-out event from the catering – which consisted of three types of doughnuts – to the Aussie-fide version of MAGA hats. In One Nation’s case, the MAGA on its blue hats stood for Make Albo Go Away. Fast-forward to Sunday, and Carroll was asked if he found Nicholson’s comments about his old comrades concerning. Not surprisingly, he said, “it is”, before going on to describe the threat as “deeply alarming”. One Nation have threatened to jail Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews. Justin McManus, Jason South “Any Americanisation of our judicial system should be deeply alarming to every single Victorian,” Carroll said.



“We have a principle in Victoria, and indeed Australia – judicial independence – and that should never be compromised or its integrity put at risk.” Back to the launch, with a “Pauline pothole detector”, a playlist raiding Aussie classics, soft focus video clips of candidates, and sugary snacks, One Nation’s campaign rally was a curious combination of showbiz, slogans and politics – with plenty of merch on the side. One Nation merch at the Victorian state election campaign launch in Melbourne on Saturday. Chris Hopkins CBD ventured inside the gathering, striking up conversation with orange-clad supporters – think tops, ties, T-shirts and the odd orange jacket, these people love a theme – and candidates mingling around the tables of doughy delicacies. Funds certainly weren’t wasted on catering. There were three types of the treats to choose from: strawberry icing with sprinkles, chocolate icing with sprinkles or cinnamon sugar.



Merchandise sales ticked over with a selection of three caps, a party orange T-shirt, Please Explain playing cards and even a Pauline Hanson bobblehead being snapped up. “They are flying off the shelf. We call it a Pauline pothole detector,” one attendee quipped when CBD inquired about the red-headed figurines placed among the caps. “I’m going to put it on my dashboard, and when we hit a pothole, she will shake her head.” Interestingly, only one cowboy hat was spotted among the throng, and, as is par for the course with the One Nation circus, the party ute was there, this time parked in the corner of the conference room foyer and being used by many as a backdrop for selfies. Pauline Hanson at the One Nation Victorian campaign launch. Chris Hopkins



Reflecting perhaps the average age of attendees, the nostalgia card was played heavily, right down to the playlist of Aussie music bangers rolled out as walk-on tracks for candidates and party leaders. Victorian upper house member Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell arrived on stage to Daddy Cool’s Eagle Rock, Rose Tattoo’s We Can’t Be Beaten was played as Colleen Harkin took to the podium, even You’re The Voice got a run as Warren Pickering was introduced to the room. CBD has to wonder what the artists would make of their songs being used at the launch. Hanson took an American option for her music, walking on stage to US rap artist Skrxilla’s Big Time before she was joined by candidates as AC/DC’s Thunderstruck boomed. Seguing from headbanger to revhead, Hanson on Sunday took a go-kart for a spin in Geelong after another One Nation event.



No laughing matter: Hughesy goes solo Time for an update on comedian turned political tub thumper, Dave Hughes. Hughesy’s progressively bolder and louder online railing against the state Labor government, Anthony Albanese’s federal government, budget blowouts, corruption and his support of Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson has been a source of intrigue for CBD over recent months. Dave Hughes has been making headlines for his criticism of Labor. Simon Schluter Just as interesting has been the reaction of some of his comedian colleagues such as Dave Thornton and Henry Bretz who have turned his political awakening into punchlines.



Now, Hughes has taken another turn, splitting with his long-term management. Hughesy has been part of Kevin Whyte’s powerful Token management stable for a couple of decades, but recently the parties agreed to part ways. Related Article Victorian election Dave Hughes to campaign for Liberals in Victorian election Hughes is no longer on the Token website. Clicking through to his former profile page, you find a note reading: “Whoops, it looks like the page you are looking for no longer exists or has been moved.” Hughes confirmed to CBD he was going in a new direction under his own steam, saying he had been heading towards being independent for a while, long before finding his political voice.



“It’s a very amicable split,” he said. “It has been a very mutually beneficial partnership for decades. But I actually do have time to organise my own stuff now, so I’m gonna do it!” With extra time on his hands, we doubt he is going pull back on his political commentary. In fact, it might even ratchet up a notch. Foxx spotting Oscar-winning actor Jamie Foxx has been spotted in Melbourne ahead of filming in the Docklands starting later this week on his new film, Deadlocked. Related Article CBD Hollywood film to have Jamie Foxx under fire in Melbourne’s Docklands



Foxx turned plenty of heads at the weekend when he got a sweat up playing pickleball at House of Pickle in Port Melbourne. The Hollywood star is something of a celebrity in the pickleball/paddleball world. In fact, he is known back in Los Angeles for throwing pickleball parties, and co-founded a paddle brand. Expect him to play on while he is in town.

World.title: ‘Makes you happy’: Classic Greek treat finds a new home on Sydney Road
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life ‘Makes you happy’: Classic Greek treat finds a new home on Sydney Road Carolyn Webb October 4, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A serious back injury ended his career as a plumber at age 20, and aside from being painful, it left Kosta Kostidis at a loss as to what to do for a living. But the love and advice of relatives, including his 89-year-old grandfather, helped Kostidis find a sweet but very different career — in the field of Greek pastries. Kosta Kostidis (right), with Yianni Palazi, serves bougatsa pastries at his new shop, Bougatsaki, in Brunswick. Chris Hopkins A few weeks ago, two years after the injury, Kostidis opened a small shop in Sydney Road, Brunswick, whose prime product is a custard-filled pastry called bougatsa. The street-side outlet is named Bougatsaki, meaning, in Greek, “little bougatsa”.



There’s a symmetry to the move, given Kostidis’s pappou (grandfather), Efthimios Oplopiadis, is a former baker. In 2024, Kostidis was a fourth-year apprentice plumber when he “did his back” on a job in Melbourne’s south-east. Former baker Efthimios Oplopiadis with grandson Kosta Kostidis at the new shop. Chris Hopkins “I was out of work for a year, seeing physios and specialists,” he said. He was bedridden for months, and he still receives treatment.



“It was not fun,” he said. “For a couple of months, it was really bad.” When Kostidis felt better, he was keen to work, but there was a problem: “I had no idea what I wanted to do.” A sample of a bougatsa pastry from the shop, Bougatsaki. Andrew Clark While at home in Coburg, he would make bougatsas with his pappou, and had the idea of selling pastries. Oplopiadis had worked as a baker in Melbourne factories for 30 years after migrating from Greece in 1968 and liked to make pastries at home.



His daughter, Kosta’s mother Martha Oplopiadis, says bougatsas have been a staple of family gatherings, as a dessert, for generations. One year ago, Kostidis started a food van selling bougatsas, which took off. He has worked at parties, festivals and soccer games. Kosta Kostidis (right) with his cousin’s husband, LaManna Supermarket CEO Patrick LaManna. Chris Hopkins In February at the Antipodes Festival in Lonsdale Street, in Melbourne’s CBD, Kostidis, his mother, his sister, Danean, and cousin Lynda LaManna helped Kosta sell more than 3000 bougatsas in three days. Opening the shop in Brunswick last month had been a huge but exciting step, Kostidis said.



He was inspired by specialist bougatsa outlets in Greece. And his mentor – his cousin’s husband, LaManna Supermarket chief executive Patrick LaManna – encouraged him to focus on bougatsas. “To be honest, I’m not too sure what I would have done without Patrick and my mum. Coming off a year when I wasn’t working and was just lost, they helped me find myself, pretty much,” Kostidis said. His grandfather, to whom he has always been close, has also been a great support, being a sounding board, and suggesting ingredients, including savoury fillings. It feels right, says Kostidis, to follow his pappou in the baking business.



Oplopiadis said he liked that Kostidis had opened a shop. “He started slowly and has been steadily progressing and coming up with new ideas,” Oplopiadis said. “I’m happy to see the family helping him. It’s a lot of hard work.” Editor's pick Exclusive

Victorian election A cinema chain’s Liberal donation broke the rules. This is why there won’t be consequences Oplopiadis, originally from the city of Serres, in northern Greece, reckons that bougatsas will draw customers. “You see, when you eat bougatsa, it makes you happy, it’s not a heavy dessert. It has light, velvety custard, it’s just delicious,” he said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘We’re going to defend the kingdom’: NRL fans prepare for grand final after tragedy
World.content:
For Newcastle Knights fan Bailey Goodacre, grand final day began 156km from Sydney’s Accor Stadium in the Del Hotel and Pub on Newcastle’s trendy Darby Street. Not long after the pub’s doors opened at 10am, Goodacre and his mates were inside, beer in hand and ready to watch their team in a grand final for the first time in 25 years. Bailey Goodacre (second from the right) and his friends at The Del Hotel and Pub. Tom Decent “We’ll steady ourselves and have some food and drinks,” he said. “Eventually, we’ll have more people come. It’s going to be unreal. I can’t wait. “We defended the table, and now we’re going to defend the kingdom.”



The city woke to promising news after the tragedy of Saturday. Several supporters, including children, were hospitalised after a car crashed into a crowd in Newcastle. But a five-year-old girl struck by the car, who underwent emergency surgery the night before, was now in a critical but stable condition. “We feel really bad for what has happened. It is sad,” Goodacre said, adding that he thought the town, already bonded by their team’s success, had become even closer after the incident. Newcastle fans at Broadmeadow Station start the journey to Sydney. Sitthixay Ditthavong At Broadmeadow Station, three kilometres closer to Accor Stadium, groups of Knights fans left every 30 minutes on trains to Sydney. Most were in Newcastle jerseys, few had any luggage and they seemed prepared to make the return journey after the match. Two of them, Cathy and Michelle Price, wouldn’t have been on the Newcastle express if not for the tickets they won in a competition on the morning of the game.



“I’ve had to change my plans,” Cathy said on the platform. By midday, hundreds had crossed the Hawkesbury River, descending on the state capital by train, bus or car. David Thompson dressed as a knight for the occassion. Oscar Colman Ashlee Storey and her mum, Anissa, were two who made the journey on the Pacific Motorway, arriving at the stadium in jerseys from the collection of their late brother and son Matthew, who died nine years ago from Hodgkin’s lymphoma. “All his friends have been sending messages saying he’ll be here with us. They’re so happy we got tickets,” Anissa said. “He was the number one Knights fan, and even his coffin, he had a Knights coffin.”



Ashlee, who attends every home game, has worn her Knights jerseys to work every day this week, much to the chagrin of her boss, a Roosters supporter. But the events at the fan parade on Saturday were in every fan’s mind. Ashlee and Anissa Storey outside Accor Stadium. Oscar Colman “Just upsetting and devastating,” she said. “I feel so sorry for all the families that were all involved in it. It’s just terrible. “It’s been such a great atmosphere in Newcastle and for one guy to ruin it all for everyone is just really upsetting.”



Although Knights fans dominated the station and pubs around Accor – including one actually dressed as a knight (“It’s not knitted by Nan; I got it on eBay,” David Thompson said) – others were there for the State Championship and NRLW grand final. Adrian Harch with his children, Ella and Lachlan, outside Accor Stadium. Oscar Colman Luckily for 10-year-old Lachlan Harch, his beloved Brisbane Broncos were still in contention in the NRLW. Otherwise, the Broncos jersey, shorts, socks and necklace he received for his birthday on Thursday wouldn’t have seen the inside of a stadium until next year. Sadly for him, the Broncos were well beaten, 30-6, by the Roosters in the women’s decider. Though fewer than the Knights fans, Roosters supporters made a pilgrimage of their own from Sydney’s east to its west and weren’t phased by being in the minority.



“It doesn’t matter,” Harry Zouroudis, who dressed up as a Rooster, said. “It’s the result that matters in the end.” Some Roosters fans made a much longer commute, and only intend to do so once. Harry Zouroudis wasn’t phased about the fewer number of Roosters fans. Oscar Colman Moruya’s Brad Fairbairn has been a fan for more than half a century but has never attended a grand final. He’s in the stands because of a drunken impulse after the Roosters’ 36-20 victory over the Dolphins in the preliminary final at Suncorp Stadium. “Well I got drunk last Friday night and said I don’t care what it costs, we’re going,” he said.



Although Fairburn spent more than $1600 on two tickets – one for himself and one for partner Karen Cooper – he didn’t wake up hungover and regretful the morning after. “It’s a bucket list thing,” he said. “We’re not getting any younger, we won’t be back again.”

World.title: New postgraduate training pathway needed for rural GPs - doctor
World.content:
A Far North doctor is calling for a new postgraduate training pathway to better equip GPs for work in rural areas.

Katharina Blattner said working as a doctor in the rural Far North wasn't easy, but it was rewarding.

"I work at Hauora Hokianga Rawene Hospital, one of the smallest hospitals in the country, and my job is fantastic," she said.

She said working in a remote area had much different demands to working in the city.

"Practising medicine in a rural area, that's shaped by a lot of interrelated factors but the notable one is geographic distance from specialist services and resources," she explained.

"That rural context means clinicians need to be able to work across a really broad generalist scope of practice and with the capacity to manage a really wide range of presentations to quite a depth, because it might be a two-hour drive to the closest ED."

Dr Blattner had trained as both a GP and a rural hospital doctor.

Katharina Blattner. Supplied / University of Otago

"It's a pretty long training process to get a fellowship in rural medicine and general practice, they're both specialties in their own right," she said.

"That would be a minimum four or up to eight years of training [after graduating medical school] before someone is a fully qualified rural medicine specialist."

The rural hospital medicine specialisation was introduced in 2008 in recognition that urban and rural hospitals required different skillsets.

"Being a rural-specific programme, that's had a real impact in terms of the doctors coming out the other end making a difference to the workforce in rural hospitals," she said.

But no such specialisation existed for rural general practice.

"What hasn't happened, and what would be great if it did happen, would be if there was also a parallel rural-specific training programme for general practice. If within the general practice programme there was a rural-specific stream."

Dr Blattner, who also worked as an associate professor at the University of Otago, last week published a study in the New Zealand Medical Journal highlighting the gap.

She said working as a general practitioner in a rural area was often seen as a "lesser" option for graduates, and offering a full postgraduate training pathway would go a long way to breaking that illusion.

"Sometimes what I'm hearing or what I'm observing is that it's seen as a dead-end choice. Graduates would like to see they can have career progression in rural medicine in the same way they would if they chose another specialty," Blattner said.

"As a clinician you want to be able to do the whole career-progression thing, work to the top of your scope, be involved in teaching and do some research.

World.title: Auckland road cordoned off after hazardous materials found in car
World.content:
Police have cordoned off a road in Auckland after the discovery of hazardous materials in a car.

The substances were found in a vehicle in Epsom at the intersection of Market Road and Great South Road.

Police searched the car after arresting the driver, who had fled from them about 5pm near the Karaka area.

The driver was caught after spikes were used near Market Road.

Fire and Emergency are at the scene.

World.title: Two men jump into river after failing to stop for police
World.content:
Police in the Ōpōtiki area in the Bay of Plenty are appealing for sightings of two men who failed to stop for officers before jumping in a river.

Duty Inspector Phil Edwards said about 3.45am on Sunday a vehicle ran a red light in Wainui.

"Road spikes were successfully deployed about 10km from Ōpōtiki shortly after 4am, before the vehicle came to a stop down Snell Road, by the Otara River," he said.

"The two occupants have then got out of the vehicle and jumped into the water."

A search and rescue operation was launched, with assistance from the Harbourmaster, Coastguard Ōpōtiki, and a rescue helicopter, but the two men have not been found.

"Police Search and Rescue staff are continuing the search this morning, and are appealing to the public for help," Edwards said.

Edwards said a "large-scale" operation was underway and police had searched the river and deployed helicopters and ground crew across farmland to find the men.

"If you are one of these males, you know who they are, or you have any other information which may help us locate them, please get in touch. We're also after information about any suspicious behaviour in the area."

Edwards said the priority at this time was ensuring the men were safe.

Urgent information could be passed on via 111, referencing job number P067829874.

World.title: 'I just wanted to get him out' - Man who saved 89-year-old from burning home
World.content:
One of the men who helped rescue an 89-year-old from his burning Gisborne home early Saturday morning, before quietly slipping away, says he did not want to make a fuss about it.

Local police hailed Tim Morris as a 'hero' yesterday after the rescue.

The 37-year-old Gisborne man was driving on Aberdeen Road at about 1am Saturday with a friend, when they saw the blaze and pulled over.

They were able to pull the 89-year-old through a broken window to safety, before checking to see if anyone else was in the property and going to neighbours for help.

Police said the rescued man was recuperating well in hospital.

Police said, once emergency services arrived, Morris and his friend quietly slipped into the night, but he revealed his involvement, after he saw an appeal from police for the hero to come forward.

"I just wanted to get him out," he said. "It's been a bit emotional.

"At the end of the day, helping people makes me feel good."

Detective Senior Sergeant John Love said the fact Morris did not want to make a fuss when he arrived at the Gisborne Police station on Sunday morning said a lot about him.

"However, thanks to his quick actions, the house occupant was able to escape a life-threatening situation.

"We put out an appeal, because we wanted to find him, not because he was in any trouble. We wanted the opportunity to shake his hand and say 'thank you'.

"We got that opportunity today.

World.title: Coloured solar panels hold potential for NZ vegetable growers
World.content:
A renewable energy researcher says coloured solar panels have "tremendous" potential for New Zealand vegetable growers.

Published in Cell Reports Physical Science, a Swedish study has found broccoli grows well beneath magenta-coloured solar panels, although the vegetable takes 25 days longer to get to full size and has lower levels of micronutrients.

Victoria University School of Engineering and Computer Science associate professor Ramesh Rayudu said further research was needed, but the initial study was a bit of a game-changer.

Rayudu told RNZ that, every now and then, researchers came across a paper that sparked the reaction: "Oh, that was so obvious, why haven't we thought of that?"

"It was one of those situations when I read that paper," he said. "It is a great idea."

The Swedish researchers said conventional dark-blue solar panels were typically opaque, creating too much shade for crops. so customised semi-transparent panels were designed for the study.

The basic concept was straightforward, according to author Silvia Ma Lu of Mälardalen University.

"The solar panels use part of the incoming sunlight to generate renewable electricity, while allowing part of the light to pass through to the crops growing underneath."

The solar panels offered a potential tool for farmers to harvest renewable energy, while sustaining crop yields, the study said.

Ramesh said it was a promising demonstration of producing both food and electricity from the same land, and opened the door for New Zealand vegetable growers to one day offset their electricity bills or sell energy back to the grid.

"If they haven't got any solar panels, now they can consider putting in solar panels. What that means is that whatever energy is generated from the solar panels is an added advantage for these growers."

He said the technology likely needed further development to make such a scheme viable, as the semi-transparent panels generated less electricity.

"Depending on the value of electricity and the price received for broccoli, that lost electricity could require roughly 1.2 to 3.2 tonnes of additional broccoli per hectare to offset its value."

However, if the benefits outweighed the cost, coloured solar panels shouldn't be limited to broccoli growers, he said.

"We can use it for other things, like cabbages, cauliflower, carrots."

Canterbury University electric power research engineer Sharee McNab said investigating how to make food production and energy generation viable and efficient was potentially crucial.

World.title: As it happened: Election campaign 4 October
World.content:
Election 2026 heated up on Sunday, when Labour released its long-awaited fiscal plan and National immediately claimed it fell billions of dollars short, which would be made up in more borrowing and taxes.

Among the promises from Labour leader Chris Hipkins was a pay rise for 65,000 care and support workers, costing $2.5b over four years, while also re-implementing pay-equity legislation.

National finance spokesperson Nicola Willis accused Labour of lying to the country, claiming an $8.5b hole in its policy.

Audio player for " Why aren't young people signed up to vote? Let's ask them! " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1710400%2Fas-it-happened-election-campaign-4-october

Why aren't young people signed up to vote? Let's ask them! Afternoons Download MP3 11m

Meanwhile, National leader Christopher Luxon visited the Takanini Gurdwara Sri Kalgidhar Sahib Sikh Temple, which has hosted several previous prime ministers.

National also launched its blue campaign bus and pledged $1.75b to build South Auckland's Mill Road, which NZ First leader Winston Peters claimed his party first announced in July.

National's Mt Roskill MP Carlos Cheung also had billboards burnt down overnight.

ACT leader David Seymour insisted government policies had attacked wealth creation for decades and other parties would "destroy wealth" with their solutions to the current cost-of-living crisis.

Instead, he promised to remove tax on KiwiSaver earnings.

The Green Party pledged to make public transport free for eligible groups, like children, students apprentices, community services cardholders and total mobility users, and cap bus and train fares at $2 for everyone else.

Te Pāti Māori announced its one-person party list, with general secretary Lance Norman the only extra candidate.

World.title: Greens eye free, fast and reliable public transport with election promises
World.content:
The Green Party has pledged to make public transport free for eligible groups and cap bus and train fares at $2 for everyone else.

It says its transport plan offers fast, frequent and affordable services.

Under the Greens' policy, public transport would be free for children, students, apprentices, Community Service Card holders and Total Mobility users, while everyone else would pay a maximum fare of $2.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406186515112

It would also build mass rapid bus and light rail services in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, offer more frequent inter-regional bus services, strengthen rural bus services and allow councils to pedestrianise more inner-city areas and increase safe walking and biking spaces.

The party has also promised overnight passenger trains from Auckland to Wellington, as well as bringing back the Southerner between Christchurch and Dunedin and extending Te Huia to Tauranga.

"In the middle of a fossil fuel crisis, these common sense investments will save New Zealanders money, stress and time," said co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick.

"It'll cut emissions and improve quality of life."

Swarbrick and transport spokesperson Julie-Anne Genter addressed media in Auckland on Sunday from outside Maungawhau City Rail Link station.

Swarbrick referred to the more than a million trips that have been taken on the CRL since it opened last month.

"What that tells us and shows us so clearly is that when we build transport infrastructure that makes it easy, affordable, and even fun to get around, people will use it.

"But right now, too many New Zealanders are driving around with the fuel light on, hoping and praying that petrol prices will drop," she said.

Swarbrick said the government could not control oil shocks like that caused by the Middle East war - but it could make investments that reduce the cost of living and reduce dependence on fossil fuels.

She described the party's plan as "straight up common sense".

Swarbrick said meaningful change could be made immediately, but some parts of the plan like light rail networks could take a decade or so.

The major investments would go through the Infrastructure Commission's assurance process, she said.

The entire plan would cost around $23.9b: $21b for mass rapid transit and rail investments, $1.3b for capped and free fares, $75m for electric buses, $290m for councils to expand walking and biking spaces, $824m for public transport improvements and $406m for inter-regional buses.

"What we are proposing today is to meet the needs not only of our immediate cost of living crisis, but also our medium and longer term needs to build infrastructure that is fit for purpose for the future. Yes, that will cost money," Swarbrick said.

She cited the Greens' wealth tax as a way of paying for some of it, but said the party's full fiscal plan would be laid out in the next few weeks.

But Public Transport Users Association national co-ordinator Jon Reeves questioned the viability of the Greens' plan.

He supported cheaper fares, but said the proposal sounded like wishful thinking.

"I'd like to see some of these things come true. On a $2 fare for everyone, it's good, it may change the attitudes of some people into using public transport but how many is the question," he said.

"The other area is who is going to fund it.

"When we do give out free transport to someone, someone else has to pay for it. Does it come at the cost and the expense of running services?" he said.

Reeves said one way to reduce the cost of public transport would be to bring services back into New Zealand ownership to keep profits in the country.

"In New Zealand multinational corporations are pretty much the ones who operate all the services, whether it's Auckland or Wellington trains or the bus services around the country. They're all majority owned by overseas foreign companies," he said.

"We need to bring it back to New Zealand and cut out the middleman, bring that money back and make it stay here so we can invest in more public transport and give cheaper fares to users."

World.title: Labour releases its fiscal plan, promises pay rise for care and support workers
World.content:
Labour has released its long-awaited fiscal plan saying every election promise is paid for, but it has not provided a cost for fully re-implementing pay equity legislation.

It does however promise an immediate pay rise to 65,000 care and support workers, costing $2.5 billion over four years, and Labour leader Chris Hipkins says there's "plenty of headroom" within the plan to pay for pay equity overall.

Finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds says Labour will keep operating allowances - that is, new day-to-day spending - at the $2.4 billion set by the coalition government in Budget 2026.

The party said it wouldn't rely on a larger operating allowance, stating new investment "must fit within these allowances, alongside cost pressures and other priorities".

"Our announced capital commitments fit comfortably within the $12 billion of future capital allowances," said Edmonds.

"We also have almost $10.5 billion of future operating allowances unallocated. We can deliver what we have promised without increasing those allowances."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406191627112

Edmonds also said Labour would return the books to surplus in 2028/29 and bring net debt down below 20 percent of GDP "over time", maintaining it will use the OBEGAL measure, rather than the government's preferred OBEGALx measure.

"We can do that because we have made better choices about where public money goes and will make every dollar work harder."

Labour has previously labelled the government's spending decisions austere, but Edmonds denied that matching allowances could also be considered austere.

"We're providing real cost of living relief pressure for our families. We are moving as much as we can to ensure that the money goes to the places it needs to," she said.

"It all comes down to choices."

Labour's already announced capital commitments were:

$200 million capital injection for the New Zealand Future Fund

$420 million for the initial student loan write-off

$200 million for hospitals

$400 million for schools

$2.9 billion for Kāinga Ora housing, spread over four years

$7 million for Ratepayer Assistance Scheme (RAS) solar expenditure

Hipkins said most of the party's big election policies had been announced.

No cost indicated for restoring pay equity law

Last year the government overhauled the Equal Pay Act, retrospectively stripping nurses, teachers, carers and other female-dominated workforces of the right to pursue pay equity claims under the existing law.

The controversial legislation stopped the 33 claims underway and raised the threshold for proving work has been historically undervalued.

On Sunday Labour confirmed it would restore pay equity legislation in its first 100 days and give an immediate pay rise to 65,000 care and support workers.

That specific payrise would cost $2.5 billion over four years, but the full cost for restoring pay equity was not provided.

"You'll see there's plenty of headroom within the fiscal plan that we've released today," Hipkins said.

"We have a $10 billion unallocated amount of headroom, we've got multi billion dollars for health cost pressures - and many of the pay equity claims are within the health system - so we're confident we will be able to meet the costs of pay equity within the flexibility that we built into the plan."

The legislation would include transitional rules so the claims that had been underway could continue, rather than be started from scratch.

Hipkins said the care and support worker payrise was a stopgap.

"This is not a final deal for care and support workers, but that could still take... a year, maybe, to negotiate and to conclude that process."

Some public sector cuts reversed

Labour promised to reversed half of the first tranche of public sector cuts announced in the government's Budget, and fully reverse the second tranche.

The party is working on the assumption that the government is already halfway through that first tranche of cuts.

"In many cases the cuts have already been made, and we're not going to reverse cuts that have already been made," Hipkins said.

"The current government aren't releasing that information, so we've had to make some assumptions about that."

Hipkins said Labour would scrap the Ministry for Regulation, and the savings realised would largely be divvied up among other agencies.

Labour stands by its promises, ridicules National's

Hipkins said National promised to grow the economy and get the books in order.

"It has done neither," he said.

"171,000 New Zealanders are unemployed, growth is weaker and debt has continued to rise. They have cut jobs and services, and New Zealanders have been left to pay the price."

Hipkins said the choice was clear: "more cuts and decline under National, or a Labour Government that will balance the books without shrinking the economy, get costs under control and back the people and businesses doing the work."

Edmonds said every election commitment Labour had made was fully costed and fully funded.

"The numbers add up and we have left room to confidently respond to whatever comes next," she added.

World.title: Up There Cazaly singer vowed to make AFL grand final after horrific fall
World.content:
He is a name synonymous with the AFL grand final.

While teams change, pre-game acts change and even the rules themselves change, Mike Brady's performance of unofficial AFL anthem Up There Cazaly has been a fixture of the big day for decades.

Last weekend's grand final was no different — but that was not always a given.

In January, the 78-year-old suffered a horrific fall during a routine evening walk near his Great Ocean Road home.

Mike Brady performed on ABC's Countdown program in 1979 to promote his Up There Cazaly single. (ABC News)

"I fell and landed on my ample backside," he said, laughing.

But the injury was no laughing matter.

Brady described the horror of having to twist his ankle back into place before dragging himself to a nearby fire station, "leaving a trail of blood and mud".

Brady would later learn he had fractured his leg, ankle and foot in 12 places.

With his doctor telling him not to push himself and that it was unlikely he would be able to walk anytime soon, his grand final call-up nine months later was all but certainly out of the picture.

Mike Brady performed before the 2013 AFL grand final between the Hawthorn Hawks and the Fremantle Dockers. (AAP: David Crosling)

When the AFL asked if he would still be up to performing, he vowed to be there even if he had to crawl on stage.

"I said, 'Try and stop me,'" he said.

"Because I love it. It's a part of me."

'The place was closing in on me'

A self-described "outdoors person" who relishes being active, Brady is the first to admit that even he doubted he would make it during parts of the nine-month journey that followed.

"I wasn't doing well," he said.

"I was waking up and felt like the place was closing in on me.

" I was put in a palliative care place, and that was tough because I felt like I shouldn't be there. "

Mike Brady performed during the 2022 AFL grand final match between Geelong and Sydney. (Getty Images: Dylan Burns)

After five months in hospital, he was able to return home with the help of a wheelchair.

He slowly transitioned to crutches, and now mostly gets around using a walking stick.

But Brady defied all expectations and ditched the walking stick to walk out on stage on September 26.

The 100,000-strong crowd gave him the strength not just to walk, he said, but to fly.

"At the beginning of the song, I'm singing it kind of normally, but then I thought, 'I've got this, I'm going to be able to sing it!'

Mike Brady was interviewed about his famed football anthem in 2002. (ABC News)

"I sang harder than I've ever sung before.

"One hundred thousand people reacted, and the roar — I've never heard anything like it.

"It was fantastic. I felt absolutely vindicated for pushing myself so hard."

Musician vows to perform for years to come

Brady says he is not one to dwell on the past and spent much of his recovery writing new poetry and music.

But many hours alone with his thoughts left him to reminisce on a career he never expected.

As an English immigrant, Brady moved to Melbourne at the age of 11.

Mike Brady performed at the 1979 VFL grand final. (Supplied)

The musician and jingle-maker had never even been to a full AFL game when he was asked to create a tune to market the Victorian Football League.

"What an honour," he said.

He went on to pen what would become a footy phenomenon.

Recalling the day he first performed Up There Cazaly at the 1979 VFL grand final, introduced by his friend John Farnham, Brady said it was the first time he felt truly at home in the country he had lived in for nearly two decades.

"I really felt like I belonged in Australia," he said.

"I'd never felt that before. But hearing men and women in the crowd shouting, 'Good on ya, Mike', I really felt the warmth."

Even 48 years later, the feeling remains every time the words "up there Cazaly" leave his mouth.

"I often say the smile on my face when I sing it is actually me chuckling at the irony," he said.

"I love the irony of being a Pommy immigrant that was taken to heart by so many Australian people, and if that's not a great honour, I don't know what is."

Mike Brady says the 1979 VFL grand final, which featured Carlton legend Alex Jesaulenko (pictured), was a key moment in his Up Their Cazaly journey. (Getty Images)

While the honour of performing the track has been handed to other performers over the years, he wants to perform for the next two years, taking it to the song's 50-year anniversary and his own 80th birthday.

"I just hope the crowd is as kind to me as they have been for all those 48 years," he said.

In fact, Brady was more determined than ever to take to the stage this year, fearing the AFL might not ask him back if he did not.

If the crowd's reaction was anything to go by, it was an unlikely fear.

World.title: Aussie duo and new world number one fall at China Open
World.content:
Australian women's involvement at the China Open is down to just one singles player after Kimberly Birrell and Storm Hunter were both second-round casualties.

World number 41 Birrell suffered a 6-4, 6-4 loss to Czech Marie Bouzkova at the WTA 1000 event in Beijing on Saturday night.

Birrell, 28, who won the Korea Open last Sunday with a win over compatriot Maya Joint in the final, raced out to a 3-1 first-set lead before dropping serve twice to lose it in 42 minutes.

Down 3-0 in the second, Birrell lifted and won the next four games but was broken twice more to see her involvement in the Chinese capital come to a premature end.

For Bouzkova, the 28-year-old 18th seed, a meeting with China's Zheng Qinwen awaits.

The 2024 Olympic champion was leading Anna Kalinskaya 6-7 (4/7), 6-4, 3-0 when the Russian retired.

Earlier, Queensland veteran and former doubles world number one Storm Hunter was beaten 6-2, 6-2 by Maria Sakkari in just 73 minutes.

The 182nd-ranked Hunter failed to join 20-year-old fellow Aussie Taylah Preston in round three, losing serve six times in her latest hardcourt tournament clash in Asia.

Next up for Sakkari, the Greek 25th seed and former world number three, is Elina Svitolina.

The sixth-seeded Ukrainian came from a set down to eliminate Czech Katerina Siniakova, 1-6, 6-4, 6-2.

Shock of the day came with newly crowned world number one Elena Rybakina crashing out ‌3-6, 6-4, 6-3 to unseeded Alina Charaeva in the second round.

It couldn't have been a worse start to her reign as the number one as Rybakina lost in her first match since defeating four-times major winner Aryna Sabalenka to capture the US Open title last month.

Charaeva, a 24-year-old Russian-born Armenian ranked 118th ​in the world, etched her name into the record books by becoming the lowest-ranked competitor since the introduction of the WTA rankings in 1975 to rally from a set down to defeat a world number one.

Elsewhere, there were wins for third seed Coco Gauff, eighth seed Iga Swiatek, 21st seed Ann Li and 24th seed Jelena Ostapenko.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: NRL and NRLW grand final day has arrived. Here's what you need to know
World.content:
The final day of the NRL and NRLW seasons is here. The grand finals for the men and women will be held today.

In the women's decider, the Sydney Roosters and Brisbane Broncos face off in a rematch of last year's grand final.

In the men's grand final, the Sydney Roosters are facing the Newcastle Knights.

Here's everything you need to know about NRL and NRLW grand finals day.

What time are the NRL and NRLW grand finals?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals will be held on Sunday, October 4, the first day of daylight saving time in many states and territories across the country.

Here is when each grand final begins in each state and territory.

NRL grand final

7:30pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

7pm ACDT: South Australia

6:30pm: Queensland

6pm: Northern Territory

4:30pm: Western Australia

NRLW grand final

4pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

3:30pm ACDT: South Australia

3pm: Queensland

2:30pm: Northern Territory

1pm: Western Australia

How can you watch and listen to the grand final?

The game will be on Channel 9 and 9Now, but be aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire NRL season that is exclusive to Channel 9.

To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.

Where are the NRL and NRLW grand finals being played?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals are being played at Stadium Australia in Sydney.

Stadium Australia has hosted every NRL grand final since 1999, with the exception of the 2021 decider which was played at Brisbane's Lang Park during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Since the NRLW's inception in 2018, all grand finals have been played at Stadium Australia, again with 2021 being the exception. That decider was played at Dolphin Stadium in Redcliffe.

Who is playing in the NRL grand final?

The Sydney Roosters face the Newcastle Knights for the NRL premiership.

The Roosters finished the season fourth on the ladder, and lost their opening match of the finals before victories over Cronulla and the Dolphins.

The Newcastle Knights finished seventh on the ladder. After defeating Souths in the first week of the finals, the Knights went to Auckland and defeated the Warriors, then beat Penrith while being down to 12 players for all of the second half.

Who is playing in the NRLW grand final?

The Sydney Roosters are undefeated in 2026, winning all 11 matches in the home-and-away season, then defeating the Canberra Raiders in last week's preliminary final.

It mirrors Sydney's fantastic NRLW season in 2025, where they were undefeated until losing in last year's decider to the Brisbane Broncos.

The Broncos finished third on the table, with a record of 8–3 in the home-and-away season. The Broncos suffered a three-game losing run in the middle of the season, but have won their past five matches, including last weekend's preliminary final against the Gold Coast Titans.
